Mr. Blue
The small bell rang several times as the front door of the shop was pushed open. Jim looked up
from the book of accounts he was working on and cast a smile at the customer.
“Welcome to Jim’s Junk Joint, my friend,” he said amiably as he had hundreds and thousands of
times before. “Feel free to look around and pick up anything you want. It’s all for sale, if it ain’t
nailed down, and even that’s negotiable.” He flashed the man a grin.
This was his first customer of the day, even though it was nearly noon. This was no surprise to
Jim; it wasn’t tourist season and it was a Sunday. He’d often been told he ought to close shop on
the Sabbath, more than half the businesses on the street did, but he insisted on being there on
Sunday every week, just the same. Anything to get out of going to church with his wife Helen.
“Are you looking for anything in particular, son?” Jim asked the man who walked in. College
kid, by the look of him. And from somewhere up north, too. The boy’s skin was a painful
looking red, not used to the unforgiving Florida sun, even this time of year.
“Yes, actually,” the college boy said with a grin, his too-white teeth gleaming. “I’m seeking
information.”
“You’ve come to the right place, son. I’ve been known to gossip as bad as any old woman.” Jim
grinned, as did his customer, those pearly whites making an encore appearance. “Take a seat,
son, and tell me what you want to know. My name’s Jim, by the way, the proprietor of Jim’s
Junk Joint.”
“My name is Thomas, Thomas Bailey. You can call me Tom.” He accepted the chair Jim offered
in front of the counter that Jim sat behind.
“You look like a college lad, if you don’t mind my saying,” Jim said, who had never in his life
cared if anyone minded what he was saying.
“Well, I used to be,” Tom said with obvious disdain. “I dropped out to pursue my writing career.
I thought I could do it better by going out and living life than sitting in some stuffy professor’s
sad idea of a creative writing class. So, I’m travelling around to small towns in my beat up old
Dodge, collecting local stories, legends, and the like. I was hoping you could help me with that.”
Jim could tell that Tom thought this was the most romantic thing in the world; even the way he
brought up his “beat up old Dodge” gave that away. Ah, the thinking of youth, Jim thought to
himself. To be young and stupid again.
“All right, son, I’ll bite. What are you looking for?”
Tom didn’t say anything for a moment. He looked as if he were trying to phrase it in just the
right way. That was one of the problems with writers, in Jim’s mind, especially wannabe
writers. They could never just come out and say something. Everything had to be poetry.
Wannabe writers were the worst.
Wonder of wonders, Tom opted for the simple thing. “What can you tell me about Mr. Blue?” he
asked.
Jim sat in silence for a moment, stunned. He hadn’t expected this question. He figured Tom
would ask him about the kids who disappeared down at the lagoon every summer or the old
yarn about Captain Johanson’s ghost that was said to still roam the beaches after his wife and
her lover did away with him 100 years ago. Some even tied those two stories together. This,
however, he had not expected. “How do you know about Mr. Blue? That story already spreading
to that fancy college of yours?”
Tom gave an uneasy laugh. “No, nothing like that. I happened to come across a rumor about
him a couple of towns down. You don’t mind talking about him, do you?”
“No, I just don’t see why you’re interested. He’s just a harmless old rich coot with strange
habits, that’s all. Hell, I’d have more strange habits myself if I could afford them. Wouldn’t you
be more interested in stories about the ghost who kidnaps teenage girls every summer? That’s a
more interesting story.”
“I don’t believe in that kind of thing,” Tom said. “What I’m looking for are real stories about
real people. Something with real substance, real meat.” Tom’s eyes lit up at the incredible
romance of his own notion.
“Are you going to try to publish this story, because I’ll tell you right now, it’s not that
interesting.”
“No, I’m a fiction writer, not a reporter,” Tom said, a seed of contempt in his voice. Obviously
fiction writers were the only real writers. “I don’t want to record you, as I surely would if I
planned to publish this story. I’m just searching for flavor, stories to widen my own human
experience that I can draw on when I write. I’m not looking for details, really, just moods,
feelings.”
Tom was definitely caught up in his religion, Jim could see. “All right, son, I’ll tell you what I
know.
“Mr. Blue, I’d tell you his full name if I knew it, moved here a couple of years ago. He bought the
old Anderson place up on the hill. It’s a nice place, sits on five secluded acres. It’s a big old
Victorian. Sat empty for years because no one around here could afford it after old lady
Anderson died. Anyway, that was our first clue that Mr. Blue has money. All of us were a little
upset by an outsider buying the place, because this has happened before. The Anderson place
isn’t the only fancy one around. These rich snobs move in, bring in people from the city to do all
their work, never buy anything from the local shops, hell, hardly speak to us at all. But
Mr. Blue, well, he’s surprised us in more ways than one, that’s for sure.
“I don’t know what you’re expecting, but he ain’t no dark mystery man full of secrets.
Mr. Blue’s a little strange, and there’s some stories going around about him, but he’s a real nice
guy, and one of my best customers. He hired local folks to go up and remodel the house, and he
comes down and shops here several times a week. If you’re lucky, you may get to see him for
yourself. Yeah, I thought that’d interest you.
“He just has this one odd thing about him, and it’s really not that odd. You see, he loves the
color blue. All shades of blue. Everything around him, everything he owns is blue. That’s it.
That’s the big mystery. A little strange, maybe, definitely eccentric, but I wouldn’t call it scary. I
wouldn’t call it mysterious even. Just a rich old guy who happens to like blue and can afford to
indulge in the whim.”
Jim stopped talking, and Tom didn’t say anything for several minutes, apparently waiting for
Jim to continue. When he didn’t, Tom asked, “That’s it? That’s the whole story?”
“I’m afraid so, son.”
“What do you mean, everything around him is blue? You mean literally everything?”
“OK, let’s put it this way. I’ve seen Mr. Blue drive several expensive cars, and they’re all blue.
That’s not so strange, I suppose. He had his house painted one shade of blue, the trimming
painted a darker shade of blue, and the walls on the inside yet another shade. I know that from
the lads who did the work. He told me himself that he moved here to be close to the blue sky
and the blue water. When he occasionally goes down to Tammi’s Diner for breakfast, Tammi
tells me that he always orders blueberry pancakes with blueberry syrup and a blueberry shake.
He’s bought all kinds of blue things from me, and only items that are blue. He’s bought a blue
lamp, a blue kazoo, a fishing rod, a ball, several books with blue covers, kid’s toys even, an ash
tray, some dishes, sheets, towels, silverware with plastic blue handles, you name it, he wants it.
As long as it’s blue. He buys things no matter what shape they’re in, too. They can be broken,
torn, dirty, it doesn’t matter. He always pays me well, in cash, never barters, sometimes gives
me more than I ask for. If you look around the shop, you won’t find a thing in here with more
than a touch of blue on it. I have to make an effort to find him anything anymore. I started
bringing in things from my own home; anything blue my wife would part with. When people
bring things in to sell me, they know to hold out for high prices on anything blue, and I give it
to them because I know Mr. Blue will pay me plenty of profit. When I go on scavenger hunts, as
I call ’em, to get more merchandise, I’ve come back with my truck filled with nothing but blue
items, and he buys them all. Not all at one time, but a couple of items almost every day. I don’t
know where he puts it all.
“Then there’s his name. Have you ever heard of anyone else with the last name Blue? He
obviously wasn’t born with it. Even his skin’s a little blue. Probably some kind of makeup he
puts on, I’m sure, but there it is. Yes, Mr. Blue is a little strange, but he’s a good customer and a
nice man and, as far as I can tell and despite the rumors, he’s never been anything but the
model citizen.”
Tom digested this for a while. He took a beer that Jim offered and sipped it thoughtfully. After a
while, he asked, “Have you ever been up to his place? You know, to see for yourself what
happens to all of his stuff. For any reason at all?”
“As far as I know, no one has after the remodeling and painting was finished. Despite being so
friendly when he’s in town, he stays pretty much secluded at home. The man likes his privacy.”
“So no one has seen his place at all since then?” Tom asked, obviously searching for more of the
story.
“Well, rumor has it that some school kids snuck up there once and had a look around. They
made up some pretty ridiculous stories and spread them around town. Pretty rude kids, if you
ask me.”
“What did they say?” Tom asked, persistent.
“It’s really rather stupid,” Jim replied, “but since you think you must know, I’ll go ahead and
repeat it. They say they snuck over Mr. Blue’s fence, which was painted blue, of course, and
tried to peek in the windows but the curtains were drawn tight. They say that they spotted an
open window on the second story of the house and climbed up to get into the house. They had
just seen Mr. Blue shopping downtown here and knew they had some time before he got back,
so they decided to explore a bit. When they got inside, so they said, they were completely
shocked. They had expected everything to be blue, fitting Mr. Blue’s reputation, but it wasn’t.
Everything was white. Purely, utterly virgin snow white. Everything from the walls to the
carpet, the furniture, the telephone, every knick-knack, every book, every single thing in that
house was pure white except for the curtains that could be seen from the outside. This
particularly disturbed one of the boys, since he had helped his father lay a blue carpet just
before Mr. Blue moved in. They explored most of the house and said that everything was that
same colorless white, everywhere they looked.
“According to their story, they were so engrossed with what they were seeing they forgot all
about the time pressure they were under, and were brought back to their senses when they
heard a car pull up outside the house. They panicked and didn’t make it out of the house in
time and ended up hiding in a closet right off the living room. Mr. Blue let himself in. They
could see through a crack in the door that he was carrying an armful of bags filled with items
bought in town, some from me I assume, all blue. The boys say that he sat down on his white
couch, dumped all the items out before him, picked them up, and inspected them one by one.
They say he smelled them, felt them carefully, and weighed them in his hand as if he were
inspecting a fine leg of lamb rather than a piece of blue garbage.
“This is where the story really gets strange, and why I’m convinced that those little snots are
full of malarkey. They say that he again picked up each item, brought them to his lips, and
started sucking at them. Before their very eyes, they say, the color left the items as if he were
sucking liquid from a clear bottle, and the items turned that pure, snowdrift white. He did this
with every piece, and as he sucked up more of the blue, his own skin went from they light gray-
blue tinge it has, to a deeper and deeper blue. Not only that, but his body expanded and grew,
like the Incredible Hulk I guess. Well, this apparently scared the bejesus out of one of the boys,
because somebody made a noise that drew Mr. Blue’s attention.
“‘Who’s in my house?’ he supposedly yelled in a voice much deeper than his normal, pleasant
tone. The boys, scared into action, ran as quickly as they could from their hiding spot. Mr. Blue
was right behind them. ‘I’ll teach you to break into my house, you little bastards!’ he
supposedly yelled at them. This new, monstrous Mr. Blue, according to them, had grown some
kind of fangs and was chasing them crouched down, almost on all fours. They said that he kept
sniffing, too, as if following their scent or some such nonsense. They say they still don’t know
how they got away, he was pretty fast, but they managed to make it out the back door and off
his property before he could catch them. They immediately began spreading stories of the ‘color
vampire’ around town. No one paid them much attention; the story was so ridiculous. I figure
they were caught trespassing, and when the old man threatened to call the cops or their
parents, they ran out and started spreading nasty rumors for revenge. You’d think they would
have thought up a better story.”
Jim paused for breath. “Well, that’s it; that’s the story. I told you it wasn’t much. What do you
think?”
Tom thought about that for a moment. “You’re right, not a very convincing story, but
interesting. Not exactly what I had expected, but I appreciate you telling it to me.” Tom stood to
leave.
Jim could see something in Tom’s blue eyes, a look of excitement, of adventure. “Whoa now,
boy, don’t go running off just yet. I know what you’re thinking, and I don’t want you going and
making trouble for old Mr. Blue. If you want to meet him so bad, just wait here for a while and
you’ll probably get a chance to see him. He almost always comes in on Sundays. Have another
beer.”
Tom accepted the offer, and didn’t have long to wait. They talked about sports, politics and
Tom’s college for a while, but not long after Jim was finished with his story the bell tied to the
door jingled for the second time since Jim had opened shop that morning.
“Ah, Mr. Blue, nice to see you. I was just thinking about you.”
“Is that so?” asked a pleasant voice in an accent that Tom couldn’t quite place. He turned and
took his first look at Mr. Blue. He lived up to his name. The short-sleeved shirt he wore was a
solid, light shade of blue and the pants were a darker shade. He had on a blue plastic bead
necklace. His hat, tennis shoes, and socks were all blue. Even the cheap looking plastic
sunglasses he wore were blue. None of this, taken by itself, would have caused more than a
funny look or two, but sure enough, the man’s skin was a very light, very soft gray-blue. He was
a short, rotund man, apparently bald under his hat, and aside from his skin tone and the
singular color of his wardrobe, he looked to Tom to be just like any other old tacky rich man
living in Florida.
“Do you have anything for me today, my friend?” he asked Jim in that unrecognizable accent.
“Sure thing, Mr. Blue,” the storeowner answered. “I have several items that may interest you.”
“Well, let’s have a look.”
Mr. Blue walked up to the counter, coming to stand right next to Tom’s stool. Tom couldn’t help
but stare. Jim pulled several things out from behind the counter. He laid them down, one at a
time, naming them as he went along.
“We have another bed sheet for you, and a pillow. Here’s another T-shirt, and a vase. Here’s a
couple of toy blocks, all blue of course, and some blue markers. Here, I think you’ll get a kick
out of these.” He sat a large pair of bright blue snorkeling flippers onto the counter, a grin on
his face.
“Those are very nice, my friend,” Mr. Blue said, inspecting the merchandise.
“I have a few other items as well, if you want them.”
“No, no, not today. Some other time. How much for these?”
“Well, you know I have been having trouble finding anything for you. I’ve had to go out of town
more often. Short of spray-painting other things blue, that’s the surest way I know to find stuff.
So, I’m afraid I’m going to ask you for $40 for this. I wish I could do better for you.”
“No, my friend, that is fine. You have done much to cater to this old man’s lunacy. I’ll even give
you a bonus today.” He pulled out his wallet, blue of course, and retrieved a $50 bill. Money was
probably the only non-blue thing on the man.
“Keep the change, my friend.”
“Thank you very much. It’s always a pleasure doing business with you.” Jim smiled charmingly.
As Jim bagged Mr. Blue’s purchases, the strange man turned his attention to Tom. “Who’s your
friend here, Jim?” he asked politely.
“That’s Tom. He left college to take up writing.”
“Is that so?” Tom nodded. “I wish you the best of luck, my friend.”
“May I ask you a question, Mr. Blue?”
“Certainly, though I bet I could guess what it is.” Mr. Blue smiled.
Tom did as well, showing off his pearly whites again. “I’m sure you do. What is it with all the
blue? Why the huge preoccupation with the color?”
Mr. Blue chuckled. “I ask myself that very question quite a lot. It must just be the crazy mind of
an old, spoiled man. I’ve always liked the color, but for some reason I now crave it. Other than
that, I don’t know what to tell you.”
“May I take you to dinner so that we can talk, or even be presumptuous enough to invite myself
up to your home? I know that’s rather rude, but you interest me.”
Mr. Blue shook his head. “I’m afraid you’d be rather disappointed. I’m sure our friend Jim here
has filled you in on all the local gossip. That’s much more fun than anything I would have to tell
you. No, I must be heading home, I’m afraid. An old man needs his rest. I’m sorry, my friend,
but I don’t have any more to tell you.” With that, he grabbed his bag of purchases, thanked Jim
again, and headed for the door. As he was about to walk out of the shop, he turned back and
addressed Tom. “I did want to mention one last thing. You have lovely eyes, Tom. My favorite
color.” He chuckled and walked out.
Silence filled the shop once again. Finally Tom said, “There’s more to this story; I can feel it.”
“Now Tom,” Jim said, “you got to meet the man. Isn’t that enough?”
“He’s not telling us something.”
“He doesn’t have to.” Jim gently grabbed Tom’s arm. “Listen, son, the man has his right to
privacy. Even if he is some kind of ‘color vampire’ or what have you, I don’t see that it hurts
anyone anyway. Better than a traditional vampire, if you ask me. Why don’t you just leave the
old man alone? Leave him in peace.”
“You’re right, Jim. It’s none of my business. I guess I’ll just head back to my hotel and move on
in the morning. There are a lot of towns along this highway. Thanks for your time and thanks
for the beer.” They shook hands and Tom left. Jim had the feeling that the boy had no intention
of leaving Mr. Blue alone.
Jim had only one other customer that day, and she didn’t buy anything. He got caught up on
some bookwork and inventory, which he hated to do, but had to anyway. Sundays were a good
day to do it. He locked up the shop a few minutes after five, when the sky was getting darker
and the sun was on its way to bed.
Jim headed home by the same route he always used. He happened to drive past the road that
Mr. Blue lived on, and decided that if he saw Tom he’d try to talk some sense into him. Not that
it would do any good; wannabe writers were stubborn. Jim genuinely liked Mr. Blue, and not
just because of the money he brought in. He was a kind soul.
Jim was not surprised to see Tom walking near the road that Mr. Blue lived on. He was
surprised, however, when he saw Tom stumbling about, waving his arms frantically to and fro,
and tripping over everything that stood in his path. He was lucky he hadn’t been hit by a car,
tramping in the middle of the road like he was. Jim pulled his car over and got out.
Tom was raving. “He’s not human! He’s some kind of monster! Help me! Will somebody please
help me?”
“What the hell’s going on?” Jim cried, angry with this fool who couldn’t leave well enough alone
and had to make a scene besides. “What the hell do you think you’re doing, Tom?”
“Jim, is that you? You’ve got to help me, Jim! You’ve got to help me!” Tom turned in Jim’s
general direction and stumbled toward him. His face, what Jim could see of it from the short
distance, was dirty and scratched; his dark hair was sticking out all over the place. He stumbled
toward Jim, falling to his knees after a few paces. Jim ran to the prostrate man.
“What’s wrong with you, Tom?” Jim asked, trying to turn Tom over, to sit him up.
“I can’t see, Jim. I can’t see,” he murmured, agony in his voice.
“What are you talking about? Look at me.” Jim raised Tom’s chin and looked into Tom’s eyes.
He looked into sightless eyes.
Tom’s blue eyes were now as white as his teeth.

The Secrets of Happiness and Genius
So I am driving along Dumfuk municipal highway 13 on route to Hoochie’s house. I am thinking
about the normal stuff I think about, you know, life, happiness, right, wrong, justice, pleasure,
pain, the ineffable tenuousness of existence, what food might be in Hoochie’s fridge when I
arrive, whether or not Mr. Kotter was ever really happy teaching at his old high school, when a
new subject bursts upon my brain: “What is the best way to raise children so that they have the
greatest chance for living a happy and healthy life?”
Hmm..easy question right? I figure I should have this one answered within the 40 minutes it
takes me to cross the great plains of mediocrity and arrive in the homeland of Hoochie my
volleyball goddess girlfriend.
So to answer the question, “What is the best way to raise children?” I naturally began with
myself. After all, I am just about the happiest healthiest person I have ever encountered. So
what makes me who I am?
Well, I am a total hedonist. For you uneducated types that means I live an Epicurean lifestyle.
Ok, Ok, it means I believe the most important thing a person can do is pursue their OWN
happiness. You know, pleasure for pleasure sake. Eat, drink, dance like a maniac, and be merry!
Suck the marrow from life! Yea, all that.
I also believe, and this is reinforced by my experience, that pursuing your own happiness is the
most wonderful thing you can do for OTHER people in this world. Once a person focuses all
their energy on their own happiness, eventually they will get to a point, where they want to
love others, because loving other people is one of the greatest pleasures in life. It shouldn’t be a
struggle. You don’t have to force yourself to give give give, sacrifice sacrifice sacrifice. Life is not
about killing yourself for others. Life is about celebration and when you truly celebrate, you fill
the lives of others with joy and beauty. (Oh yea, am I a flake or what?)
So I believe in the noble pursuit of pleasure. And I have found that the greatest pleasures are
not simply being able to sit in front of the TV, eat Cheetohs, have sex, watch reruns of Welcome
Back Kotter, have more sex, eat more Cheetohs, and sleep. No, I have found, that though these
things are an essential part of happiness, to be a truly successful hedonist actually means loving
other people often and generously. It is kinda ironic eh? I set out willing to be a selfish bastard
and it turns out the most selfishly pleasurable thing for me to do is to live a virtually saintly life.
What a nasty trick God is playing on me.
Anyway, I am a hedonist, so naturally, when it comes to raising children, my first instinct is to
assume one should raise children as hedonists. “Hey kids, do whatever you want to do! I am
sure in the end, you will figure out that work is joyous and laziness is for miserable losers!”
Unfortunately, I am starting to think it is not so simple.
It seems when kids are growing up, the things they do make emotional impressions upon their
psyche that lasts their entire lives. And if you just let them run wild and free, they tend to grow
up undisciplined, lazy, flaky, and constantly at the mercy of their emotional whims. I mean, you
start telling them do whatever makes you happy, and then they start something and once they
feel a little emotionally turned off then they stop. In essence, I see value in encouraging
children to force themselves through seemingly unenjoyable work, so that they can learn the
satisfaction of completing a difficult task.
This is all highly theoretical. It is not like I have raised lots of children. But I have seen the
children of lots of people. Hippees tend to raise children with a type of hedonistic attitude and
hippee children, in my experience, often grow up pretty undisciplined and flaky. Saying this
pains me, because I hate authoritarianism in all its forms. I hate the word discipline. But I
believe, in order to be happy, a person must have strength to challenge their emotions, and
persevere through hardship, and to stick to difficult tasks. Somehow, these things need to be
instilled in children, and pure hedonism is not the answer.
Ok, so I won’t go into the rest of my reasoning. But trust me it is really crystal clear and if I did
explain it, you would not have any doubt in your mind. In any case, to save time, I am just going
to skip to the answer. Just trust me on this, ok? If you want your children to be happy and
healthy when they grow up, raise them Catholic.
So there it is. I found the answer and there were still 10 minutes before I arrived at Hoochies
house. So I decided to quickly answer another question.

Genius
Still By Matt
I start thinking that I don’t just want children to grow up to be happy and healthy. I want
children to grow up to be joyously overflowing productive geniuses. How can that be arranged?
Well, wait a minute. Is there a difference between being a genius and being a happy healthy
person? Weren’t many of the most impressive creative geniuses throughout history miserable
most of their lives? Poets, authors, musicians, artistsoften they lived painful tumultuous
livesoften they died unappreciated and unrecognized and it is not unusual for a brilliant artist
to have ended his or her life in suicide.
Geez, what a quagmire. So do we want happy healthy people or do we want geniuses? Are there
any happy healthy geniuses out there (besides myself of course)?

Again, I wont bore you with the crystal clear unassailable reasoning behind this answer. I know
you will just trust me. How do you raise a child so that they grow up to be a genius? Raise them
Southern Baptist.
Wow, another question resolved and still a couple minutes before I arrived at Hoochie’s. So

Well, as I drove up to Hoochies house I found the secret formula. Again skipping the boring
reasoning. If you want your child to not only grow up to be happy and healthy but ALSO a

I know at first glance that might sound like the ridiculous ramblings of a maniac, but trust me,

solid 20% chance that they will grow up to be a happy healthy genius by the time they reach
the age of 55. You heard it here first.

Part II: The Wisdom Project Forum Archive —
2004–2007
An Open Source Think Tank — By Matt Ready and the Wisdom Project Community

Introduction
The Wisdom Project was an “Open Source Think Tank” founded by Matt Ready in 2003. Its
mission was to foster wisdom through online dialogue.
What made the Wisdom Project unique was its rating system. Every post in the forums could be
rated by community members on a scale of 1 to 10 — not for agreement, but for wisdom: the
quality of reasoning, openness to other viewpoints, and thoughtfulness of argument.
The hypothesis was simple: if you rate posts for wisdom rather than agreement, the most
thoughtful contributions will rise to the top — regardless of which “side” they represent.
This archive contains 20 discussion threads and 440 posts recovered from the Wayback
Machine in March 2026.

By Matt Ready and the Wisdom Project Community

Are you Democrat or Republican? This is gonna be a looooong story.
When I left the US Navy in June of 1991 I had already become tired of complaining about
politics and wanted to do something.
At the time Ross Perot was running and had alot of good, common sense things to say about
what was wrong with government and how to fix it.
I, as did most of my family, joined his campaign.
I gathered signatures to get him on the Ballot, I was the coordinator for the town I lived in at
the time, I worked phones, I passed out flyers, I wrote to editors, called radio stations, I
organized local rallies, and always stepped up to argue for him when discussions of politics
came up at social gatherings.
When he ended his campaign abruptly I was crushed, but I learned something I thought was
true for a long time.
If you want to really Effect change in America Politics, you need to work from the inside.
As a result I joined the Democratic Party, and my local Democratic club.
My family is a long line of union members and had be democratic supporters for a long time.
My Grandfather had once even been a card carrying member of the Socialist party back in his
days as a union organizer.
After about another year of watching C-Span, and discussing issues with fellow Democrats I
really began to feel out of place.
It was not just that I didn’t frequently agree with the position of the Democratic side of the
Aisle, I frequently could not “get” how they came to their position in the first place.
Then, one night at a Democratic club meeting events were put into motion for my departure
from the party.
The subject of gun control came up.
I asked the group the following: Quote: If I wanted one of you dead, and I did not have the
means to hire someone to do it then I have to ask you.
Why would I goto a local gun store, get the forms, then goto the local police department, get my
fingerprints taken three times for local state and federal background checks, turn in all the
forms with the associated filing fees and wait 1 - 2 months to get a Firearms Purchasing Card
(which is only good for Rifles and Shotguns).
Then, go back to the gun shop, get the pistol purchase forms (must be done per handgun), go
back to the police department, present my Firearms purchasing card, get finger printed 3 times
for all three background checks again, turn in the forms and associate filling fees, wait 4-6
months (why it takes so much longer for the same background checks to come back is beyond
me).
Then take the not yet finalized form I get back to the gun shop, Then pick out my pistol of
choice then turn in the paperwork to have the specific gun and serial number added and
submitted to the police department.
Wait another week or so for word that the police department accepted the form, then return to
the gun shop ( now at least 6 months from when I originally wanted to purchase the gun ), and
pay the balance of full retail for it and take it home? Why would I do this when I could simply
get in my car, drive north for 30 minutes to the bad side of Newark, buy a weapon on the street
corner, probably at a discount, drive home with it on the same night, without paying all those
filing fees, and without any offical record of my owning a gun or of that specific gun being
associated to me, shoot you and toss it in the ocean? Note : The above was based on the Gun
Control Laws of New Jersey at the time (Early 90s).
Regardless of your agreement or disagreement with gun control, the above does have a certain

Thread 4: The Next Revolutionary Advance for Internet Forums
like this: Voice
Matt
1/29/2004 at 09:55 PM
With this type of voice message board-you could have engaging, interesting, convenient, and
fairly natural conversations over the Internet.
The experience could be liberated from sitting at a computer-and it would be enhanced by
being able to hear human voices-rather than reading text.
You could have all the fun and convenience of natural conversation-but enhanced through the
reach and expertise and convenience available over the Internet.
It may seem daunting, but the technology already exists and is available.
All this idea requires is a MySQL based message board (such as the XMB Forum) and a pretty
basic client side application.
The SQL database could store all the voice messages in mp3 format.
The client side application would run on a pocketpc phone or palm phone.All this application
would need to do is 1) interface with the MySQL database (the message board).
Be able to upload and download the mp3 files in the appropriate thread-and play them on
demand. 2) encode into mp3 format as people recorded their posts. 3) This part is optional, but
would be the ultimate addition: be able to recognize some simple voice commands such as
“Record” “Post” “Replay” “Skip” “Next” “Back”.
If you can program or hack MySQL and make pocketpc Apps, then you can make this amazing
voice enabled internet forum.
Limitations: Bandwidth for moble internet access is an obvious limitation.
But remember, voice forums will be just as fun and convenient on desktop computers and
where high bandwidth is available.
Voice messages will be much bigger.
The MySQL database will grow fast.
But hey, it will be so fun, I think users will be willing to pay the message board host a little to
help cover storage costs.
Another alternative is to delete or archive all messages after 3 days-limiting discussions to
fairly current threads.
I know this will arrive someday.
But why not sooner rather than later? Any programmers out there interested in a little project
like this? If so, go for it.
I maintain no copywrites on this idea.
But if you are going to run with this idea, please just let me know so I can use the forum on my
website.
The best way for this to be developed is through an open source project.
Anyone who wants to collaborate on this project with other programmers feel free to post on
my website to make contacts.
Or just go for it if you already know how to do something like this.
I look forward to hearing all about it!

Natural Language translation is not necessary.

The point of this system is not simply to be able to use speech to get right answers to questions.

I dont want a google search, I want the equivalent of walking into a room of people and asking a

Science is not the new world religion.
The fact is this: science and religion are two very different things, and do not necessarily have
to clash.
I have seen good science and good religion coexist within the same person, let alone the same
lifestyle.
Some people know where the borders of science and religion are, and some just don’t.
When these borders are distorted, and science or religion invades the other, then you get the
problems that can be found today that cause such questions as “is science the new world
religion?” Science is, always has been, and will continue to be, a method of searching for an
explanation of what we have around us and the natural phenomena that come with it.
Science changes as new information is gained, new observations are made, and ideas are tested
over again.
Religion is a belief system based upon faith.
Religion should not be able to be proven or disproven, because religion requires a “leap” of
faith, trusting in something that is unknown and cannot be known.
There is no way to prove that God exists, but there is no way to prove that God doesn’t exist.
There is no “test” by which one can confirm the existence of God.
That’s what makes religion what it is.
If science and religion are such different things, why do fundamentalists speak out against
science? Some religious groups try to prove their religion true.
Such a group is the fundamentalist Christians.
Whether arguing with the uncertainty of Darwin’s theory of evolution by natural selection, the
Shroud of Turin (a cloth that was supposedly used to clothe the dead Jesus after his crucifixion)
or the Grand Canyon, these religious try to prove their God’s existence.
In this example, religion crosses the border of faith and into science, using evidence in an
attempt to prove their religion.
In response, scientists will challenge the claims within the scientific spectrum, because that’s
how science works.
If the religious want to use science, they have to expect that someone will test their hypotheses.
Archaeologists and anthropologists have shown the errors in these religious arguments, and the
end result is a religious/scientific conflict that one would hear about in the news.
A determined scientist does not have to be an atheist by any means, because religion and
science do not have to conflict with each other.
As long as science and religion stay true to their real meanings (science with evidence and
religion with faith), they will not need to conflict.
Science is not a religion, and religion is not a science.

Thread 6: Carbon Reduction Project in Wisconsin
mandias
9/13/2007 at 04:48 PM
This is an article cut and pasted from the blog on jsonline (journal sentinal
online(Milwaukee)).
It is about our electric company WEenergies and a project they are working on.
Pleasant Prairie is a community just south of Milwaukee.
Construction has begun in Pleasant Prairie on a pilot project that will test whether a key gas
linked to global warming can be removed from the smokestack of a coal-fired power plant
before it is released into the air.
We Energies is hosting the pilot project at the state’s largest coal-fired power plant.
Construction of the carbon separation facility is scheduled to be completed late this year, with
the project slated to start at the end of the year.
Carbon dioxide is the leading greenhouse gas, and coal-fired power plants, cars and trucks are
the primary sources of rising carbon dioxide emissions in the atmosphere.
The Milwaukee utility is working with Alstom, which developed a process that would use
chilled ammonia to cool the carbon dioxide and other gases in the smokestack, making it easier
to separate the greenhouse gas.
The test is a joint project of the two companies and the Electric Power Research Institute, the
research arm of the utility industry.
The project will be in operation for at least a year, with results expected to be published in late
2008, We Energies said.

Clyde
6/3/2004 at 05:57 AM
Truth can never be anything but a guidepost or marker or policy.
Policies and such are only there to guide.
We approximate the truth.
As more information is added, as new situations arise, we can approximate the truth to a
greater extent.
That truth may have been truth for a given context, but change the context and that truth can
change, relative to the observer and to the time.
Ultimately, since knowledge is infinite, so to is truth.
Any knowledge added to a domain of any system, will change that domain and everything in it
to some small degree, hence changing that policy or “truth” slightly.
Take gay marriage for example.
There is the problem of the acceptability of homosexuality and religion since marriage is a
religious institution that has become a civic one as well.
Here are some of the issues that I can think of (none of these are my value judgements, just
what society has deemed important): should the same sexes be together? There are scientific
arguments and religious arguments and moral arguments.
What actual harm is being done? Is marraige a religious institution such that it was made
merely for man and woman? Is marriage a civic union with legal implications that two people
in love ought have as a protection? These are only the arguments and questions that I think are
most commonly found.
I’m sure that there are many more, and many more that have not even been thought of which
will change the discourse.
As man/woman evolve, say 2,000 years from now, what sort of information will we be
composed of that will make our arguments look ridiculous and narrowminded? The best we
can do is approximate based on our capabilities and the utility with respect to its unversal
utility of goodness.
Lastly, we also need to take into account the phenomenological issues that arise from the
moment.
We are never in a vacuum and will never have a perfect scenerio.
Variables and circumstances are always changing as well as our individual collective context.
I’m not so sure that it is the “truth” that is as big an issue as it is how we discuss and determine
that “truth” that is the issue.
If the “truth” is never perfectly resolved, it may matter more to maximize the process of the
determination of that “truth” than to try to take a razor’s edge to it and proclaim it forever.
If we collectively worked toward the truth with honesty, energy, humility, facility, etc, at least
we could be sure that a greater approximation of “truth” were not shrouded in the abscurity of
argumentation, pride, ego, fear, the disintegrative societal affects of the division that is born
from the quest for fire that has become the quest for “truth.” I believe that “truth” is an ongoing
process, IMHO.
I am not saying that there are not things of substance that can be built upon and that have an
eternal essense or quality.
Ideas may approach circumstatial absolutism, but universal, eternal absolutes will forever be
policies modified by time, place, practitioner, and phenom.
Ideas will always require modifications, caveats, etc.
We are not perfect beings (nor, again IMHO, will we ever be), therefore, how could we ever
expect to find a universal, eternal, perfect, form, even in a vacuum of time, place, etc?

It is my opinion that there is.
I also think that there are at least two different things being discussed here. the first one is
whether or not there is absolute truth.

whether or not it is possible to know absolute truth.
Is there actually absolute truth? The way that I see it, there is.
What the absolute truth is is based upon free will.
Because all people are equal (of course, you could do away with this assumption and my
argument would fall, but it is my belief that I am no better than you), one person does not have
the right to detract from the free will of another unless it is nessessary for the preservation of
the free will of one of the involved parties (in other words, it is OK to punish criminals because
this helps to dissuade them from detracting from the free will of the general public).
Having laid this out, we can see that there must be absolute truth as long as all people are
created equal.
Everyone bigins life with a right to free will.

I believe that federally endorsed gay marriage is wrong because it encourages a practice that
does not provide a stable base for society (there is plenty of research supporting this).
I believe that the government should not be able to ban contractual (non-government endosed)

free will).

I choose absolute truth.

Truth is relative to perspective.
When we speak of truth, we are really speaking of the truth AS WE SEE IT.
For example: I am an atheist.
Due to lack of supporting information, I am not convinced that God (or any other such deity)
exists.
I can’t prove that there ISN’T a God, but there’s no proof that there IS a God.
I live my life in the belief that there is no God.
To me, it’s true - God does not exist.
One of my friends is a devout Catholic.
She can’t prove that there is a God, but she has faith that there is.
She feels God’s presence in her personal life.
She knows that God exists.
To her, there’s nothing more true than that.
Can we really be certain about anything? Sure, 1+1=2 now, has equaled 2 before, and will always
equal 2.
But what exactly is “two”? “Two” and “2” are merely representative of a common value that just
we’re familiar with.
We can only describe it as Two… or 1+1, but how do we define “one”? Clearly it is a matter of
perspective, and a truth as we see it.
If I believe that 1+1=3, how can you contradict me? My 3 could actually be your 2.
It may be confusing, but accurate nonetheless.
We speak the truth as we see it; unless your religious beliefs involve the belief in an
omnipotent, omniscient, infallible being (such as God), absolute truth can’t exist.
A Catholic would, for example, believe that the word of God is absolute truth, because God is
infallible.
He is never wrong, so God must always be right.
He must always speak the truth, and since this truth cannot be misinterpreted, it is absolute
truth.
Personally, I’m an atheist, fitting my above description in my example.
I’m not convinced of the idea of absolute truth.
There are truths that we all hold as “absolute”, since we know that 1+1=2 by our standards.
But again, we can only interpret the truth AS WE SEE IT.

Looking at the issue of absolute truth from an Einsteinian perspective perhaps it would be
better to consider relative and absolute as the yin and yang of a larger whole.
Einstein’s relativity theory declares that the speed of light is absolute measured from any
source under any conditions.but time and space measured from an original space-time
continuum are relative and alter as one accelerates toward the speed of light.
Also semantically ‘absolute’ implies ‘relative’ as a necessary sine qua non precondition and vice
versa like hot implies cold.
Alan Nicoll
9/10/2004 at 05:42 PM
Quote: Originally posted by demosthenes Is there really such a thing as absolute truth? This is a
question thrown around a lot in today’s society.
Should people really be able to choose what is right for themselves? Or, is there a pre-ordained
right and wrong? With gay mariages, death penalties, and abortion all in debate I think that
this is a question worth debating.
This question has provoked some abysmal responses, mostly because they don’t address the
question.
Unfortunately, an adequate answer would require book length, so the best I can offer is some
inadequate thoughts.
First, not all truths are created equal.
I am sitting at a keyboard typing at this moment.
If I am wrong about this, then I cannot be right about anything.
Immediate sense perceptions like this are very close to “absolute truth,” yet are not truly
absolute because I can be mistaken.
It could be that I have been anesthetized and my brain removed from my body, and artificial
sensations are pumped into my brain by evil scientists.
This is fanciful, of course, but when you’re talking about “absolute” people tend to get fanciful.
The truths of mathematics (1+1=2) are formalistic and rule-bound.
If you correctly follow the rules you can produce an endless series of tautological mathematical
truths.
Do these count as “absolute truth”? Is it absolutely true that a bachelor is an unmarried man? It
seems to me a matter of taste if one wants to use the word in this way.
I don’t think it makes any practical difference whether one calls these truths “absolute.” The
question of truth tends to get more interesting as we get away from being as close as possible to
absolute.
Most of the posts above immediately jump to this position and start in discussions of morality
and religion.
My take on the logical status of moral terms is that they are essentially teaching terms.
A parent says to a child, “It is bad to tell lies.” The child learns and believes this (let’s assume)
and so adopts a particular attitude towards lying, making it less likely that he will tell lies in
future.
But what does the parent mean by this use of the word “bad”? Probably something like, “most
people disapprove” or “it will lead to problems” or maybe just “I don’t want you to.” Clearly
these are subjective and very far from “absolute truth.” The parent might be appealing to a
particular standard, and so mean “God forbids it” or “it is tabu.” But again, although this may be
objective based on the standard, overall this must be subjective because the adoption of a
particular standard is just a kind of choice which will be different for everyone.
Standards compete, and so I see none as being absolute.
What is “absolute truth”? To me it is a truth that must be objective (as with sense impressions
and mathematics), and it must be (at least approximately) the same for everyone (which
applies more to mathematics than to sense impressions, since senses differ).
This is inadequate, but at least it tries to address the topic.

Is there really such a thing as absolute truth? YES This is basic ontology, the specification of a
conceptualization.
Consider the statement: “No absolute truth can exist.” In order for this statement to be true, it
in itself must be an absolute truth.
Then it is self-negating.
Ergo, an absolute truth does exist.
Does man know the absolute truth? NO Like Euclid’s greatest prime number, each time one
conceives of the greatest or the absolute, there is the possibility of extending it by one.
Yet this contradiction doesn’t exclude the reality that such exists as it speaks only to our ability
to conceive.
For us, the best we can surmise is a relative truth based on individual and consultative
knowledge, references and experience.
In order for this to be true we must be dealing in a number system greater than base 2.
The equation in base 2 would be 1+1=10, and in base 1 it would be 1+1=11.
As we’ve agreed in general mathematics to utilize base ten as our starting point, of course most
will conclude 1+1=2 is correct: there is an assumed reference.
Still, this statement would be true for any system above a binary so even if I were thinking in
base 3 while baka was delving into hexadecimals, we’d concur that this statement is correct
while our frames of reference were totally different.
We’d run into problems when I in turn said 2+1=10 while baka insisted it was 3.
And we’d be at total loggerheads when she’d insist (22)+(22) + 2 = A and I said it’s 101.
I agree with Alan that the question of an absolute truth was not addressed by most
respondents, but rather perceived and received truths, and as with baka and my mathematic
discussions, the validity of these will depend on agreed reference.
I have a problem with Demosthenes’ correlation of absolute truth with a preordained right and
wrong.
The first, truth, is a state of being, while the latter, judgment, is a matter of perspective. “I am” –
neither inherently good or bad, just a statement of fact.
Contained within the concept of “preordained” is an element of volition, requiring an
originating agent to determine rightness and wrongness in relation to existence.
If such an agent knew absolute truth and associated it with “all that is right,” why would it
create that which is wrong? Therefore, all that exists is right – for the agent of origin.
That does not mean it is “right” for humans, who are not the originators.
For humanity, the best we can do is determine whether our continued existence is of value to
us and what we need to do to sustain, or end it, accordingly.
It would seem if we begin from the premise that humanity is fundamentally flawed, ie, is wrong
or bad in essence, that we will inevitably see to our demise.
One way inwhich we’ve historically circumvented this is by placing a belief in a deity who
grants us salvation from our essential flawed state, allowing us to transcend it.
The problem with this is somewhere along the line many decided that we’d received all the
knowledge we needed regarding this transcendence millenia ago and attempt to force our
reality to comform with it.
Disregarded is the idea that the perceived realities and agendas of that time may have skewed
how the information was filtered and presented.
Operating from the binary OR/AND assumption, (you’re either with us or against us), they’ve
concluded 1+1=1 and there are no alternatives.

You defined “absolute”, so I will define “truth” in a way that you probably won’t like. “Truth”
for me is simply an attribute of a statement.
The nature of this attribute is so fundamentally hard-wired into my brain that describing it
adds no value.
It is like the attribute “tasty” is to food.
Since “truth” is an attribute value of a statement, a statement that cannot be understood by
another intelligent being in the same way that I understand it, may have a different truth value
for that being, or no truth value at all if that being can’t understand the statement.
To get more concrete, intelligent life from other worlds may use very different abstractions
than we do to understand the world.
They may not use numbers, in which case “1+1=2” would have no truth value to them.
All of us humans agree that statement like this are true because these statements are composed
of concepts wired into our brains.
So going back to your definition of absolute truth, I don’t believe in objective truth or objective
anything in a pure sense.
I would call one statement more objective than another if it is substantially more widely
believed, but I disagree that there exists anything that is completely objective in the sense that
every intelligent being should necessarily agree with it.

demosthenes
10/9/2004 at 02:49 AM
In regards to the possibility of living in such a life that ignores absolute truth (living as a moral
relativist): To make a sound argument in favor of absolute truth it is first necessary to
understand the opposite belief, moral relativity.
A moral is defined as: A concisely expressed precept or general truth; a maxim.
To be relative is to be: Dependent on or interconnected with something else; not absolute.
Ergo, moral relativity is the belief that there is not any absolute truth, that a truth is based on a
situation.
The problem with moral relativity lies in the fact that its system of beliefs requires absolute
truth to function.
This fundamental paradox is the basis for many other problems in moral relativity, making its
system of beliefs impossible from any logical perspective.
To examine the core beliefs of a moral relativist is to find that they do not believe in absolute
truth in any shape or form.
They believe there is absolutely no absolute truth.
Therein lies the paradox.
The fundamental belief of a moral relativist is their version of an absolute truth.
With this fact, it is not possible for moral relativists to denounce absolute truth without
contradicting themselves.
This paradox is only one example of how the beliefs of a moral relativist are fundamentally
incongruent.
Even ignoring the first major paradox, it is possible to find more problems with moral
relativism.
Moral relativists decide for themselves what is right and wrong.
While this seems to work on a personal level it falls apart on a societal level.
Because each moral relativist decides their own right and wrong, they are always correct in
their decisions.
Also a moral relativist vows to respect the decisions of all others.
However, in a society where right and wrong are different for each moral relativist, they are
constantly breaking their own laws.
For one person to act on what they believe is right, would be to go against another persons
belief of right, therefore violating respect for their beliefs.
These two paradoxes make moral relativism not only illogical, but also impossible.
The fundamental paradoxes in moral relativity cause its system of beliefs to completely collapse
under examination, in the same way a building without a foundation would collapse under a
strong wind.
In no way is it possible to logically argue in favor of moral relativism, because doing so would
be a contradiction to that system of beliefs.
Moral relativity, when questioned, examined, and scrutinized reveals itself as an irrational
system of beliefs and a senseless way of living.

generally as certain as we shall ever need.

not fall into a completely nihilistic absurd relativism.

render life meaning while having internal consistency and few contradictions within a larger
holistic social system.

two fundamentally different worldviews.
If you have ever debated with a deeply religious person, you will understand what I mean by

deeply held than his belief in reason.
A person’s worldview cannot be changed by reasoned debate because a worldview is axiomatic
to its holders.
A person’s worldview can only be changed by attacking its emotional foundations.

worldview is, and all the practical implications that that has.

Thread 10: What is wisdom and how do you foster it within
yourself and society?
Matt
7/8/2003 at 07:30 PM — Wisdom Rating: 6.0
What is wisdom and how do you foster it within yourself and society? My answer is here in my
summation of the purpose of The Wisdom Forum.
Since the emergence of consciousness, a battle has been waged upon the geography of the
human condition.
This battle, this struggle has been between two eternal foes.
Satan, it is not even good vs. evil, but rather it is Wisdom vs.
Perhaps the easiest way to explain what I mean by Wisdom and Folly is by using a problem-
solving example.
Lets suppose there is a space ship waiting to be launched.
Lots and lots of people are eager and waiting for this ship to launch, for it is expected to be a
spectacular event.
Now lets suppose on the morning of its long awaited launch, an engineer notices that ice has
formed on many of the space ships vital components.
This engineer has gone to school many years studying the science of rocketry and has learned
that ice is an extremely unpredictable variable in relation to launching space ships successfully.
So this engineer goes to the person in charge and says, We should delay this launch because
there is ice on the rocket engine.
I am not comfortable with launching the spaceship under these conditions.
It might explode (and kill everyone on board).
The person in charge responds to the engineer, Oh you are so paranoid.
Lots of people are eagerly awaiting this launch.
We are going to launch it anyways.
After all you arent certain it will explode right? The person in charge then gives the go ahead
for launch.
The person in charge bases this decision upon 0 years of studying the science of rocketry and
many years of being a person who ignores the advice of snobby academics other so called
experts who claim to know everything.
The result? The space shuttle explodes shortly after launch due to leaking via a frozen rubber
seal.
In this story, I see two forces at work: Wisdom and Folly.
The engineer possessed more insight into the state of that space ship.
He or she possessed greater wisdom in this debate.
The person in charge didnt really know much of anything about space ships compared to the
engineer.
He was simply the person put in charge.
In this scenario, folly won the debate, but obviously everyone lost the day.
Now simply because the engineer had more knowledge than the person in charge does that
mean the engineer is wiser than the person in charge in all matters? No.
The engineer may very well be a dimwit when it comes to many subjects and many types of
problems.
For instance, perhaps if that engineer had better communication skills he could have convinced
the person in charge to delay.
He could have gone to the media or done some other extreme measure to try and save the lives
of the crew.
In every decision, in every example of problem solving, wisdom and folly are players.
It is not the case that one side is always the side of total wisdom and the other is always the side
of total folly.
Wisdom and folly are always players on both sides.

life imaginable.
But finding your way towards wisdom demands immense amounts of effort and courage.

escape).
Yet, if you give in to fear and laziness you will not get to where you want to go.
You will be moving aimlessly and very well could end up crashing upon rocks to the detriment
of your life and the lives of others.

12/4/2003 at 06:21 PM — Wisdom Rating: 10.0
To use your example – the Challenger disaster – the question is by what criteria do you judge
the “wisdom” or “folly” of the decision made? I have recently learned of an interesting concept
in an area called “decision theory.” That is the distinction between a “good decision” and a
“good outcome.” The best example I can think of is the good old game of “Russian Roulette.”
Were I to offer you the chance play the game exactly once, you have a 5:1 chance of surviving.
Were you to play, and survive – as the probabilities indicate you would – you might be tempted
to think your decision was “wise” because you survived.
That would be to confuse a “good outcome” with a “good decision.” Playing Russian Roulette is
a profoundly stupid thing to do – precisely because those odds, as measured against the
consequences of a “bad outcome” or horrible.
Would you fly with a 1 in 6 chance of dying? Would you undergo elective surgery with such a
chance? To continue the flying analogy, suppose your decision was “fly or drive.” Statistically,
flying is safer.
But suppose the particular flight you took crashed? Bad decision? Nope.
Good decision, bad outcome.
Thus, you can’t really measure the “wisdom or folly” of the launch decision by the outcome.
You have to measure it by the known risks, and the consequences of being wrong.
Everything I have seen says that deciding to “launch” was a bad decision – and would have
been just as bad, if nothing had happened.
They knew those rubber seals became brittle and shrank in cold weather.
Thus they knew that a failure of those seals had a substantially higher probability of occuring,
and that the consequences of a failure would be not only the loss of the crew, but a major
setback to the entire program.
Even measured by the yardstick of “self-interest” on the part of the administrator making the
final decision, the decision was a bad one.
The risks of not launching was a bad day in front of his supervisor – assuming he couldn’t
convince higher-ups of the genuine risks.
The risk of launching meant it was his responsibility for the bad decision – a responsibility
hard to evade since he was warned of the problem.
Returning to our Russian Roulette example, we can modify that.
Suppose you had eight hours to cross the country to collect 10 million dollars, and suppose the
only to get there would be to fly some experimental, problem plagued or otherwise “unsafe”
aircraft – with say a 1 in 6 chance not making it.
Do you get on the plane? How important is 10 million dollars to you? If you’re Bill Gates, you
might take a pass – since you’ve already got a lot more than 10 million dollars.
If you’ve otherwise got what you want out of life, and 10 million dollars might actually create
more problems for you than it solves – and it might – you might also take a pass.
But if you have a defined, well conceived use for 10 million dollars, no other way to get access to
those kind of resources, and this represents your “big chance,” you may well decide to get on
that plane and take your chances.
I can tell you I would, and “white nuckle” it all the way there.
All of which gets back to an even more basic question of “wisdom or folly,” namely what’s
important to you.
That is question of values, and those question are notoriously difficult to answer.

Now, to your essay: I believe the greatest and most profound question, and the fundamental
question of wisdom, is what are the most important problems (or what goals are most worth
seeking)? I believe the second greatest and most difficult question of wisdom is what is the best
way to solve those problems (or achieve those goals)? Often, the greatest folly occurs when
people skip real fast past the first question and spend all their time on the second.
In other words, they poorly choose their goals and use all of their effort and brainpower
pursuing folly.
By what criteria do I judge the “wisdom” or “folly” of a decision made? I judge it first, by the
nature of the goal being sought and second by the strategy used to try and achieve that goal.
In my writing, I emphasize that each of us seeks happiness as our ultimate goal (even if we
label it things like fulfillment, enlightenment, inner peace etc..).
Moreover, we elect leaders to represent all of us and help create a world in which all of us have
the best opportunity possible to live a happy life.
This goal is of course a value, but I like to assume we all share it, or at least should.
With that in mind, when a decision is made, I first evaluate it in relation to the goal: a world
where all people have a good opportunity to live a happy life.
When a politician or corporate leader ignores this goal and instead pursues the goal of power
for power sake or individual wealth at the expense of others-I believe they are being fools.
When it comes to politicians and public officials such as the NASA administrator I think we are
free to presume their goal is to work for the well being of all citizens.
They may not actually have that goal, but I believe we can judge them based upon it
nonetheless.
The only question remaining for politicians and such is how good are their decisions in relation
to this goal.
If a person wants to play dice with their own life and happiness-that is their choice.
I would be hesitant to declare a person a fool for taking chances with their own life if they
sincerely believed it made them happy. (They may be using foolish reasoning, but that is
another question.
Doing something risky that you believe makes you happy is every person’s inalienable right.)
But if a person is making decisions that directly impact the well being of others-then they are
entrusted by those people to act wisely on their behalf.
Betting your life on a 1 in 6 chance for 10 million dollars is a crazy thing to do.
Risking the lives of people you have under your control-that is a decision we expect our leaders
to make using the utmost caution and critical thinking in relation to our shared goal: a happy
peaceful flourishing world.
A leader who works toward that goal with “good” decisions is wise.
A leader who seeks another goal or makes absurd decisions is a fool.

Thread 11: Can a Corporation have a more noble purpose than
making money?
Matt
9/16/2004 at 02:55 PM
A “for profit” corporation obviously exists to make money as one of it’s activities.
But can a “for profit” corporation have a more noble fundamental purpose such as: “To foster
and promote wisdom” while distributing profit to the people who assist in that effort? I have a
lot of research to do, but I believe there is more flexability in existing as a “for profit”
corporation rather than a “non profit” educational corporation, so I am exploring that option.
Are there any “for profit” corporations out there that you consider good and noble

Mike
9/17/2004 at 03:26 AM
A for-profit corporation certainly can follow purposes other than pure shareholder value
maximisation.
The main issue is ownership - the shareholders own the residual value of the firm.
If you are a 100% owner of a firm, you can do pretty much what you like with the profits, since
they are effectively yours after the taxman takes his cut.
The problems start when you have outside shareholders.
At that point, you have a legal duty to maximise shareholder value in most countries.
Unless all shareholders agree to your actions, you could be liable for damages if you use
company money for purely “altruistic” purposes.
You might be able to get round this by specifying non-monetary objectives in shareholder
agreements (i.e. write the objectives before you issue the shares, so that all share purchasers
have explicitly agreed to the objectives) but there is always a degree of uncertainty in legal
matters.
Merck is an example of a company that does something like this: if you buy the shares, you are
implicitly agreeing that you will accept that management will spend company resources on
non-financial objectives.
If you look at their mission statement their number one value is: Quote: 1.
Our business is preserving and improving human life.
All of our actions must be measured by our success in achieving this goal.
We value, above all, our ability to serve everyone who can benefit from the appropriate use of
our products and services, thereby providing lasting consumer satisfaction.
Notwithstanding this, I still think that non-for-profit is the best model for a think tank.
You can still pay salaries, after all, and you gain a significant degree of additional credibility if
you can demonstrate that you are not just in it for the money.

I simply recognize that the free market is also a democratic system, and every dollar is a vote.
Not only is every dollar a vote, but it is a vote that has more value than the political vote,
because an individual must earn his dollar-votes, whereas the political vote costs him nothing.

vote.

ascertainable, with a greater chance for relief if found to be unsatisfactory, than his political
vote.
It is therefore obvious that he will care more about what happens to his dollar-vote than his
political vote, and put more deliberation into the act of voting.
The great problem of political (as opposed to economic) democracy has always been to
convince the voter that his vote is worth something while the reality of the process convinces
him it is worth nothing.
He does nothing to earn it, has no implied warranty for his purchase, and ultimately it controls
very little that directly affects his life.

Why should corporations need a more noble purpose then just making money? When a
company makes money and seeks to make more, they frequently investing money into more
ways to make it.
They do this through expansion.
Maybe they add a few jobs, maybe the build a new location, maybe they buy a floundering
competitor.
When they do this they create jobs.
They create jobs at their company, and their support industries, at the financial instutions that
loan and manage their money at the deli near their new location, etc. etc.
More jobs mean more people putting money back into the economy.
We build more stores, and that creates jobs, stores order more goods, which requires more
manufacturing, and that creates more jobs, etc. etc.
IMHO the most noble act one can commit is to help someone else become capable of supporting
themselves and securing their own future.
That, is ultimately what corporations do when their goal is to “only” to make money.
fschmidt
3/2/2005 at 05:59 AM
I just skimmed this thread and most of it seems to be arguing about whether corporations are
good or bad, which wasn’t Matt’s original question.
Matt should talk to a lawyer to get a clear answer, but I believe that corporations can be
structured to pursue various goals.
It’s true that the board of directors has a “fiduciary responsibility” to the shareholders to
maximize share value.
But what happens in practice? Does paying CEOs huge salaries maximize shareholder value? Of
course not.
The legal requirement of fiduciary responsibility only comes into play in the most blatant cases
of ripping off shareholders.
Otherwise, the board acts in the best interest of whoever has power over the board, usually the
CEO and a few large shareholders.
So the determining factor over how a corporation behaves is who has the real power to choose
the board of directors.
The original idea was to let the shareholders elect the board, but this system has largely been
broken because of lack of interest from small shareholders and the use of various rules to limit
the power of small shareholders.
In my ideal corporation, the employees would elect the board.
If the employees are motivated by some non-financial goals, these goals would then be reflected
on the board and therefor by company actions.
The way to accomplish this in a corporate structure is to have 2 classes of stock.
The first class would be non-voting stock that is transferable and represents the financial
interest in the company.
The other would be voting stock that is non-transferable (accomplished with buy-back rules)
that is issued only to employees.
This effectively separates money and power, and thereby prevents money from buying power
within the company.
This is an idea that I have been thinking about for a long time, and I am right now putting into
practice.
I am working with my lawyer to structure a business that I am starting along these lines.

There is nothing wrong with a company having noble goals.
Many companies start with just such an idea.
The problem is, that in order to achieve any goals a company must be profitable.
I am working on starting a company.
The idea is to provide installation, service and education of all mannors of low-voltage systems,
from Cable TV to computer networks to people.
My goal is to bring great services to people at a reasonable price.
The idea being that everyone is better off with better access to information as well as services
that make their daily life easier.
Note such a bad goal.
However, for this company to work it needs to be profitable enough to be able to support itself
as well as my family.
Now, I would also like to start a non-profit organization designed to help the elderly and
disabled in my home town by taking care of things they cannot, like their lawns, snow removal,
painting, home repairs etc.
My comapny could be a major force in this.
Assuming it does well enough, it might be able to finance this organization.
However, it would need to be quite profitable in order to do so.
Outside of ensuring that the people working for the company have the best understanding
possible of the companies goals, policies, proceedures, as well as the individuals job, and the
benefits they have access too, there is really no benefit for the company to directly seek to
“wisen” their employees.
However, many companies can see that better educated employees will be better employees and
possibly better managers in the future.
This is why so many larger companies provide tuition assistance.
It depends on what the company does.
A financial services company helps itself as well as the public if it provides free information via
website, newspaper article, handout or whatever, on what the various financial investment
vehicles are.
A company like the one I want to create serves the public and itself by providing free
information on what home automation services are, how alarms can protect you from more
then buglaries, etc.
Outside of that, I see it as the job of the individual to “wisen” themselves through reading,
exploring, and just plain living.
Remember, all companies are not Profit only motivated.
The largest donations to various charities come from corporations.
But in order to make such donations, a company as to make a profit.

Matt
12/12/2003 at 07:05 PM
Think of the post rating in the Lyceum as “wisdom ratings”.
People should rate posts based upon how wise or foolish they judge the opinion, idea,
reasoning, or offered solution.
For example, imagine two people both favoring a solution you abhor.
The first recites precanned arguments like a broken record and ignores any compelling
questions or counter arguments.
You might rate most of this person’s posts with a 1.
The second person expresses their view with apparently well thought out reasoning and a
seemingly genuine effort to find the best answer.
They respond to questions and they admit when counter arguments have some validity.
Although, you still abhor thier ideas, you might rate some of their posts 3 or 4.
Jon Q Republican
1/14/2004 at 01:09 PM
The nation sales tax on the surface seems like a good idea.
There are however two problems I see with it that need to be addressed before the tax could be
enacted.
The first is the poor.
Those in this country with families that make $30000.00 or less a year don’t pay taxes now.
They get it all back in April.
Those under $28000.00 actually get more back then they paid in due to the earned income tax
credit.
Going to a national sales tax would put large tax burden on these people that have not had that
burden under the current system.
The idea that everything not be taxed and we somehow focus this tax on the wealthy will not
work.
We tried this with luxury taxes on yachts and the like.
The result was the destruction of the yacht industry in this country (where regular people
worked) as the rich just began to purchase these craft outside of the USA.
Furthermore, to avoid food and clothing under 100.00 would be to avoid consumables.
Without such a tax on consumables the percentage would have to be outrageously high to come
close to the revenue currently made by the income tax.
Another problem is getting it past congress.
Congress is not likely to pass this type of reform because it takes away one of there biggest
areas of power.
Legislating the tax code.
Congress has used the tax code to reward supporters for a long time and is not likely to give it
up easily.
And of course there are all the accountants and poor IRS agents that would be put out of work.
My two favorite benefits are public education and the taxation of illegal or quasi-legal incomes.
If you ask the average person on the street what they make, they tell you what their last
paycheck was.
The don’t see it as make $800.00 a week and paying $300.00 to the government, they see it as
making $500.00 a week.
A national sales tax would put the cost of government right in front of the eyes of every
American every time they went to the store.
I think this would result in many more people becoming politically involved and calling
congress on all that pork.
Then there is the taxation of illegal and quasi-legal incomes.
Drug runners buy a lot of toys.
The resulting sales tax revenues from the criminal element will likely be significant and easily
balance the budget.
Also Rich people keep a lot of their money off shore.
With a national sales tax there would be no incentive to do this.
This could lead to a surge in investment in American companies and a massive, sustained boost
to the economy.
Anyway, that’s my take on it.
I’d love to hear peoples ideas on how to make this program work without crushing the poor and
retired.
