3/19/2004 at 02:40 AM
The current problem with sales taxes are that they aren’t sales taxes, they are purchase taxes.
You buy something (other than food or clothes) and the store adds 8%(in RI).
Now if the tax were on the sale the store would pay that percentage on the price it got.
This could be extended to every facet of commerce.
You sell labor for $15.00/hr you pay X% in taxes on the receipts of the sale.You sell stock for
$15,000 you pay X% in taxes on the receipts of the sale.You sell brokerage services for Y% of the
deal you pay X% of that in taxes on the receipts of the sale.
No loopholes, no shelters.
No waiting for projected income.
The national income becomes a true fraction of the national commerce.
I have a feeling that this method, let’s call it a transaction tax which is a variation the excise
taxes that founders did approve of, would generate more than enough to fund all levels of
government at less than the current average state sales tax and would eliminate the need for
income and property taxes.
In times of stress small incremental adjustments would cover the difference and be easily rolled
back when the crisis passed.
Border tariffs are protectionist and therefore diplomatically a problem.
Plus we’d just be taxing our own consumption which falls disproportionately on the less
wealthy.( Imagine the prices at Wal-Mart doubling since they sell almost nothing made in the
US) I have a problem with the notion of a financed based social structure that affords more
worth to an individual for what they have as opposed to what they do, but that’s a non-starter
argument in the current situation.
QU2R’s concept of a stateless private society was tried.
It was called feudalism, Russia is still suffering through it last phases.
The US had a couple of recent versions in the institutions of share cropping and company-
owned coal towns and aside from the song 16 Tons and Loretta Lynn not much good came of
them.
The idea he puts forth presumes an idealized level playing field and unbiased enlightened self
interest that has never been shown to exist.
The current government spending( all levels, I believe) is about 17% of GDP, among the lowest
in the industrialized world and then we spend an additional 14% on health care without
covering everyone.
The problem is not ability or resources it is allocation and distribution.
The Swedes pay 59% of GDP in taxes, but they have a much higher standard of living than we
do.
By any accounting method life costs X how that X is created and apportioned is the root
question.
Who is in, who is not and how is that determined.
The current system is barely rational and less than equitable.

3/23/2004 at 04:57 AM
As my original post stated . . .
Quote: The current problem with sales taxes are that they aren’t sales taxes, they are purchase
taxes.
You buy something (other than food or clothes) and the store adds 8%(in RI).
Now if the tax were on the sale the store would pay that percentage on the price it got.
This could be extended to every facet of commerce.
You sell labor for $15.00/hr you pay X% in taxes on the receipts of the sale.You sell stock for
$15,000 you pay X% in taxes on the receipts of the sale.You sell brokerage services for Y% of the
deal you pay X% of that in taxes on the receipts of the sale.
No loopholes, no shelters.
No waiting for projected income.
The national income becomes a true fraction of the national commerce.
The basic idea is that all transactions are considered sales and are taxed at the same rate.
Labor, stocks ,property, services, etc.
If you RECEIVE money in exchange for something that amount is taxed i. e. the SELLER is taxed
as opposed to the seller merely collecting a percentage of the purchase and passing it on to the
state.
This will not eliminate the cash economy, but it should allow the nominal rate to be low enough
that it will be easier to pay it than to try to avoid it.
Try to envision every sale on the NYSE taxed at the time of the sale, just like an over the counter
sale, everyday at a rate of about 1%.
No figuring out deductions or multi-year delays in paying up and the rate is exatly the same as
that coming out of the factory worker’s check.
I haven’t done the precise math, but the stats are available to figure a ball park figure pretty
easily.
The nice part is that rich people get to keep their money and spend it however they like until
they sell something then they pay at the same rate as everyone else.
Simply its a tax on the proceeds of any sale paid by the beneficiary of the sale.
qu2r
3/23/2004 at 05:46 PM
Transaction taxes are superior to income taxes, in my opinion.
So, we basically agree despite all the thrashing about.
Taking different tack (and move this to a new thread if appropriate, Matt, as I realize threads
can get stale with length, regardless of content).
Taxation is one of those things that is most successful for those involved if it causes the least
pain to they that lose it.
Just as a low price on goods gets more customers, more payers are available when the costs are
low.
The perceived costs, not necessarily reality.
Just as an example, when cigarette taxes are raised high enough, more people smuggle
cigarettes to avoid the tax and profit on the margin between the tax-increased-price and the
price it would be otherwise.
People are more willing to pay less and ask no questions, and supplier are more willing to
undergo the expenses of smuggling to make the additional profit of charging above normal
price, but less than taxed price.
So, whats a tax that is nearly imperceptible? Transaction taxes are good when low.
Sales tax, purchase tax, whatever-you-want-to-call-it taxes on the events where money changes
hands.
Ideally, the difference between price listed and price paid is imperceptible.
Government would even prefer that the final price be marked rather than the pre-tax price, but
obviously a retailer wants to list a lower price.
Raising this tax too high would drive people to black markets (like the example above) or back
to barter, which both avoids the tax, and goes backwards in economic progress.
Income taxes shouldnt work well, but using a technique like withholding, people dont perceive
its being taken.
They dont read their stubs and they get their net check, and not since their first job back in
High School have they thrown a fit over the tiny numbers on their paycheck compared to what
they calculated their hourly rate to yield in a week.
Most people are employed rather than own a business, so this income/withholding
combination works well on everyone who doesnt write those quarterly checks.
Payroll taxes work well for similar reasons, since people dont realize that they are losing
money.
Their employer pays the tax out of what could be their income, but they never saw it, so it
doesnt feel taken.
Again, its important for their to be employees for this technique, since employers are the agents
of collection, so it doesnt work so well on business owners without employees.
Another way to collect taxes in a painless manner is by inflating the currency.
If you can convince people to use a money substitute that has no relationship to real value, then
you can print as much as you like.
Of course, keeping the inflation rate low is important to postpone the problems of inflating so
much that people stop using the money.
But, as long as they keep using it, you can print more, getting the full value of the money when
you spend it first.
The price-increasing effect dictated by basic economics will take some time to work its way
through the economy.
The lowered value of the money is felt by the last user, like those who save money or otherwise
dont use it for a period of time over which that inflationary effect is felt.
This creates a steady stream of income that people dont notice at all, and payment is made very
subtly and incrementally as the large pool of money slowly, though surely, absorbs the new into
the economy.
Actually, this would work even if it werent a tax (meaning an individual rather than a
government could make money this way).
If you could perfectly counterfeit money (I mean absolutely perfect, perhaps replacing
destroyed dollars or otherwise being totally un-noticeable, so that what you make is basically
real money) you could make money the same way.
The money could never be detected as counterfeit, and the detectable affect (price increases
over time) is hardly noticeable, and people wouldnt even be looking for you, and you can
benefit from being the first spender of the new money, just like the gov

4/29/2004 at 05:23 PM
Assuming that any revised taxation system would have to produce at least as much revenue as
is produced by the current system, my thoughts are as follows: - Corporations and the wealthy
are undertaxed under the present system; - The tax burden on lower income taxpayers is too
heavy.
Any increase in a sales tax would exacerbate this problem; - Corporations (and their wealthy
controlling owners) have so much political power that meaningful reform is now politically
impossible.
My solution would be as follows: - Ban political contributions other than by registered voters; -
Having reduced the political power of corporations, all loopholes and special interest provisions
in the corporate tax code should be removed; - A modest annual wealth tax (proposed here by
Radiant1 on 2/18/04 and 3/20/04) should be imposed on net assets of individuals and trusts
(excluding owner-occupied homes and farms) with a high threshold; - Corporate compensation
of any individual that is in excess of 100 times the minimum wage should be treated as a
dividend, not a deductible expense, thus placing the burden of excessive compensation on the
shareholders not the taxpayers; - The additional revenue produced should be used to reduce
the tax burden on the lower income groups.

6/9/2004 at 05:36 AM
Here’s a novel tax idea.
How about a flat assets tax? It’s honest.
Unlike income and sales tax it is unavoidable on at least the major items.
No millionaire avoidance schemes.
You list your assets on one page, minus one and only one deduction of say $10,000 so you don’t
waste the time of the IRS tracking down some old pickup or guitar, and then total and pay a
fixed percentage.
The rich generally spend a smaller percentage of their assets than the poor so it would in affect
be progressive.
To take a tack from above it’s transparent because assets again are harder to hide than income
or sales.
It would encourage peer pressure to play it straight because people would feel that if somebody
else wasn’t paying they would get stuck with the additional tax.
Now the tax system is all so full of dodges people just get mad because they don’t have as good a
deal as the other guy.
A principle here is that what a government gives it should give over the table and not call it a
deduction or a credit.
It’s a government handout called something more palatable to the receiver.
So no deductions or credits except the sole one mentioned above.
The little old lady with the house and the limited fixed income which everyone brings up when
I mention my proposal can be helped first by her drawing on her house equity and then by
government programs, even grants, to help her.
The principle is taxes are there to raise money as simply, fairly and transparently as possible.
They should not be in the charity business by offering under the table kick backs or to engineer
social policy.
These under the table tax manipulations and too much complexity is what causes
disillusionment with federal taxation.
The government should fund their policies through direct payments visible to everybody.
This is called transparency and is critical to a well managed open democracy.
I will save my ideas on real cost pricing for later.

I agree that we benefit from government.
Anyone (like Richard Cheney in his debate with Lieberman) that claims government has not
played a part in the success of the greatest capitalists is quite foolish.
Through government we have transportation, mail, national defense, and a host of other things
that rely on centralized taxes.
What I do have a problem with; however, is when government oversteps the bounds of its
constitutional mandate.
Congress has the power under Section 8, clause 1 of the constitution to lay and collect Taxes,
Duties, Imposts and Excises, to pay the Debts and provide for the common Defense and general
Welfare of the United States.
My problem is a lot of governmental programs (whether enacted today or not) do not meet the
criteria our forefathers set.
To tax one individual in order to provide a service to another that is not required to preserve or
enhance the “general welfare,” (among the other criterion) is not constitutional.
Is it constitutional to tax us in order to subsidize some farming initiatives… yes, if that is what
it takes to keep farmers from moving on to other ventures.
My sense, however, is that government spends a lot of dollars on issues that only effect one
distinct segment of society (classified by either circumstance or geography).
Should we have healthcare for all? Absolutely not - we should only offer healthcare to those
groups who will have a substantial future impact on our general welfare (like young people for
instance).
Should we gather the funding so guarantee that every child go to college? No - we should only
gather the funding so enough children go to college to satisfy the demands of our economy.
This is not to say that on a personal basis - we shouldn’t try to ensure all people have access to a
quality university, but it is frankly unfair to demand, through taxes, that one person pay for the
schooling of another, under threat of jail time if they don’t pay their taxes, if that does not get
them something in return (preservation or enhancement of general welfare).

2/11/2004 at 06:36 PM — Wisdom Rating: 7.0
This is very common to this type of government.
The more the government is involved in what you do, the more you want to influence it.
Money is influence, so it flows to where the control is.
Its the incentive structure.
If you have money, and the governments in a position to influence how you make it, use it, etc,
then youll have a business case to use some of that money to protect yourself and your
interests.
One way to stem this is shrink government.
The less control government has, the less it matters to big money interests, the less incentive
theyll have in trying to influence government.
Why bother influencing something that doesnt matter? This still leaves the incentive to pump
money in to attempt to increase control again (mercantilist trend of many many decades), but
it would be a step in the right direction.
Another big step (perhaps it is the same one) is to somehow get the government back in the
mode of being legal.
Actually ruled by the Constitution.
That people would actually comply with their oaths.
Using a fixed Constitutional guide to decisions would be a standard independent of money.
Of course, this idea is considered antiquated by a government whose every branch ignores or
bends the fixed standard to their whim, increasing their particular power along the way.
Courts that legislate, legislatures that fail to check the courts, presidents who go to war without
declaring it, legislation that ignores the Constitution and courts that interpret it opposite to
what it says.
Said another way, to reduce apparent or real corruption in government, actually return to a
government that rules by law.
Perhaps thats too high-minded and unrealistic.
The pessimist in me says you cant solve it in a republic.
The incentives are set that those who want power spend money to get it, whether that means
buying votes with government programs or buying influence with campaign donations.

Throughout the American political system, a palpable shift towards conservative policies is
continually leaving the US in the stone age.
In the past, the synthesis of liberal and conservative ideals created some of the most notable
social solutions ever seen in the history of democracy.
However, as this balance shifts away from the progressive end of the spectrum, this debate
takes on a distinctly conservative character and stale institutions will never be toppled.
Furthermore, in such a conservative climate, the societal situations that gave rise to such
conditions will be self-preserving.
For the essence of conservative thinking is maintaining the institutions that have worked in the
past, especially the most pervasive ones firmly entrenced in our society.

The family is the fundamental unit of society where all basic things are taught, from civility to
morals to work ethic, and its decay is contributing to many problems.
The courts are supposed to have no will of their own; their purpose is to exercise the
legislature’s will and to check the legislature, according to the constitution.
Were there no set measure by which to size the laws, then the judiciary would be, in effect, a
legislature themselves, only much smaller and with almost ultimate power.
As said by Thomas Jefferson: It has long, however, been my opinion, and I have never shrunk
from its expression,… that the germ of dissolution of our federal government is in the
constitution of the federal judiciary; an irresponsible body, (for impeachment is scarcely a
scare crow,) working like gravity by night and by day, gaining a little today and a little
tomorrow, and advancing its noiseless step like a thief, over the field of jurisdiction, until all
shall be usurped from the States, and the government of all be consolidated into one.
To this I am opposed; because, when all government, domestic and foreign, in little as in great
things, shall be drawn to Washington as the center of all power, it will render powerless the
checks provided of one government on another, and will become as venal and oppressive as the
government from which we separated.
This has happened through misinterpretation of the commerce clause of the constitution
(despite what is said in the Federalist Papers, the definitive Constitutional commentarys, as
they were written by the founders themselves), and has progressed to the creation of new
rights, the applying of the Bill of Rights to the states when it was never meant to be applied that
way (again, see the Federalist Papers), and other abuses.
It has been gradual, but needs to be stopped.
Bad laws are usually not a slippery slope - you can elect someone else and repeal the laws - but
decisions made by the courts have no such stay.
See The Federalist Papers and the Constitutional Freedom Foundation .
These set out what I have said about the Constitution in detail.

7/31/2004 at 05:06 AM
Davidjanca wrote: Quote: What the communities need is an enviable example of participatory
government.
When folks see other groups of folks thriving because their government is working for their
benefit instead of often to their detriment they will seek out similar solutions.
Gem replies: Absolutely correct, davidjanca! I am of the opinion that this ‘democracy’ of “WE,
THE PEOPLE” has been subverted by politicians that have forgotten who the real bosses are in a
democracy.
The “special interest groups” that have their own agendas and pour money and/or gifts into the
pockets of those they wish to manipulate needs to come to an abrupt and immediate end.
Giving those special interests whatever it is they want without regard to the impact their
demands have on the rest of America and the world is a major source of dissension and
resentment in the world, the majority of which seems to be directed at the United States at the
present time.
How, then, can this be remedied? By returning to a form of “Participatory Government”.
Ideas: (1) Reducing Congress and the Administration back to the level “Public Servants” that
would be beholden to the desires and will of “We, the People”and become the implementors of
the public will and not the determiners of the ‘public will.’ (2) Complete separation not only of
Church and State but of Business and State as well. (3) Bills and Legislation passed only after
approval by a referendum vote of the people. (4) Referendum voting on all issues by a popular
vote of the people at least three times a year. (5) Shifting the focus of Congress from a ‘creator
of laws’ to a think-tank type of institution that would come up with several possible solutions
to national and international issues, with the solution to be utilized decided by the popular
referendum vote. (6) No political contributions of any kind.
Electoral funding to come from taxpayer coffers, equal amounts per candidate per election to
level the playing field. (7) No ‘riders’ on bills- a bill must either stand or fall on it’s own merits.
(8) Pay raises for legislators to be requested of and voted for or against by the constituents the
legislators represent. (9) The institution of a “Vote of No Confidence” referendum vote that can
remove a government official immediately if the people feel the government official no longer
represents the best interests of the country. (10) Supreme Court Justices to be voted in by the
people, not installed by appointment- with definite term limits.
These are just ten suggestions that I have thought about for a long time that I feel might help
alleviate the problems that currently beset our nation.
I look forward to debate, discussion and critique of these ideas in the hopes that they may lead
to a more democratic form of government that will benefit not only America but all nations.

Paul Johnson
9/14/2004 at 11:49 PM
Who will buy cheap imported products if the consummers are out of job and have no money? It
doesn’t work like that.
If people are out of work because someone else will do their job cheaper, it implies that
somewhere else someone is in work and willing to buy the stuff.
Think of the classic supply-demand curve.
As demand for workers goes down, so do wages.
So people will be able to find work, just at lower wages.
Meanwhile, back in the “cheap” country demand for workers has pushed up wages from their
previously low level, so its not as cheap anymore.
And since you have a lot of newly rich people overseas with money burning holes in their
pockets, you can start making things here to sell to them.
That pushes wages here back up.
In the long term everyone wins: the rich get richer, and the poor get richer too.
The problem lies in the short-term dislocation as old industries are shut down and lay off
workers who (in the short term) can’t find new jobs.
The role for Government here is not to hobble local industry with regulations that make it
difficult to reduce costs, or to slap on import tarrifs to keep out cheap goods (one day historians
will look in amazement at the popular delusion that you could make people wealthier by
making stuff more expensive).
Instead it they should be easing the transition for areas and groups hit by these changes.
In the UK there is a long standing tradition of offering tax breaks, grants and other incentives
to industry if they will move to economically depressed areas, which explains why there are so
many Japanese car plants in South Wales for example.
When a low skill job is outsourced, you can provide more training to the people to give them a
higher skill job.
But what are you going to do when the higest skills jobs are outsourced? Same thing.
I’m a programmer by trade, and well aware that I am in competition with ambitious young
men in India who see $20,000 as a good annual salary.
But a few years ago that was $10,000, and the price is still going up. (Aside: India has such lousy
telecoms infrastructure that in most of the country you couldn’t make a profit out of IT if
people worked for free, and even in Mumbai things are not ideal.
Employees are not the only cost) Life is not a zero-sum game.
Just because someone else is winning does not automatically mean that you are losing.
Just because a job position is filled in India does mean that one less position exists to be filled
here.

Paul Johnson
9/21/2004 at 05:49 AM
Quote: Originally posted by davidjanca I would like to comment on the continually repeated
assertion that lack of -health insurance- is a problem.
I am sure that insurance companies are thrilled to have acheived such pervasive political
catchphrase adoption.
Is there someone who disagrees with me when I say that the relevant problem is “Lack of access
to quality HEALTHCARE for children and for the poor, NOT lack of health insurance”? Well, yes
as far as it goes.
However I don’t think that the “no insurance” rhetoric excludes a solution that bypasses the
insurance companies, nor do I think that the insurance companies could use this term in that
way as part of their lobbying.
So I don’t see it as an issue.
To pick up a more general point, let me talk a bit about my experiences with health care in both
the UK and US (where I have worked, and been insured through my employer).
In the UK your point of access to health care is either through your “General Practitioner” (GP)
or through the Accident and Emergency department at a nearby hospital (A&E).
If its a routine thing then you make an appointment with your GP, typically a week in advance.
The appointment will last about 10 minutes, and the doctor will usually be running 30 to 60
minutes behind the schedule.
If it won’t wait a week then you can explain to the receptionist and get an “emergency”
appointment that day or the next.
If its a real must-treat-now issue then you go to A&E.
Ambulances are available by phoning 999 (equivalent of 911).
At A&E they decide how urgent your problem is, and assign priority accordingly.
If you have something really serious then you get seen immediately.
If its just a cut then you can find yourself waiting for hours because there is always someone
coming in who needs care more urgently than you do.
Saturday at 11pm is a really bad time to get careless with a knife.
While you are waiting you get to sit with everyone else, including the drunk who got into a fight
and lost. (Assault on staff at A&E is a serious problem, BTW) If the GP or doctor who sees you at
A&E thinks you need specialist care then s/he can refer you to a Consultant.
Again, waiting time depends on seriousness.
If you are about to die then stuff happens fast.
But if you don’t fall in to the “about to die” cateogory then you get put in a queue, where you
wait.
It can take 18 months to see a consultant, and waits of 6 months are not uncommon.
When the consultant sees you (again, for 10 minutes) s/he may order tests or surgery.
Into the queue again.
Test results are generally available within a couple of weeks, followed by a second 10 minute
appointment with the consultant the next week.
Surgery generally takes longer.
So its surgery, but not urgent.
Then you get a letter from the hospital telling you when your appointment is.
You can change it if you have to, but only to a small range of later dates.
You go in at the appointed time.
The operation may be postponed if there is too much demand from more urgent cases.
Some people wind up going in several times.
The chance of administrative cock-up during all this is high.
My son was supposed to be operated on for an undescended testicle.
We went in, but the operation was postponed.
We were told we would get a letter with a new appointment.
When we hadn’t heard anything after 6 months we phoned up.
A brief check showed that my son had been flagged as “discharged” even though the operation
hadn’t happened, so it didn’t get rescheduled.
My father in law missed chemotherapy during his last days because of some mix up over the
ambulance that was supposed to take him in.
By the time it was sorted out he was too ill for the treatment.
When we came to the US my son’s testicle had still not been sorted out.
So we made sure that my new employer’s health plan included pre-existing conditions, and got
an appointment with a specialist.
He scheduled an operation and asked us when it would be convenient.

7/20/2004 at 10:31 AM
Same-Sex Unions Are A Fun Topic Opponents of the legalization of marriage like to pretend that
there’s no real difference between a civil union and a marriage, so why not settle for a civil
union? This of course begs the question, if there’s no real difference, why not let them marry?
Let them talk long enough and you’re likely to hear something along the lines of “tolerance will
destroy our culture” - which would be a good reason to restrict the enjoyment of our basic
human rights to white male christian landowners, the way their white male God, landlord of
Eden, intended it to be.
As for marriage being about children, many heterosexual marriages have been economic
unions first and foremost, regardless of whether or not the couple had children.
If it becomes clear to the State that a couple does not plan to raise children, should the State’s
recognition of that marriage be withdrawn? Should marriage licenses in fact only be granted to
couples with children, and revoked when the children can no longer be counted as dependents?
The impact of the legalization of same-sex marriages will be to extend benefits currently
enjoyed by heterosexual spouses to homosexual spouses.
These benefits include enrollment in the spouse’s health insurance, enjoyment of the spouse’s
pension and social security, visitation rights, inheritance, etc.
Beyond that, I would expect the debate to open up not to questions such as “Why can’t I marry
my dog?” - although that question will be asked - but rather “Why are certain partnerships
recognized, while others are not?” If you have decided to combine your destiny and your
finances with other members of your household, why is there a limit to the extent to which
these lifemates can share in your fortune, good or bad, regardless of whether or not you intend
to have sex with them? There are a few ways to dodge that bullet; one is the existing polygamy
laws, another is to point out that such voluntary associations are called “corporations”, another
is to extend the social “safety net” to the point that we all enjoy such benefits as health care and
pension simply as members of our society regardless of marital status.
We still haven’t worked all the bugs out after abolishing slavery.
Legalization of same-sex marriages will have foreseen and unforeseen, intended and
unintended consequences which we will have to sort out down the road.
In the meantime, the tiny risk posed is far outweighed by the benefit of treating our fellow
human beings like fellow human beings.

The debate on gay marriage has been hashed, re-hashed and probably corned beef hashed as
well.
When discussing Same-Sex Marriage we are talking about the Legal Definition of Marriage in
the form of State sanctioned marriage.
In this country, the law is what matters.
If you feel that things outside of the Legal Definition of Marriage need to be included in the
legally recognized definition of marriage then you need to work to change that law.
I agree that is some instances, changing laws have been bad for society (I just do not see it in
this case).
However, you don’t get to apply your own morals and views to existing laws in court.
The courts decision is based on the law.
Currently the Legal Definition of Marriage represents a commitment between a man and a
woman, there is NOTHING else in marriage law other then that commitment and the legal
obligations connected to it.
The oppositions frequent argument is along the lines of: “We cannot allow it because it will
harm the children if we change the definition of marriage”.
But, where are the protections for children in the Legal Definition of Marriage ? Nowhere.
Legal protections for children are actually found in Parental rights laws, child abuse laws, child
custody laws, etc.
This is where the laws that protect children reside.
Marriage gives some a small leg up when dealing with some of these laws, however marriage is
NOT a requirement for any part of any of them.
Another argument is that it separates marriage from procreation.
The implication here is that the state sponsors marriage to promote procreation.
I fail to see how, allowing homosexuals to marry will somehow reduce procreation in
heterosexual couples.
More to the point, procreation is not mentioned ANYWHERE in the Legal Definition of
Marriage .
If it is not legally defined as part of marriage in the eyes of the state then how can it be a valid
argument to deny same-sex couples marriage? I fail to see the difference between a mandate
restricting what racial combinations can marry and what sex combinations can marry.
Based on The legal definition of Marriage .
I fail to see how this will negatively effect society any more then allowing interracial marriages
did.
The argument is continually made that this is about protecting the children, yet there are no
protections for children defined in the definition of LEGAL MARRIAGE, anywhere in any
marriage license, and as far as I can tell children are never mentioned in any religious vows of
marriage.
Even if you believe (I don’t) that homosexuality is: a> learned behavior and not genetically
based b> a negative form of behavior c> a negative for children You can not use that as an
argument against same sex marriage because: A> Two Convicted Child Molesters can Legally
Marry B> Two Convicted Child Abusers can Legally Marry C> Two Convicted Child Murderers
can Legally Marry So, there is absolutely no protections afforded to children by the Legal
Definition of Marriage , other then the marginal leg up married parents have in dealing with
the actual laws dealing with child protection.
Marriage is NOT a requirement of any of those laws.
Futhermore, when the opposition claims that they have to oppose same-sex marriage “for the
sake of the children” they don’t seem to take into account the 1000s of children currently living
in same sex households.
If you believe that marriage is such an important part of the protection of children they why
would you deny that protection to these children? Are they somehow second class citizens
because of the type of household they live in? Is this a “Sins of the Father” (or Mother) Issue?
The only difference between Marriage of heterosexual and marriage of homosexual couples
when dealing with legal / state marriage is the sex of the participants.
The Civil Rights act clearly states that you cannot discriminate based on sex.
So, IMHO, this is a clear case of discrimination.

6/30/2004 at 03:37 AM
The Public education system in the US solves one very important problem, but creates several
other problems.
The problem it solves: Providing every child an opportunity for an education.
The problems it continues to have: 1.
Public education, like all government run programs, is shoddy and inefficient.
It does not have to compete on a balanced playing field, therefore it is substandard. 2.
The curriculum in public schools is determined by the state and federal government.
Why should the government be in control of what your child is taught in school? 3.
Parents who are unhappy with public education for either of the above two reasons, have to
pay out of their pocket for a private education.
This means they have to pay twice for their childs education: Once in taxes and again in tuition
and fees.
Wouldn’t it make sense to charge people only once for the education of their children-and allow
them to educate them in the way deemed best by them? What is your solution to the state of
public education in the US and the above 3 issues? Note From Matt: This thread has generated
a ton of great posts.
The quickest way to read the best solutions to this topic is to click the ” Topic Solutions Report ”
link which appears in the lower left hand corner of every post.

6/30/2004 at 03:44 AM
I believe all citizens should help pay for the gauranteed education of all children.
I believe this because we all benefit from having an educated populace-and we all suffer if we
are surrounded by uneducated illequipped people.
The trick we need to master is how to fund something without destroying our ability to do it by
over-regulating it.
We should fund it- and allow the free markets to compete for the best solution.
It seems charter schools achieve this exact combination of goals for publicly funded education.
Quote: Charter schools are nonsectarian public schools of choice that operate with freedom
from many of the regulations that apply to traditional public schools.
The “charter” establishing each such school is a performance contract detailing the school’s
mission, program, goals, students served, methods of assessment, and ways to measure success.
The length of time for which charters are granted varies, but most are granted for 3-5 years.
At the end of the term, the entity granting the charter may renew the school’s contract.
Charter schools are accountable to their sponsor– usually a state or local school board– to
produce positive academic results and adhere to the charter contract.
The basic concept of charter schools is that they exercise increased autonomy in return for this
accountability.
They are accountable for both academic results and fiscal practices to several groups: the
sponsor that grants them, the parents who choose them, and the public that funds them
Charter School info The Charter school movement is giving education what it needs: an infusion
of money and freedom to innovate.
These charter schools are experimenting, coming up with new ways to make sure the teachers
and principals are held accountable-in essence they are finding ways to make sure CHILDREN
LEARN and receive a high quality education.
The best thing about it: If a school is not doing what we are paying it to do, we can fire it and
hire someone else to give it a try.

We pulled our daughter out of a private school because it was rotten and put her into the public

fewer benefits.
If you think public schools have low quality, the answer is to give them more money, not blame
the victim. 2.
Government control: So what? Better to have a central body setting standards and making sure
they are met than no control at all.
Remember that private schools are in business to make money, not to educate your kids.
The kind of private schools that most parent can afford are not worth going to.
With public schools the government can draw on funding from all over the state and even the
nation, and the gov’t can make sure the schools meet certain standards.
What often happens in private schools – especially the more exclusive ones – is that parents can
threaten to take their business elsewhere if things don’t go well: “My little Johnny is a genius!
Why is he getting such bad grades? If he doesn’t start getting A’s, we’re taking him (and our
money) to a school that recognizes his potential!” 3.
Unfair: Education isn’t a private affair like going to the movies.
If other children aren’t getting educated, it will affect your own kids in the future, the same as
if other kids never learn how to drive safely.
The answer here is for parents to get more involved in the process. re charter schools: The
worrisome thing about charter schools is that they are publicly-funded private schools – the

For many problems in the world we spend too much time arguing like this: “If we did this this
would happen.” “No, if you did this that would happen.
We need to do this.” “They do that there and it doesn’t work.” “They didn’t do it right, it needs
to be done like this.” “You wouldn’t be able to do it like that because of this this and this.” “Yes
we would.” “No you wouldn’t” “uh huh!” “uh uh.” “uh huh.” “uh uh.” and so on getting us
nowhere.
I believe we need to figure out ways to stop arguing over theories and start putting theories to
the test.
Let’s use a little scientific method to find the best and most effiecient solutions to the problems
in health care and education.
Instead of bashing our highly abstract visions of the future against one another, why not give
each State funding and encourage them to innovate-and try to find a formula for success-
rather than force feeding everyone a single formula? If we give communities an equal amount
of money per student and the freedom to innovate and create the best educational system they
can, I wonder what they would come up with? Let the proof be in the pudding.
Let people test the ideas out there and study the results.
How about a 10 year plan to see what ideas really can be used to transform our public school
system from a mediocre stagnant day care into a palace of wisdom and learning.
lisafaz
8/1/2004 at 03:27 PM
All three of the questions posed initially are important and complicated, so in this post I will
only address the issue of quality.
I must begin by telling you that I am a teacher in a public school in North Carolina.
I also taught in Ohio for five years before moving south.
In my experience, the quality of schools varies significantly from district to district.
In Ohio, this translated into how wealthy the tax base of the school district was.
For example, in Columbus, Ohio, New Albany’s schools aer excellent.
They can afford to pay teachers more than some of the other schools in the county, thus
attracting a bigger pool of applicants and allowing them to choose the best.
Conversely, Groveport had awful schools and was in a low income area.
Teachers didn’t dream of working for that district… it was kind of a “well, I guess it’s a job”
kind of school when I was there.
The funding inequities caused lower income school districts to fall behind in quality.
Accountability is another issue in school quality.
First, who gets to create the yardstick by which schools are judged? Federal, state or local
governments? And do the people who comprise a school quality investigative committee have
any expertise in the field of education? Giong through school yourself as a student does not
qualify you to judge the quality of a school, just as going to a doctor for a physical does not give
you the qualifications to prescribe for yourself.
In North Carolina, all public schools must adhere to the Standard Course of Study created by
the state’s Department of Public Instruction.
Because I teach students with special needs, I will only discuss their curriculum.
My students have full scale IQs ranging from 50 to 75.
In North Carolina, theses students are offered the Occupational Course of Study, which is
designed to help them become good entry level employees and live as independently as possible.
I teach math, English, social studies and science, while my partner teacher employability skills.
Junior year, our students must satisfactorily complete an unpaid internship.
Senior year, they compleet a paid work experience and move directly into jobs upon graduation.
In English, I help them improve their functional reading skills.
Math: how to balance a checkbook & work with taxes and paystubs.
In social studies, they learn citizenship and self-advocacy under the Americans with Disabilities
Act.
In science, we focus on personal health, which includes family planning.
For these students, this is a quality education.
The curriculum was designed to suit the needs of the students and our society.
Every five to seven years, the North Carolina Department of Public Instruction revises the
curriculum of every subject taught in its schools.
This is done by a panel of teachers, parents, businesspeople and professors.
This ensures that the curriculum always stays current and relevant.
In the mountain region, where I live, there is not that much variance in teacher pay.
However, we are paid significantly less than our Ohio counterparts.
Teacher training also greatly effects quality.
In NC, schools will pay for teachers to earn their National Board Certification, and we now have
more nationally certified teachers than any other state.
In addition, in the mountain region, special education teacehrs are encouraged to apply for the
Mountain Connection Grant (of which I am a recipient) which pays for them to earn their
Master’s in Teaching on the condition that these teachers will continue to teach in a public
school in North Carolina for three years after completing the program.
If more states took these kinds of initiatives, we would have better trained teachers using
research-based practices in classrooms across our nation. (Note: I changed the title to more
accurately describe the solution contained in this post.
It was merely titled “School Quality”. -Matt)

8/6/2004 at 01:07 AM
I am a teacher, and also only three classes form my Master’s in Teaching, so I think I could be
considered to be somewhat of an authority on the subject.
That said, standardized testing for the masses is not an effective tool with which to measure the
achievement of our schools or students.
At least, not the way they are handled now.
To truly measure whether schools are doing their job (educating students), we need to establish
a baseline for each student at the start of each school year or semester.
Then, it needs to be immediately graded and returned to the teacher, who can then create an
individualized learning plan for each student, addressing what is not yet known.
After a specified time period, there should then be a post-test, verifying that the teacher did his
or her job of teaching those facts to the student.
That would truly be “leaving no child behind”.
Don’t forget though, that the assessment tool itself must incorporate a variety of methods to
measure the student’s knowledge.
There must be selection questions (multiple choice, fill in the blank from a word bank,
true/false), production qustions (the student must produce an answer… none may be offered
as options) and applications (a student is given a situation in which they would use this
knowledge that is meaningful to them personally).
With the testing system we have in place now, we rely almost entirely on selection, use some
production and very few application, therefore, we test efw higher level thinking skills
adequately.
Could we do it correctly? Right now, this is impossible.
We don’t have the extremely low staff to student ratio needed or the funds for the teachers or
test creation or even the test administration and grading itself.
So instead, our government has simplified the whole thing down to giving all students in a
grade level the same test, which in many cases is poorly designed and is incapable of measuring
the actual learning that happens.
It’s as if we’ve decided to judge dentists by how many cavities their patients have.
The dentists may do all he or she can do to care for the patient’s teeth, but ultimiately, it’s the
patient’s responsibility.
And some people have a familial history of “good” teeth, just as some families tend to be more
verbal or math oriented.
lisafaz
8/6/2004 at 01:11 AM
Consider this quote taken from the website of California Educator (
http://www.cta.org/CaliforniaEducator/v6i5/TakingStand_3 ) The improvement in test scores
that results from these strategies is short-lived, at best.
This is because of the “sawtooth effect”described by researcher Robert Linn.
He has found that, sadly, the experience with test-driven reform has been quite consistent
across the country: When a new test is introduced, students do not do well.
Gradually over the next several years, scores improve.
However, scores tend to plateau three to four years out in spite of the best efforts to the
contrary.
Then they plummet when the test is re-normed or a new test is introduced, hence the
“sawtooth” effect.
A false sense of accomplishment is followed by the uneasy suspicion that, in fact, conditions are
unchanged or, worse, have deteriorated.

RepublicanPlatform
8/25/2004 at 04:47 PM
Real Education Reform: Strengthening Accountability and Empowering Parents “No child in
America should be segregated by low expectations . . .imprisoned by illiteracy . . . abandoned to
frustration and the darkness of self-doubt.” George W.
Bush The question is “Are our schools better off now than they were eight years ago?” At a time
of remarkable economic growth, when a world of opportunity awaits students who are
prepared for it, American colleges and universities are offering remedial courses and American
businesses are unable to find enough qualified or trainable workers to meet the demand.
Worst of all, so many of our children, Americas most precious asset, are headed toward failure
in school, and that will hold them back throughout their lives.
Republicans desire a better result.
We believe that every child in this land should have access to a high quality, indeed, a world-
class education, and were determined to meet that goal.
Its long past time to debate what works in education.
The verdict is in, and our Republican governors provided the key testimony: strong parental
involvement, excellent teachers, safe and orderly classrooms, high academic standards, and a
commitment to teaching the basics from an early start in phonics to mastery of computer
technology.
Federal programs that fail to support these fundamental principles are sadly out of date and,
under the next president, out of time.
For dramatic and swift improvement, we endorse the principles of Governor Bushs education
reforms, which will: Raise academic standards through increased local control and
accountability to parents, shrinking a multitude of federal programs into five flexible grants in
exchange for real, measured progress in student achievement Assist states in closing the
achievement gap and empower needy families to escape persistently failing schools by allowing
federal dollars to follow their children to the school of their choice.
Expand parental choice and encourage competition by providing parents with information on
their childs school, increasing the number of charter schools, and expanding education savings
accounts for use from kindergarten through college.
Help states ensure school safety by letting children in dangerous schools transfer to schools
that are safe for learning and by forcefully prosecuting youths who carry or use guns and the
adults who provide them.
Ensure that all children learn to read by reforming Head Start and by facilitating state reading
initiatives that focus on scientifically based reading research, including phonics.
Nothing is more important than literacy, and yet many children have trouble reading.
This problem must be addressed at all grade levels.
And as is so often the case in education, the solution is parent and child working together with
teachers to help break a cycle of illiteracy that may have extended from generation to
generation.
We want to replace that pattern with the rich legacy of reading.
We recognize that under the American constitutional system, education is a state, local, and
family responsibility, not a federal obligation.
Since over 90 percent of public school funding is state and local, not federal, it is obvious that
state and local governments must assume most of the responsibility to improve the schools, and
the role of the federal government must be progressively limited as we return control to
parents, teachers, and local school boards.
Programs beginning the process by congressional Republicans to return power to the people,
such as “Straight As” legislation and “Dollars to the Classroom” are a good step to reach this
goal.

The Issue: Government schools lead to the indoctrination of children and interfere with the free
choice of individuals.
Compulsory education laws spawn prison-like schools with many of the problems associated
with prisons The Principle: Education, like any other service, is best provided by the free
market, achieving greater quality and efficiency with more diversity of choice.
Solutions: We advocate the complete separation of education and State.
Government ownership, operation, regulation, and subsidy of schools and colleges should be
ended.
We call for the repeal of the guarantees of tax-funded, government-provided education, which
are found in most state constitutions.
We condemn compulsory education lawsand we call for an immediate repeal of such laws.
Until government involvement in education is ended, we support elimination, within the
governmental school system, of forced busing and corporal punishment.
We further support immediate reduction of tax support for schools, and removal of the burden
of school taxes from those not responsible for the education of children.
Transitional Action: As an interim measure to encourage the growth of private schools and
variety in education, including home schooling, we support tax credits for tuition and other
expenditures related to an individual’s education.
We likewise favor tax credits for child care and oppose nationalization of the child-care
industry.
We oppose denial of tax-exempt status to schools because of those schools’ private policies on
hiring, admissions and student deportment.
We support the repeal of all taxes on the income or property of private schools, whether profit
or non-profit.

Just a couple of observations on your long post.
First, consider the following two quotes together: Quote: Regarding spanking- you dont wait a
minute.
Like a kid touching a hot stove, the resonse hasta be immediate.
Quote: Naturally, they too had an aversion to corporeal punishment; but for one, it was not
adminstered by the teachers.
They played good cop/bad cop, and the principle was the heavy.
The principle also had some emotional distance from the passions of the moment which
produced the outburst, so that he could, in true Stoic fashion, deliver the paddling in a
dispassionate manner.
It seems clear that the principal won’t be administering the punishment “immediately.”
Children are not rats.
When rats are “punished” all they know is that they are experiencing pain, usually from an
electric shock (i.e., from an unknown source).
And the rat will do what it can to avoid future pain.
When a child is punished, he knows it’s coming and he knows who is doing it.
The result is likely as not going to be resentment and growing fear of the punisher.
Unlike the rat, the child will do what it can to avoid future contact with the punisher.
And I am not the first to point out that physical force is characterized by parents and teachers
as a bad way to solve problems, and that non-violent problem resolution is the way to go.
Corporal punishment teaches the opposite lesson, and “actions speak louder than words.” Is
physical force as a problem solving approach what you want to teach? Regardless of the
effectiveness of corporal punishment, I think that its use must be an admission of failure of
authority.
If the child respects the parent’s (or teacher’s) opinion and demands, corporal punishment
won’t be necessary; and if he doesn’t, it won’t work very well.
Having said all this, I will also mention that I and my wife have spanked our son about five
times.
This was generally the result of major anger on our part, where we couldn’t think of a better
way to handle what we saw as extreme provocation by our son.
I would never apply corporal punishment in the manner you suggest; I think it is important
that it be applied in a moment of anger, and typically with an apology afterwards.
As usual, it’s not an easy question.

9/21/2004 at 06:13 PM
This is a difficult subject to tackle because it involves so many preliminaries to be decided, such
as: what makes a good education? how do current practices measure up in providing a good
education? what kinds of changes would be helpful toward providing a good education? what
kinds of changes are possible given the current climate of public opinion? Without provisional
answers to such questions, its difficult to say anything sensible towards the initial question.
In another thread (
http://www.thesearchforwisdom.com/community/boards/viewthread.php?tid=288 ) I argued
that a good education must provide both preparation for adulthood and an enjoyable
experience for the child.
Current practices attempt to provide a good preparation for adulthood, but do so at the expense
of enjoyment for the child.
So the kind of changes I recommend would all be directed toward improving the day-to-day
experience of the child in school, i.e., make school less demeaning, less controlling, less
punitive, and less boring, or in positive terms, make school more respectful, freer, without
punishment, and more interesting.
Such proposals are often dismissed as progressive education which has been tried and failed
and characterized as children swinging from the chandeliers by critics who doubtless think of
themselves as tough minded.
Yet the very words come back in school mission statements and other statements of objectives:
respectful of students and so on.
The current trend in U.S. public education is the No Child Left Behind (NCLB) initiative of the
Bush administration, and the approach is thoroughly tough minded: punitive towards failing
schools and failing students.
Also, the programmed lecture method of the Open Court and other modern curricula create a
rigid and controlling environment in the classroom.
According to Herbert Kohl, this top-down, authoritarian, and rigid approach is stupefying for
teachers and students alike ( Stupidity and Tears: Teaching and Learning in Troubled Times ,
W.
Norton, 2003); that is, it makes students and teachers do things the system requires even
though those things are contrary to their conscience and better judgment.
Marva Collins and other educators who have achieved great things in public schools, within
normal funding, are often held up as models of how things ought to be done without throwing
money at the problem.
My take on this is that these educators are exceptional people who succeed because of their
exceptional ability and determination.
Most teachers and principals do not have that level of ability and determination, and tinkering
with their methods is not going to produce comparable results in their schools.
And, as Kohl also points out, exceptional teachers find NCLB and its increasingly popular top-
down mind set ties their hands.
The first thing Id do today to improve public education in the U.S. is to let teachers teach.
Junk the programmed lecture straitjacket and let teachers respond according to their wisdom
to the needs they see in their students.
Everyone seems to be against social promotion these days, but it is no secret that children do
not do well when they are held back.
In school, the official stamp of failure on a student is a virtually certain guarantee of future
failure.
The second thing Id do to improve public education in the U.S. is to junk the idea that all
students must progress in all subjects at the same rate, and start treating them like individuals
with individual interests and needs.
In other words, abandon the factory model of empty heads on the conveyor belt awaiting the
input of knowledge and skills.
What model, then? Open classroom.
It seems to me that the ideal model that everyone knows about is Summerhill.
Unfortunately, one important reason for Summerhills success was A.
Neill, the founder, another exceptional educator whose results are unlikely to be duplicated by
lesser beings.
Even so, a Summerhill-like environment is the best environment I

has flatly stated that the DoE has no business messing with them.

If a politician proposes shutting down schools that are failing miserably, that politician is
excoriated instead of the people in charge of the school who are either not doing their jobs or so
focused on bureaucracy that they cannot do them.
The great tragedy of public schooling is the fact that its existence has convinced parents that
someone else is taking care of their child’s education, which lets them off the hook.
Put a parent in charge of their child’s education again, especially paying for it, and they will
treat education as it should be treated: as a business that is expected to produce satisfactory
results.

material and then give them ideas on how to help their children with it.

big deterrents to learning is the classroom itself.

matter, when studying weather, why not hold classes outside when there is a storm? When
studying history, why not bring the kids to the history and visit the local city history museum,
local historical landmarks, etc? I realize we have liability issues when it comes to field trips, so
we would have to enact a law that makes the parental permission slips truly binding and limit
legal actions to incidence of GROSS neglect(drunken bus driver and the like).

Quote: Originally posted by OverlandSailor The main point of tests is ensuring that someone

Should we abandon all tests in school? No more chapter tests, pop quizzes, mid-terms etc.? How

By interacting with the kids and liking them and wanting to help them.
Let me tell you another story from that year I was a substitute.
In one classroom an overhead projector was set up with transparent orange disks made to look
like coins, in various sizes.
I think this was a first grade class.
I put some coins on the projector and asked what they added up to.
Nobody could tell me.
I quickly realized that these kids had too little experience with real coins to recognize that these
orange circles on the screen were somehow related to the actual physical money they’ve
handled on occasion before.
The situation was completely misbegotten and foolish, as so many things in schools are.
In another class we were doing “learning centers,” where the kids break up into small groups.
I sat down with one group and laid out some coins and asked them questions, I no longer
remember what.
They were completely helpless.
Eventually, we just started counting pennies, a radically simpler task, and the kids took to it
with enthusiasm.
They needed the fundamental skill of counting pennies before they could get anywhere near
making change and the like.
My point: testing isn’t needed.
Just imagine what kind of pencil and paper test these kids would get: pictures of coins, and
circle the picture where the coins add up to twenty-seven cents.
Some classes will do all right because they’ve had money in their hands since age four.
Others will be completely helpless because all they’ve seen of coins is orange circles projected
on a screen, or at best, play money in the classroom that they get five minutes with every other
week.
A sensitive, intelligent teacher who likes kids and wants them to do well doesn’t need a paper
score to tell him who needs help.
The public school system doesn’t TRUST anyone.
Not teachers, not students.
Everyone has to PROVE themselves, every day, in every subject, or they will be PUNISHED.
Can’t you see how hateful this is? Alan Nicoll

  1)   Make the teacher responsible for the student grade 2) Teach to APPLY not to get grade

Money is not the answer.
We spend thousands more per child today then we did in the 50s (even when adjusting for
inflation) and yet or schools have consistantly performed poorer then the years before.
Most of the Answers put forward here do not require more funding, but they require cultural
change in education.
If we want teachers to step up and maintain discipline in the class room so that they can
properly teach those who want to learn, then we need to insulate those teachers and
administators from nusinance lawsuit brought by parents who feel that the discipline their
child recieved was too harsh.
We need to return to the reform school approach so that the most disruptive students are only
harming themselves.
If we want the schools to focus more on the traditional subjects like math, science and english,
then we need to stop trying to use our public schools as a soap box for every social issue in
existance.
There is no reason the schools cannot be used for evening classes on such subjects for those
who want to learn more about them, but we are failing our kids when it comes to the basics and
we need to return the regular school day to focusing on them.
If we want our schools to try new ways to engage children in learning, and return to some old
ones, then we need to make it so the schools are legally insulated from lawsuits in regards to
anything less the gross neglect when it comes to field trips and the like.
Barely any trips happen anymore.
This is NOT a money issue, it is a legal liability issue.
Those permission slips parents have to sign state clearly that they will not hold the school liable
in most cases when it comes to these trips.
Yet, when something does happen, those slips have shown themselves to not be worth the paper
they are written on once the case reaches the courtroom.
If we want to ensure that the teachers are best suited to teach then we need to take on the NEA
and institute standards testing for our educators.
Those that fail such tests need not be fired.
Perhaps they failed these tests in math but excelled in history, move the teachers to work on
the subjects they are strongest in.
Then, create a training / teaching program for the teachers to have the ability to improve
themselves so that they can better serve our children.
We need to start looking at the real problems here if we are ever going to find real solutions.

Sailor, what you’re advocating sounds to me like the two most popular prescriptions for school
reform: more discipline, and “back to basics.” These prescriptions have been refuted (or at least
challenged) in Alfie Kohn’s most recent book, The Schools Our Children Deserve .
In the Appendix he provides a summary of recent studies, all the facts and figures a layperson
would likely want.
I’ve discussed this book in this thread previously, starting in January ’05, as well as arguing
extensively in my own words that these methods are failures and only make the situation
worse.

Granted this company would have to manage and secure the towers necessary for the task, but
this company would also be able to employ leverage to secure military backup for the project.
Therein would lay the question of strategic placement that is the crucial obligation of this
entire strategy.
What would initially occur would be the systematic destruction and replacement of these
towers.
In conjunction with military operations to recover abductees and neutralize captors, this would
become a game of triangulation and re-establishment.
We could eventually (over months) use this system to predict as well as prevent and pursue
abduction cases.
I do not know the numbers of dollars involved, but I imagine it is in the one billion range given
the time frame and overall construction-coordination-reconstruction costs.
The government should find the financial means to parlay this into reality given both the
eventual and immediate win-win nature of the transaction.
Comments are always welcome.

reliable network.
Getting a company to do this would likely be no problem at all.
Allowing them in and deciding who can / should do it is another matter.

Intro to Process (10mins)
Welcome
  •    “Welcome to the Port Townsend General Assembly! Thank you for your participation!”
  •    Confirm all can hear the speaker. If not, teach group human microphone.

       everything else will be found on occupyporttownsend.org
  •    Reminder of purpose of General Assembly
  •    The purpose of a General Assembly is to help us find our common ground so we can
       work together to solve problems and improve our world. A General Assembly is open to
       all people.
  •    A General Assembly is a Consensus Based Group. Consensus Decision making means:
  •    We are not here to debate and win arguments. We are here to collaborate.
  •    The aim of Consensus Building is to build upon our common ground.
  •    All participants are asked to actively listen, rather than merely be preoccupied with
       preparing our response.
  •    all opinions need to be considered when generating consensus, making it difficult to
       assimilate and apply, thus it may require a long process….all that’s needed is time.
The process and methods used to facilitate this general assembly are designed to make the most
directly democratic, horizontal, participatory space possible; each tool (hand signals, etc) is
about opening space . If you have suggestions for how to improve the process of facilitating,
please participate in the Process and Facilitation Working Group which is meeting Tuesday 5-
6:30pm at the Undertown in the back room.
  •    LiveStream/Video of this GA: “We are setup to video and livestream this meeting on the
       Internet. The purpose of this live stream is to allow as many people as possible to learn
       about this meeting, stay informed, participate, and help us.”
  •    Identify Roles:
  •    Facilitator(s): Matt and Alex
  •    Stack Taker: Jeanne
  •    Minutes:
  •    Time Keeper:
  •    Other facilitators here to help us make today as successful as possible.
  •    Temp check for approval of Facilitation team?
Introduction to Process
  •    Explanation of hand signals, which enable communication without disruption of
       speaker’s voice
  •    Twinkling one’s fingers in an upward motion means you agree with that is being said
  •    Twinkling one’s fingers with the hands flat means you are on the fence; you are not sure
       about whatever is being said
  •    Twinkling one’s fingers in a downward motion means that you are opposed to what is
       being said; you don’t agree.
  •    Silently holding up one’s hands while creating a diamond shape between the fingers
       means ‘point of process.’ This is used to signal the facilitators that the process is not
       being followed.
  •    Silently raising one’s index finger means, ‘point of information.’ It is a signal that a point
       of factual information the speaker has articulated is incorrect or needs further
       clarification.
  •    Rolling one’s hands in a circular motion in front of the body means; wrap it up, we
       understand your point. This is used when someone is over-clarifying. In the interest of
       time, clear and concise statements are appreciated.
  •    Step up/Step Back: The facilitators articulate the idea that there are people in our
       society who have been taught that their ideas are more important than others.
      Additionally there are those groups who have been conditioned to believe that they
      should constantly question the voicing of their own opinions. The step-up, step-back
      concept asks that those who often speak step back to make room for others, and that
      those who speak less often step up to assert their voices.
  •   Crossing both arms in front of one’s self is called a block. This is done when someone
      has a severe ethical or moral concern with a proposal. More on that later.
Open Mic (Up to 30 Minutes)
  •   In a few minutes, we will be doing a crowd storming exercise in which we break up into
      small groups and ask you all to speak and collaborate on the following questions:
  •   Who are you?
  •   What is touching you in the Occupy protest movement?
  •   What change would you like to see?
  •   What are the actions you are willing to take responsibility for?
  •   (Alternate question: hopes, concerns, ideas, burning questions?)
  •   Before we break up into groups, we want to have an open mic. If you are ready and
      eager to speak now to the GA on one of these questions, this is your first chance to do so.
      So who has something they want to say to the GA right now? Please raise your hand and
      get on stack. Great. We ask that you try to keep your statement right now to under 1
      minute (depending on attendance).
  •   If someone asks a question that you really want someone to answer- twinkle it- so
      facilitators may decide if we need to set aside time to answer it either now or later.

       back to the full GA. (10-15 minutes)
Proposal for Date/Time of next GA Proposal for GA 12/3/2011: It is proposed that the next GA be
Saturday Dec 10, 12-2pm outside on the Community center lawn- where the weekly Occupy
protest has been happening.
Order of Presenting a Proposal
  •    The proposer reads the proposal, twice if necessary.
  •    The floor is open to clarifying questions or concerns, speakers should get on stack. The
       proposer can answer questions or address concerns directly as they come.
  •    The floor is then open to ‘friendly amendments’. These are amendments to the current
       proposal, not a new proposal or question/concern. It is up to the proposer to accept or
       decline friendly amendments.
  •    Once everything has been discussed and friendly amendments have been address the
       facilitation team will move for consensus by asking for a temperature check.
  •    If the check is a mix of agree and disagree, that is not a meaningful consensus and the
       item will probably need to be tabled, set aside until the next GA, and refined. If it is
       about 70/30 in agreement with the proposal and the proposer isn’t interested in tabling
       the item, the facilitator can move for a 8/10 vote.
  •    If there is consensus, everyone seems to agree, the facilitator must asks for ‘blocks’.
       Anyone presenting a block will need to explain why and if the block is not rescinded or
       the proposal is not removed the facilitator will move for a 8/10 vote.
  •    We DO NOT want to vote, that means some people are excluded or ignored. But if the
       issue is critical we will do a straw poll, raising of hands in agreement, and if the
       facilitation team sees 8/10 agreement the proposal passes.
To contest an old proposal that has already been passes, draft a new proposal that would
remove or invalidate the old one.
Occupy Port Townsend Decision Making Process (Still a work in progress)
  •    Proposal: When ready to decide on a proposal, The facilitator will say, “We are now
       going to decide on this proposal. How does everybody feel about this proposal –
       temperature check.
  •    If it appears a clear majority feel good about the proposal, then ask for blocks. …. Then
       try and resolve.
  •    If large number of blocks, consider tabling the proposal for later meeting to discuss and
       reach consensus on proposal before bringing back to GA.
  •    If a small number of blocks, then set a time limit, and the blocker then voices the
       reasons for the block, and a conversation that attempts to deal with the block ensues. If
       conversation has been exhausted and the blocker is clearly not willing to reach a
       compromise, the group moves to a 8/10 majority vote or tables the proposal. Consensus
       is not always reached on the first try- and that’s ok.
Facilitating to consent technique
Alex explained a really interesting technique for facilitating towards consent – especially useful
when time is critical. Suppose you have 8 minutes to decide something important such as…how
many people should be required to be a quorum for a GA? Facilitator asks for or offers a
proposal in this manner: Would anyone object to the Quorum for a GA being set at 8 people? If
no hands are raised, you have consent. Quorum is 8 people. If you cannot agree to any proposal
for another quorum number in the next 8 minutes, your Quorum is 8. Facilitator may then ask
for a new proposal. Someone may propose 10. Repeat same exact question. Each time a
proposal is offered, if no one objects then it is done. The moment their is an objection- you can
begin discussion- but discussion is over at 8 minutes- (unless everyone consents to extending
the time), so the meeting can move on to the next item. This strategy will help enable a group
to quickly make bare minimum decisions- stay within time limits – and not constantly get
bogged down debating minor details and tweaks to proposals.
Matt’s Idea for encouraging restraint with using the Block
  •    Crossing both arms in front of one’s self is called a block. This is done when someone
       has a severe ethical or moral concern with a proposal. This should be used rarely.
  •    Have you ever had a good friend that has made a bad decision? Ever had a good friend
       make a bad decision despite your firm advice to do otherwise? It happens. Is it always
       appropriate for you to say to your friend, you forbid them from making this decision
       and will never talk to them again if they do so? No. That is a card you only play in rare
       circumstances- or you don’t have many friends. Hopefully, your good friend will learn
          from their bad decisions- or there is the chance you were wrong. Time will tell and if
          you both continue to communicate and learn, you will both learn and grow from it, and
          hopefully it will all work out eventually.
  •       The GA is your good friend. Once in a while, the GA may form a consensus on an issue
          that you disagree with. This is ok, this happens in friendships. You will have your
          chance to tell your good friend the GA your firm reason for why you disagree-your
          concerns will be heard. But having your say does not mean always getting your way.
          The GA may still want to proceed. This is ok. Like your other good friends, this GA will
          learn from it’s mistakes and miscalculations. Keep communicating and participating,
          and we will all learn and grow from these decisions.
