Many Worlds Theory PHysics and Philosophy
6320What Sean Carroll Gets Wrong About Many Worlds Theory
What Does Many Worlds Theory Tell us About God?
“I want to know God's thoughts - the rest are mere details.” ― Albert Einstein
Sean Carroll writes in his book Something Deeply Hidden that Many-Worlds Theory is “the
most straightforward reading of our best understanding of quantum mechanics.” According to
Many-Worlds theory, quantum systems do not evolve linearly into one outcome, rather all
possible quantum outcomes occur, we just happen to find ourselves in one of the branching
universes, so we see only one outcome when we observe quantum systems. The necessary
implication of this precept of Many-Worlds, is that every human being is frequently branching
into multiple future versions of our self, each existing in one of these branching universes.
Sean Carroll writes, “in Many-Worlds all outcomes happen, weighted by the amplitude squared
of the wave function.” We will come back to this “amplitude squared of the wave function”
business one day, but for now let’s focus more narrowly on the most profound philosophical
implications of Many-Worlds theory, and specifically upon what Sean gets wrong.
In the chapter “The Human Side” Sean Carroll asks the critical question, “Should the branching
of our current selves into multiple future selves affect the choices we make?...Does the existence
of all those extra worlds have implications for how we should act, personally or ethically?” To
explore these questions, Sean sets up some thought experiments, but he conditions his analysis
upon a strange monumental assumption. He writes, “Assume for the purposes of the thought
experiment, we believe that life itself is a purely physical phenomenon, so we can set aside
considerations of life after death.” What could a quantum physicist possibly mean when he
says “life is a purely physical phenomena?” Quantum mechanics demonstrates to us that
everything in the universe is nothing like the “physical” thing it appears to be, so why should
we suddenly assume life, our conscious minds, our memories, and everything that you consider
you, is somehow a purely “physical” thing for which we can ignore what it might be in terms of
quantum theory and wave functions?
So let us explore the juicy questions regarding the implications of Many-Worlds theory to our
everyday human lives, but let us cast off Sean Carroll’s “life if a purely physical phenomenon”
assumption. Let us assume, our conscious mind exists in quantum reality just as everything
else in the universe exists in quantum reality. So then it follows, according to Quantum
Mechanics and Quantum Field Theory, every quantum particle/wave/thingy that exists inside
our physical brain (which I will assume is the host of our conscious mind and self) is ultimately
a wave in a quantum field. We should then be able to safely assume, our conscious mind itself
is in some way, simply a wave in quantum fields. And if our conscious mind is a wave in
quantum fields, then does this lead to any important implications for how we think of ourselves
and how we live our lives? It absolutely does- and we will find there is good reason Sean Carroll
did not want to venture down this rabbit hole.
If Conscious Life is a Wave Function, then Death is Dubious
If our conscious mind is ultimately a wave function within quantum fields, there is no clear
reason to assume this wave function is utterly destroyed when our physical brain is destroyed.
According to quantum theory, waves are never really destroyed, they just transform into other
waves. When a photon “hits” an electron they may say “it was absorbed and the energy caused
the electron to change energy levels,” but the photon is not really “destroyed,” rather its wave
simply collides with the wave function of the electron and they interact- as waves do. Quantum
Field Theory describes quantum events this way, and all the best physicists on Youtube say it
has been proven to be the most accurate theory we have of the quantum universe. (Check out
PBS Spacetime on this topic https://youtu.be/ATcrrzJFtBY) . The entire universe is simply an
ocean of quantum waves interacting- and that necessarily includes us. So is death in this world
really the end for all of us? Maybe not. Many-Worlds theory on its own throws some serious
wrenches in how we might look upon both the possibility of dying and what we might
experience after bodily death.
Is Death the End?
Is this a simulation?
Life Isn’t Fair...Or Is It?
I can still hear the sound of my mom’s voice as she replied to my outburst, “That’s not fair!”
with “Life isn’t fair!” In fact, I’m pretty sure I heard her say that on more than one occasion.
“Life isn’t fair” is one of those brutal truths most parents have to either teach their children or
fearfully wait for them to learn on their own. After all, even parents who try to raise their kids
in a world where justice and fairness prevail at all times- whenever for example two siblings
fight or somehow experience a different quality of life moment to moment - such parents act as
the ever wise and fair justice of the peace, listening with compassion to everyone’s point of view
and then metering out fair and just adjustments to reality to preserve the neverending equity of
life for their children- even these parents must realize, at some point, the true unfair nature of
life will catch up with their child’s experience. Life is indeed unfair. Yet, according to Many-
Worlds theory, this may not ultimately be true at all. Life might actually be perfectly fair to
every human being who lives.
According to Many-Worlds theory, you are likely branching into different universes at least
5000 times a second due simply to the radioactive decay of atoms inside your physical human
body. For real world implications of this, every human being since the moment of their
conception, has a descendent in one of a gargantuan number of different realities. In fact, Sean
Carroll sums up the implications of all these branching possibilities in this wonderful interview
where he is asked, “Does this mean there is a universe in which you are President of the United
States?” and Sean Carrol replies, “Yes!”. (https://youtu.be/kTXTPe3wahc?t=891)
Think about that response for a moment. (It helps if your brain really can imagine the Many-
Worlds theory being true. If your brain just rejects that outright, then you won’t get as big a
kick out of the implications of the rest of this.) According to Many-Worlds theory of quantum
mechanics, the most straightforward and most elegant theory for explaining the bizarre results
of every quantum experiment ever conducted, every human being (over 35 and born in the
USA) has a parallel self who is currently the President of the United States. Let that sink in for
a moment.
Sean Carroll and Many-Worlds theory says that every human life branches into a
incomprehensibly large spectrum of life outcomes limited only by what is physically possible to
occur. Sean Carroll makes it clear, that truly impossible events do not occur, but that leaves a
still ridiculously vast number of possible life outcomes. There is a parallel you who is President
of the United States, a movie star, a famous author, a wealthy entrepreneur, a prestigious
academic, the greatest parent who ever lived, a cult leader, and any other thing you can
imagine. Unfortunately, this also means there is a parallel you who is a loser, a drug addict, a
failed author, a homeless person, a widely despised person, and an outcast. According to Many-
Worlds theory, every human life branches into an essentially infinite spectrum of possible
outcomes. You just happen to find yourself in one sliver of these branches, the reality in which
you currently live.
The fact that millions of parallel you’s exist does not absolve you from the responsibility of
valuing your unique life. Sean Carroll emphasizes, once these branches occur, the other you is
not you, it is a totally different person now, just with a common ancestor in your timeline. The
fact that your choices lead to near infinite universe branching, does not mean you shouldn’t try
to choose the most ideal branch of reality in which to live. If anything, you might just let this
branching help you be more ambitious about what goals you aim for in life- for there is always
a chance of reaching the goal- and there is also likely a version of you who achieves it. But this
branching might impact your brain a bit when we go back to discussing that pronouncement
many of our parents enjoyed declaring, “Life is not fair!” For maybe from one point of view, it is
nearly perfectly fair.
If every single human from conception has a life that branches into, let’s say, a million different
outcomes, and every human has basically the same number of “positive” outcomes and
“negative” outcomes, then suddenly, we must admit, this is essentially “equal” and therefore
arguably “fair”. It may not be fair from the perspective of a person currently living in one of
those “negative” and unpleasant life versions, but from an outside perspective, you could argue
that the universe was fair to every human being on average. Even if you happen to be
randomly crippled by a tree falling spontaneously upon you, every other human will also have
a version of themselves where similiarly random tragic things happen. None of us are alone in
our suffering. We all can take some solace in the fact that there is a version of reality where
every human suffers similarly to ourselves. The Many-Worlds theory is a theory of a fair
universe from a certain point of view.




Due to the radioactive decay of atoms in your human body, 5000 times a second you are
branching into multiple universes.
Albert Einstein, one of the greatest human minds to ever exist in this branch of reality once
said, “I am not interested in this phenomenon or that phenomenon...I want to know God's
thoughts – the rest are mere details."

Egalitarian Activist Economy
What is the Egalitarian Activist Economy?
The Egalitarian Activist Economy (EAE) is an alternative economy within the current world
economy. It is an economy in which participants and supporters believe all people are
fundamentally equal and that we should always work to improve equality wherever it is
healthy and reasonable to do so. It is an activist economy in that it functions in an active effort
to replace the current world economy which is not egalitarian. Participating in the egalitarian
economy includes therefore not merely creating businesses and trade which is more equal, it
includes every form of economic action imaginable to subvert and replace the non egalitarian
businesses and economies in the world.
What is an Economy?
An economy “consists of the economic systems of a country or other area; the labor, capital,
and land resources; and the manufacturing, production, trade, distribution,
and consumption of goods and services of an area.” The EAE is an egalitarian economy in that
it aims to make all economic systems (the labor, capital, land resources, manufacturing
production, trade, distribution, and consumption of goods as egalitarian (as equal) and fair as
possible. Egalitarian means equal.
Why is this an “Activist” economy?
“Activism consists of efforts to promote, impede, or direct social, political, economic,
or environmental change.” The EAE is an activist economy because the participants in it are
actively engaged in promoting egalitarian systems. This activity must be active, because the
non egalitarian forces in the world, the wealthy and the powerful, are always actively working
to increase their greater power and wealth. To transform the world economy into an
egalitarian economy, to make an egalitarian economy exist and thrive amidst the forces that
exist to prevent it from existing, action is essential. Power is never given up without fierce
resistance. The EAE is an economy of people working to make the economy and the equality it
stands for spread, thrive, and subvert the alternative.
If you support an Egalitarian Economy then what is the current world economy?
Well, the opposite of Egalitarian is Elitist. So I suppose we could call the current dominant
capitalist economy an Elitist Economy.
What would our world look like if the EAE replaced the Elitist Economy of the world?
Most or all large corporations that operate in your town would be replaced by worker owned
cooperative businesses. These cooperatives would not have the single minded purpose of
making money and only making money. They would have a purpose that aligned with the
interests of all the people who work there including making money, helping the workers have a
healthy work environment, helping the workers live happy healthy lives, and helping the larger
community be healthy and happy. The key to making power be used in a healthy positive way
is to put the power into the hands of the people it effects. A worker owned cooperative will
effect the people who work there and live around it so all power can be in the hands of the
people who work there- who will have a natural interest in the lives of their neighbors.
The EAE also supports more egalitarian political power. Rather than have political power
controlled by wealth in that elections are funded by the winners of the Elitist Economy,
political institutions are made as egalitarian as humanly possible. This will help prevent any
very large cooperatives from dominating and exploiting people.
This is all crazy talk. Is any of this really possible?
Let’s find out!
How do I participate in and support the Egalitarian Activist Economy?
You use the labor, capital, and land resources; and the manufacturing,
production, trade, distribution, and consumption of goods and services in your area in a way
that is Egalitarian and Actively competes with the Elitist economy. This means you compete
with the winners of the elitist economy, those entities that have the most power. This may
mean the big corporations in your area, whatever your area is.
I don’t understand. What do I do?
Create Egalitarian alternatives to the labor, capital, and landresources; and the manufacturing,
production, trade, distribution, and consumption of goods and services in your area.
You mean like I start an Egalitarian donut shop?
Exactly.
But that’s a big pain… What legal structure should I make it? Should I be an LLC or a
non profit corp?
Make it Egalitarian. Why “register” it with the state at all? If you register it with the state and
the federal government then you are playing by the rules of the elitist economy. Who cares
about the rules of the elitist economy? Forget the rules. Make an egalitarian donut shop. Don’t
worry about the rules you are told to obey.
But this is illegal! I don’t want to break the law!
Why not? Grow some balls. This is activism. We are trying to change the world here. What’s
the worst that can happen? Let’s all work together and we can come up with amazingly clever
ways to make this economy thrive.
But…but…but… What if they…?
I don’t have all the answers. If you want to collaborate on this, let’s talk.
Hey I have started my Egalitarian Donut cooperative! Now what do I do?
Now use every idea you can come up with to compete, crush, and replace any large elitist
economy donut connected corporations that are in your area. Tell everyone who gets a donut
why you exist, what you are about, educate while you feed the donut hunger of our populace.
Any other great ideas to help my egalitarian donut cooperative crush the local
Starbucks and Safeway donut operations?
Remember, this is activism and the entities you are competing against are monsters.
Corporations are monsters. The people in them may not realize they are working for monsters,
but they are. You don’t need to play nice. Sell your donuts on the front steps of the large
corporations you want to crush. Educate while you economate. This is activist economics
baby! Park your operation every day on their doorstep. Sell tasty alternatives. Or give your
tasty alternatives away! Who cares about the money. You want to starve that corporation out
of business. You want to educate every person who uses it. Remember, you are not doing this
for money. You are helping transform the elitist economy into an egalitarian economy. Act
with love, patience, persistance, but act boldly.
What if I get arrested? What if people yell at me? What if everyone calls me a
socialist?
Activism can be extremely challenging. But it can also be inspiring and fun. Don’t do this
alone. Find like minded people who will work with you to change the world. Start an EAE
group in your local town. Support each other. Learn with one another. Let’s change the world.
It’s about time.
Are you saying that every city and town needs to create an Egalitarian Activist
Economic group which collaborates and supports creating egalitarian worker owned
coop businesses and drive out all large for profit corporations from their cities and
towns?
Yup. Yehaaa! Let’s get to it! But this is not just about the USA. This is the world baby. Every
town and every city in every country in the world. One egalitarian world economy. Wouldn’t
that be something to see!?

Dear Mike,
I would like for us to work together to avoid any further public confrontations or drawn out
conflicts over the issue of audio recordings of commission public meetings.
To best do my job as a hospital commissioner I require a complete record of our public
meetings. I require this complete record to be in my possession the moment our public
meetings conclude so that I might immediately review any portion of the meeting events and
begin considering next steps. I also need to be able to easily share the complete records of our
public meetings with any interested members of the public so that I might ascertain their
opinions, ideas, feedback, suggestions, and advice on any aspects of hospital district
governance that they are interested in.
I am willing to consider not recording the meetings myself, if I have an equally reliable
solution that will guarantee I walk out of every public meeting of the hospital commission
with a complete record of the meetings events. I would like to work with you to find such a
solution that is convenient for everyone involved.
I believe the simplest solution is that I record the meetings on my personal recording device
and immediately provide a copy of the file to administration after the meeting. I could simply
walk over to the commission office, plug in my usb cable, and upload the file to a directory on
the file server. The file is already dated by the software. The hospital Information Technology
department keeps backups of all files on the file server. If anyone ever requests one of the
audio files from a meeting, then someone could simply copy the file to a thumb drive for the
person. The cost of storing hundreds of hours of audio files is negligible. Also the labor
involved with copying a file onto a thumb drive is negligible. Such a process is not complex or
costly which is probably one of the reasons why so many other public governing bodies record
audio or video of their public meetings.
As you noted, any handwritten notes a hospital commissioner makes during a public meeting
is subject public records standards. Audio recordings, are simply a form of note taking. We
may need to refine it, but the policy regarding commissioner notetaking you described is
already in place and as long as I make my recordings available in a timely manner, we appear
to be keeping with the policy we already have.
I hope this is sufficient to resolve this matter. I believe we would all prefer to be spending our
time working to improve our efforts at addressing the healthcare needs of our community. I
need an audio recording of our public meetings to do that work.
We have another public meeting on 4/16/2014. I would like to record this meeting. Please let
me know if my recording the meeting will result in yourself and/or the board chair delaying
 the meeting progress on the agenda, recessing the meeting, or adjourning the meeting as
 happened at the 3/19/2014 meeting. I believe all these actions in response to me recording the
 meeting are unnecessary and unseemly disruptions to board business. Yet, if I know these
 actions are going to be your response, I will make extra efforts to find interested members of
 the public who want to record the meetings and can attend the 4/16/2014 meeting. Please
 understand that many of the people I would ask are working poor and unable to attend
 though interested – which is another reason I record these meetings.
 I would like to resolve this matter and move on to our work. Part of my ability to do this work
 involves making a recording of our meetings as I believe I am allowed to do now.
 Can you please let me know by 3PM next Wed 4/2/2014 if we can agree to this?
 Respectfully,
 Matthew Ready

Creative writings that Jefferson Healthcare commission candidate Matt Ready uploaded on a
personal blog in 2012 have prompted one voter to question whether someone who advocates
against corporations ought to be elected to a position in a corporation.
“What tweaks me off is he advises breaking the law and I think it’s scandalous we could elect a
commissioner who would do so,” complained Tony Harriman, who brought Ready’s blog and
writings to the Leader’s attention last Friday after a political forum Thursday night where
Ready, who is running against incumbent Marc Mauney, urged voters to check out his blog
at mattready.net.
Harriman, who acknowledges that he is candidate Jill Buhler’s treasurer, said he was shocked
when he read a piece titled “Egalitarian Activist Economy,” that asks questions and answers
them.
In the post, which Ready said Monday were really whimsical writings that don’t represent
how he feels today, Ready suggests creating an egalitarian activist economy and alternatives,
such as, hypothetically, an egalitarian donut shop.
“But that’s a big pain … What legal structure should I make it? Should I be an LLC or a
nonprofit corp.?” he asks in the essay, then answer by saying, “Make it Egalitarian. Why
‘register’ it with the state at all? If you register with the state and the federal government, then
you are playing by the rules of the elitist economy. Who cares about the rules of the elitist
economy? Forget the rules … Don’t worry about the rules you are told to obey.”
Ready says he wouldn’t urge people to start a business and not pay taxes, but he does believe
that civil disobedience is an important tool in democracy. “But you have to be ready to face the
consequences of that,” he said.
Ready, who participated in the Occupy movement in 2012 and was a (not “leader”)
participant in a protest at Bank of America, goes on to call corporations monsters in one essay.
In another essay titled “We need to create the world we want. It is time to end Corporations,”
Ready suggests ending for-profit corporations.
Ready said he’s never had any traffic on the blog before – he considers it more of a personal
journal for his creative writing and art work – and has since moved the “Egalitarian Activist
Economy” piece into a draft section, meaning its no longer on active on his blog.
“It was an idea that I threw against a wall. I don’t do a lot of writing on economics,” the
philosophy major said. Suggested addition?

Me talking to people about irrational beliefs.
I have changed. I have slipped over a line that I find somewhat dangerous.
I have wandered clearly over the line of agnosticism to a new type of potential gnosticism, a
gnosticism about the world around that is unprovable, yet seemingly powerful. And I am
gently discussing and exploring this world with people. I am somewhat disturbed by this step,
this change. Yet, I am also excited and inspired by it.
Am I opening a road to a type of insanity? Or am I opening a road to a greater life and sanity? I
am truly uncertain. Yet, I am certain of my level of joy, excitement, and happiness. This is
indisputable. All that is disputable is my rationality.
[What is a rational world view? Is it rational to believe the Earth itself is alive and might speak
with you? What is the evidence? Ask the Earth a question and listen for the answer. If your
mind seems to produce an answer, are you creating that answer yourself or is the Earth
communicating through a channel in your mind? Which is the rational answer to believe?
Occam might say the former, and though Occam’ Razor is a rational principle, it is not absolute.
It is merely a tool one can use when one must split the difference between choices. A less
complicated answer is a less complicated answer, yet the truth is the truth, and it may be more
complicated than some alternatives. What is the rational choice? Is it rational to be simplistic
in the absence of absolute evidence?
I ask the Earth a question and I hear an answer. The answer emerges in my mind. Where does
it come from? Earth or my imagination? Earth or my unconscious? I cannot say with absolute
certainty- and so I simply listen and respond. I converse. Am I talking to myself? Am I acting
crazy? Am I letting my mind loose on a path from which I might lose it? Still I don’t know.
Perhaps we need a new principle of rationality in the spirit of Occam: Be simple or beware.
Neglect Occam’s Razor at your own risk. It is not that Occam is right, just that the world
beyond Occam’s meridian is vast, colorful, and powerful. If a rational being crosses it, they
might no longer recognize themselves. They might find themselves in surprising company and
gazing upon startling vistas.]

Jefferson Community Health Council. Invite members, participants. The purpose of this
organization is to work together to improve the health of our community. This organization
has no authority on its own and will only effect change through the powers and actions of the
participating members. As such, this organization will operate strictly through a consensus
model, whereby all actions are undertaken through consent of all members. This model is only
viable in so far as essential stakeholders in community health actively participate in the
organization decision making process.
We propose that the Jefferson Community Health Council has permanent membership and
participation from all major stakeholders in the health and welfare of the residents of Jefferson
County Washington. This membership will include at a minimum leaders from:
Jefferson Healthcare
Jefferson County Health Department
Jefferson Mental Health
Safe Harbor
Jefferson County Government
Port Townsend City Government
Jefferson County and Port Townsend Law enforcement

i see the energy in my base. I see myself like a tree. My trunk touches the earth, my roots
engulf the soil. I see the tree i photographed embracing and married to the boulder. I wish to
flourish. Like the tree, I must feed the trunk, it feeds on rest, nutrients, water, and moves via
energies such as sexual and emotional energies. Yet, in addition to feeding and nurturing the
trunk, I must also extend my branches and stretch to leaf and flower and bloom. The past few
weeks have been very nurturing to my trunk and base. I feel a craving to stretch my branches,
to balance my growth.
Sunlight glowing through the ceramic of my coffee cup. The smoky steam of my coffee.
Swirling and rising in patterns shifting too fast to hold or name. It reminds me of the ocean
shore ripples at Hanalei. The shore was near perfectly calm, yet small gentle waves continue to
form and softly break upon the shore. The waters ripples, like the coffee steam swirled and
moved and changed rapidly, too fast to hold. I see time always is moving thus. I see this, I
allow myself to ride the wave of change through these racing moments. I feel my being
shifting, now I ride upon the racing wind of time, I am like a winged cliff jumper streaking
down a mountain side, or a surfer on a powerful ocean wave. I feel energy emerging from time,
though i sit perfectly still in my ergonomic Ikea chair. Is this a source of energy and power one
might tap into, feed off of moment to moment? I wonder, could I suck more power from it if I
allow myself to see an even faster rhythm to time? For if time moves like a fast wave, it also
might be seen to move like an even faster wave, and then faster still? Perhaps I could perceive
and ride the streaking wave of time to channel a virtually infinite power? I glance at this
possibility, but I do not pursue it.
Savannah or Jack might emerge. Do I move upstairs? They too will merely be a part of this
racing energy of moment to moment time. They too are merely a part of this energy. I don’t
fear their emergence as I once did, worrying they will disturb me mid meditation. I close my

MARCH 19, 2014 JEFFERSON HEALTHCARE
COMMISSION MEETING TRANSCRIPT OF
DIALOGUE
Marie Dressler: …Calling the meeting to order at 3:33. This is Jefferson County Public Hospital District N.2, Board of
Commissioners meeting and Commissioner Jill Buhler is excused. Could I ask you what is in front of you? Are you
recording this meeting?
Matt Ready: Yes. I’m making an audio recording of this meeting to help me remember what has happened.
Marie Dressler: Okay. Actually that sounds like a good opening for discussion about doing something like that with
one of the concerns with the Public Meetings Act as it is being recorded and the Public Hospital District is responsible
for safekeeping and so it can all be accessed, maybe this is something that you ought to step in [unclear 00:00:55].
Mike Glenn: Yeah. I think that — I believe there was going to be a discussion at tonight’s meeting about recording
board meetings, which I think is a reasonable thing to discuss. There are implications associated with recording
board meetings that recording become part of the record and is also part of the Open Public Meeting Act and Records
Act, so a recording provided by a hospital, a hospital recording for the purpose of records has to be disclosed when
requested and any recording by a board member, according to Council, would be considered that official record. So I
think what the discussion tonight was going to go along the lines of discussing it at the board level and then if the
board is interested in pursuing that to direct administration to develop a policy, a procedure, and a methodology to
make sure that we do it correctly we — it’s in line with our Record Retention Act and Open Public Meeting response
team and we do it right. So I think the recommendation from Council is that [if] absent of the hospital doing it, that a
board member should not.
Matt Ready: Well, based on my research I don’t think that’s accurate. I mean, this is a public meeting, citizens have a
certain right to record these meetings; I don’t surrender that right because I’m a Commissioner, just like we each
have the right to vote, you know, we have certain rights, the right to breathe, the right to take notes, I don’t think it’s
— I would disagree with that assessment of what is legal, or that this constitutes a board act, this is an act as a private
citizen.
Mike Glenn: Well, it might be an act of a private citizen but because of your — because you’re a board member, just
like the notes you take at a board meeting, they are subject to the Open Public —
Matt Ready: Sure.
Mike Glenn: — Record Act, so that any tape that you record is also subject to that act, so it becomes part of the record

Subject: Audio Recording Public Meetings
Dear Mike,
I would like for us to work together to avoid any further public confrontations or drawn out conflicts over the issue of
audio recordings of commission public meetings.
To best do my job as a hospital commissioner I require a complete record of our public meetings. I require this
complete record to be in my possession the moment our public meetings conclude so that I might immediately
review any portion of the meeting events and begin considering next steps. I also need to be able to easily share the
complete records of our public meetings with any interested members of the public so that I might ascertain their
opinions, ideas, feedback, suggestions, and advice on any aspects of hospital district governance that they are
interested in.
I am willing to consider not recording the meetings myself, if I have an equally reliable solution that will guarantee I
walk out of every public meeting of the hospital commission with a complete record of the meetings events. I would
like to work with you to find such a solution that is convenient for everyone involved.
I believe the simplest solution is that I record the meetings on my personal recording device and immediately provide
a copy of the file to administration after the meeting. I could simply walk over to the commission office, plug in my
usb cable, and upload the file to a directory on the file server. The file is already dated by the software. The hospital
Information Technology department keeps backups of all files on the file server. If anyone ever requests one of the
audio files from a meeting, then someone could simply copy the file to a thumb drive for the person. The cost of
storing hundreds of hours of audio files is negligible. Also the labor involved with copying a file onto a thumb drive is
negligible. Such a process is not complex or costly which is probably one of the reasons why so many other public
governing bodies record audio or video of their public meetings.
As you noted, any handwritten notes a hospital commissioner makes during a public meeting is subject public
records standards. Audio recordings, are simply a form of note taking. We may need to refine it, but the policy
regarding commissioner notetaking you described is already in place and as long as I make my recordings available
in a timely manner, we appear to be keeping with the policy we already have.
I hope this is sufficient to resolve this matter. I believe we would all prefer to be spending our time working to
improve our efforts at addressing the healthcare needs of our community. I need an audio recording of our public
meetings to do that work.
We have another public meeting on 4/16/2014. I would like to record this meeting. Please let me know if my
recording the meeting will result in yourself and/or the board chair delaying the meeting progress on the agenda,
recessing the meeting, or adjourning the meeting as happened at the 3/19/2014 meeting. I believe all these actions in
response to me recording the meeting are unnecessary and unseemly disruptions to board business. Yet, if I know
these actions are going to be your response, I will make extra efforts to find interested members of the public who
want to record the meetings and can attend the 4/16/2014 meeting. Please understand that many of the people I
would ask are working poor and unable to attend though interested – which is another reason I record these
meetings.
I would like to resolve this matter and move on to our work. Part of my ability to do this work involves making a
recording of our meetings as I believe I am allowed to do now.
Can you please let me know by 3PM next Wed 4/2/2014 if we can agree to this?
Respectfully,
Matthew Ready

Excerpt from Attorney General’s Opinion
This document is available online here:
http://www.atg.wa.gov/AGOOpinions/Opinion.aspx?section=archive&id=9332#.UzL47q1dVK5
PUBLIC MEETINGS – OPEN PUBLIC MEETINGS ACT – COUNTIES – RECORDING OFFICIAL PROCEEDINGS –
Authority of county to restrict video and/or sound recording of county meetings.


      1. A county does not have authority to ban video or sound recording of a meeting required to be open to
         the public by the Open Public Meetings Act (RCW 42.30); the county could regulate recording only to
         the extent necessary to preserve order at the meeting and facilitate public attendance.
      2. A county has authority to ban video or sound recording of any lawful executive session of a public
         meeting.
      3. If a meeting is not an “open public meeting” as defined in RCW 42.30, but is required to be an open
         meeting by some other statute, the extent of the county’s authority to restrict recording of such a
         meeting would depend on the language and the intent of the controlling statute.
      4. If a county officer conducts a “private meeting” as may be defined in law, the county has authority to
         restrict or prohibit the recording of such meetings.


*********************
November 30, 1998
The Honorable Randall K. Gaylord
San Juan County Prosecuting Attorney
350 Court Street
P.O. Box 760
Friday Harbor, WA 98250
Cite As: AGO 1998 No. 15
Dear Mr. Gaylord:
By letter previously acknowledged, you have requested our opinion on the following paraphrased questions:
May a county legislative body prohibit an individual from using a video or audio recording device to record a meeting
or hearing conducted by county officials? If such recording cannot be prohibited, may the legislative body impose
restrictions on the use of such recording devices?
BRIEF ANSWER
A county is subject to the Open Public Meetings Act which generally requires that meetings of the governing body be
open to the public and that no conditions precedent to attendance by the public, except for orderly conduct, may be
imposed. Therefore, a county legislative body may not ban the use of recording devices from the open portion of a
meeting held pursuant to the Open Public Meetings Act. The county legislative body may impose restrictions on the
use of recording devices, but only to the extent necessary to preserve the orderly conduct of the meeting. Executive
sessions held pursuant to the Open Public Meetings Act are not open to the public, and the county legislative body
may ban the use of recording devices at executive sessions. The county legislative body may ban the use of recording
devices at public meetings that are not subject to the Open Public Meetings Act or to some other state statute that
limits county authority. A county legislative authority may ban the use of recording devices to record conversations
at private meetings not open to the public.

police being called into board meetings to stop me from recording. Many times I had mentally prepared myself for
such confrontations and had long ago decided I would continue recording under all circumstances and simply see
what levels of force might be used against me. Yet, on this day, I was not so mentally prepared as I had no reason to
believe all the commissioners would suddenly try to stop the recording again- which they hadn’t done for months.

  Blog post: JEFFERSON HEALTHCARE
COMMISSION MEETING – 06/29/2016
July 2, 2016 | Author Matt Ready | Edit

In Chelan, Wa the Jefferson Healthcare Board of commissioners met in regular session following the annual WSHA
conference. Since our normal audio recording equipment does not travel with us, I recorded the meeting with my
own handheld digital recorder.
To my surprise, the majority of my fellow commissioners took exception to me recording the meeting. When I
refused to stop recording the meeting, they decided to conclude the meeting rather than continue. You can hear
commissioner De Leo leave the meeting in protest of my recording. He later rejoins the meeting at about the 5:50
mark.
As I say during this brief meeting, I make sure a recording of all meetings is made because I feel it is essential for me
to do my job. Everyone in that room needs to be held accountable for what we say- because what we say and do
matters. Without a complete record of the meetings, too much time can be spent arguing about what we agreed to or
said in the past, rather than discussing actually important and difficult subjects.
I truly thought this board was done debating the issue of recording our public meetings. A year earlier, I recorded
our regular meeting in Chelan, WA in the exact same manner, but last year none of the objections raised during this
year’s meeting were raised. The recording a year ago is here.
If you listen to the recording the following are the two objections raised as best I can discern.


       1. A hospital lawyer has advised that if a commissioner records the meeting, then the recording may be
          argued to be an official record and therefore needs to be archived with other recordings. The resolution
          to this point, as I say in the meeting and have said since this point was first raised two years ago: I will
          give the recording to the hospital to store with the other recordings.
       2. The second objection seems to be referring to the board policy on recording meetings which was
          intentionally drafted in a way to give the board the freedom to not record a meeting if it so chooses.
          The reason for this flexibility was to allow the board to meet with people off campus who might be
          disinclined to meet with us if we insisted on recording the meeting. If we insisted on recording such
          meetings, we might hamper our ability to serve our district if our access to elected officials became
          more limited. The policy in place at the time of this meeting reads as follows:


                     In addition to the written minutes of regular and special meetings, official audio recordings
                     of all open public meetings may be made by board designated staff and said recordings will
                     be processed, retained and made available in accordance with the Open Public Records Act.

Since this meeting was not with any outside entities and was merely a meeting of our board off campus, there was no
reason for it not to be recorded. So I recorded it as I did the meeting in Chelan the year prior. Moreover, though this
policy gives the board the choice to record a meeting or not, it does not take away every individual commissioners
right to record the meeting if they so choose. I continue to be unsure exactly why my fellow commissioners decided
to suddenly raise these objections and refused to continue the meeting while it was recorded.

Flannary Collins mrsc.org via mrscenter.onmicrosoft.com                          2019, 2:08 PM

to (readyforhealthcare email address)



Matthew:


While I can give you some general guidance on public meetings and the OPMA, MRSC’s role is
not to be the legal counsel for an agency or for an employee/official of an agency. We
provide general guidance on municipal issues, but we do not provide specific legal advice. Thus,
I cannot tell you whether there were any OPMA violations or crimes committed in the
transcript you provided. You will need to consult with your agency’s attorney or with a private
lawyer on that question.


I did spot a question in your email that I am able to answer: Can a commissioner or a private
citizen record a public meeting of the hospital commission?


The answer is, yes, any person can audio record an open public meeting of the commission so
long as it is not done in a disruptive manner. See AGO 1998 No. 15. However, while a recording
done by a private citizen is not a public record, a personal recording done by a commissioner
may be. This area is not crystal clear from a PRA perspective, but the Washington State
Archives has previously indicated that, if the agency itself doesn’t record the meeting and the
only recording is made by a commissioner on a personal device, that recording is subject to a 6-
year retention. If the Archives considers this type of recording to be subject to retention under
chapter 40.14 RCW, then it should be considered a public record under chapter 42.56.RCW. I am
not aware of any case law on this issue, although there are some cases addressing records on
personal devices/accounts (see our blog posts on this issue here and here). PRA/retention
issues is likely one reason why an agency would want to adopt a policy outlining expectations
for recording of a meeting.


Flannary P. Collins
MRSC Managing Attorney

On March 17, 2014 elected hospital commissioner for Jefferson Healthcare, Matthew William Ready
emailed his fellow hospital commissioners and the CEO Mike Glenn informing them:

“After much consideration, and in the spirit of transparency, accuracy, and openness, I have decided to
personally begin making audio recordings of our regular session commission meetings and making those
recordings readily available to anyone interested in hearing them. I for one cannot remember
everything that is said during our meetings and I believe it will be helpful for everyone to have a
complete and accurate record of our meetings for review and reference.”

On March 19, 2014 Commissioner Ready took out his audio recorder upon the opening of the meeting
and began recording.
The argument that followed is still unresolved as of 11/9/2019. Below is a transcript from the March 19,
2014 meeting:

Questions for legal researchers regarding March 19, 2014 meeting incident
1.       I believe it is beyond dispute that every citizen of the United States has the constitutional right
(US Constitution 1st amendment) and right by state law (the Open Public Meeting Act) to record any
open public meeting. Am I wrong?
2.       In the transcript and audio recording of March 19, 2014 you can clearly see the CEO aggressively
verbally pressuring Commissioner Matt Ready to stop recording the meeting. I don’t believe the
details of the verbal argument used is relevant, since the right to record the meeting is beyond dispute.
a.       Was the OPMA violated by the act of pressuring Commissioner Matt Ready to turn off his audio
recorder?
b.       Commissioner Dressler was the chair of the meeting March 19, 2014. Since the commission
follows Roberts Rules of Order, is Commissioner Dressler responsible for the violation of the OPMA at
the March 19 meeting, even if she didn’t say very much? She did in her actions tacitly
approve of everything the CEO was saying.
c.       The pressure exerted on Commissioner Ready succeeded in pushing him to turn off the audio
recorder. Does this qualify as a successful ban of audio recording?
d.       I believe it has been ruled many times that the right to record a public official in the public
execution of their duties is protected by the 1st amendment. Were Commissioner Ready’s
constitutional right to free speech guaranteed in the 1st amendment of the US Constitution violated
during this exchange on March 19?

I believe my rights were violated and perhaps laws were broken in the brief exchange on June 19,
2014. I hoped after this meeting the CEO and other commissioners would realize how wrong they were
to attempt to subsume the right to record, but sadly 2 and half years later, on June 29, 2016 a very
similar, but much more verbally violent incident occurred over the exact same issue.

At the June 29, 2016 meeting commissioner Ready took out an audio recorder and announced he was
recording the meeting. Immediately commissioner Deleo ordered him to turn it off. Commissioner
Ready refused, clearly indicating again his intention to exercise his right.
Commissioners Buhler (the chair), Commissioner Dressler, and CEO Mike Glenn then spent about 14
minutes arguing with Commissioner Ready attempting to pressure him to turn off his recorder. When
Commissioner Ready refused they adjourned the meeting rather than continue recorded. The
transcript of this meeting is below.

#####

As you can see from the transcript above, the CEO and Commissioners Buhler and Dressler continue to
be under the belief that the desires of the majority of the board to not be recorded is somehow a reason
for harassing a citizen exercising a protected right of free speech and transparent government,
guaranteed by the US Constitution and the OPMA. After the above meeting, I was again hoping they
would reflect upon this incident and realize they were deeply in the wrong. Unfortunately, on October
14, 2019 at another open public meeting of the Jefferson Healthcare Hospital Commission, the entire
argument came up again.

October 14, 2019 Commission Meeting
The 10/14/2019 Jefferson Healthcare Commission meeting was officially recorded by Jefferson
Healthcare- but I do not have a copy of it handy, but you can confirm these details with the recording.

At this meeting I attempted to resolve these insane, inappropriate, immoral, and possibly illegal actions
taken at previous meetings in attempts to stop personal audio recordings of the meeting by asking the
chair to make an official ruling whether a commissioner personally recording the meeting is in order or
out of order. The chair person (Commissioner Buhler) and the CEO (Mike Glenn) were extremely hostile
to the suggestion and significantly aggressive verbal reactions occurred. The meeting was then
recessed and the subject dropped.

Throughout this same meeting, it was argued by the consultant running the meeting that day and the
CEO that public hospital districts are not really full government agencies and shouldn’t be treated as
such. At the beginning of this open public meeting, the commissioners were all given the insane request
to keep the discussions “confidential” even though we were not in executive session. At one point the
CEO called the hospital district “pseudogovernmental” to emphasize this point. It seems this belief in
the “pseudogovernmental” nature of public hospital districts is at the heart of their beliefs why it was ok
to aggressively “discourage” (ban) recording of the two previous meetings – because to non government
agencies, the profits and privacy of the corporation is more important (and has legal and moral
authority) over personal rights. Indeed, in non-government healthcare agencies, the meetings are not
open public meetings, and the agency and board majority would have the full right to stop someone
recording.
Someone just needs to inform my fellow commissioners and CEO, that Jefferson Healthcare is a public
hospital district, and that every action they take to suppress basic individual rights to transparent
government and free speech are wrong. Are they legally wrong too? I don’t know. I am not a lawyer.

My attempts to use currently employed hospital counsel to resolve this have been unsuccessful. I
believe this may be because the lawyers work for the CEO and not the commissioners. One hospital
lawyer I contacted refused to discuss the topic with me I believe after checking with the CEO. On
another occasion, Commissioner Dressler said if I contacted a hospital lawyer to discuss this, I would
have to pay for it out of my own pocket- a very strange attempt to create an economic barrier between
a hospital commissioner and legal counsel benefiting the district.

Questions for legal researchers regarding June 29, 2016 meeting incident
1.       Was the OPMA violated by the act of ordering Commissioner Matt Ready to turn off his audio
recorder?
2.       At the 14 minute mark of the 6/29/2016 meeting, Board Chair Commissioner Buhler seems to
rule the recording out of order because it does not follow hospital district policy. Is hospital district
policy relevant to the exercise of a constitutional right? Did this action violate the OPMA? Does it
matter that they were all completely misstating the actual board policy?
3.       If the hospital district has a policy that forbids an individual commissioner from recording a
meeting, is that a violation of the OPMA? This would be a ban on recording written into a policy.
4.       I believe it has been ruled many times that the right to record a public official in the public
execution of their duties is protected by the 1st amendment. Were Commissioner Ready’s
constitutional right to free speech guaranteed in the 1st amendment of the US Constitution violated
during the clear attempts to ban recording on June 29, 2016?
5.       If employees of a public hospital district and elected commissioners all verbally harass another
commissioner regarding the exercise of a basic constitutional right, is this to be considered criminal
harassment? If similiar time was spent arguing with a member of the public or press attempting to
dissuade them from recording an open public meeting, wouldnt that be considered criminal harassment
or i suppose an act that could be civilly litigated? Again I am not a lawyer.
6.       Since I believe a recording is essential for the competent performance of my duties as a public
servant, is it not “intimidation of a public servant” to attempt to verbally nag me for 14 minutes to turn
off my recorder?
7.       From both transcripts above and the Oct 14 meeting record which is available- as well as all the
email exchanges available about this issue which could easily be obtained by interested parties, it is
clear that Commissioner Deleo, Commissioner Dressler, Commissioner Buhler, CEO Mike Glenn, and two
or more hospital employed attorneys all seem to have collaborated on this brilliant strategy to stop me
from recording the two meetings mentioned. If the attempts to stop me from recording a public
meeting constitute criminal harassment or intimidation of a public servant (which I am not qualified to
judge), then the group of them working together to commit these possibly criminal acts could further
constitute a criminal conspiracy. Do you think the actions constitute a criminal conspiracy?
8.       If the actions taken to suppress my right to record are considered criminal, then since I was
exercising my constitutional right of free speech and freedom of the press to record public officials in a
public space, do these actions to suppress my right to free speech (as well as free press since I am also a
writer), constitute a Conspiracy against Rights (a federal crime)?
####
Please note: I am not trying to have the immoral actions taken above prosecuted to the full
extent of the law. I simply want to feel free and safe to exercise my right to record any open public
meeting I attend, regardless of my status as a public hospital commissioner. I want to continue to enjoy
all the rights gauranteed to me by the OPMA and US constitution while serving in my role as hospital
commissioner- and I see no valid reason that should be repeatedly called into question in heated public
confrontations.

I believe the actions taken to suppress my right to record were highly immoral but over the past 6 years,
none of the commissioner nor the CEO, nor the Jefferson Healthcare lawyers have seen fit to admit
that. They all seem ready to take similiar actions if I again attempt to exercise my rights.

Is there anything you can do to help resolve this conflict and stop my colleagues from continuing to
commit immoral and possibly illegal actions if I decide to take out my audio recorder once again and
exercise my right to record?

Thanks!

motion that the commission adopt the policy that “if a commissioner decides to record a meeting on their own device,
uh, it will be announced and no further discussion of it will be had since they’re exercising their basic right.”
The motion was rejected 3-1.
The hospital attorney present at the 12/18 meeting said this in regards to the motion: “The, the threshold question is
whether or not, uh, a board member can record over the objection of other board members and, uh, I don’t know the
answer to that, so I would have to research that before our next meeting. Uh, I need some time to look into that.”

January 20, 2020 Press Release

  LOCAL POLITICIAN MATT READY CREATES
NEW WASHINGTON HEALTHCARE
ORGANIZATION TO COMBAT PRIVATE
CORPORATE INFLUENCE OVER HEALTHCARE
February 27, 2020 | Author Matt | Edit



THE ASSOCIATION OF WASHINGTON PUBLIC
HOSPITAL COMMISSIONERS (AWPHC) CREATED TO
COUNTERACT UNDUE INFLUENCE OF PRIVATE
LAWYERS AND CORPORATIONS INCLUDING THE
AWPHD (ASSOCIATION OF WASHINGTON PUBLIC
HOSPITAL DISTRICTS) AND MRSC (MUNICIPAL
RESEARCH SERVICE CENTER) OVER ELECTED
LEADERS IN WASHINGTON STATE HEALTHCARE
INDUSTRY
PORT TOWNSEND, Wash., January 20, 2020 (Newswire.com) – Elected Public Hospital Commissioner Matt
Ready (http://readyforhealthcare.org) is officially inviting all Washington State Public Hospital Commissioners to
join the newly formed Association of Washington Public Hospital Commissioners (http://awphc.org).
“Currently, there is no reliable organization to help elected public hospital commissioners to collaborate or receive
independent legal support,” Ready explains.
Ready has been embroiled in a 6-year dispute with fellow commissioners over the basic right of a person to record an
open public meeting of hospital commissioners. On two occasions, when the hospital was not officially recording the
public meeting, Ready began recording the meetings on a personal device yet was asked to stop. On one of the
occasions Ready was ordered to turn off his recorder, yet Ready refused. Ready explains, “I believe every word we say
in these meetings is important. So I need a complete and accurate record of what we say. I don’t believe this job can
be done ethically or competently without an accurate record of our public process.”
Ready believes something is wrong with public officials and public employees attempting to stop an elected official
from recording the activities of the elected body during an open public meeting. “I am pretty sure every person in
Washington State has the right to record any open public meeting. I don’t know why I have had to repeatedly defend
this right. The arguments used against me have been a bunch of legalistic mumbo jumbo. This controversy has been
an enormous waste of time and tax payer money.”
Frustrated by the 6-year dispute over the recording issue, Ready decided to reinvigorate and relaunch the concept
organization of the Association of Washington Public Hospital Commissioners. Ready posted on the association’s
Facebook page (https://www.facebook.com/groups/awphc) the following stirring prose:
“I created the Association of Public Hospital Commissioners several years ago when I first realized the Association of
Washington Public Hospital Districts was structured to prevent publicly elected officials from ever having power in
the institution. Elected commissioners are banned from serving on the AWPHD Board. Now, after 6 years of
struggling with a clear civil rights issue related to the recording of open public meetings (The Jefferson Healthcare
Recording Fiasco) I am crystal clear that a non-corrupt networking institution for public hospital commissioners is
needed.”
“Public hospital commissioners are elected by the people. As a public hospital commissioner, I have sought support
and guidance from the AWPHD and the nonprofit institution it funds to provide legal support to municipal
corporations, the MRSC, to help resolve the 6-year dispute over recording public meetings. The MRSC and AWPHD
refuse to offer an opinion.”
“The AWPHD is controlled by hospital CEOs. The MRSC is funded by the AWPHD. The money controls the work as
always.”
“We can do better. Let’s build an organization that actually supports the fair functioning of democracy.”
As one of the first proposed actions of the newly launched association, Ready proposed the following on his Twitter
feed:
“As one of the founders of The Association of Public Hospital Commissioners, I ask the association to consider the
following proposal: we help fund the creation of a network of competent legal researchers and lawyers to support
public hospital Districts.”
A “network of competent legal researchers and lawyers to support public hospital Districts” could replace the role the
Municipal Research and Service Center (MRSC) plays for public hospital districts.
Why is this important?
The multiyear conflict between Matt Ready and the municipal corporation he serves as elected representative for,
may indicate an interesting edge in the fundamental struggle between private corporate power and public power in
the US Healthcare system. Ready says, “If our elected leaders don’t have the basic right to document the use of power
in open public meetings, then people willing to abuse power will have no reason to fear accountability. The fact that
an elected official has been repeatedly pressured by a corporate agency and other commissioners to cease exercising
a basic civil right such as recording a public meeting, without a single comment from local news media, local leaders
of either party, or any local citizens seems to indicate there is something strange afoot in Jefferson County
Washington.”
To contact Matt Ready please direct message him on Twitter or Instagram (@MeditationMatt).
https://www.newswire.com/news/local-politician-matt-ready-creates-new-washington-healthcare-21079597

Hello!

In March 2014, elected hospital commissioner Matt Ready (that’s me) informed his fellow
board members and Jefferson Healthcare CEO Mike Glenn he would be exercising his right to
audio recording future meetings. During two open public meetings that followed when no
official recording was being made (2014, 2016), several other commissioners and the hospital
CEO with the apparent backing of multiple hospital attorneys repeatedly aggressively asked
Matt Ready to stop recording. Transcripts of these incidents and audio recordings are available
here in one of my blog posts:

http://readyforhealthcare.org/?p=528



Recording an open public meeting is an action protected by the open public meeting act, and
the state and US constitution. Therefore repeatedly badgering and pressuring a person
exercising this right is wrong and should be stopped by authorities. I am not a lawyer, but I
think harassment, intimidation of a public servant, and since these criminal acts were clearly
done in planning by commissioner Dressler, CEO Mike Glenn, and a Seattle lawyer named Brad
Berg- starting in a 2014 phone call before the first recorded incident, then I assume
“conspiracy” is also a valid charge. FYI, if it is agreed these are crimes against my civil

On Jan 29, 2020, at 9:10 AM, Krier, Nancy J (ATG) <nancy.krier@atg.wa.gov> wrote:

Dear Mr. Ready,


Thank you for your email below and the attachment. Please note we cannot provide you legal
advice or a legal opinion. We are not your or your agency’s attorneys, and we cannot advise or
represent you. However, we can provide some general information about open government
laws. You have asked about recordings of open public meetings by the public agency officials
serving on the board/commission. Here is some general information.


       ·    Public agency boards/commissions subject to the Open Public Meetings Act
       (OPMA) at RCW 42.30 are not required to make audio or video recordings of meetings.
       If an agency board chooses to record its meetings, agencies typically have recording
       procedures because the recordings are public records (see discussion further below).
       The recording procedures may vary in some details from agency to agency, such as
       whether an audio or a video recording will be made as the official recording.


       ·   In formal Attorney General Opinion (AGO) 1998 No. 15, we were asked to give an
       opinion on recordings of county meetings made by members of the public. We
       concluded that recordings by members of the public for meetings subject to the OPMA
       are permitted if the recording procedures are not disruptive, and that restrictions on the
       public’s recording of public meetings can be provided only if the restrictions are
       necessary to ensure the orderly conduct of a meeting. We also determined there is no
       right to record executive sessions that are closed to the public.


       ·    Elected public hospital commissioners attending commission meetings are doing so
       in their capacity as a commissioner. Regarding public records, elected hospital
       commissioners preparing (creating), owning, using or retaining records of hospital
       commission meetings in their capacity as a commissioner, including but not limited to
       recordings of commission meetings they are attending, and including but not limited to
       recordings on a personal device such as a personal cell phone, are creating presumptive
       public records of the agency and public records are subject to the Public Records Act at
       RCW 42.56. RCW 42.56.010(3); Mechling v. City of Monroe, 152 Wn. App. 830, 222
       P.3d 808 (2009); O’Neill v. City of Shoreline, 170 Wn.2d 138, 240 P.3d 1149
       (2010); Forbes v. City of Gold Bar, 171 Wn. App. 857, 288 P.3d 384 (2012); Nissen v.
       Pierce County, 183 Wn.2d 863, 357 P.3d 45 (2015); West v. Vermillion, 196 Wn. App
       627, 384 P.3d 634 (2016); West v. Puyallup, 2 Wn. App. 2d 586, 410 P.3d 1197 (2018).
       The PRA is to be “liberally construed.” RCW 42.56.030.


       ·   Public records are also subject to the records retention requirements in RCW
       40.14. RCW 40.14.010(1). Public records are the property of the State of Washington.
       RCW 40.14.020. They must be preserved, transferred, destroyed or disposed of only in
       accordance with RCW 40.14. Id.

The above are some statutes to consider. While you referenced your First Amendment rights,
we cannot conduct constitutional analysis for you. And, you referred to your belief that there
may be criminal conspiracy, harassment and intimidation involved in your communications
concerns the recordings. If you have evidence to indicate a crime has been committed, you
would need to contact your county prosecuting attorney.


Thank you again and I trust this assists you. As noted this is general information only and is
not legal advice or a legal opinion. You will need to consult with your agency’s attorney or
private legal counsel if you need legal advice or a legal opinion, or if you need legal research
conducted for you.


Sincerely,


Nancy Krier
Assistant Attorney General for Open Government
Office of the Attorney General

Jan 15, 2021 blog post

   JEFFERSON COUNTY PUBLIC HOSPITAL
DISTRICT COMMISSION VOTES UNANIMOUSLY
ON AMENDMENT ABOUT RECORDING ISSUE
January 15, 2021 | Author Matt | Edit

On 1/14/2021 the Jefferson County Public Hospital District Commission voted unanimously to add language to the
Board Book (the board policy book) that states if a commissioner independently records an open public meeting of
the commission, the commissioner will promptly give a copy of the recording to the district for public records
storage. The commissioners present seem to all indicate this policy will prevent future public confrontations and
conflicts over a commissioner recording meetings as happened in 2014 and 2016 and which led to several public
confrontations in the years following where those incidents were discussed. Many questions are still unanswered
about this controversy but the commission is considering taking steps to answer at least some of those questions.
The two questions that seem to be answered and agreed to by all members of the commission:


       1. A commissioner has the right to record any open public meeting of the commission whether regular or
          special session, on site or offsite (as do all residents of the United States)
       2. No one can (or should try to) prohibit a recording of anyone in an open public meeting, even if they
          personally object to the recording.


Neither of these two points were ever in doubt for me personally, but it is good that all the commissioners have now
agreed on these to facts of law (and ethics).
Everyone also agreed it was appropriate to require by policy that commissioner give a copy of any personally made
recordings to the district for safe keeping, but this was never controversial and has been the defacto standard of
practice by me since the very first meeting I recorded in 2014.
It is unfortunate and concerning that it has taken 7 years and enormous amounts of energy to get to this point but at
least some progress is being made.
Jan 24, 2021 :
The board voted to hire outside legal counsel to answer any an all lingering questions related to
a commissioner recording a board meeting on a personal device including how the board
should handle the situation to avoid public conflict, confusion, or confrontation.

FROM THE PORT TOWNSEND LEADER )

HOSPITAL DISTRICT WILL GET LEGAL LOOK AT
RECORDING POLICY FOR BOARD MEETINGS
Posted Friday, February 5, 2021 8:30 am
Nick Twietmeyer
ntwietmeyer@ptleader.com
Nick Twietmeyer
ntwietmeyer@ptleader.com
Jefferson Healthcare’s Board of Commissioners has agreed to get legal advice on whether board members acted
appropriately in asking a commissioner to discontinue his audio recording of public meetings.
The issue dates back to a March 2014 board meeting, when Commissioner Matt Ready attempted to record the
discussion topics for later reference.
Other commissioners and hospital administrators present during the meeting pushed back, stating that it would
place the hospital district in a compromising position by requiring it to maintain his recordings as public records.
Ready declined subsequent requests to stop recording by both board and administrative staff members.
In the years following the initial incident, Jefferson Healthcare has begun publishing on their website the audio from
meetings going back to 2017.
The issue came up again at a special session last week that had one agenda item: a self-evaluation for the hospital
district board.
Commissioner Jill Buhler Rienstra said she thought the board had established an adequate policy that properly
addressed the matter of board members recording meetings, but added that some questions still remain.
“I think that what’s left on the table is … were your rights violated early on?” Buhler Rienstra asked Ready during the
Jan. 24 meeting.
“Do you feel that this is resolved going forward?” she asked.
“I do not think really critical questions have been answered,” Ready replied. “I don’t see how we can move forward
without feeling like we have adequate legal support to the board … it shouldn’t be this hard to get questions
answered.”
At multiple times throughout the meeting, Ready and others referenced a series of questions drafted by Ready and
sent to the board members in advance of the meeting.
(The hospital district did not respond to The Leader for a copy of the questions before the newspaper went to press
Tuesday.)
During the Jan. 24 meeting, Commissioner Kees Kolff said the board should seek legal assistance in answering
Ready’s lingering questions in order to encourage the board members to move past the matter.
“I would strongly recommend that we just go ahead and get a written legal opinion, right now, using Matt’s
questions,” Kolff said. “I will make that motion, because I don’t think we’re going to get anywhere discussing the past
any further.”
“I think we owe it to Matt to allow him to ask his questions and we will all learn from it,” he added.
The motion was seconded by Ready.
Just before the board voted, Commissioner Marie Dressler said she was worried about the costs of pursuing legal
answers to the questions raised by the commissioner.
“You can probably get several different opinions from several different lawyers, so that is a concern of mine because
they’re pretty expensive,” Dressler said. “If this is the final adjudication of these questions, then I think that’s
reasonable.”
The board voted unanimously to get the questions answered by a lawyer.
Board Chair Jill Buhler Rienstra said she hoped settling the matter would lead the group to “being a cohesive board
that’s dedicated to going forward for the best of the district.”
END Article from Port Townsend Leader

repeated requests between 2016 and 2021 for written legal answers to the issues related to this recording conflict.

commissioner records a meeting on a personal device, crafted sensible policy based on the written expert legal

The above transcript is a snippet from a public meeting of a hospital commission and
suggests that there are differing opinions among the commissioners about what
happened in the past. The consultant, Karma B, is trying to bring the issue to a close
and move the conversation forward, but Commissioner Dressler raises a concern about
the organization being put in jeopardy. Commissioner McComas acknowledges that he
came on the board after the events in question and feels that the policy was improved
in 2021, while Commissioner Kolff believes that there is a subjective call when it comes
to what is best for the organization.


This transcript has shed light on tensions between Commissioner Ready and the rest of
the hospital administration. The transcript, which was recorded during a meeting
between Commissioner Ready and Consultant Karma B, reveals Commissioner Ready's
frustration over the handling of the recording issue by the hospital's lawyer, John
French.
According to Commissioner Ready, he had previously met with and asked Hospital
attorney John French to address his concerns about the recording issue, but never
received a response. Commissioner Ready suggests that French may have been told
not to work on the issue. If someone instructed a hospital attorney to ignore the
notification by a board member of possible legal wrongdoing, this might be a
problematic action. This lack of action by French, combined with the administration's
decision to withhold a 2016 legal opinion on the issue of recording until 2021, has led
Commissioner Ready to question whether the actions of the hospital administration
could be considered "pointless fraud."
Fraud is a serious matter and could have significant consequences for the hospital and
its administration. However, it's important to note that Commissioner Ready's
comments are only a perspective and that it's up to the relevant authorities to determine
whether any wrongdoing has occurred.
The transcript serves as a reminder of the importance of transparency and open
communication within any organization. It's crucial for all parties to work together and
address any issues in a timely and effective manner to ensure the smooth functioning
of the organization.

(FROM THE PORT TOWNSEND LEADER )
HOSPITAL DISTRICT WILL GET LEGAL LOOK AT
RECORDING POLICY FOR BOARD MEETINGS
Posted Friday, February 5, 2021 8:30 am
Nick Twietmeyer
ntwietmeyer@ptleader.com
Nick Twietmeyer
ntwietmeyer@ptleader.com
Jefferson Healthcare’s Board of Commissioners has agreed to get legal advice on whether board members acted
appropriately in asking a commissioner to discontinue his audio recording of public meetings.
The issue dates back to a March 2014 board meeting, when Commissioner Matt Ready attempted to record the
discussion topics for later reference.
Other commissioners and hospital administrators present during the meeting pushed back, stating that it would
place the hospital district in a compromising position by requiring it to maintain his recordings as public records.
Ready declined subsequent requests to stop recording by both board and administrative staff members.
In the years following the initial incident, Jefferson Healthcare has begun publishing on their website the audio from
meetings going back to 2017.
The issue came up again at a special session last week that had one agenda item: a self-evaluation for the hospital
district board.
Commissioner Jill Buhler Rienstra said she thought the board had established an adequate policy that properly
addressed the matter of board members recording meetings, but added that some questions still remain.
“I think that what’s left on the table is … were your rights violated early on?” Buhler Rienstra asked Ready during the
Jan. 24 meeting.
“Do you feel that this is resolved going forward?” she asked.
“I do not think really critical questions have been answered,” Ready replied. “I don’t see how we can move forward
without feeling like we have adequate legal support to the board … it shouldn’t be this hard to get questions
answered.”
At multiple times throughout the meeting, Ready and others referenced a series of questions drafted by Ready and
sent to the board members in advance of the meeting.
(The hospital district did not respond to The Leader for a copy of the questions before the newspaper went to press
Tuesday.)
During the Jan. 24 meeting, Commissioner Kees Kolff said the board should seek legal assistance in answering
Ready’s lingering questions in order to encourage the board members to move past the matter.
“I would strongly recommend that we just go ahead and get a written legal opinion, right now, using Matt’s
questions,” Kolff said. “I will make that motion, because I don’t think we’re going to get anywhere discussing the past
any further.”
“I think we owe it to Matt to allow him to ask his questions and we will all learn from it,” he added.
The motion was seconded by Ready.
Just before the board voted, Commissioner Marie Dressler said she was worried about the costs of pursuing legal
answers to the questions raised by the commissioner.
“You can probably get several different opinions from several different lawyers, so that is a concern of mine because
they’re pretty expensive,” Dressler said. “If this is the final adjudication of these questions, then I think that’s
reasonable.”
The board voted unanimously to get the questions answered by a lawyer.
Board Chair Jill Buhler Rienstra said she hoped settling the matter would lead the group to “being a cohesive board
that’s dedicated to going forward for the best of the district.”

 Whispered Meeting




 If 5 public board members of a 5 member board are in a public meeting. 4 in person and one over
 audio on phone. During the public meeting one of the four in person members whispers
 communication with all 4 in person board members about a question they want asked if the 5th
 board member, is that whispering an illegal serial meeting of a quorum of board members while
 intentionally not including the 5th?
Whether or not the whispered communication constitutes an illegal serial meeting would depend on

the laws and regulations governing the board in question. In general, a serial meeting occurs when a

quorum of board members communicate with one another outside of a properly noticed public

meeting. This can be considered illegal if the applicable laws and regulations prohibit such

communication.


However, in this case, the communication you described involves four of the five members being in the

same physical location, so it might not be considered a serial meeting if the applicable laws do not

prohibit members from communicating with each other in person.


Additionally, if the communication was not part of a prearranged plan to circumvent the open meeting

requirements and if the members did not take any formal action during the whispered conversation, it

might not be considered an illegal serial meeting.
It is important to note that the laws and regulations governing public boards vary by jurisdiction, so it

would be best to consult with legal counsel to determine whether the communication in question was

an illegal serial meeting.

meetings and making those recordings readily available to anyone interested in hearing them.

reference.”

 I believe my rights were violated and perhaps laws were broken in the brief exchange on June

At the June 29, 2016 meeting commissioner Ready took out an audio recorder and announced
he was recording the meeting. Immediately commissioner Deleo ordered him to turn it off.
Commissioner Ready refused, clearly indicating again his intention to exercise his right.
Commissioners Buhler (the chair), Commissioner Dressler, and CEO Mike Glenn then spent
about 14 minutes arguing with Commissioner Ready attempting to pressure him to turn off his
recorder. When Commissioner Ready refused they adjourned the meeting rather than continue
recorded. The transcript of this meeting is below.
