[Matt Ready’s personal account of this moment in the meeting:

I was seated to his right with at least one person in between us, but nonetheless, I remember

When someone is angry with you and they suddenly rise from the table, you don’t know
what will happen next. My brain immediately started evaluating possibilities. I must
admit, my body experienced a shot of extra adrenaline instinctively, since I suppose at a
primal level, I perceived some sort of violence towards me was possible.

I saw my recorder sitting on the table out in front of me and thought, “Is he going to grab at
my recorder?” The possibility seemed plausible as I had imagined such things happening
at previous debates about the recording of meetings. In fact, I had played through many

circumstances and simply see what levels of force might be used against me. Yet, on this

Reply from Washington State Assistant Attorney General for
Open Government, Office of the Attorney General Reply
regarding OPMA and possible crimes committed
On Jan 29, 2020, at 9:10 AM, Krier, Nancy J (ATG) <nancy.krier@atg.wa.gov> wrote:


Dear Mr. Ready,


Thank you for your email below and the attachment. Please note we cannot provide you legal
advice or a legal opinion. We are not your or your agency’s attorneys, and we cannot advise or
represent you. However, we can provide some general information about open government
laws. You have asked about recordings of open public meetings by the public agency officials
serving on the board/commission. Here is some general information.



· Public agency boards/commissions subject to the Open Public Meetings Act (OPMA) at
RCW 42.30 are not required to make audio or video recordings of meetings. If an agency board
chooses to record its meetings, agencies typically have recording procedures because the
recordings are public records (see discussion further below). The recording procedures may
vary in some details from agency to agency, such as whether an audio or a video recording will
be made as the official recording.



· In formal Attorney General Opinion (AGO) 1998 No. 15, we were asked to give an opinion
on recordings of county meetings made by members of the public. We concluded that
recordings by members of the public for meetings subject to the OPMA are permitted if the
recording procedures are not disruptive, and that restrictions on the public’s recording of public
meetings can be provided only if the restrictions are necessary to ensure the orderly conduct of
a meeting. We also determined there is no right to record executive sessions that are closed to
the public.



· Elected public hospital commissioners attending commission meetings are doing so in their
capacity as a commissioner. Regarding public records, elected hospital commissioners
preparing (creating), owning, using or retaining records of hospital commission meetings in their
capacity as a commissioner, including but not limited to recordings of commission meetings they
are attending, and including but not limited to recordings on a personal device such as a
personal cell phone, are creating presumptive public records of the agency and public records
are subject to the Public Records Act at RCW 42.56. RCW 42.56.010(3); Mechling v. City of
Monroe, 152 Wn. App. 830, 222 P.3d 808 (2009); O’Neill v. City of Shoreline, 170 Wn.2d 138,
240 P.3d 1149 (2010); Forbes v. City of Gold Bar, 171 Wn. App. 857, 288 P.3d 384
(2012); Nissen v. Pierce County, 183 Wn.2d 863, 357 P.3d 45 (2015); West v. Vermillion, 196
Wn. App 627, 384 P.3d 634 (2016); West v. Puyallup, 2 Wn. App. 2d 586, 410 P.3d 1197
(2018). The PRA is to be “liberally construed.” RCW 42.56.030.



· Public records are also subject to the records retention requirements in RCW 40.14. RCW
40.14.010(1). Public records are the property of the State of Washington. RCW 40.14.020.
They must be preserved, transferred, destroyed or disposed of only in accordance with RCW
40.14. Id.



The above are some statutes to consider. While you referenced your First Amendment rights,
we cannot conduct constitutional analysis for you. And, you referred to your belief that there
may be criminal conspiracy, harassment and intimidation involved in your communications
concerns the recordings. If you have evidence to indicate a crime has been committed, you
would need to contact your county prosecuting attorney.


Thank you again and I trust this assists you. As noted this is general information only and is
not legal advice or a legal opinion. You will need to consult with your agency’s attorney or
private legal counsel if you need legal advice or a legal opinion, or if you need legal research
conducted for you.


Sincerely,


Nancy Krier
Assistant Attorney General for Open Government
Office of the Attorney General

       approval or disapproval.

02/05/2025 Matt Ready’s Notes on the February 5 Executive Session and the
Potential Illegal Straw Poll
It appears that after the February 5, 2025 executive session, Jefferson Healthcare CEO Mike
Glenn left the meeting under the impression that he had board approval to work extensively
with staff to craft and submit a proposal to Olympic Medical Center (OMC) aligned with the
framework he had just presented. Unfortunately, such approval would have been legally
impossible under the Open Public Meetings Act (OPMA), as no action can be taken during an
executive session.
Therefore, one of the following two statements must be true:
  •    An Illegal Straw Poll Occurred: CEO Mike Glenn and certain commissioners of
       Jefferson Healthcare engaged in an illegal, secret straw poll—either within the executive
       session or outside it—that resulted in informal approval for the CEO to proceed. This
       straw poll led to the creation and submission of a detailed proposal titled “Commission
       Packet.pdf” sent to commissioners on February 5 and discussed during the session.
  •    The CEO Acted Unilaterally Without Board Approval: CEO Mike Glenn created a
       far-reaching proposal for a strategic partnership with OMC involving the formation of a
       new, nongovernmental nonprofit corporation—Peninsula Health Alliance—which
       would potentially assume authority over both public hospital districts. He submitted
       this proposal as if it represented Jefferson Healthcare without:
  •    Board approval;
  •    Providing full and clear information to the board;
  •    Allowing board members to ask legal questions about risks or ramifications;
  •    Sharing any financial analysis, projections, or studies justifying the proposal as a sound
       fiduciary decision.
As an attendee of the February 5 executive session, I am prepared to swear under oath that I
directly asked CEO Glenn whether he was seeking board approval to submit a proposal to OMC.
He answered affirmatively. I further affirm that each commissioner present took a turn to
verbally express support for the CEO’s action. This was, by all definitions, a textbook illegal
straw poll. CEO Glenn left the meeting with de facto—but not legally authorized—approval
from the board.
As a result, the proposal was submitted to OMC without legal board approval. The board never
received a fair opportunity to review the proposal, ask questions, or recommend changes in a
public and lawful process.
Had I been given the chance to provide input, I would have strongly opposed giving Clallam
County a 7-to-5 majority over the new alliance board. I would also have insisted on a
transparent and open process to select leadership—rather than agreeing in advance that CEO
Mike Glenn would assume the role of executive director. During the executive session, I was left
with the distinct impression that his leadership had already been preselected as part of the
proposal.

Key Concerns Regarding the Peninsula Health Alliance Proposal
This proposal outlines a major governance restructuring for both hospital districts under a
new not-for-profit entity (Peninsula Health Alliance) while stating that the individual
hospital boards would retain autonomy. However, there are several critical legal and
governance concerns that must be addressed before moving forward.

1. Lack of Formal Board Authorization
   •  If this proposal was drafted based on informal “voice consent” in executive session,
      it lacks legal board approval and may be invalid under OPMA.
  •   Any major proposal like this should have been voted on in a public session before
      submission.
  •   Key Question: Who authorized this submission, and does it legally bind either hospital
      district in any way? The proposal says “Jefferson Healthcare” is making the proposal-
      but without board consent, can such a proposal be made- or should it be made?

2. Governance Risks & Potential Power Shift
   •  The creation of a “super board” consolidates decision-making over regional
      healthcare into a new entity that could change its governance structure over
      time.
  •   While the proposal states that current hospital commissioners would serve on the new
      Peninsula Health Alliance Board, this structure could be changed later to reduce
      elected oversight.
  •   The proposal states that decision-making will be driven by an “alliance executive
      director” and a “strategic leadership team,” raising concerns about who will truly
      control healthcare decisions moving forward.
  •   Key Question: What legal safeguards prevent future bylaw changes that could remove
      elected commissioners from meaningful oversight?

3. Possible OPMA Violations & Transparency Issues
   •  This proposal suggests a phased approach—but when was the board ever formally
      presented with this plan for open discussion?
  •   The public has not been informed or consulted about this potential restructuring.
  •   If this proposal has already been sent to OMC without proper board approval, it
      raises serious transparency concerns.
  •   Key Question: Why was this proposal not reviewed and approved in a public board
      meeting before submission?

4. Financial & Operational Impact Unknown
   •   The proposal does not include any financial projections, service impact
       assessments, or cost-benefit analysis.
  •   Before approving or discussing this further, the board needs a full independent
      financial impact analysis detailing:
  •   Cost of forming and running the new entity.
  •   Potential tax revenue impacts.
  •   Effect on patient care, service accessibility, and operational sustainability.
  •   Key Question: Without financial data, how can the board or the public determine if
      this is a good idea?
Recommendations Before Moving Forward
  •  Independent Legal Review – A third-party attorney should assess:
  •    Whether this proposal was submitted legally and if any board actions were taken
       improperly.
  •    The future governance risks of the Peninsula Health Alliance and how to ensure
       permanent public oversight.
  •    Independent Financial Analysis – A full assessment of the financial, operational, and
       service impact must be conducted before any further discussion.
  •    Public Transparency &** OPMA Compliance** – The board must:
  •    Discuss this proposal in an open public meeting.
  •    Ensure the public is properly informed and consulted before any commitment is
       made.
  •    Board Vote in Public Session – No further action should be taken unless the full
       board votes in an open meeting to proceed with discussions.

Final Thought:
🚨fullAlegal,
       major governance change like this cannot be rushed behind closed doors without
             financial, and public review. This proposal should not move forward until all
concerns are addressed in a fully transparent and legally compliant manner.

Incredibly Important Discussion
February 24, 2025 | Author Matt* | *Edit
A public hospital district is a municipal corporation. What does that mean?
A Public Hospital District in Washington State is a governmental entity created by voters
within a specific geographic area to provide publicly funded healthcare services. These
districts are municipal corporations, similar to cities and counties, and operate under
Chapter 70.44 RCW of Washington State law.

Key Features of a Public Hospital District in Washington:
  •   Publicly Owned &** Governed** – Managed by an elected Board of >**
      Commissioners**, typically five members, who oversee operations > and finances.
  •    Taxing Authority – Can levy property taxes to support > healthcare services.
  •    Healthcare Services – Operate hospitals, clinics, nursing >** homes, ambulance
       services, and wellness programs** depending on > community needs.
  •    Local Control – Voters within the district determine leadership > and financial support
       through elections.
  •    Broad Service Scope – Can provide not just hospital care, but > also preventative
       care, mental health services, and emergency >** medical services (EMS).**
  •    Nonprofit-Like Function – Although government-run, they often > collaborate with
       private healthcare providers to improve > services.

Example:
Jefferson Healthcare in Port Townsend is a public hospital district (Jefferson County Public
Hospital District No. 2) that operates a critical access hospital and various clinics, serving the
local population.

 A map of the state of washington AI-generated content may be incorrect.

A map of the state of washington AI-generated content may be incorrect.

Financial & Legal Structure of Public Hospital Districts in Washington State
1. Legal Structure
   •  Public hospital districts are municipal corporations established > under RCW 70.44,
      similar to cities and counties.
  •    They are political subdivisions of the state, meaning they are subject to public
       records laws, open meetings laws (RCW 42.30), and public bidding
       requirements.
  •    Governed by a Board of Commissioners (usually five members) elected by district
       residents for six-year staggered terms.

2. Financial Structure

Revenue Sources
Public hospital districts operate as nonprofit-like entities but have multiple funding sources:
  •    Property Taxes
  •    Can levy up to 75 cents per $1,000 of assessed property >** value** without voter
       approval.
  •    Can seek additional levies (e.g., EMS levies) with voter approval.
  •    Patient Service Revenue
  •    Most revenue comes from Medicare, Medicaid, private insurance, >** and direct
       patient payments**.
  •    Some services (e.g., critical access hospitals) receive cost-based reimbursements from
       Medicare.
  •    Bonds &** Loans**
  •    Can issue general obligation bonds (subject to voter > approval) for capital projects.
  •    Can take out loans for equipment, facility expansions, or infrastructure improvements.
  •    Government Grants &** Subsidies**
  •    Eligible for federal and state grants (e.g., rural > healthcare funding, emergency
       response grants).
  •    Some districts receive special state funding for essential healthcare services.
  •    Partnerships &** Contracts**
  •    May enter into agreements with private healthcare providers, >** universities, or
       nonprofits**.
  •    Some districts contract out services such as ambulance services, mental health
       programs, or specialty care.

Financial Accountability
   •   Must submit annual financial reports to the Washington State > Auditor’s Office.
  •    Subject to public budgeting and auditing requirements under RCW 43.09.
  •    Required to hold public meetings for major financial decisions, ensuring
       transparency.

Example of Financial Operations
A typical public hospital district might:
  •    Collect $2 million from property taxes.
  •    Earn $50 million in patient service revenue.
  •    Receive $3 million in grants.
  •    Secure $10 million in bonds for hospital expansion.
IF YOU GIVE CONTROL OF YOUR PUBLIC HOSPITAL DISTRICT TO A NON PROFIT
CORPORATION, YOU LOSE PUBLIC CONTROL AND ACCOUNTABILITY SAFEGUARDS. Just
a theoretical comment irrelevant to anything except… is it?
But why would you even think about giving control of your public hospital district to a non
profit corporation? Maybe healthcare has changed and a big restructuring would be good for
the community in some way. Is the best thing to do, to abandon the safeguards of a publicly
controlled municipal corporation governed by democratically elected commissioners in favor of
a non profit corporation that could at any time vote to changes its governing structure and
transparency to whatever it wants whenever it wants? Is this type of radical restructuring the
only type worth considering?

Analysis
If two or more Washington public hospital districts want to radically restructure, there are
several possible models besides forming a nonprofit corporation to oversee them. Below is a
comparison of potential restructuring options.

1. Nonprofit Corporation Oversight Model
   •  Description: The hospital districts create a new nonprofit >** corporation** to
      oversee operations, governance, and potentially > financial management.
  •    Pros:
  •    Increased operational flexibility (nonprofits can operate > outside some government
       constraints).
  •    Can raise private funds and enter into partnerships more easily.
  •    Unified leadership without dissolving individual districts.
  •    Cons:
  •    May reduce public oversight as a nonprofit board isn’t > publicly elected.
  •    Could lead to conflicts over accountability between the elected commissioners and the
       nonprofit board.
  •    Potential for mission drift if nonprofit governance does not align with public interest.

2. Full Merger Into a Single Public Hospital District
   •   Description: The two or more hospital districts merge into one >** larger district**
       with a single elected Board of Commissioners.
  •    Pros:
  •    Unified budget and governance streamline decision-making.
  •    Eliminates redundant administrative costs.
  •    More tax revenue pooling, allowing better investment in healthcare infrastructure.
  •    Cons:
  •    Requires voter approval.
  •    Risk of local communities losing influence in decision-making.
  •    Could be disruptive to existing labor agreements and management structures.

3. Interlocal Agreement for Shared Governance
   •   Description: The districts remain independent but sign an > interlocal agreement
       (ILA) to share administration, > facilities, or specific services.
  •    Pros:
  •    Retains separate identities while allowing cost-sharing.
  •    No need for voter approval.
  •    Can focus collaboration on specific departments (e.g., emergency services, IT, or
       billing).
  •    Cons:
  •    Coordination challenges if leadership has conflicting > priorities.
  •    Not as strong as a full merger in terms of financial and operational integration.
  •    Potential for unequal benefit distribution if one district has greater financial need.

4. Creation of a Joint Operating Authority (JOA)
   •  Description: The hospital districts form a separate public >** entity** under RCW
      39.34, which has independent taxing > authority and management.
  •    Pros:
  •    Maintains public ownership and control but allows joint > decision-making.
  •    Can issue bonds and levy taxes to support regional healthcare.
  •    Clear legal framework under Washington law.
  •    Cons:
  •    Complex governance structure may slow decision-making.
  •    Requires voter approval and legal agreements.
  •    Can create bureaucratic layers, adding to costs.

5. Public-Private Partnership (PPP)
   •  Description: The hospital districts enter into a contract with >** a private company**
      to manage operations while retaining public > ownership.
  •    Pros:
  •    Private expertise can improve efficiency.
  •    Possible cost savings through operational streamlining.
  •    Avoids the political difficulties of a full merger.
  •    Cons:
  •    Less direct public control over healthcare decisions.
  •    Risk of profit-driven priorities conflicting with community needs.
  •    Potential staffing changes and wage adjustments.

 rtnership (PPP)
Conclusion
 •   If efficiency and flexibility are the priority, the nonprofit >** oversight** model
     makes sense.
  •    If strong public control and accountability are key, a merger or Joint Operating
       Authority is better.
  •    If they want minimal disruption, an Interlocal Agreement might be the best option.
  •    If they need private sector expertise, a Public-Private Partnership could work.

Readyforhealthcare.org Post: February 25, 2025 Matt Ready posts to
website: “Are Our Elected Leaders Sworn to Abide and Comply with
Corporate Controlled Policies?”
February 24, 2025 | Author Matt* | *Edit
A bureaucracy worships the rule of bureaucracy. A bureaucrat uses the bureaucracy to get
what they want for their personal agendas.
A public hospital commission is a government entity of elected leaders. The leaders swear to
uphold the constitutions of the USA and Wa state. A bureaucrat who claims that elected leaders
have sworn to abide and comply with the “policies” chosen by the majority of the board of
elected leaders, wants to remove the ability of an elected leader to have any dissent to the
actions of the board majority. This is a method of destroying the basic concept of democracy-
where each elected leader is elected to voice their opinion and do and say things they believe
are in the interests of the greater good.
Forcing elected public hospital commissioners to oversee a public hospital district – but do so as
members of a non profit board overseeing the public hospital district – is a way to force those
leaders to obey corporate policies – which will be used to limit public oversight, accountability,
transparency, and the ability of your elected commissioners to do anything about it.

When)

Hi Mike and Jill, can you let me know when the commissioners are going to be informed
whether or not Jefferson Healthcare is has been selected as a finalist with the OMC partnership
proposal. I would like to know if this is something that is moving forward or if it has completely

Matt
March 2, 2025 - 9 days later Jill Buhler email replies to Matt Ready, Mike
Glenn (Re: When)
5:59 PM - Jill Buhler to Matt Ready, Mike Glenn (Re: When)
Hi Matt,
I apologize for the delay; I was out of town until Saturday.
In answer to your question, Yes and No. Allow me to explain.
First, a summary of the process, as we understand it:
We submitted an “indication of interest” (OMC’s term) on February 12. Mike was notified
February 19 that we were selected to present our indication of interest concept paper to OMC.
Accordingly, JH admin was invited to site visit OMC and review our document in late March. If
this goes, we are selected to proceed: “refined proposals from phase two participants would be
requested in late April 2025.”
THIS is when we decide to proceed, or not, and fill in the many blanks of our concept proposal.
Lawyers and other consultants will no doubt be involved. At this point, we also expect to get the
all clear from OMC to discuss their process and our proposal in public meetings, which we
agree is critically important to do.
So, yes, we made it to the next step, but no, we have not begun the next phase.
Further complicating things is OMC’s and their counsel’s need to maintain confidentiality.
Mike and I spoke with Brad Berg about this and agreed the request needs to be lifted if we are
to continue in phase 2. We expect it to be.
I hope this answers your question.
Jill

directly. This legal counsel should be retained solely by the Board of Commissioners,
independent of the CEO and administration, to ensure unbiased legal advice on matters related
to governance, compliance with the Open Public Meetings Act, Hospital District operations,
strategic partnerships, and any legal concerns impacting the board’s oversight responsibilities.
The selected legal counsel should report exclusively to the Board of Commissioners, attend
meetings as necessary, and provide legal opinions directly to the board without intermediary
oversight from administration or administration lawyers.
We should initiate a selection process for this kind of legal support. We probably should have
had this all along - other public Hospital District boards have their own legal counsel. Many
corporations have boards with their own legal counsel; it’s completely a best practice.
I think that needs to be done, and I think we need our legal questions answered.”
Commissioner Jill Buhler: “You are welcome to make that motion at the next meeting, Matt.”

Executive Summary from attachment in Sheriff email
Executive Summary
This packet documents a coordinated effort by leadership at Jefferson Healthcare to develop,
conceal, and submit a major regional governance proposal—the Peninsula Health Alliance
—without legal board authorization, public vote, or transparency. The process involved:
  •    Improper use of executive sessions,
  •    Likely serial meetings,
  •    Suppression of dissent and oversight,
  •    False public statements,
  •    Concealment of legal risk by the district’s attorney,
  •    And enabling or misleading advice from advisory bodies.
The actions detailed may rise to the level of fraud, misconduct, OPMA violations, and
criminal conspiracy.

What Happened
❗   On February 12, 2025, a 50+ page proposal was submitted to Olympic Medical
Center (OMC) to create a nonprofit entity—the Peninsula Health Alliance—which
would oversee both public hospital districts.
  •   This proposal was never approved in a public board vote.
  •    It was discussed only in a closed executive session under a dubious legal
       justification.
  •    Some commissioners were consulted and edited drafts; others were excluded
       entirely.
  •    Commissioners were instructed to keep the proposal secret from the public.
  •    No financial projections, service impact analysis, or legal safeguards were
       presented to the board before submission.

Why It Matters
 •    The public was misled.
  •    The board was fragmented.
  •    The law was likely broken.
  •    Governance of two public hospital districts is at risk of privatization.

Governance Risks of the Peninsula Health Alliance Proposal
 •   Creates a new nonprofit “superboard” to oversee two public hospital districts.
  •   Initial board includes elected commissioners—but bylaw changes could remove
      them later.
  •   Decision-making driven by a CEO-appointed executive director—reducing
      accountability.
  •   Could become a privatized governance shell—insulated from public oversight.

Legal Analysis & Violations
  •   OPMA Violations: Improper use of executive session; “real estate” exemption
      misapplied.
  •   Illegal Board Action: If any “voice consent” was given in closed session, it is not valid
      under law.
  •   Suppression of Public Discussion: Board members were told to stay silent; public
      kept unaware.
  •   First Amendment Concerns: Pressure was applied to Commissioner Ready to remove
      public content.
  •   Legal Counsel Complicity: Brad Berg enabled or ignored legal irregularities.
Recommendations
  •  Criminal Investigation Refer all records to the Jefferson &** Clallam County Sheriffs
     and Prosecutors, Washington State Attorney General, and U.S. Attorney**.
  •    State Oversight &** Audit Request immediate review from the Washington State
       Auditor** and MRSC of executive session conduct and proposal submission.
  •    Independent Legal Review Hire outside counsel, independent of CEO and existing
       staff, to advise the board and public on OPMA and governance risks.
  •    Independent Financial Impact Analysis Analyze how the Peninsula Health Alliance
       could affect local finances, taxes, patient care, service quality, and staffing.
  •    Halt Further Action Until Public Vote Require that no governance changes occur
       until the full board votes in public and the community is informed.
  •    Bar Referral for Attorney Misconduct Submit complaint to the Washington State
       Bar Association regarding attorney Brad Berg’s advice and conduct

Final Statement
“The people do not give their public servants the right to decide what is good for them to know
and what is not.” – Washington OPMA Legislative Intent
This situation is not just a legal crisis—it’s a moral and democratic one. The public has a right
to know when its hospital is being handed off to a private structure. Every step must be visible,
legal, and accountable.

Attachment Text
Summary Report: Legal Concerns Raised by Attorney Austin Hatcher Regarding the
Peninsula Health Alliance Proposal
Prepared by: Commissioner Matt Ready
Date: March 26, 2025
Overview:
Attorney Austin Hatcher of Hatcher Law, PLLC reviewed the actions taken by Jefferson
Healthcare regarding the Peninsula Health Alliance proposal and found multiple areas of legal
concern, particularly regarding compliance with Washington’s Open Public Meetings Act
(OPMA), board authorization procedures, and the use of executive sessions.
Key Legal Concerns Quoted from Attorney Hatcher:
   1.      Questionable Use of Executive Session:
“The executive session was under a very stretched reading of the ‘lease’ purposes of
RCW 42.30.110(1)(b) and (c)… That is not the case here.”
— Austin F. Hatcher
Hatcher argues that using the real estate exemption to hold an executive session to
discuss a broad strategic alliance—absent a specific property negotiation—is likely not
legally valid under OPMA.
   2.      Improper Action in Executive Session:
“It seems the Board did in fact decide to submit the proposal in an executive session (or
somewhere else off the record)… then action was taken in executive session.”
— Austin F. Hatcher
Since no action can legally be taken in executive session, any consent or authorization
to submit the proposal given during such a session would be invalid and potentially
illegal.
   3.      Submission of Proposal Without Clear Board Approval:
“Mike, Jill, and Bruce have a weird position that ’nothing concrete has been discussed
or merits discussion.’ Your point is well taken that there is in fact a very concrete step
that has been taken…”
— Austin F. Hatcher
Hatcher identifies a contradiction in statements made by leadership downplaying the
proposal, despite a formal submission having been made, which may indicate a lack of
transparency or improper procedure.
  4.   Concerns Over Legal Advice and Governance Integrity:
“I think the history of questionable executive sessions is worrisome.”
— Austin F. Hatcher
Hatcher’s concern about past executive sessions suggests a recurring pattern that may
require legal and governance reform, particularly the hiring of independent legal counsel
for the board.
  5.   Legality of Proposal Mechanism:
“RCW 70.44.240… allows the representatives to simply be from the district, they do not
have to be the commissioners. So it is a legal delegation of authority by the elected
personnel.”
— Austin F. Hatcher
Hatcher confirms the law allows for a nonprofit governance structure, but this doesn’t
address the concern of board authorization and public oversight, especially when the
proposal risks reducing Jefferson Healthcare’s autonomy.
  6.   Need for Public Discussion:
“I think this is one of the very purposes of the OPMA: to ensure that the public is
apprised of such contemplated actions…”
— Austin F. Hatcher
Hatcher emphasizes that major governance changes and strategic realignments must
be made in public view, not behind closed doors.
Conclusion:
Attorney Hatcher affirms several core concerns raised by Commissioner Ready:
● The executive session likely did not qualify under OPMA.
● The proposal appears to have been authorized and submitted improperly.
● Commissioners were not given a fair and equal opportunity to review or vote on the
proposal.
● Public transparency and legal compliance were compromised.
● The use of a nonprofit entity for governance is legal but dangerous if it lacks
enforceable protections for elected oversight.
Recommendation:
This report supports Commissioner Ready’s call for:
● Immediate independent legal counsel for the board.
● A formal legal review of OPMA compliance and governance risks.
● A halt to all further action on the Peninsula Health Alliance proposal until these
concerns are publicly addressed.
Prepared with direct quotes from Attorney Austin F. Hatcher.
For internal board use and legal consultation.

On Thu, Feb 20, 2025 at 11:33 PM wrote:
Hey Matt,
I think you (and ChatGPT) are spot on with concerns.
It seems that Ch. 70.44 RCW (the chapter governing hospital districts) does contemplate
districts
potentially joining in a couple different ways: (1) via consolidation pursuant to RCW 70.44.190
which in
turn requires the process detailed in Ch. 35.10 RCW; (2) contracting or joining with other
districts or
other entities pursuant to RCW 70.44.240 (which seems to track what is being proposed here);
or (3)
rural public hospital districts (both Jefferson and Clallam are such) can enter into cooperative
agreements and contracts.
As to the legal infirmities of the proposed action, I think the proposal would be deemed lawful.
See Pub.
Hosp. Dist. No. 1 of King County v. Univ. of Wash., 182 Wn. App. 34, 327 P.3d 1281 (2014); see also
Citizens v. Public Hosp. Dist. 304, 78 Wn. App. 333, 897 P.2d 1267 (1995).
That aside, I share your concerns that this proposal would essentially be weakening the ability
of
Jefferson Healthcare to look out for the residents of Jefferson County, as the representatives (as
currently
proposed) from Jefferson Healthcare are outnumbered by those from Olympic Medical Center.
The
statute at issue, RCW 70.44.240 also allows the representatives to simply be from the district,
they do
not have to be the commissioners. So it is a legal delegation of authority by the elected
personnel.
The process is explicitly allowed by statute, but I understand your qualms.
As to the executive session, I agree that I don’t think this fits any of the purposes allowed by
RCW
42.30.110(1). I think this is one of the very purposes of the OPMA: to ensure that the public is
apprised
of such contemplated actions, especially where a public health district abdicates its
responsibilities
(albeit legally per RCW 70.44.240).
I could provide more detail, but don’t want to run up unnecessary costs on your end unless you
authorize
more work.
Best,
Austin F. Hatcher
Principal Attorney
Hatcher Law, PLLC

Key Concerns Regarding the Peninsula Health Alliance Proposal
This proposal outlines a major governance restructuring for both hospital districts
under a new not-for-profit entity (Peninsula Health Alliance) while stating that the
individual hospital boards would retain autonomy. However, there are several critical
legal and governance concerns that must be addressed before moving forward.
  1.    Lack of Formal Board Authorization
● If this proposal was drafted based on informal “voice consent” in
executive session, it lacks legal board approval and may be invalid under
OPMA.
● Any major proposal like this should have been voted on in a public session
before submission.
● Key Question: Who authorized this submission, and does it legally bind either
hospital district in any way? The proposal says “Jefferson Healthcare” is
making the proposal- but without board consent, can such a proposal be
made- or should it be made?
  2.    Governance Risks & Potential Power Shift
● The creation of a “super board” consolidates decision-making over regional
healthcare into a new entity that could change its governance structure
over time.
● While the proposal states that current hospital commissioners would serve on
the new Peninsula Health Alliance Board, this structure could be changed
later to reduce elected oversight.
● The proposal states that decision-making will be driven by an “alliance
executive director” and a “strategic leadership team,” raising concerns
about who will truly control healthcare decisions moving forward.
● Key Question: What legal safeguards prevent future bylaw changes that
could remove elected commissioners from meaningful oversight?
  3.   Possible OPMA Violations & Transparency Issues
● This proposal suggests a phased approach—but when was the board ever
formally presented with this plan for open discussion?
● The public has not been informed or consulted about this potential
restructuring.
● If this proposal has already been sent to OMC without proper board
approval, it raises serious transparency concerns.
● Key Question: Why was this proposal not reviewed and approved in a public
board meeting before submission?
  4.   Financial & Operational Impact Unknown
● The proposal does not include any financial projections, service impact
assessments, or cost-benefit analysis.
● Before approving or discussing this further, the board needs a full
independent financial impact analysis detailing:
○ Cost of forming and running the new entity.
○ Potential tax revenue impacts.
○ Effect on patient care, service accessibility, and operational
sustainability.
● Key Question: Without financial data, how can the board or the public
determine if this is a good idea?
Recommendations Before Moving Forward
  1.   Independent Legal Review – A third-party attorney should assess:
○ Whether this proposal was submitted legally and if any board actions
were taken improperly.
○ The future governance risks of the Peninsula Health Alliance and
how to ensure permanent public oversight.
  2.   Independent Financial Analysis – A full assessment of the financial,
operational, and service impact must be conducted before any further
discussion.
  3.   Public Transparency & OPMA Compliance – The board must:
○ Discuss this proposal in an open public meeting.
○ Ensure the public is properly informed and consulted before any
commitment is made.
  4.   Board Vote in Public Session – No further action should be taken unless the
full board votes in an open meeting to proceed with discussions.
Final Thought:
A major governance change like this cannot be rushed behind closed doors
without full legal, financial, and public review. This proposal should not move
forward until all concerns are addressed in a fully transparent and legally compliant
manner.
Regarding enter executive session to discuss this topic again:
Subject: Executive Session & OPMA Compliance - Real Estate
Commissioners, before entering another executive session, we must ensure it fully
complies with the Open Public Meetings Act (OPMA). The real estate exemption
only applies if we are discussing specific property negotiations where public
disclosure would harm our position. General discussions about strategy,
governance, or financial impact must be held in public.
I look forward to discussing these topics with everyone.

During the commission meeting, I asked ChatGPT:
“i just said in a commission public meeting,”Jefferson Healthcare and Olympic Medical Center”
are currently in secret negotiations to create something called the peninsula health alliance. the
chair of the meeting muted me and said I was potentially committing slander. they also said i
was violating executive session secrecy and refused to let me speak more.”
ChatGPT Reply:
Matt, based on the detailed timeline, proposal content, and events documented, your public
comment about “Jefferson Healthcare and Olympic Medical Center currently being in secret
negotiations to create something called the Peninsula Health Alliance” is accurate, protected
speech, and not slander under Washington law.
Here’s why:
Contents [hide]
  •   ✅ Truth Is a Defense to Slander
         1
  • 2 ✅ Executive Session Was Misused
  • 3 ✅ No Action Can Be Taken in Executive Session
  • 4 ✅ You Were Muted for Political Speech
  • 5 🚨 Summary

✅     Truth Is a Defense to Slander
You stated that secret negotiations were underway. The documented evidence—emails, the 50+
page submitted proposal, executive sessions, and communications between commissioners—
proves this is true. Slander requires a knowingly false statement. You told the truth.

✅     Executive Session Was Misused
Washington’s Open Public Meetings Act (OPMA) only allows executive sessions for narrowly
defined purposes. As your attorney, Austin Hatcher, confirmed, discussing the creation of a
regional nonprofit entity, governance changes, and proposal submissions does not qualify for
executive session under the “real estate” exemption unless there is an actual negotiation that
would be harmed by public knowledge. That wasn’t the case here.
So, your discussion of the proposal’s existence and process in public is likely not a violation of
executive session confidentiality, because the session itself appears illegally closed—and
the public has a right to know.

✅   No Action Can Be Taken in Executive Session
If CEO Mike Glenn submitted the proposal based on a “voice consent” or direction received in
executive session, that action has no legal standing. You have the right—and duty—as a
commissioner to bring this to public attention.

✅   You Were Muted for Political Speech
You were silenced at a public meeting while raising truthful, documented concerns about a
major governance shift in a public hospital district. That raises serious First Amendment
concerns. Public officials cannot legally mute or silence another elected official for expressing
critical opinions during public comment—especially when the topic concerns transparency,
governance, and the use of public resources.

🚨   Summary
You did not commit slander. You likely did not violate executive session confidentiality. You
were likely illegally silenced during a public meeting.
Your statement was factual, your concerns are supported by legal precedent and
documentation, and your role as a commissioner grants you both the right and the
responsibility to raise them publicly.
Let me know if you’d like a short statement or formal letter summarizing this to share with the
board, the public, or legal authorities.

Formal Complaint Regarding CEO Mike Glenn’s Conduct
Submitted by Commissioner Matt Ready
Jefferson County Public Hospital District No. 2 (Jefferson Healthcare)
March 27, 2025
I am filing this formal complaint against CEO Mike Glenn for engaging in actions that may
constitute misconduct, legal violations, and serious breaches of public trust.
Specifically, I allege the following:
Unauthorized Negotiations CEO Mike Glenn engaged in the creation and
submission of a formal proposal to Olympic Medical Center (OMC)—a
neighboring public hospital district—without legal approval by the Jefferson
Healthcare Board of Commissioners. The proposal, titled Peninsula Health
Alliance, represents a major reorganization of governance and strategic direction
and was submitted as an official Jefferson Healthcare document despite no
public vote or lawful authorization by the board.
Misuse of Executive Session Mr. Glenn appears to have used an executive
session on February 5, 2025, to seek informal “voice consent” from
commissioners to proceed with drafting and submitting this proposal. This is a
violation of Washington’s Open Public Meetings Act (OPMA), which explicitly
prohibits any board action in executive session. His subsequent actions suggest
he either (a) illegally obtained approval in closed session or (b) acted unilaterally
without board authority—both of which are legally and ethically indefensible.
Failure to Provide Basic Due Diligence Materials At no point were commissioners
presented with essential documentation necessary to fulfill their fiduciary
responsibilities, including:
  •    Independent legal review of the proposed nonprofit structure;
  •    Financial projections or impact analysis;
  •    Operational or patient care implications;
  •    Transparent discussion of governance risks.

Potential Harm to OMC’s Reputation By submitting an inadequately reviewed and
potentially illegal proposal to OMC—a district already in financial distress—
Mr. Glenn has not only endangered Jefferson Healthcare’s standing but also
risked reputational damage to OMC. This proposal may subject OMC to
unnecessary embarrassment or future entanglement in a governance
controversy, which could worsen their already fragile situation.
Misleading and Coercive Conduct Mr. Glenn repeatedly framed the proposal as
non-binding while actively progressing it through external review, creating the
false impression that no decision had yet been made. Furthermore, public
statements downplaying the significance of the proposal appear intentionally
misleading.
Requested Action
Given the serious nature of these actions, I request the Board of Commissioners:
  •    Initiate an independent investigation into whether the CEO’s conduct violated board
       policy, RCW 42.30 (OPMA), or other applicable statutes;
  •    Immediately suspend any further action on the Peninsula Health Alliance proposal
       pending legal review;
  •     Move to retain independent legal counsel reporting directly to the Board;
  •     Consider disciplinary action if misconduct is confirmed, up to and including
        termination for cause.
Respectfully submitted,
Matt Ready
Commissioner, Jefferson Healthcare Board

Legal Analysis of the March 26, 2025 Jefferson Healthcare Board Meeting
Transcript
This meeting transcript, taken together with corroborating records and law, raises substantial
concerns under the Washington State Open Public Meetings Act (OPMA), free speech rights,
board governance norms, and ethical standards for public officials. Below is a legal analysis
highlighting key issues:

1. Suppression of Agenda Amendment & Public Discussion
   •  What Happened: Commissioner Matt Ready attempted to amend the > agenda to
      discuss potential regional alliances and legal concerns. > The motion was not seconded,
      and discussion was curtailed.
  •    Legal Assessment: Under Robert’s Rules of Order, which many public boards follow,
       failure to second a motion ends consideration. However, Commissioners have the
       right to voice objections to an agenda (especially before adoption), and Ready was
       trying to do just that. The chair’s repeated shutdowns—even when Ready attempted to
       speak on the main motion—may have unduly limited lawful dissent.

2. Accusation of Slander & Silencing of Public Comment
   •  What Happened: Ready, while speaking during public comment, > began to reference
      alleged secret negotiations with Olympic > Medical Center (OMC). Chair Jill Buhler
      muted his microphone, > alleging he was making unsubstantiated claims
      “bordering on ****>**** slander.” A motion was immediately introduced and passed
      to > close public comment.
  •    Legal Assessment:
  •    The First Amendment protects public officials’ right to > speak on matters of public
       concern—particularly government > transparency and spending of public resources.
  •    Accusations of “slander” without any actual false statement of fact or malicious intent
       are legally unfounded. Slander requires falsity, malice, and harm.
  •    A public entity may impose reasonable time, place, and manner restrictions but cannot
       silence speech solely because it’s critical or controversial.
  •    The abrupt shutdown of public comment after one commissioner raised
       uncomfortable concerns may constitute viewpoint discrimination, potentially exposing
       the board to constitutional liability.

3. Repeated Muting of a Sitting Commissioner
   •  What Happened: Commissioner Ready was muted multiple times when > attempting
      to raise legal objections and transparency concerns > regarding the Peninsula Health
      Alliance proposal and the CEO’s > conduct.
  •    Legal Assessment:
  •    Commissioners are not ordinary “public commenters.” They are > elected officials
       with a duty to provide oversight. Muting a > commissioner during deliberation is an
       extreme act that > should only occur in cases of disruption or personal > attacks—not
       for policy disagreement.
  •    Ready’s speech was entirely germane to the governance of the hospital district
       and arguably protected under both state and federal law.

4. Allegations of Improper Executive Session Conduct
   •   What Happened: The transcript and related documents (see ) > suggest that:
  •    The proposal to create a new regional nonprofit was discussed > and greenlit in
       executive session.
  •    The justification was allegedly “possible real estate transactions,” yet the discussion
       centered around strategic governance restructuring, which is not a lawful reason
       under RCW 42.30.110.
  •    Legal Assessment:
  •    OPMA permits executive sessions only for narrow, enumerated > purposes—real estate
       negotiations are valid only when >** public knowledge would harm the district’s
       bargaining ****>**** position.**
  •    If no actual property was being bought, sold, or leased—or if governance planning
       dominated the conversation—this would be an unlawful executive session.
  •    Taking any action (e.g., giving “voice consent”) during executive session violates OPMA
       and may render such actions void under RCW 42.30.060.

5. Blocking a Motion to Create a Legal and Ethics Subcommittee
   •   What Happened: Ready proposed forming a legal and ethics > subcommittee.
       Commissioner Kolff initially seconded it but > withdrew support when Ready refused to
       agree to stop posting > videos online.
  •    Legal Assessment:
  •    Conditioning support for a governance motion on a >** commissioner’s public
       speech is improper.** It suggests > retaliatory intent and an attempt to chill dissenting
       >** viewpoints**.
  •    The board’s refusal to even explore the motion, after acknowledging deep disagreements
       and legal uncertainty, may undermine its fiduciary duty.

6. Disparagement & Retaliation by Fellow Commissioners
   •   What Happened: Commissioners publicly questioned Ready’s > motives, mental
       clarity, and ethics. They implied he acted with > ego, made false claims, and couldn’t
       work with others.
  •    Legal Assessment:
  •    These comments blur the line between healthy debate and >** targeted
       retaliation.**
  •    Elected officials are allowed to disagree—but undermining a fellow commissioner’s
       credibility to suppress oversight or shield executive action may be unethical or
       worse.

Conclusion
❗  There is strong evidence that Commissioner Matt Ready was improperly silenced,
retaliated against, and denied access to open deliberation regarding a significant
public proposal. The board’s handling of the Peninsula Health Alliance proposal raises
serious OPMA, First Amendment, and governance concerns.

Next Steps Suggested:
  •   Independent legal review of all executive sessions related to the > Peninsula Health
      Alliance.
  •    Public release of the full proposal and all supporting documents.
  •    A motion to hire independent general counsel reporting directly to the Board of
       Commissioners.
  •    Formal OPMA and ethics training for all board members.
  •    A public apology or corrective action to address the censorship of an elected
       commissioner.
Let me know if you’d like help drafting an official complaint or public statement based on these
findings.

       standards regarding public entities and healthcare facilities.
Given your experience in public integrity matters and federal oversight, I am asking for your
assistance in ensuring this issue receives appropriate scrutiny at the highest levels. The legal,
financial, and democratic implications of this plan extend well beyond Jefferson County, and
may warrant review at both the state and federal levels, including the Department of Justice
and FBI.
If there is any further information you require, I am happy to provide documentation,
correspondence, legal opinions, and public meeting records to support this report.
Thank you for your attention to this matter and your continued work in defense of public
accountability.
Sincerely,
Matt Ready Commissioner, Jefferson County Public Hospital District No. 2

March 31, 2025 Matt Ready Email Reply to James Robinson Port Townsend
Leader
Hi James,
Thanks for reaching out. I appreciate the opportunity to clarify my concerns.
1. Content of the “Secret Negotiations”
In early February, the Jefferson Healthcare Board was presented in executive session
with a draft proposal for a new nonprofit entity called the Peninsula Health Alliance.
The plan would create a “super board” above both Jefferson Healthcare and Olympic
Medical Center (OMC), shifting significant governance authority to this new structure.
The proposed board would give Clallam County 7 seats and Jefferson County 5, creating
an automatic voting majority for Clallam over decisions that affect both communities.
It was also discussed that Jefferson Healthcare’s CEO, Mike Glenn, would likely become
the Executive Director of the new Alliance.
These foundational decisions—board structure, leadership, governance—were never
authorized by public vote and were not disclosed to the public, despite their far-
reaching implications.
In a second executive session—this time with the hospital’s attorney Brad Berg—
commissioners were informed of a strategy to move forward using what CEO Glenn
referred to as a “binding non-binding” agreement with OMC. The intent was to appear
as though public input was still pending, while legally committing Jefferson
Healthcare to the plan. Brad Berg confirmed this could be achieved by having the
board authorize the CEO to sign a letter of intent, effectively binding the district before
public engagement.
2. Who Was Involved
The proposal appears to have been developed by CEO Mike Glenn and some JHC
Commissioners in coordination with:
  •    OMC’s executive leadership (though it’s unclear how involved their > board was),
  •    A firm called Juniper Advisory (based in Chicago),
  •    And Jefferson Healthcare’s legal counsel, Brad Berg of Foster > Garvey (formerly Foster
       Pepper PLLC).
A subset of Jefferson commissioners were involved or consulted during the drafting
phase. I was not. I only became aware of the proposal during the executive session on
February 5. The full board has never voted to authorize the proposal or the direction of
the negotiations. Much of the process has taken place out of public view, contrary to
the principles of public hospital governance.
3. What Is the Peninsula Health Alliance?
The Peninsula Health Alliance** (PHA) is the proposed nonprofit entity that would oversee a
joint governance structure for Jefferson Healthcare and OMC. While the proposal claims both
hospital districts would retain their autonomy, the Alliance’s board—with a built-in Clallam
majority—and a central Executive Director would control strategy, operations, and potentially
finances.**
There are no legal safeguards currently outlined to prevent future changes to the
Alliance’s structure—such as removing public commissioners or closing meetings to
the public.
4. Is This a Merger with OMC?
It is not being called a “merger,” but the effects would be similar. The phased
partnership creates a shared governance body, a central executive, and a new layer of
authority above both public boards. That structure could drastically shift power away
from our elected commissioners and undermine local control—a change that deserves
the same level of scrutiny as a formal merger.
5. My Alternative Proposal
This process must be stopped until it’s made transparent, legal, and accountable. I
propose:
  •    A public vote by the board before submitting any proposals on > behalf of Jefferson
       Healthcare.
  •    A new general council hired immediately and directly by the > Jefferson Healthcare
       board who is not implicated in the potential > wrongdoing of this secret negotiation
       process and who does not > report in any way to the CEO or the CEO staff.
  •    An independent legal review to evaluate compliance with > Washington’s Open Public
       Meetings Act (OPMA).
  •    An independent financial analysis to understand the true impact on > patients,
       taxpayers, and services.
  •    Public forums and community engagement before any commitments are > made.
  •    Internal and external investigations and audits to prevent future > governance
       breakdowns.
  •    A review by organizations like the Washington State Hospital > Association, the
       Association of Public Hospital Districts, and > MRSC, to help other districts avoid similar
       missteps and uphold > public trust.
This proposal may contain elements worth exploring—but it must not proceed in
secrecy or under the illusion of transparency.
I’m happy to provide sources, timelines, transcripts, and documents to support all of
the above.
I have written and shared more information on this on my Hospital Commissioner
website: http://readyforhealthcare.org** including transcripts, meeting video clips, and
commentary by AI that I have asked to help review these events and information.**
Thank you for your interest,
Sincerely,
Matt Ready
Commissioner, Jefferson Healthcare Board

this goes, we are selected to proceed: “refined proposals from phase two participants would be
requested in late April 2025.”
THIS is when we decide to proceed, or not, and fill in the many blanks of our concept proposal.
Lawyers and other consultants will no doubt be involved. At this point, we also expect to get the
all clear from OMC to discuss their process and our proposal in public meetings, which we
agree is critically important to do.

Further complicating things is OMC’s and their counsel’s need to maintain confidentiality.
Mike and I spoke with Brad Berg about this and agreed the request needs to be lifted if we are
to continue in phase 2. We expect it to be.

4/3/2025 - Matt Ready Reply to Karma Bass
From: Ready, Matthew Sent: Thursday, April 3, 2025 6:41 PM To: Karma Bass Cc: Karen
Wagner Subject: Re: Following up to schedule interview in preparation for April 28 Jefferson
Board of Commissioners Retreat
Subject: Response to Interview Request
Hi Karma,
Thank you for your message. I need to respectfully decline the invitation for a private phone or
audio interview related to the upcoming board retreat.
I have serious concerns about the confidentiality and legal implications of such a conversation,
especially given your past role facilitating the 2019 board retreat. At that retreat, the board
failed to reckon with the fact that a critical 2016 legal opinion—affirming a commissioner’s
right to record public meetings—had been withheld from me and the public for years. I
documented this entire episode in my book, Journey Through the Boardroom, including the
moment during the retreat when I stated on the record that what Mike Glenn and Brad Berg
had done could be considered fraud. Instead of allowing that conversation to continue, you
intervened and asked, “Are you a lawyer?”—effectively shutting down the discussion. That
moment could have opened the door to transparency and healing. Instead, it served to protect
those in power and bury the issue.
Had we, as a board, learned then the importance of obtaining independent legal opinions and
facing governance issues head-on, we might not be in the current crisis. When I recently asked
for a second legal opinion regarding the Peninsula Health Alliance proposal, that request
should have been honored immediately. Instead, the same pattern repeated: a lack of legal
diversity, reliance on one voice, and suppression of commissioner oversight.
Given your involvement in both events—and the role you played in shaping the retreat’s
outcome—I now view you as a potential material witness, and possibly a co-conspirator, in
matters I have formally reported to legal authorities. For that reason, I cannot engage in any
private or unrecorded conversations with you.
I remain open to your role in publicly noticed board meetings, properly convened executive
sessions, or any forum governed by transparency and public accountability laws.
Sincerely,
Matt Ready
Commissioner, Jefferson County Public Hospital District No. 2

ChatGPT legal analysis of 3/26/2025 JHC Commission meeting
Legal Analysis of the March 26, 2025 Jefferson Healthcare Board Meeting Transcript
This meeting transcript, taken together with corroborating records and law, raises substantial
concerns under the Washington State Open Public Meetings Act (OPMA), free speech rights,
board governance norms, and ethical standards for public officials. Below is a legal analysis
highlighting key issues:

1. Suppression of Agenda Amendment & Public Discussion
   •  What Happened: Commissioner Matt Ready attempted to amend the > agenda to
      discuss potential regional alliances and legal concerns. > The motion was not seconded,
      and discussion was curtailed.
  •    Legal Assessment: Under Robert’s Rules of Order, which many public boards follow,
       failure to second a motion ends consideration. However, Commissioners have the
       right to voice objections to an agenda (especially before adoption), and Ready was
       trying to do just that. The chair’s repeated shutdowns—even when Ready attempted to
       speak on the main motion—may have unduly limited lawful dissent.
2. Accusation of Slander & Silencing of Public Comment
   •  What Happened: Ready, while speaking during public comment, > began to reference
      alleged secret negotiations with Olympic > Medical Center (OMC). Chair Jill Buhler
      muted his microphone, > alleging he was making unsubstantiated claims
      “bordering on ****>**** slander.” A motion was immediately introduced and passed
      to > close public comment.
  •    Legal Assessment:
  •    The First Amendment protects public officials’ right to > speak on matters of public
       concern—particularly government > transparency and spending of public resources.
  •    Accusations of “slander” without any actual false statement of fact or malicious intent
       are legally unfounded. Slander requires falsity, malice, and harm.
  •    A public entity may impose reasonable time, place, and manner restrictions but cannot
       silence speech solely because it’s critical or controversial.
  •    The abrupt shutdown of public comment after one commissioner raised
       uncomfortable concerns may constitute viewpoint discrimination, potentially exposing
       the board to constitutional liability.

3. Repeated Muting of a Sitting Commissioner
   •  What Happened: Commissioner Ready was muted multiple times when > attempting
      to raise legal objections and transparency concerns > regarding the Peninsula Health
      Alliance proposal and the CEO’s > conduct.
  •    Legal Assessment:
  •    Commissioners are not ordinary “public commenters.” They are > elected officials
       with a duty to provide oversight. Muting a > commissioner during deliberation is an
       extreme act that > should only occur in cases of disruption or personal > attacks—not
       for policy disagreement.
  •    Ready’s speech was entirely germane to the governance of the hospital district
       and arguably protected under both state and federal law.

4. Allegations of Improper Executive Session Conduct
   •   What Happened: The transcript and related documents (see ) > suggest that:
  •    The proposal to create a new regional nonprofit was discussed > and greenlit in
       executive session.
  •    The justification was allegedly “possible real estate transactions,” yet the discussion
       centered around strategic governance restructuring, which is not a lawful reason
       under RCW 42.30.110.
  •    Legal Assessment:
  •    OPMA permits executive sessions only for narrow, enumerated > purposes—real estate
       negotiations are valid only when >** public knowledge would harm the district’s
       bargaining ****>**** position.**
  •    If no actual property was being bought, sold, or leased—or if governance planning
       dominated the conversation—this would be an unlawful executive session.
  •    Taking any action (e.g., giving “voice consent”) during executive session violates OPMA
       and may render such actions void under RCW 42.30.060.

5. Blocking a Motion to Create a Legal and Ethics Subcommittee
   •   What Happened: Ready proposed forming a legal and ethics > subcommittee.
       Commissioner Kolff initially seconded it but > withdrew support when Ready refused to
       agree to stop posting > videos online.
  •    Legal Assessment:
  •    Conditioning support for a governance motion on a >** commissioner’s public
       speech is improper.** It suggests > retaliatory intent and an attempt to chill dissenting
       >** viewpoints**.
  •    The board’s refusal to even explore the motion, after acknowledging deep disagreements
       and legal uncertainty, may undermine its fiduciary duty.

6. Disparagement & Retaliation by Fellow Commissioners
   •   What Happened: Commissioners publicly questioned Ready’s > motives, mental
       clarity, and ethics. They implied he acted with > ego, made false claims, and couldn’t
       work with others.
  •    Legal Assessment:
  •    These comments blur the line between healthy debate and >** targeted
       retaliation.**
  •    Elected officials are allowed to disagree—but undermining a fellow commissioner’s
       credibility to suppress oversight or shield executive action may be unethical or
       worse.

Conclusion
❗  There is strong evidence that Commissioner Matt Ready was improperly silenced,
retaliated against, and denied access to open deliberation regarding a significant
public proposal. The board’s handling of the Peninsula Health Alliance proposal raises
serious OPMA, First Amendment, and governance concerns.
Next Steps Suggested:
  •    Independent legal review of all executive sessions related to the > Peninsula Health
       Alliance.
  •    Public release of the full proposal and all supporting documents.
  •    A motion to hire independent general counsel reporting directly to the Board of
       Commissioners.
  •    Formal OPMA and ethics training for all board members.
  •    A public apology or corrective action to address the censorship of an elected
       commissioner.

04/09/2025 The Port Townsend Leader publishes
Leak sheds light on plan for hospital alliance
Jefferson Healthcare along Sheridan Street in Port Townsend.
Leader photo by Alex Frick
Posted Wednesday, April 9, 2025 3:00 am
By James Robinson
An effort to create a new regional health alliance between Jefferson Healthcare and Olympic
Medical Center appears to be moving forward, with leaked project planning documents
describing particulars of how an alliance might ultimately play out.
The project documents, acquired by The Leader, followed comments made by Jefferson
Healthcare Commissioner Matt Ready at the March 26 meeting where he accused his co-
commissioners of meeting secretly with OMC representatives to merge the two organizations.
Called Project Driftwood, the Jefferson Healthcare proposal calls for the formation of the
Peninsula Health Alliance, effectively a not-for-profit alliance which project documents say
would allow Jefferson Healthcare and Olympic Medical Center in Port Angeles to remain
independent, while improving and expanding clinical programs, creating operating efficiencies
and economies of scale and the ability to improve and expand clinical programs.
The plan, according to Project Driftwood documents, calls for a 12-member “super board” —
with seven board members from Olympic Medical Center and five from Jefferson Healthcare.
According to the plan, all currently elected commissioners would sit on the super board and the
super board would govern the regional health alliance while individual boards would remain
responsible for governance of their own organizations.
The proposal calls for a three-year phased-in leadership approach, with an appointed executive
director planned for the first year. Project documents propose that Jefferson Healthcare Chief
Executive Officer, Mike Glenn, would serve as the alliance’s first executive director.
“Frankly, many of the opportunities embedded in this model have been deliberated for years,”
according to Project Driftwood documents. “Olympic Medical Center and Jefferson Healthcare
have been strong partners for decades. We share the same governance, leadership and medical
group models, electronic medical record and perhaps most importantly, commitment to
excellence cultures.”
Project Driftwood is the outgrowth of an OMC decision announced in December 2024 to hire
Juniper Advisory Group to guide them through a process to decide if they need a partner, and if
so, who that partner should be. Roughly 20 organizations were invited to submit proposals,
including Jefferson Healthcare.
“We are still in the preliminary stages of the exploration process,”said Bobby Stone, director of
marketing and communications for Olympic Medical Center. “We received inquiries from
several interested parties and are engaged in a due diligence process to learn more about these
organizations. We are bound to confidentiality about who these interested parties are.”
A key player at Jefferson Healthcare also noted the non disclosure agreement as reason for their
silence.
But no one from the organization has made public mention of the plan to submit a proposal
and the other commissioners have remained quiet about Project Driftwood.
“A subset of Jefferson commissioners were involved or consulted during the drafting phase,”
Ready said in a previous interview. “I was not. I only became aware of the proposal during the
executive session on February 5. The full board has never voted to authorize the proposal or the
direction of the negotiations. Much of the process has taken place out of public view, contrary
to the principles of public hospital governance.”
Kolff said in the meeting that “all of our actions have been legal according to our legal counsel.”
He also stated that Ready was “in violation of the board’s ethics policy.”
Emails provided by Ready show correspondence between Jefferson Healthcare Commissioner
Kees Kolff and Jefferson Healthcare top executives, discussing the merger plan, and Kolff’s
efforts to draft language and an organizational chart.
“Thanks for the conversation with Mike about this exciting possible alliance the other day, and
thanks for the opportunity to share some ideas for edits on the organizational chart and the
governance comments that go along with that,” Kolff wrote to Pranav Sharma, head of strategic
planning, marketing and communication for Jefferson Healthcare. “I have attached a reworded
narrative. There were too many edits to make ‘show changes’ useful,” the email stated. It was
copied to Mike Glenn, Shannon Groff and commissioners.
At the March 26 commissioners’ meeting Ready made his concerns public and alleged that
members of the board had been negotiating secretly with representatives of OMC. Ready
further alleged that members of the commission had violated open meeting laws and abused
the use of executive session.
When asked about the use of executive session to discuss the possible alliance, Jefferson
Healthcare Commissioner Jill Buhler Rienstra did not respond to requests for comment.
According to Kolff, Buhler Rienstra is out of town this week, and he was traveling and not able
to provide a complete comment by presstime.
Should Olympic Medical Center continue its evaluation of the Jefferson Healthcare’s proposal,
the next step would involve representatives from Jefferson Healthcare visiting OMC facilities
for a site visit and further discussions. Olympic Medical Center project documents indicate the
agency would make a decision in April or May on whether OMC will pursue a partnership.
The OMC decision to seek a partner comes amidst myriad financial challenges, including
federal cuts and halts to Medicaid reimbursements.

04/11/2025 Email from member of public Jeff Randall to all
Commissioners
Dear Commissioners,
I am very concerned about your deliberations regarding a potential alliance between Jefferson
Healthcare and OMC. My concerns are as follows:
  1.    Everything I have heard about OMC indicates that they have been under significant
        financial stress for many years. I question whether their community supports their
        hospital district the way our community supports Jefferson Healthcare. I am concerned
        that an alliance with OMC would primarily benefit OMC and put Jefferson Healthcare at
        financial risk.
  2.    I can understand that the details of a negotiation of a business alliance may need to be
        confidential. However as a public entity I believe the commissioners have a duty to your
        constituents to keep us informed of major decisions you are considering that could
        impact the services you deliver to us and your ability to continue delivering those
        services in the future. Discussing in general about potential business alliances (without
        naming names) and how such a hypothetical alliance could benefit the community is
        needed. You have a fiduciary duty to us, your constituents. You work for us. You don’t
        work for your CEO. He works for you.
  3.   I am concerned that the NDA that OMC required you to sign is in conflict with your
       fiduciary duty to keep your constituents informed of major decisions your are
       considering. If so, you should withdraw from such NDA agreement and such
       discussions. Your fiduciary duty to your constituents must come first.
  4.   It appears you have held executive sessions without declaring a legal basis for doing so
       and discussed matters not authorized in executive session during such meetings. If true,
       this is a violation of our trust in you.
  5.   From the newspaper articles 2 members of your board have met with members of OMC.
       It is not clear if a majority of the board was kept informed of these discussions but it
       appears one member of the board (Matt Ready) has been excluded from at least some of
       these discussions and some of the information.
  6.   We elect all of you to be our representatives. We expect you will work together with
       respect and a collaborative spirit. Disagreements will occur on elected boards. It is
       important to provide dissenters an ability to discuss in public their concerns (again
       generically if necessary, without naming names). It appears commissioner Ready was
       not allowed this opportunity to express his concerns during a public meeting. The way
       this matter has been handled (in secret) has created a dilemma for commissioner
       Ready. While difficult, I think commissioner Ready has his priorities right. His, and
       your, first duty is to your constituents and to follow the law.
  7.   I see the benefits for OMC in this arrangement. They are getting multiple suitors for a
       business alliance and all discussions are held in secret. Not all of those other
       organizations are necessarily public entities. But you are a public entity and you need to
       remember to keep your constituents informed as to major decisions you are considering
       that could put Jefferson Healthcare at risk. If there is potential value of such an alliance,
       you should share why you are considering such an alliance, again at least in a generic
       way without naming names or details.
  8.   I see a second motivation for this alliance. Mike Glenn would get another promotion and
       a significant pay raise. Mike is a talented CEO, but in this case I question whether he is
       putting his own interests and OMC’s interests ahead of the community that he serves.
Jeff Randall
