04/14/225 Email to Karen Wagner Via Consulting from Matt Ready
Subject: Response to Self-Assessment Survey Invitation
Hi Karen,
Thank you for reaching out with the invitation to participate in the Jefferson Healthcare board
self-assessment survey. I’m writing to inform you that I will not be participating in this survey
or any other private preparatory activity associated with the upcoming board retreat being
facilitated by Karma Bass and or Via Healthcare Consulting.
This is not a personal decision about you or your professionalism, but rather a principled
response to a serious governance and legal situation that remains unresolved. I have ongoing
concerns related to transparency, legality, and the role Karma Bass and her company Via
Healthcare Consulting previously played in events that are now central to a formal criminal
complaint I’ve filed as an elected commissioner of Jefferson County Public Hospital District
No. 2.
Karma Bass served as the facilitator for Jefferson Healthcare’s 2019 board retreat. During that
retreat, I raised deeply concerning facts regarding a 2016 legal opinion that had been withheld
from me and the public for years—an opinion that affirmed a commissioner’s legal right to
record public meetings under Washington law. When I stated in that meeting that the actions
taken by then-CEO Mike Glenn and attorney Brad Berg in concealing that opinion could be
considered fraudulent, Karma intervened not to help the board reflect or take accountability,
but to shut down the discussion by asking, “Are you a lawyer?”
This moment, which I consider a pivotal failure of the board to reckon with wrongdoing, is one
of many I documented in detail—including transcripts and internal emails—in my book
published in 2023, “Journey Through the Boardroom: An Insider’s Perspective on Hospital
Governance: A true story about corporatism, truth, tactics, life, liberty, and wisdom. Please abide
and comply.” That book outlines how institutional power and professional facilitators were
used to suppress accountability rather than promote it. Karma Bass is named in that
documentation as a central figure in enabling this suppression during two separate retreat
facilitation incidents.
Now, in 2025, your firm is again facilitating a board retreat at the request of the same CEO who
has been at the center of multiple OPMA and transparency controversies. I cannot, in good
conscience, participate in any retreat preparation process run by Karma’s firm. I consider her
not a neutral facilitator, but a potential material witness in matters I have reported to legal
authorities, and possibly a co-conspirator in efforts to obstruct governance oversight.
Furthermore, I have significant legal concerns that the structure of this “self-assessment”—
where your firm gathers individualized responses from each commissioner and compiles them
to prepare retreat content—may constitute a hub-and-spoke serial meeting, which would be
in violation of Washington State’s Open Public Meetings Act (OPMA). I will not participate in
any activity that risks exposing the board to further legal jeopardy or contributes to a pattern of
concealed decision-making.
That said, I remain entirely committed to participating in publicly noticed board meetings,
properly convened retreats, and executive sessions conducted in accordance with the
law. I will continue to serve as a fully engaged commissioner, advocating for transparency,
legal integrity, and genuine public accountability.
Thank you for your understanding. Please do not interpret this as a lack of commitment to
board effectiveness—but rather, as a commitment to lawful, ethical governance that serves the
public first.
Sincerely, Matt Ready Commissioner, Jefferson County Public Hospital District No. 2 Author,
Journey Through the Boardroom

On 4/8/2025 1 was assigned to an investigation by Sheriff Pernsteiner. Sheriff Pernsteiner
requested I review, analyze and investigate the complaint for any criminal wrongdoings. The
email I received from Sheriff Pernsteiner consisted of three (3) documents: raw transcripts

       Peninsula Health Alliance Proposal (l).pdf
Below outlines my examination and evaluation of the documents, RCW’s, legislation and case
law.
Key Points —
  •    It seems likely that the actions described may violate the Washington State Open Public
       Meetings Act (OPMA), with potential civil penalties, but criminal charges are less
       certain and would need further investigation.
  •    Research suggests possible official misconduct, a gross misdemeanor, if actions were
       taken with intent to benefit or deprive rights, but proving intent is complex.
  •    The evidence leans toward unauthorized board actions and suppression of
       transparency, raising concerns about public trust and governance.
Background —
The complaint alleges misconduct by Jefferson Healthcare leadership, including misuse of
executive sessions, unauthorized actions, and suppression of public information, potentially
impacting criminal law in Washington state.
Analysis —
The allegations center on violations of the OPMA, which requires public meetings for governing
bodies like hospital district boards, with limited exceptions for executive sessions. The
complaint suggests executive sessions were misused to discuss a governance proposal under a
real estate pretext, likely violating OPMA, as only specific real estate price discussions are
allowed in private (Washington State Legislature - RCW 42.30). Unauthorized submission of a
proposal without public board approval may also breach district governance laws under
Chapter 70.44 RCW, potentially constituting official misconduct under RCW 9A.80.010 if intent
to benefit or deprive rights is shown. Suppression of commissioner speech and misleading
statements could further complicate legal standing, possibly involving civil penalties but with
criminal implications less clear without proven intent.
No single section of Chapter 70.44 RCW explicitly states “unauthorized submission of a
proposal is prohibited.” However, RCW 70.44.060 establishes the commissioners as the
governing body with decision-making power. An unauthorized action by an individual (ie., a
superintendent or employee) could be interpreted as exceeding their delegated authority,
violating the governance structure set forth in this section. Additionally, RCW 70.44.050
requires commissioners to act collectively at “regular or special meetings,” reinforcing that
official actions, like approving proposals, must occur through formal board processes—not
unilaterally.
Regarding the connection to RCW 9A.80.010 (official misconduct), a violation of RCW 70.44.060
could potentially align with misconduct if intent to “obtain a benefit or deprive another of a
benefit” is proven, as this criminal statute requires a public servant to knowingly commit an
unauthorized act under color of law. However, this would depend on evidence of intent, which
Chapter 70.44 RCW itself does not address—it focuses on structure and authority, not
criminality.

Unexpected Details —
An unexpected aspect is the potential involvement of legal counsel as a co-conspirator, which
could raise ethical issues for the Washington State Bar Association, though criminal liability
remains uncertain.
Note -
This note provides a comprehensive analysis of the allegations in the complaint submitted by
Commissioner Matt Ready regarding suspected misconduct at Jefferson Healthcare, focusing on
potential violations of Washington state criminal law. The complaint, dated March 26, 2025,
details issues such as misuse of executive sessions, unauthorized board actions, suppression of
public transparency, and coordinated behavior possibly rising to criminal conspiracy or
racketeering. The evaluation considers relevant statutes, case law, and the provided evidence,
including emails, meeting transcripts, and legal opinions.
Legal Framework and Relevant Statutes —
Washington state law, particularly the Open Public Meetings Act (OPMA) under Chapter 42.30
RCW, mandates that meetings of governing bodies of public agencies, including public hospital
districts, be open to the public, with specific exceptions for executive sessions. Executive
sessions are permitted for limited purposes, such as discussing the minimum price for real
estate sales or leases when public knowledge could affect prices, as outlined in RCW and (l)(c)
(Washington State Legislature - RCW 42.30). The Washington Supreme Court, in Columbia
Riverkeepers v. Port of Vancouver (2017), narrowed this exception, ruling that only price
minimums, not broader negotiations, can be discussed privately (MRSC - The Supreme Court
Narrowly Construes the “Minimum-Value” Executive Session Exception to the OPMA).
Public hospital districts are governed by Chapter 70.44 RCW, with board powers and duties
detailed in RCW 70.44.060, including contracting, property acquisition, and operational
decisions (Washington State Legislature - Chapter 70.44 RCW). Criminal laws potentially
applicable include official misconduct under RCW 9A.80.010, defined as a public servant
intentionally committing unauthorized acts or refraining from duties with intent to obtain a
benefit or deprive rights, classified as a gross misdemeanor (Washington State Legislature RCW
9A.80.010). Criminal conspiracy is covered under RCW 9A.28.040, requiring an agreement to
commit a crime with a substantial step taken (Washington State Legislature - RCW 9A.28.040).
Racketeering, under Chapter 9A.82 RCW, involves a pattern of criminal profiteering activity for
financial gain, with definitions including acts like murder and robbery (Washington state
Legislature - Chapter 9A.82 RCW).
Analysis of Allegations —

Misuse of Executive Sessions
The complaint alleges that executive sessions were held under the pretense of discussing
’possible real estate transactions” but actually centered on a regional governance restructuring
with Olympic Medical Center (OMC) through the Peninsula Health Alliance, a nonprofit entity,
without specific property negotiations. This appears to violate OPMA, as the Washington
Supreme Court limits executive session discussions to minimum prices for real estate, not
governance strategies. Attorney Austin Hatcher’s legal opinion, dated March 26, 2025, states,
“The executive session was under a very stretched reading of the ‘lease’ purposes of RCW
42.30.110(1)(b) and (c)… That is not the case here,” supporting the likelihood of an OPMA
violation (Digital Media Law Project - Open Meetings Laws in Washington).
Timeline evidence, such as the February 5, 2025, executive session discussing the proposal
without real estate specifics, and CEO Mike Glenn’s email on February 12, 2025, mentioning
potential leasing assets, suggests misuse. However, the primary focus was governance, likely
exceeding OPMA exceptions.

Unauthorized Board Action
The complaint states the proposal, a 38-page core document within a 160-page package, was
submitted to OMC without formal board authorization in a public vote, potentially via informal
’voice consent” in executive session. RCW 70.44.060 grants boards broad powers, but major
decisions, especially binding proposals, typically require public meetings. The complaint’s
assertion, “If informal ‘voice consent’ was obtained in executive session, that constitutes illegal
board action under OPMA,” aligns with OPMA’s prohibition on final actions in executive
sessions. Emails, such as Glenn’s February 12, 2025, note of scrambling to meet the deadline,
indicate action without public approval, possibly unauthorized under district laws.

Suppression of Public Transparency and Misrepresentation
Officials, including CEO Mike Glenn and Chair Jill Buhler, allegedly misrepresented the proposal
as “inconsequential” or “airy-fairy,” despite its formal nature, misleading the board and public.
This is evidenced in meeting transcripts from February 19, 2025, where Glenn stated, “There’s
really nothing to talk about right now,” despite submission. Commissioner Ready was
discouraged from public discussion, with Buhler calling on March 14, 2025, to remove website
content, potentially raising First Amendment concerns, though not directly criminal. This
pattern, detailed in the complaint’s table of misleading statements, suggests suppression,
impacting public trust and transparency.

Coordinated Conduct and Potential Criminal Conspiracy or
Racketeering
The complaint suggests a pattern of withholding legal opinions, avoiding public processes, and
private communications resembling serial meetings, possibly meeting conspiracy thresholds
under RCW 9A.28.040, requiring an agreement to commit a crime with a substantial step.
Official misconduct under RCW 9A.80.010 could be the underlying crime if actions were
unauthorized with intent to benefit, such as consolidating control. However, proving intent is
complex and emails show efforts to avoid serial meetings. Like Kolffs February 8, 2025,
instruction not to respond. Racketeering under Chapter 9A.82 RCW, requiring a pattern of
profiteering acts like murder or robbery, seems unlikely, as definitions (effective until April l ,
2025, adding catalytic converter trafficking post-April) don’t fit governance issues.
Legal counsel Brad Berg’s role, advising on executive session use despite invalidity, may raise
ethical concerns, potentially reported to the Washington State Bar Association, but criminal
complicity is uncertain without clear evidence of intent.

Penalties and Criminal Implications —
OPMA violations carry civil penalties, increased to $500 for first-time knowing violations and
$1 ,000 for repeats, as per recent legislation (Governor to sign AG-request bill to strengthen
open public meetings law. increase penalties I Washington State). Criminal implications hinge
on official misconduct, requiring intent, which is not clearly evidenced here. Conspiracy would
need a proven agreement and step(s), possibly a stretch given civil nature of OPMA.
Racketeering is improbable without financial gain from listed crimes.
Conclusion —
The actions likely violate OPMA, with civil penalties applicable, and may constitute official
misconduct if intent is proven. Criminal conspiracy or racketeering seems less supported,
requiring much further evidence. The complaint’s detailed documentation, including emails
and legal opinions, suggest a review by the Washington State Attorney General’s Office —
Assistant Attorney General for Open Government who oversees possible OPMA violations.

05/20/2025 Letter to Attorney General
Dear AGO,
I am writing in my official capacity as an elected Commissioner of Jefferson County Public
Hospital District No. 2 (Jefferson Healthcare) to formally request an opinion and guidance from
your office regarding potential violations of the Open Public Meetings Act (OPMA), RCW 42.30,
by our Board of Commissioners.
On February 5, 2025, our Board entered executive session under the justification of discussing
potential real estate leasing. However, the actual subject of the session was a major governance
restructuring proposal: a formal response to Olympic Medical Center’s (OMC) public Request
for Proposals, involving the creation of a new nonprofit entity—the Peninsula Health Alliance
—that would oversee both public hospital districts. I was informed of this plan for the first time
during that executive session, while it appeared other board members had been previously
briefed.
Subsequent events raise serious legal and ethical concerns:
  •    A 50+ page proposal was submitted to OMC on February 12, 2025, without a public vote
       or board authorization.
  •    Commissioners were instructed by our CEO to keep the proposal confidential even after
       submission.
  •    My efforts to raise these concerns in public meetings were obstructed, including having
       my microphone muted multiple times by the board chair.
  •    I was not provided prior drafts of the proposal nor kept informed about its development,
       while other commissioners appeared to have been actively engaged.
  •    The executive session did not meet the standards for a valid exemption under RCW
       42.30.110, as no actual real estate pricing or negotiation was discussed. Instead, a
       governance overhaul was debated—this appears to exceed the permissible scope
       defined by the Washington Supreme Court in Columbia Riverkeeper v. Port of Vancouver.
  •    A formal complaint submitted to the Jefferson County Sheriff’s Office led to a report
       from Detective Sergeant Derek Allen and an analysis by Chief Criminal Deputy Chris
       Ashcraft. While criminal charges were not pursued, both concluded that OPMA
       violations were “likely” and highlighted concerns around misuse of executive session
       and unauthorized board action.
  •    Legal counsel Austin Hatcher further confirmed that the real estate exemption cited for
       the executive session was inapplicable, and that if the proposal was authorized in that
       session or submitted without a public vote, both acts would be OPMA violations.
Requested Guidance
Given the importance of transparency and public trust in the operation of municipal
corporations like public hospital districts, I respectfully request your office provide:
  •    A formal opinion on whether the use of executive session in this context violated the
       OPMA, particularly in light of the narrow interpretation of RCW 42.30.110 under
       Columbia Riverkeeper.
  •    Clarification on the legality of submitting a binding or semi-binding proposal (with
       governance and financial implications) absent a public vote of the Board, and whether
       doing so violates RCW 70.44.050 and RCW 70.44.060, which collectively affirm that
       commissioners act collectively through formal meetings.
  •    Guidance on the applicability of civil penalties or injunctive relief under RCW 42.30.120
       and RCW 42.30.130. As someone who attended these meetings but publicly and
       repeatedly objected, I seek clarity on whether I may be subject to any statutory liability
       despite dissenting.
  •    Any model language, case law summaries, or procedural resources your office or MRSC
       recommends to prevent such governance breakdowns and ensure full compliance with
       open meetings law.
  •    If appropriate, legal insight into whether a Declaratory Judgment action under RCW
       7.24 or injunctive relief under RCW 42.30.130 would be an effective and applicable
       remedy to address and prevent further misconduct. A ruling clarifying whether this
       proposal is legally valid or binding would serve the public interest.
Ongoing Urgency
I must emphasize the current and active nature of this matter. Despite all of the above, this
proposal appears to still be under ongoing consideration by Jefferson Healthcare’s CEO, Olympic
Medical Center, and Juniper Advisory. As an elected commissioner, I am not being informed of
the status of these negotiations, even though they involve the future governance of our hospital
district.
This ongoing secrecy, combined with the legal issues described above, represents a live and
escalating risk. If left unchecked, it may lead to an agreement being presented as a fait accompli
—crafted outside public view, possibly on the basis of invalid authorization—and could
severely undermine the credibility, reputation, and financial integrity of both Jefferson
Healthcare and OMC.
Immediate legal guidance from your office is essential to prevent further erosion of public trust
and to protect the legal standing of both hospital districts.
Please contact me at mattready@gmail.com or (360) 477-1447 if you require additional
documentation, including the full proposal, transcripts, emails, the complaint materials, or the
complete investigative reports. I can provide a compiled digital or print version upon request.
Thank you for your time and attention to this serious matter. I look forward to your response.
Sincerely, Matt Ready Commissioner Jefferson County Public Hospital District No. 2

5/20/2025 Ethics Complaint against Lawyer Brad Berg for
Washington State Bar Association
ETHICS COMPLAINT for Attorney Brad Berg – Enabling Executive Session Abuse, Facilitating
Governance Secrecy, and Obstructing Oversight
Respondent: Brad Berg, Attorney, Foster Garvey Law Firm Filed by: Commissioner Matt Ready,
Jefferson County Public Hospital District No. 2 Date: May 20, 2025
Summary of Allegations
This complaint concerns Attorney Brad Berg’s conduct as legal counsel to Jefferson Healthcare.
Although Mr. Berg did not attend the February 5, 2025 executive session where the Peninsula
Health Alliance proposal was first introduced, upon entering the process he failed to investigate
or acknowledge the questionable and potentially illegal conduct that preceded him. Instead,
Mr. Berg advised the Board of Commissioners to continue concealing and advancing the
proposal through executive sessions using legally invalid justifications. His legal advice actively
enabled secrecy, obstructed legitimate commissioner oversight, and suppressed public
accountability regarding a major governance restructuring plan that remains under
undisclosed negotiation.
Factual Basis
  1.   Improper Legal Justification for Executive Session Secrecy
On March 18, 2025, Mr. Berg attended an executive session of the Jefferson Healthcare Board of
Commissioners and advised that the Peninsula Health Alliance proposal could continue to be
discussed privately under the “real estate exemption” of RCW 42.30.110. However, the
discussions at hand centered on creating a new nonprofit entity and radically restructuring
hospital governance—not negotiating the lease or purchase of specific properties.
“Lawyer Brad Berg describes how to use the Real Estate exemption and ‘legal concerns with
actions’ to keep the discussions of this proposal in executive session until they want to bring it
out.”
This interpretation of the law has since been challenged by law enforcement and legal
authorities. A formal review by the Jefferson County Sheriff’s Office and Chief Criminal Deputy
Prosecutor Chris Ashcraft found:
“The executive session was under a very stretched reading of the ‘lease’ purposes of RCW
42.30.110(1)(b) and (c)… That is not the case here.”
The prosecutor further stated that OPMA violations were likely, and the misuse of executive
session exemptions was central to those concerns.
  2.   Advice Used to Enable Secrecy and Advance the Proposal Without Oversight
By the time Mr. Berg became involved, a 50+ page proposal had already been submitted by CEO
Mike Glenn to Olympic Medical Center without any formal vote or public board authorization.
This action appears to have been based on a straw poll taken during the February 5 executive
session—an illegal practice under Washington’s Open Public Meetings Act.
“Each commissioner present took a turn to verbally express support for the CEO’s action. This
was, by all definitions, a textbook illegal straw poll.”
Rather than advising the board to disclose this procedural breach and remedy it with proper
public process, Mr. Berg endorsed continuing the secrecy through executive sessions using the
same dubious “real estate” exemption.
In addition, Mr. Berg proposed a strategy to obscure the true status of the deal from the public
while signaling commitment to OMC. He recommended using a “letter of intent” that could
appear nonbinding to Jefferson County residents, while OMC would understand it as a de facto
binding agreement:
“You could achieve that by authorizing the CEO to sign a letter of intent, and then take time
until a final board vote.”
This maneuver served to delay public involvement while assuring OMC that Jefferson
Healthcare was locked in. It allowed the board to postpone public scrutiny while giving the
appearance of transparency and due process—when in fact a major governance decision was
already being advanced behind closed doors.
  3.   Suppression of Oversight and Encouragement of Single-Source Legal Control
Mr. Berg’s legal opinion became the board majority’s shield against scrutiny, and his silence in
response to formal concerns effectively blocked further inquiry. Since February 19, I have
repeatedly submitted written legal concerns to the board and administration. Mr. Berg has not
responded to these concerns directly, nor has he provided neutral legal analysis in any public
setting.
Instead, his perceived authority has been used to discredit dissenting views and silence calls for
transparency:
Commissioner Kolff: “Brad is the definitive person on this particular type of issue. He has
actually written the code that we follow.” Commissioner Buhler: “Our legal counsel… has said
that nothing we have done is illegal… He is preeminent in this discussion.”
This monopoly on legal interpretation has resulted in repeated efforts to mute me during
meetings, block my motions from discussion, and falsely accuse me of slander and ethics
violations when I attempted to inform the public.
Ethical and Legal Violations
  •    Violation of OPMA Principles: Endorsing the use of executive session under legally
       unsupported claims of real estate discussions.
  •    Failure to Provide Impartial Legal Advice: Ignoring formal concerns from a sitting
       commissioner and refusing to address the legality of board actions.
  •    Complicity in Suppression of Oversight: Facilitating a climate where dissent was
       penalized, commissioners were silenced, and public comment was shut down.
  •    Conflict of Interest: Providing legal strategies that protect the CEO and board majority
       while sidelining the board’s broader obligation to the public and the law.
Relief Requested
Currently, Attorney Brad Berg is the only legal counsel being made available to commissioners,
despite his direct involvement in the conduct described above. I strongly urge Jefferson
Healthcare to immediately retain independent legal counsel who reports directly to the full
Board of Commissioners—not the CEO—to rectify this ongoing conflict of interest and ensure
lawful oversight.
The continued reliance on Mr. Berg—especially while the Peninsula Health Alliance proposal
remains under active, undisclosed negotiation between the Jefferson Healthcare CEO and
Olympic Medical Center—exposes the board to legal liability and further erodes public trust in
the integrity of our governance.
I respectfully request that this complaint be referred to the Washington State Bar Association
for formal review and potential disciplinary action. This review should examine:
  •    Whether Mr. Berg knowingly advised or condoned board conduct in violation of
       Washington’s Open Public Meetings Act;
  •    Whether his failure to respond to legal objections and concerns raised by a
       commissioner violates professional standards of impartiality and competence;
  •    Whether his dual role in defending the CEO while advising the board constitutes a
       breach of ethical obligations under the Rules of Professional Conduct.
Jefferson Healthcare and its elected commissioners deserve neutral, independent legal advice—
not legal guidance tailored to protect administration at the expense of the public. The failure to
provide such counsel risks irreparable damage to public accountability, institutional integrity,
and legal compliance.
Sincerely, Matt Ready Commissioner, Jefferson County Public Hospital District No. 2
mattready@gmail.com

05/20/2025 Matt Ready Letter to Olympic Medical Center
Subject: Legal and Governance Concerns Regarding Peninsula Health Alliance Proposal
Dear Members of the OMC Board of Commissioners,
I am writing to you in my capacity as an elected commissioner of Jefferson County Public
Hospital District No. 2 (Jefferson Healthcare) to offer a professional courtesy and share
important information regarding the proposal submitted to you on February 12, 2025, by our
CEO, Mike Glenn, concerning the formation of the Peninsula Health Alliance.
As you may be aware, serious legal and governance concerns have been raised about this
proposal, including whether it was lawfully authorized by the Jefferson Healthcare Board of
Commissioners. A formal complaint triggered an official review by the Jefferson County
Sheriff’s Office and Prosecuting Attorney’s Office.
On May 14, 2025, the Jefferson County Prosecuting Attorney’s Office concluded that although no
criminal charges would be filed, the process by which this proposal was developed and
submitted likely violated Washington’s Open Public Meetings Act (OPMA). Specifically:
  •    The proposal was discussed in executive session under a highly questionable “real
       estate” exemption.
  •    No formal public vote was taken to authorize submission of the proposal.
  •    Informal voice consent or a straw poll appears to have been used, which is not legally
       valid under state law.
The detective’s report and legal analysis also noted that the proposal may have been crafted
and submitted without board approval, independent legal review, or proper financial due
diligence.
Given these facts, I urge OMC to approach any current or future discussions involving this
proposal with caution. Moving forward with an agreement that lacks lawful authorization from
one of the participating public entities could expose both parties to significant reputational and
legal risk.
To ensure legitimacy and transparency, I recommend that both Boards of Commissioners
convene jointly in open public session to (1) clarify the status of the proposal, (2) determine
whether it reflects the lawful will of either district, and (3) commit to full compliance with
Washington State law in all future deliberations.
Please know that I am not opposed to forming a healthy, legally sound alliance between our
districts if we proceed through proper, transparent, and lawfully authorized pathways. The
public deserves a process that upholds both the letter and spirit of open government.
I am attaching the May 14, 2025 report from the Jefferson County Sheriff’s Office and

Initiate a Formal Internal Review of Potential Misconduct Related to the Peninsula Health

Whereas, Jefferson County Public Hospital District No. 2 is governed by an elected Board of
Commissioners responsible for all major decisions regarding governance, legal compliance, and
strategic direction, in accordance with RCW 70.44 and RCW 42.30;
Whereas, on February 5, 2025, during an executive session, CEO Mike Glenn presented a
proposal for a significant restructuring of governance through the formation of a new nonprofit
entity—the Peninsula Health Alliance—in partnership with Olympic Medical Center;
Whereas, the proposal was formally submitted by the CEO to Olympic Medical Center on
February 12, 2025, without a public vote or formal authorization from the Board of
Commissioners in open session;
Whereas, Commissioner Matt Ready raised immediate objections during the February 5
executive session, citing the legal prohibition on board action or consensus during executive
sessions, and has since publicly stated that multiple commissioners gave verbal expressions of
support for the proposal in a manner that may constitute an illegal “straw poll” under RCW
42.30.060;
Whereas, on May 14, 2025, the Jefferson County Prosecuting Attorney’s Office and Sheriff’s
Department concluded an independent review of these events and found that:
  •    The executive session was likely misused under Washington’s Open Public Meetings Act
       (OPMA);
  •    A major proposal was submitted without lawful board authorization;
  •    The use of informal “voice consent” in executive session may constitute unauthorized
       board action;
  •    While no criminal charges were filed, the conduct raises serious legal, ethical, and
       governance concerns that warrant further review;
Therefore, I move that:
  1.   Internal Misconduct Review
The Board of Commissioners shall initiate a formal internal review to determine the extent to
which any violations occurred, the individuals involved, the timeline of events, and potential
remedies or corrective actions, specifically:
  •    Whether CEO Mike Glenn engaged in misconduct by submitting the Peninsula Health
       Alliance proposal without lawful board approval, in potential violation of RCW
       70.44.060 and RCW 42.30.060;
  •    Whether any commissioners knowingly participated in or allowed an illegal straw poll
       or informal consensus process during executive session in violation of the Open Public
       Meetings Act;
  •    Whether any actions or omissions by the CEO or commissioners constituted a breach of
       duty, abuse of process, or failure to uphold statutory governance responsibilities.
  2.   Review Process
  •    The review shall be conducted by an independent team composed of at least five
       Jefferson Healthcare employees not named in any allegation, supported by
       administrative staff as needed;
  •    The team may consult with external legal or HR professionals who have no prior
       involvement with the CEO or legal counsel Brad Berg;
  •    The CEO shall be asked to disclose any active Non-Disclosure Agreements (NDAs) that
       limit his ability to answer board questions regarding governance, negotiations, or
       strategy.
  3.   Reporting and Transparency
  •    A written report with findings and recommendations shall be delivered to the full Board
       of Commissioners within 30 days;
  •    The Board shall formally vote to receive the report and publicly discuss the findings,
       with any confidential personnel matters addressed appropriately in executive session;
  •    Based on the report, the Board shall determine whether further corrective, disciplinary,
       or policy actions are warranted.
Final Note: This review is essential to restore public confidence in the lawful governance and
transparency of Jefferson Healthcare. It follows the conclusions of law enforcement and
prosecutorial authorities that serious concerns exist regarding compliance with the Open
Public Meetings Act and statutory board governance.
Submitted respectfully, Commissioner Matt Ready Jefferson County Public Hospital District

 to Chris
Dear Mr. Ashcraft,
I am writing to respectfully request that your office reconsider its determination that no
criminal intent existed in the actions surrounding the Peninsula Health Alliance proposal.
Your rationale—that no one intended to “harm anyone, including the public”—fails to address
the ongoing legal and ethical consequences of these actions and does not reflect the correct
standard for criminal intent under RCW 9A.80.010. As you know, that statute defines official
misconduct as knowingly committing an unauthorized act under color of law to obtain a
benefit or deprive another of one. Malice is not required—only awareness and willful action
beyond legal authority.
As of today, the proposal has not been withdrawn, and the negotiations and planning it set into
motion have not been formally ceased. The public has received no assurance that these
activities are over. By declining to recognize the criminal implications of this conduct, your
office is allowing an unlawful governance process to continue unchallenged—deepening the
damage to democratic oversight of a vital public institution.
Submitting a 160-page, governance-altering proposal to another public hospital district without
a public vote, legal board authorization, or basic financial analysis is not a procedural error—it
is a deliberate act. Both the Jefferson County Sheriff’s report and independent legal analysis by
Attorney Austin Hatcher confirm that the proposal was submitted outside lawful public process
and that the “real estate” exemption for executive session was improperly invoked to conceal it.
Furthermore, if CEO Mike Glenn submitted the proposal based on informal “voice consent”
during executive session, that act constitutes an illegal board action and likely a violation of
OPMA. It may also qualify as official misconduct under RCW 9A.80.010. These statutes exist to
protect the public from precisely this kind of covert consolidation of power.
The harm here is not theoretical. It is tangible—eroding public trust, compromising
institutional legitimacy, and undermining our community’s right to transparent governance.
This is not a resolved matter. The core actors continue to obscure the status of the proposal, and
I, as an elected commissioner, remain uninformed about whether it is still under active
consideration.
I urge your office to recognize this as an ongoing and urgent issue. Your determination carries
consequences. To decline action is to signal that public officials may violate open meeting laws,
suppress oversight, and restructure public institutions without accountability—as long as they
claim good intentions. We need your office to use the authority and purpose of the criminal
justice system to stop ongoing misconduct and restore lawful order.
Every branch of government must fulfill its role in upholding the law. We rely on your office
not only to prosecute bad faith, but to protect the integrity of our democracy. I respectfully ask
that you take this matter up again with the seriousness it warrants.
Thank you for your time and consideration.
Sincerely, Matt Ready Commissioner, Jefferson County Public Hospital District No. 2

Official Notice of Criminal Exposure Related to the Peninsula Health Alliance Proposal
Request for Joint Public Meeting and Internal Investigation
Commissioner Matt Ready Jefferson County Public Hospital District No. 2
mattready@gmail.com | (360) 477-1447 May 22, 2025
To:
Board of Commissioners, Olympic Medical Center Board of Commissioners, Jefferson County
Public Hospital District No. 2 (Jefferson Healthcare)
Subject: Official Notice of Criminal Exposure Related to the Peninsula Health Alliance
Proposal Request for Joint Public Meeting and Internal Investigation
Dear Commissioners,
This letter serves as a formal and urgent legal notice. Based on the available evidence, your
collective roles in the development, submission, and concealment of the Peninsula Health
Alliance proposal may constitute criminal violations of Washington State law, including RCW
9A.80.010 (Official Misconduct) and RCW 9A.28.040 (Criminal Conspiracy), as well as Open
Public Meetings Act (RCW 42.30) violations. These are not theoretical risks—if proven, they
carry maximum penalties of 364 days in jail and a $5,000 fine per count, along with civil
liability and reputational harm to your institutions.
I. Basis for Criminal Exposure
The Peninsula Health Alliance proposal:
  •    Was submitted without a public board vote or legal authorization from Jefferson
       Healthcare;
  •    Was drafted and discussed in private, under a legally questionable executive session
       exemption;
  •    Was concealed from at least one commissioner during development;
  •    Was presented to Olympic Medical Center as an official act of Jefferson Healthcare;
  •    Was moved forward without public disclosure or open board deliberation.
The facts, preserved in internal emails, transcripts, and public statements, demonstrate that
individuals within both institutions took actions that may meet the legal standard for official
misconduct and conspiracy.
II. Criminal Intent Requires Knowledge—Not Malice
Under RCW 9A.80.010, a public servant commits official misconduct when they: “Knowingly
perform an act which the public servant knows is unauthorized by law…”
This statute does not require malicious motive. It is enough that the act was taken knowingly,
outside proper legal authority, and under the guise of public office. The Jefferson County
Prosecutor’s refusal to pursue charges based on a lack of “intent to harm” is a misapplication of
law. The legal threshold is clear, and the facts are already in the record.
III. Referral and External Investigation Underway
I have submitted notification and documentation of these potential crimes to:
  •    The Washington State Attorney General – Open Government Division
  •    The Jefferson County Sheriff and Prosecutor
  •    The Clallam County Sheriff
  •    Notification packets are also under preparation for federal authorities since these
       activities involve multiple jurisdictions.
IV. Demand for Immediate Internal Investigation
Whether or not external bodies act, I strongly urge both Jefferson Healthcare
and Olympic Medical Center to:
  •    Immediately initiate a thorough internal investigation into the proposal’s creation,
       submission, and concealment; 2066_001.pdf
  •    Determine which individuals were involved, what internal policies were bypassed or
       ignored, and which governance safeguards failed;
  •    Remedy procedural or legal violations through formal internal review, retraining, and if
       necessary, corrective disciplinary action;
  •    Secure and preserve all documentation, communications, emails, drafts, and attorney
       correspondence related to the Peninsula Health Alliance;
  •    Prepare formal institutional responses and briefings for external agencies who may
       request cooperation.
Doing so is not only legally prudent—it is vital to preserving institutional credibility and
rebuilding public trust.
V. Call for Immediate Joint Public Meeting
I further call on both boards to convene a joint open public meeting to:
  •    Disclose the full authorship, status, and legal justification for the proposal;
  •    Present findings from internal investigations;
  •    Receive public comment and answer questions;
  •    Consider formally rescinding and renouncing the proposal;
  •    Commit to future governance transparency.
This meeting must be fully noticed, recorded, and open to the public and press.
VI. Legal Counsel Must Report to the Board—Not the CEO
In my experience as a long-serving hospital commissioner, I have observed that legal counsel
retained by public hospital districts often appear to view the CEO as their primary client and
superior. These attorneys tend to defer to the CEO’s authority, advocate for the CEO’s positions,
and protect the CEO’s legal interests as though the CEO were the equivalent of a private
business owner. This structural bias presents a profound conflict of interest, particularly when
allegations of misconduct or legal violations involving the CEO arise. For this reason, it is
imperative that all public hospital district boards retain their own independent general counsel
—separate from any attorney hired by or reporting to the CEO. This is the only effective way to
establish a legal check and balance, safeguard the public interest, and ensure that the board
receives unbiased advice aligned with its fiduciary and statutory obligations.
VII. Bar Complaint Against Legal Counsel
I also regretfully inform you that I have been forced to file a formal complaint with the
Washington State Bar Association against Jefferson Healthcare’s legal counsel, Brad Berg. This
step was necessary due to mounting concerns, supported by the county prosecutor’s own
report, that Mr. Berg may have actively participated in or facilitated the concealment of critical
legal risks and governance violations from the public and from the full Board of
Commissioners. The prosecuting attorney explicitly flagged the potential complicity of legal
counsel in suppressing transparency and helping executive leadership avoid legal scrutiny. In
light of these findings, Jefferson Healthcare’s reliance on Mr. Berg’s legal advice must be viewed
with caution by both boards until the matter is resolved through appropriate oversight. For the
record, despite these concerns, the other Jefferson Healthcare commissioners continue to rely
exclusively on Mr.Berg’s legal advice in this matter – in my opinion, a serious act of fiduciary
negligence.
VIII. Notice
You are now officially on notice. Each day of inaction increases potential exposure—for
individual commissioners, executives, and your institutions. You have the opportunity to take
lawful corrective action now. I strongly encourage you to act quickly, transparently, and
decisively.
Sincerely, Matt Ready Commissioner, Jefferson County Public Hospital District No. 2
mattready@gmail.com | (360) 477-1447

05/23/2025 Alison Arthur emails Jefferson Healthcare
commissioners about confirmed OPMA violations by the
commission including an illegal use of an executive session.
Dear Jefferson Healthcare Commissioners:
Jefferson Healthcare’s future is crucial to the welfare of all residents.
If you agree with that statement, please stop discussing the possible alliance with Olympic
Medical Center behind closed doors with or without an attorney.
It’s we, the “peeps” as CEO Mike Glenn called the people of Jefferson County during a recent
board meeting, you need to be talking to in public meetings.
It’s not just the right thing to do; there is no legal exemption under the state Open Public
Meeting Act to allow you do go into a closed-door meeting to discuss alliances or mergers or
affiliations.
That’s not my opinion. It’s the opinion of Allied Law Group, which represents a raft of
newspapers, broadcast media, nonprofits and individuals like me who care about open
government.
After the March 26 board meeting in which chair Jill Buhler-Rienstra silenced commissioner
Matt Ready, scolding him as if he were a naughty child for wanting to talk about this issue, I
reached out to attorney Michele Earl-Hubbard of Allied Law Group. I know her professionally,
not personally. Her advice when I was working on some controversial stories years ago were
invaluable. She made me think about every word.
To be clear, I did not ask her to come to any conclusion but her own. I did pay for her opinion.
I provided her with the board agendas, access to board minutes and Mr. Ready’s PowerPoint
on the OMR request for proposals for an alliance that Ready had made public on his website.
The following is verbatim what she wrote in response to my request for her analysis:
“First, no, the agency absolutely cannot legally use the”real estate” or “potential litigation”
Executive Session grounds to hold an ES to discuss creation of this new entity or merging with
other entities. If they merge and get around to selling off surplus properties or buying new
ones, they can have an ES for that narrow discussion, but not for what they are discussing
now. The fact someone might sue them someday to stop some action they are considering
taking – liking forming this entity, etc. – is not an appropriate grounds for an ES. They can
have narrow ES’s to discuss with legal counsel and get legal advice under 42.30.110(1)(i) but
only in very specific circumstances (quoted below):
  (i) To discuss with legal counsel representing the agency matters relating to agency
      enforcement actions, or to discuss with legal counsel representing the agency litigation
      or potential litigation to which the agency, the governing body, or a member acting in
      an official capacity is, or is likely to become, a party, when public knowledge regarding
      the discussion is likely to result in an adverse legal or financial consequence to the
      agency.
This subsection (1)(i) does not permit a governing body to hold an executive session solely
because an attorney representing the agency is present. For purposes of this subsection (1)(i),
“potential litigation” means matters protected by RPC 1.6 or RCW 5.60.060(2)(a) concerning:
  (i) Litigation that has been specifically threatened to which the agency, the governing body,
      or a member acting in an official capacity is, or is likely to become, a party;
  (ii) Litigation that the agency reasonably believes may be commenced by or against the
       agency, the governing body, or a member acting in an official capacity; or
  (iii) Litigation or legal risks of a proposed action or current practice that the agency has
        identified when public discussion of the litigation or legal risks is likely to result in an
        adverse legal or financial consequence to the agency;
The only one that might even remotely apply – down the road – would be (1)(iii) – but they
have to show public discussion of the legal risks “is likely to result in an adverse legal or
financial consequence to the agency”. There is no current litigation. So they have to be saying
they worry there could be legal risks of a proposed action – AND that there will be adverse legal
or financial consequences to the agency of public discussion of the legal risks. That is rare and
very narrow. And it cannot cover ES to discuss the idea with people other than the lawyer –
and anyone from the other groups present defeats the alleged attorney client privileged nature
of the ES this exemption is meant to cover. So no they are breaking the law meeting in secret
under either of those two exemptions.
They also cannot hold an ES without saying which subpart of Section 110 covers it. The reason
they have to give the reason is so they think hard whether there is an ES ground that allows it.
If they cannot even figure it out to put it on the agenda, they are showing they have not thought
that through. And there probably isn’t such a ground.
The Commissioner who leaked the materials – if he is sanctioned – can perhaps file a lawsuit
appealing it. Anyone who participated in that ES with knowledge it violated the OPMA can be
sued for violating the OPMA and individually fined. Any ethics rule that punishes someone for
exposing illegal actions should be void for public policy reasons and unenforceable.
Anyone could sue this entity and all the Commissioners for that one ES OPMA violation.”
That last line is not my conclusion; it is the conclusion of an attorney who has successfully sued
many public agencies over the course of many years.
I have no interest in suing Jefferson Healthcare. So please do not take this as a threat so that
you can discuss it with your attorney. It’s not.
What I am asking is that is that you all think before you go into executive session.
Commissioner Ready wasn’t throwing you “under the bus” as one commissioner implied when
he tried to have a conversation with you all about the alliance. He wasn’t trying to “libel and
slander” you as another stated.
He was telling you the truth. And you shot him down without thinking about it.
Commissioner Kees Kolff came close to realizing the subject matter was in question for a closed
session. Then he went with the majority and dismissed Mr. Ready.
This issue is huge. It has serious implications for the delivery of healthcare across the Olympic
Peninsula.
And frankly, as someone who has listened to this board and values the breadth of knowledge
you all have, and who also understands the magnitude of the healthcare situation today, it
sounds like an alliance has potential merit. Partnerships like the one proposed could be a
solution for the dire situation we face in healthcare today.
It will not be a solution if it’s done in private and without rigorous public consideration – not
between high paid CEOs, not between private companies or Chicago-based specialty groups, not
between “select” commissioners but with all parties involved onboard for a public discussion
about the survival of our vital healthcare infrastructure.
And stop meeting in executive session on this. It’s not legal.
Thank you.
Allison Arthur
Community member and OPMA advocate

To: Brittany Huntingford, Executive Assistant
Cc: All Jefferson Healthcare Commissioners;
Subject: Response to Interview Request – OPMA Concerns and Legal Process Integrity
Dear Brittany,
Thank you for your message. I am writing to formally respond to the request for a one-hour
meeting between myself and legal counsel from Ogden Murphy Wallace PLLC (OMW),
regarding matters tied to the Peninsula Health Alliance.
I decline to participate in such a meeting for the following reasons:
  •    OPMA Compliance Concerns: A series of one-on-one private interviews between legal
       counsel and commissioners on a matter of active board deliberation creates a strong
       risk of violating the Washington State Open Public Meetings Act (OPMA). This
       resembles a “hub-and-spoke” serial meeting, a structure explicitly criticized by courts
       and the Attorney General as subverting open governance. As a public hospital district,
       we must not compound past OPMA concerns with further questionable practices.
  •    Legal Representation Conflicts: OMW’s retainer appears to have been initiated by the
       CEO without formal vote or direction from the full Board. If legal counsel is engaged to
       investigate matters where the CEO is a controlling central figure, the Board must secure
       legal representation that reports directly and solely to the full Board. Without that
       independence, the integrity and credibility of the process is compromised. If the goal is
       to understand what occurred in prior executive sessions, then Board Secretary notes or
       recordings (if any) should be reviewed before repeating private conversations under
       legal ambiguity.
  •    Transparency and Documentation: I am fully willing to correspond via email with
       legal counsel. If there are questions OMW wishes to ask me, I will respond in writing.
       This ensures everything is documented, accessible to all commissioners, and preserves
       transparency for the public and future record review. I encourage any such
       correspondence to be conducted openly and with full Board awareness.
If legal counsel or the Board wishes to discuss these issues with me, I respectfully request it be
done either in a lawful public meeting, a properly noticed executive session with all
commissioners present, or through written email communication shared with the full Board.
Sincerely, Commissioner Matt Ready Jefferson County Public Hospital District No. 2

inquiry
Hi James,
Thanks for reviewing the detective’s report and for reaching out.
My goal is a healthy, well-governed hospital district—led with integrity, intelligence, wisdom,
creativity, and compassion. When I realized that the board and CEO appeared to be
coordinating a public deception around the Peninsula Health Alliance proposal, I believed it
could rise to the level of fraud. When the board chair muted me repeatedly at the March 26
meeting as I attempted to speak about the proposal, it became clear that the wrongdoing had
gone too far. At that point, it was both my fiduciary duty and my duty under oath of office to
report the matter to the sheriff (and other authorities such as the Washington State Auditor)
for review.
My first and most immediate goal was to disrupt the illegal process and prevent the proposal—
crafted and advanced without public debate or board authorization—from being adopted
without a valid democratic process. That said, I remain open to building alliances, as long as
they are pursued with transparency and full public participation.
Detective Allen’s in-depth investigation and written report have now provided the community
with a clear legal analysis showing that the February 5 executive session and the submission of
the proposal violated the Open Public Meetings Act. This recognition of wrongdoing should
serve as a foundation for Jefferson Healthcare to begin the internal work necessary to
understand what happened, why it happened, repair any damage, ensure it never happens
again, and work to restore public trust.
I’ve emailed my fellow board members and the OMC Board of Commissioners, informing them
of the detective’s findings and requesting a public meeting between our two boards to
reestablish legal communication and coordination. If our two districts want to transform our
relationship, then let’s do it in the open, in full view of the public, as the law requires.
Yes, I am seeking re-election. Our public hospital district is one of the most positive and
valuable institutions in our community, and it remains my continued honor to serve on its
board of commissioners.
Let me know if you have any more questions.
Kind regards, Matt Ready Public Hospital Commissioner, Jefferson Healthcare

06/11/2025 Port Townsend Leader publishes: “Sheriff’s report
supports hospital whistleblower”
By James Robinson
Jefferson Health Care Commissioner and whistleblower Matt Ready will see his complaint move
forward against the Jefferson Health Care Board, key leadership and legal counsel, according to
a report from the Jefferson County Sheriff’s Office.
“The actions likely violate OPMA (Washington State Open Public Meetings Act), with civil
penalties applicable, and may constitute official misconduct if intent is proven,” wrote
Detective Sergeant Derek Allen, of the Jefferson County Sheriff’s Office.
Jefferson County Sheriff Andy Pernsteiner assigned the complaint to Allen after Ready
submitted his complaint and supporting evidence to Jefferson and Clallam County sheriff’s
offices. Ready said the Clallam County Sheriff’s Office had not responded to his complaint.
“Criminal conspiracy or racketeering seems less supported, requiring much further evidence.”
Hospital officials said they were surprised with the involvement of the sheriff’s. They undergo
audits annually, a process that includes compliance with open meetings laws.
“We believe we are in full compliance with the state’s open public meeting act, said Pranav
Sharma, director of strategic planning and marketing for the hospital.”The act allows for
certain discussions to be held in executive session but requires all action take place in a public
meeting.” Sharma added that they were working “closely with legal counsel to make certain
this compliance continues.”
 “The complainant’s detailed documentation, including emails and legal opinions, suggest a
review by the Washington State Attorney General’s Office — Assistant Attorney General for
Open Government who oversees possible OPMA violations. An unexpected aspect is the
potential involvment of legal counsel as a co-conspirator, which could raise ethical issues for
the Washington State Bar Association, though criminal activity remains uncertain.”
Ready’s complaint stems from a March 26 hospital board meeting where Ready accused his co-
commissioners of meeting secretly with Olympic Medical Center representatives on “Project
Driftwood,”a plan to merge the Port Angles-based medical center with Jefferson Healthcare.
Ready further alleged that members of the Jefferson Healthcare Board had violated open
meeting laws, abused the use of executive sessions, and suppressed public information. Ready
provide emails between his co-commissioners and Jefferson Healthcare executives to support
his allegations.
“This report has been sent to the full boards of both OMC and Jefferson, the Washington State
Auditor’s office, and to the Washington State Attorney General’s office for further advice and
guidance,”Ready said. “I have requested a full impartial investigation within Jefferson
Healthcare into possible misconduct by my fellow commissioners and the CEO.
Allen’s report does not suggest evidence of criminal behavior, however the report appears to
support violations of the state’s open meeting laws.
Ready leaked Project Driftwood documents after his fellow hospital board commissioners
attempted to squelch his concerns at a board meeting. Those documents detail a not-for-profit
alliance which would allow Jefferson Healthcare and Olympic Medical Center in Port Angeles to
remain independent, while improving and expanding clinical programs, creating operating
efficiencies and economies of scale and the ability to improve and expand clinical programs.
The plan calls for a 12-member “super board” — with seven board members from Olympic
Medical Center and five from Jefferson Healthcare. According to the plan, all currently elected
commissioners would sit on the super board and the super board would govern the regional
health alliance while individual boards would remain responsible for governance of their own
organizations.
The proposal calls for a three-year phased-in leadership approach, with an appointed executive
director planned for the first year. Project documents propose that Jefferson Healthcare Chief
Executive Officer, Mike Glenn, would serve as the alliance’s first executive director.
Emails provided by Ready show correspondence between Jefferson Healthcare Commissioner
Kees Kolff, Jefferson Healthcare top executives and Jefferson Healthcare’s legal counsel, Brad
Berg of Foster Garvey discussing the merger plan, and Kolff’s efforts to draft language and an
organizational chart and discussions of the use of executive session.
“A subset of Jefferson commissioners were involved or consulted during the drafting
phase,”Ready said in a previous interview. “I was not. I only became aware of the proposal
during the executive session on February 5. The full board has never voted to authorize the
proposal or the direction of the negotiations. Much of the process has taken place out of public
view, contrary to the principles of public hospital governance.”

06/12/2025 Matt Ready blog post: Why Are Our Public Hospital
Leaders Only Using Secret Illegal Meetings to Address the
Peninsula Health Alliance?
June 12, 2025 | Author Matt | Edit
By Commissioner Matt Ready Jefferson County Public Hospital District No. 2
If someone told you your local public hospital might be secretly planning a major change—one
that could shift control to a private nonprofit group—you’d probably expect open meetings,
public discussion, and transparency, right?
But that’s not what happened.
Earlier this year, the CEO of Jefferson Healthcare submitted a major proposal to merge
oversight of our hospital district with Olympic Medical Center. This proposal would create a
new nonprofit corporation called the Peninsula Health Alliance with authority over both
hospitals.
Here’s the problem: There was no public vote. No financial review. No open discussion.
Instead, the proposal was quietly discussed behind closed doors in an executive session—a type
of meeting only legal under very limited circumstances, like for real estate deals or pending
litigation. This wasn’t that.
So I informed the board that our process was violating Washington’s Open Public Meetings Act
(OPMA), blew the whistle to the public, and I filed a criminal complaint. The Jefferson County
Sheriff investigated. A detective wrote a detailed report. The Chief Criminal Deputy Prosecutor
reviewed it. Their conclusion? OPMA violations likely occurred—even if there wasn’t enough
proof to press criminal charges.
That should have been a wake-up call.
Instead, hospital leadership is doubling down on secrecy.

Two Tries at Illegal Serial Meetings
First, in April after I raised my concerns and submitted the complaint, CEO Mike Glenn and
board chair Jill Buhler arranged for each commissioner to meet privately for 30 minutes with a
consultant named Karma Bass—who reports directly to him. These were unrecorded, one-on-
one phone calls. No minutes. No public notice.
This is a textbook example of a serial meeting—when public officials avoid legal public
meetings by holding one-on-one discussions behind the scenes. That’s illegal under OPMA. I
refused to participate.
This is the response I sent to Karma:
Subject: Response to Interview Request
Hi Karma,
Thank you for your message. I need to respectfully decline the invitation for a private phone or
audio interview related to the upcoming board retreat.
I have serious concerns about the confidentiality and legal implications of such a conversation,
especially given your past role facilitating the 2019 board retreat. At that retreat, the board
failed to reckon with the fact that a critical 2016 legal opinion—affirming a commissioner’s
right to record public meetings—had been withheld from me and the public for years. I
documented this entire episode in my book, Journey Through the Boardroom, including the
moment during the retreat when I stated on the record that what Mike Glenn and Brad Berg
had done could be considered fraud. Instead of allowing that conversation to continue, you
intervened and asked, “Are you a lawyer?”—effectively shutting down the discussion. That
moment could have opened the door to transparency and healing. Instead, it served to protect
those in power and bury the issue.
*Had we, as a board, learned then the importance of obtaining independent legal opinions and
facing governance issues head-on, we might not be in the current crisis. When I recently asked
for a second legal opinion regarding the Peninsula Health Alliance proposal, that request
should have been honored immediately. **Instead, the same pattern repeated: a lack of legal
diversity, reliance on one voice, and suppression of commissioner oversight.*
Given your involvement in both events—and the role you played in shaping the retreat’s outcome
—I now view you as a potential material witness, and possibly a co-conspirator, in matters I
have formally reported to legal authorities. For that reason, I cannot engage in any private or
unrecorded conversations with you.
I remain open to your role in publicly noticed board meetings, properly convened executive
sessions, or any forum governed by transparency and public accountability laws.
Sincerely,
Matt Ready
Commissioner, Jefferson County Public Hospital District No. 2
Second, on May 23, 2025, a Jefferson Healthcare Executive Assistant—acting under the CEO’s
direction—emailed the board to schedule private one-hour meetings between each
commissioner and an attorney from Ogden Murphy Wallace. Again, one-on-one, off the record.
Again, I refused. This is what I wrote to all the commissioners in response:
Subject: Response to Interview Request – OPMA Concerns and Legal Process Integrity
Dear XXXXXXXX (executive assistant),
Thank you for your message. I am writing to formally respond to the request for a one-hour
meeting between myself and legal counsel from Ogden Murphy Wallace PLLC (OMW), regarding
matters tied to the Peninsula Health Alliance.
I decline to participate in such a meeting for the following reasons:
  •    OPMA Compliance Concerns: >*** ****A series of one-on-one private interviews
       between legal counsel > and commissioners on a matter of active board deliberation
       creates > a strong risk of violating the Washington State Open Public > Meetings Act
       (OPMA). This resembles a “hub-and-spoke” serial > meeting, a structure explicitly
       criticized by courts and the > Attorney General as subverting open governance. As a
       public > hospital district, we must not compound past OPMA concerns with > further
       questionable practices.*
  •    Legal Representation Conflicts: >*** ****OMW’s retainer appears to have been
       initiated by the CEO without > formal vote or direction from the full Board. If legal
       counsel is > engaged to investigate matters where the CEO is a controlling > central
       figure, the Board must secure legal representation that > reports directly and solely to
       the full Board. Without that > independence, the integrity and credibility of the process
       is > compromised. If the goal is to understand what occurred in prior > executive
       sessions, then Board Secretary notes or recordings (if > any) should be reviewed before
       repeating private conversations > under legal ambiguity.*
  •    Transparency and Documentation: >*** ****I am fully willing to correspond via
       email with legal counsel. > If there are questions OMW wishes to ask me, I will respond
       in > writing. This ensures everything is documented, accessible to all > commissioners,
       and preserves transparency for the public and > future record review. I encourage any
       such correspondence to be > conducted openly and with full Board awareness.*
If legal counsel or the Board wishes to discuss these issues with me, I respectfully request it be
done either in a lawful public meeting, a properly noticed executive session with all
commissioners present, or through written email communication shared with the full Board.
Sincerely, Commissioner Matt Ready Jefferson County Public Hospital District No. 2
It remains unknown whether the other four commissioners took those meetings. If they did, it
could constitute yet another serial meeting violation.

A Non Disclosure Agreement creates a conflict of interest with fiduciary
responsibilities
Meanwhile, whenever members of the public asked about the Peninsula Health Alliance, the
CEO and other commissioners claimed they were bound by a nondisclosure agreement
(NDA). Yet this NDA was never voted on or approved by the full board—and to this day, as a
sitting commissioner, I still don’t know who signed it, what it says, or even who it was
signed with.
Signing an NDA in this context raises serious ethical and legal concerns. For a CEO or
commissioner of a public hospital district to prioritize the secrecy of an NDA over their
statutory fiduciary duty to the public may represent a profound conflict of interest. Public
hospital officials are accountable first and foremost to the people—not to private consultants,
corporate advisors, or secret deals. The public has a right to know what is being negotiated on
their behalf. Silence protected by private agreements has no place in public governance.

A Pattern—and a Lawyer Reported to the Bar
These weren’t innocent mistakes. Jefferson Healthcare’s former attorney, Brad Berg, helped
design and justify the strategy to keep these discussions hidden from the public using a
stretched interpretation of the law.
Because of his role in advising and enabling these secret discussions, I filed a formal complaint
with the Washington State Bar Association. His conduct was flagged in the Jefferson County
Prosecutor’s report. Yet the Jefferson Healthcare board has made no public acknowledgment of
any of this. Here is an excerpt from my Bar ethics complaint:
*Mr. Berg’s legal opinion became the board majority’s shield against scrutiny, and his silence in
response to formal concerns effectively blocked further inquiry. Since February 19, I have
**repeatedly submitted written legal concerns to the board and administration. Mr. Berg has
not responded to these concerns directly, nor has he provided neutral legal analysis in any
public setting.*
Instead, his perceived authority has been used to discredit dissenting views and silence calls for
transparency:
Commissioner Kolff: “Brad is the definitive person on this particular type of issue. He has actually
written the code that we follow.” Commissioner Buhler: “Our legal counsel… has said that
nothing we have done is illegal… He is preeminent in this discussion.”
This monopoly on legal interpretation has resulted in repeated efforts to mute me during
meetings, block my motions from discussion, and falsely accuse me of slander and ethics
violations when I attempted to inform the public.

What They’re Not Doing
They’re not addressing the sheriff’s findings. They’re not holding public meetings to fix the
damage. They’re not apologizing to the voters.
Instead, they’re calling in lawyers and consultants—in secret—trying to isolate each elected
commissioner, possibly coordinate their stories, and shape the outcome without any public
accountability.

What Needs to Happen Now
To protect the public interest and begin restoring trust, I’m calling for:
  1.   A joint open public meeting
between Jefferson Healthcare and the OMC Board of Commissioners. This is essential to
stabilize, clarify, and legally define any current or future relationship between the two hospital
districts.
  2.   A full internal investigation
by both Jefferson Healthcare and Olympic Medical Center into:
  •    What happened;
  •    Why it happened;
  •    How to prevent it in the future;
  •    And how to repair the damage, including a public apology for the deceptive process.
We can’t rebuild trust through silence. We rebuild it through truth, accountability, and
transparency.
Thank you for your time. Sincerely, Matt Ready
