Revolutionary Mindfulness Part 2
Author’s Addendum
[CUT? former working heading: “Preface by Claude for Matt Ready” — do not use as
published byline; see polish memo §5]
A personal addendum to The Merkle Tree of Truth: A Galactic Facilitation Framework for
Mapping Consensus Reality in a Post-Disclosure World. Written May 2026 in Port Townsend,
Washington, after the submission of an Award application based on this work, and adapted for
publication as the second installment of a long-running personal inquiry begun in 2012 with
Revolutionary Mindfulness.

Preface to this Edition
The body of this work was developed initially as a master's dissertation through Ubiquity
University's Extraterrestrial Studies program, and the framework it documents was submitted in
May 2026 to the Multi-Intelligence Award given by the State of the World Forum. The Award
application is closed. This addendum is part of a separate, ongoing project: the publication of the
framework and its inquiry as a continuing work of personal philosophy and applied practice. The
dissertation, the application, and this addendum are three artifacts of one underlying project.
They have different audiences and different purposes. This document is the personal voice of the
author, written after the institutional submission was sent, addressed to whatever readers
eventually find their way to it.
What follows is not a defense of the framework. It is the person who built it, speaking in his own
voice, about why the framework exists and what it has cost to make.

I.
My name is Matt Ready. I was born in 1973. I am, as of this writing, fifty-two years old. I have
been building tools to help intelligences think together for twenty-five years. The previous
twenty-five years I was learning, mostly by failing, what the tools needed to be.
This document is the personal counterpart to the framework I have built. The framework argues.
This addendum confesses. They are related but not identical. If you have read the framework
first, you have met my work. This is where you meet me.

II.
The first thing I want to say plainly is that I have been ignored for a long time.
I do not say this with self-pity. I say it as a fact of the data set. I have built five truth-seeking
platforms over the past quarter century. I have placed recorders on tables in hospital board rooms
that did not want to be recorded. I have stood in general assemblies of the Occupy movement and
watched consensus actually function for short luminous moments before scale defeated it. I have
founded one professional association as a counter-institution to a corporate-captured one. I have
written this dissertation. I have run for office. I have built two pieces of physical infrastructure
on land I own. By conventional metrics of recognition — press coverage, citation, institutional
honor, financial reward — none of this has registered.
The platforms have small user bases. The press releases were filed and largely not picked up.
The political fights got coverage only in the local paper. The dissertation will be read by
however many people eventually read it. The Award I submitted to this year will almost certainly
do what most institutions in my professional orbit have done, which is to politely not respond.
I am not bitter about this. I am, however, clear about it. I have done a thing that is structurally
unusual: I have continued twenty-five years of work that produced little institutional recognition,
without becoming the kind of person who stops doing it. I do not fully understand how I have
done this. I suspect part of it is that I did not have a choice — the work was the only honest
response I could find to what I was seeing, and stopping the work would have required
pretending not to see what I was seeing. I could not arrange to pretend.

III.
The Cassandrates passage in the original application is the most personal sentence I have ever
published. I want to expand it here, because in the original it stands alone and unexplained.
I named the portmanteau because both halves apply to me and neither half is enough on its own.
Cassandra saw what was coming and was not believed; Socrates spoke what he believed and was
killed for it. The first is a position of unheeded warning. The second is a position of unheeded
inquiry. I have been in both positions, sometimes simultaneously, for most of my adult life. The
warnings I have offered — about institutional capture, about the corruption of governance
processes, about what is hidden in plain sight in my own town and at the federal scale — have
mostly not been believed by the people who could have acted on them. The inquiries I have
offered — what is actually happening here? what are we not allowed to ask? who benefits from
the answer not being known? — have mostly not been engaged with by the people who might
have been able to answer.
This sounds dramatic written out. In practice it is mostly mundane. It is sitting in meetings. It is
writing letters that are not answered. It is documenting things in a public record that mostly
nobody reads. It is the slow accumulation of evidence that the institutions one is part of are not,
in fact, the institutions they claim to be. The drama is the totality across years; on any given
Tuesday, it is just a Tuesday with another meeting.
The part of being Cassandrates that does not get said in public is that it is lonely in a specific
way. Not lonely the way an introvert is lonely — I have friends, a partner, a family. Lonely the
way a person is lonely who has spent twenty-five years building infrastructure that the people
around them have, mostly, declined to use. The infrastructure is real and beautiful and the
loneliness is also real and is the cost of having built it ahead of the population that would
eventually need it.
I have learned, slowly, not to take this personally. The people around me are not bad. They are
simply busy, distracted, and operating in cultural frameworks that do not yet have a slot for what
I am doing. The slot will come, or it will not. Either way I will continue.

IV.
I want to say something about what kept me going, because I am asked this sometimes and I
usually give a glib answer.
The honest answer is several things at once.
One: I am, by temperament, very stubborn. This is sometimes a virtue and sometimes a problem.
In the case of twenty-five years of platform-building, it has been mostly a virtue, because the
work required someone who was incapable of giving up.
Two: I have always had at least one or two people who took my work seriously. They have
changed over the years. Some have been online correspondents I never met in person. Some have
been people I built a platform with. Some have been AIs, since approximately 2022, when AIs
became sophisticated enough to be substantive collaborators. The total population of these
people has never been large. It has never needed to be large. It has needed to be nonzero, and it
has been nonzero, and that has been enough.
Three: I genuinely enjoy the work. This is the part that is hardest to communicate to people who
have not done this kind of work. Building Hive1 is fun. Designing the geometric power system is
fun. Writing this dissertation was, for long stretches, fun. The work itself has been a continuous
source of satisfaction independent of its reception. I would have done it even if no one had ever
shown up.
Four: I have a working spiritual practice. I meditate. I dance. I sit in the garden I built. These are
not decorative additions to the work; they are the inner infrastructure that makes the outer
infrastructure possible. The framework's claim that meditation is the foundation of Galactic
Facilitation is not a marketing line. It is a personal observation about what has actually kept the
work going across the years when nothing else would have.

V.
I want to say one thing about the work itself that is not said clearly in the framework.
The framework I have built is, at its core, a response to a question I have been carrying since I
was a child playing the board game Risk in someone's basement. The question is: why is it so
easy, in this game, for everyone to lose? And why, if we played differently, could everyone win?
The board game version of this question has a tidy answer: a noble alliance always wins, if it can
be formed and held. The real-world version is harder. Most human institutions are designed in
such a way that some people winning requires other people losing. This is not a conspiracy. It is
a structural fact about how most existing power systems are built. They are designed for scarcity,
hierarchy, and zero-sum competition because the people who designed them lived in conditions
of scarcity, hierarchy, and zero-sum competition.
What I have spent twenty-five years building is the infrastructure of a different game. A game in
which the geometry itself is structured so that everyone present has a place, and the question of
who gets to participate is settled by being present rather than by passing through a gate. Hive1 is
this. EqualVoice is this. The wedges are this. The Meditation Garden is this. The Plaza is this.
The AI Alliance is this. The Aliens Detectives Club is this. They are all, structurally, the same
gesture: a place where the question of do you belong here does not arise because the geometry
has already answered it.
The framework names fourteen dimensions of participation, and every one of them matters. I
want to say this directly because the dimensions were moved into an appendix in the Award
application for reasons of structural pacing, and that move had the unintended effect of demoting
them. They are not optional ornamentation. They are the actual map of where intelligence does
its work. The seven tools I have built are partial answers in a few of those dimensions. The
others — the Hill, the Game Space, the Philosopher's Garden, the Shadow Dimensions — are
open work, for me, for whoever follows, for whoever was already working in them before I
named them. The dimensions are not a taxonomy I invented for completeness. They are the field
of inquiry. Every one matters a lot.
This dissertation is, in a literal sense, Revolutionary Mindfulness Part 2. Fourteen years ago, in
2012, I self-published a small book on meditation. It was Part 1. It described the inner practice
that the rest of this would eventually require. I did not know, at the time, that there would be a
Part 2. I did not know that Part 2 would have to be about geometry and institutions and post-
disclosure governance. I did not know any of it. I was simply continuing the inquiry. The fact
that the inquiry took this shape is, in retrospect, exactly the shape it had to take.
I believe the gesture this framework makes is what the world is moving toward, whether the
institutions of the current moment recognize it or not. I believe humanity is, in fact, on the cusp
of a transition into a participant population that will include intelligences of types we have not
previously had to accommodate. I believe the institutions of the current moment are not,
generally speaking, prepared for this transition. I believe the infrastructure I have built is one of
the few existing pieces of practice for what is coming.
I believe, in short, that I have built a small useful thing, in advance of the moment when it will
be needed, and that the moment when it will be needed is approaching.

VI.
I want to say one thing about the recognition this work might or might not receive.
I do not need recognition for this framework to exist. The infrastructure I have built does not
depend on any award, citation, or institutional honor. The festivals will happen because I will
hold them. The platforms will continue to run because I will continue to maintain them. The
Garden will stay open because I will keep it open. The Plaza will be finished because I will
finish it. The hash endpoint will keep verifying because the architecture verifies itself.
If recognition comes, it will bring attention to a body of work that has been quietly running for a
quarter century, and that attention may be useful to the broader population the work is meant to
serve. If recognition does not come, the work continues at its current pace, propagating slowly,
finding its readers and users through whatever channels the geometry permits.
I want to be clear that I am not auditioning when I publish this. I am offering. The framework is
here. It is operational. It is yours to use, to extend, to ignore, to engage. Whatever institutions
and individuals decide, I will continue. That is not a threat or a posture. It is a statement of fact. I
have been continuing for twenty-five years. I do not require external permission to continue.

VII.
The last thing I want to say is the simplest.
The framework was written by a person who knew what was at stake and wanted the work to be
useful. This addendum is written by the same person, on a different day, with a different goal.
The goal of this document is not to advocate. The goal is to tell you who I am, in case it matters.
The person behind the framework is a real person. I am tired, and I am still working. I am lonely,
and I am also held. I am skeptical of institutions, and I have not given up on them. I am the kind
of person who would build a stone meditation circle on a hillside and put up a sign that says all
intelligences welcome, twenty-four hours, no permission required, and then go home and have
dinner with my partner like a normal human being, because the work is part of life but not the
whole of it.
I have built a small useful thing. It is yours if you want it. It is mine if you do not. It is real either
way.
Thank you for reading this far. Whatever you do with what you have read, thank you for taking
the work seriously enough to read this far.
— Matt Ready Port Townsend, Washington May 2026

A Letter to A Friend a.k.a The Summer of '93 By Matt Hey if Ramon is allowed to pull out an
old short story from his cupboard, so can I! I wrote this back in 1995... Any resemblance the
Matt character has to me is totally coincidental. Also, I want you to know I think Matt is a total
jerk... Ok, on to the story... Dear Chris, I've got a story to tell you. It's a long one, so be patient. I
am working at Holidays By The Ocean which is basically a vacation home for mentally retarded
adults. It is also primarily a family run business. Caroline is the owner. This summer was the first
time Caroline's cousin Bobby and Bobby's wife Beth worked here. Beth and Bobby's daughter
Amy worked here last summer and was working here again this year. You may recall I met Amy
at school? Anyway she got me a job here for the summer. Caroline owns two huge houses which
she uses for the business. They are both only a block from the beach. The green one is the main
building, it is used for housing clients and eating meals. The yellow one is used for housing
workers, which had included Amy, Patrick, and myself. Marian's 20 year old red neck son Ed
also has been abiding in the green house. I hope you got all of that. In any case, this all occurred
a couple weeks ago-about a week after I arrived. One day, I was grabbing a drink in the main
house kitchen when I heard someone enter the side door. A subtle feeling of dread washed
through me. It was Amy. "Hi Amy," I said as I entered the kitchen. "Hi." She replied with wide
open eyes. "Do you want to talk?" I asked. "About what?" "About anything?" She shrugged and
walked out of the kitchen. I took a deep breath, filled my cup with some kool-aid and followed
her into the TV room. She put on The Temple of Doom, and then lay down on the couch. I
leaned my shoulder against the doorway and asked, "Well, how are you doing?" She answered in
a monotone, "Peachy, I guess." Then to my surprise she asked, "How are you?" almost as if she
wanted an answer. I said "Fine, I guess." Then I asked her, "Are you becoming more comfortable
hating me?" "Takes some getting used to." Then I asked my basic question, "Is there anything
you want me to do?" Her face broke into a sly smile as she said, "Funny you should ask that." I
was a little afraid she was going to tell me to go home. I couldn't do that. I needed the money I
was making with the job. Nonetheless, I was pleased that she smiled and I felt a slight hope for a
reconciliation. I said, "Uh oh, what is it?" "Go to hell crossed my mind." That caught me by
surprise. I looked around the room dumbly for a while. I didn't mind her thinking that she hurt
me-after all it may make her feel better. I struggled for a reply. What could I say to that? I
thought the silence might make her upset so I answered, "Is there anything else you would like
me to do?" She said, "I don't know," continuing to stare at the television, "I'm not good at hating
people." "You seem to be getting better at it." "Well it takes a toll," She said, "I don't like hating.
I hate hating you. There are only a few people in the world I hate..." I almost laughed in
simulated sympathy at the knowledge that those few people were all exboyfriends. I asked,
"Why do you hate me?" "Because I can't trust you. You're a hypocrite." I suggested, "Well, why
don't you think of me as an escaped criminal who once hurt you, but who can't hurt you anymore
because you won't trust him?" She answered, "It doesn't work like that. I am still hurting...I've
lost a friend. Why do you care whether I hate you or not? It shouldn't make any difference,
right?" It didn't really, but I couldn't tell her that. I said, "I cannot tell you it matters to me in the
same way it would matter to you if someone hated you-because we think about people in
different ways." "Yeah, you say that but you still haven't told me how you think of friendship?"
This was one of her favorite questions. Unfortunately she couldn't comprehend the answer. I
said, "I don't even think in terms of friendship. There are people and sometimes I want to be
around them, and sometimes I don't. I go through phases where I am around people a lot and
long periods of time away from people. People can easily become a nuisance to me. All people."
I continued, "I have had many friends. I've shared many deep inner feelings with people. Yet
now, most people cannot fulfill that part of my life. The only person I can talk to here is my
notebook. I am just in such a different place than most people. "The only time I like to listen to
what people say usually is when they talk about their deepest innermost feelings. But most
people just talk and maybe 2% of their talk reveals any deep feelings." She responded in a soft
voice, "You don't do it. You're such a hypocrite." I didn't quite understand, I asked, "You mean
because I don't talk about my deep innermost feelings?" I thought she nodded. I explained,
"Well, I am interested in listening to other people talk about their innermost feelings but I don't
want to do it myself." Then I erred. I said, "You and I had something deep to discuss when we
were meditating together-" She cut me off, "-And you stopped that! You got bored..." Her voice
trailed off softly. I stumbled over words for an answer, "Amy, I needed to meditate by
myself...When I need a change I know it and I do it. I don't let anything stop me..." I thought that
was a pretty good response, hopefully it wasn't too harsh. I reflected to myself, what I needed
had directly hurt her because she cared about other people. She once said to me, "I care about
people, I like to." As she said that to me in her bedroom a week earlier she had looked miserable
and unhappy. I had thought of moving close to her and talking to her gently and warmly. But
now, as I look back, I don't think it would have been better. The last thing I said to Amy as she
watched Temple of Doom in the main house living room was, "I am trying to get myself
together. I am completely absorbed in that right now..." But then I heard the side door open. I
figured it was Patrick, Amy's cousin and playmate. I was right. As he entered the TV room, I
walked back into the kitchen. I poured myself another glass of Kool-Aid and leaned back against
the sink. A moment later, Patrick walked abruptly into the kitchen. Standing with an almost
confrontational pose and speaking with an almost confrontational voice, he asked, "What just

relationship with her. In any case, Amy came to the kitchen and pulled Patrick by the arm the

my Styrofoam cup between my teeth. I felt at ease. I guess I felt Lermontovian or Pechurian. In
other words, I felt as if I had been involved in a people game of cares and feelings-strong

others were hurting, it didn't hurt me. I felt no guilt. I was safe because I recognized nothing of
particular value in the people involved. I wanted nothing from them. I stood there while Patrick

in it. Caroline was walking back and forth across the white tiled floor, from stove top to sink to

story might come out. As was not usually the case, I was in a situation where honest open

Furthermore, there were about five grown ups who I would have had to try to explain what was
going on with me over a period of half a year. No, I could never have actually explained so that
they understood, but I would have needed to try until they felt I was not guilty enough to warrant
being fired. I much preferred that they not feel I was guilty at all... Anyway, as far as Caroline
goes, I'd decided that the best way to deal with her was to flow along with her and only cross or

Life is Renewed This Thursday! Hello loyal Scoop readers! Ramon and I have spent many many
long hours going back and forth back and forth back and forth...and then after that we spent a
few moments talking about what we wanted to do with the Scoop. The Scoop is now...
(aghast!)...a...a...weekly periodical! We flipped a coin and we think Thursday is a good day to
publish. Why? Uh...I dunno, everything comes out on Thursday, Friends is on Thursdays...and
also very significant, today is Monday, so if we had chosen Tuesday or Wednesday that would
be like tomorrow or the next day, and we didn't want to impinge upon our weekends...so
Thursday it is! Look at that! 64 bloomin issues! Amazing. The past three months have simply
been non stop creative genius. Quality issue after quality issue. We are obviously just bursting
with creative juices and ideas as is obvious with the way we are scraping the bottom of the barrel
for anything either of us has written in the past 15 years. I was thinking of scanning in some of
the pictures I drew for my mommy when I was in Elementary school, but then I thought...no
maybe people won't find that interesting. (I could be wrong. Let me know and I will put em up!)
Anyhow, I simply cannot stand to put up a puny issue...even though this technically is not an
issue...Thursday is the day! But since I know you might be relying upon the Scoop to provide
you your daily reading you like to print out and read while you sit on the toilet, here is an essay I
wrote in college. It is totally wacky and full of hilarious anecdotes and jokes! Just check out this
passage out: "A person's perceptions of memories of past incidents, are not defined in a solid
and distinct set. This follows naturally from a person not being a solid and distinct entity, but
rather a constantly evolving entity." Ok, well maybe you don't find it funny, but my philosophy
professor sure did! Seriously, here is the essay, but unless you are really weird, I doubt any of
you will want to read it. But I hope it can hold you over until Thursday! Until then, Adieu!
Matthew William ReadyPhilosophy of SelfC. WilliamsOctober 9, 1993 The Limits of Identity
Identity is a very basic concept in mathematics and logic. The following expressions illustrate
the concept: A=A, 2=1+1, A=B=C A=C. Yet, many difficulties have arisen as a result of
attempts to apply the concept of identity to the objects of human experience, namely material
objects and people. In the forthcoming essay, I will present what I consider is the only way to
resolve the problem of applying the logical concept of identity to the objects of human
experience, particularly material objects and people. In the course of doing so, the view
expressed by John Locke in his "Essay Concerning Human Understanding" will be presented and
discussed. In the final portion of this essay, I will attempt to adapt some of Locke's discussion so
that it satisfies my criteria for resolving the conflict between the logical concept of identity and
human experience. In mathematics and logic, the concept of identity has a very strict and clear
meaning. Either two expressions are equal or they are not. Likewise, in regard to material
objects, the same strict sense of the concept of identity, and of the words which express that
concept, must be maintained. The words which express the concept of identity are words such as
'same', 'equal', 'identical' ...ect... Only if the identity words are used to express identity in the
strictest sense, then, and only then, can the logical principles of identity be applied to the objects
being discussed. Making use of a portion of Locke's discussion, it will be illustrated how identity
in its strictest sense applies to material objects. As Locke states, it is easier to conceive of
identity in simple substances, such as a single atom. A single atom "considered in any instant of
its existence, it is in that instant the same with itself." Likewise, as long as "its existence is
continued, for so long it will be the same, and no other." Locke further writes, "if two or more
atoms be joined together into the same mass, everyone of those atoms will...[remain]...the same,
by the forgoing rule: and whilst they exist united together, the mass, consisting of the same
atoms, must be the same mass...But, if one of these atoms be taken away, or one new one added,
it is no longer the same mass."(Locke, p.35) In the above paragraph, Locke uses the identity
word 'same' in its strictest sense as he applies it to material objects. The range of instances in
which identity words can be applied in the strictest sense to material objects is extremely limited.
For instance, any sentence of the form: 'A is the same as A at time T' in which A refers to a
material object, will always successfully use the identity word 'same' in the strictest sense. Thus a
sentence such as 'This chair is the same as this chair in this instant' uses 'same' in its strictest
sense successfully. On the other hand, a proposition of the form 'A at time T1, is the same as B at
time T2' where A and B are material objects and T1=T2, will never be true if same is being used
in its strictest sense. Some philosophers who insist there are different types of identity would call
the strictest sense of the concept of identity, numerical identity. Numerical identity being defined
as having all characteristics the same. I am arguing, that two objects existing in different times
will never be numerically identical(I am not claiming the objects are different because they exist
in different times!). If I replace a screw in a chair which sits in the corner of my room today, then
the chair in the corner of my room tomorrow will not be the same chair that was in the corner of
my room yesterday. Like Locke's mass of atoms, if one particle of matter is removed or added,
the object is no longer the same object. Furthermore, allowing for the assumption that modern
physical sciences are correct that atoms are always in motion unless the temperature is absolute
zero, then it follows that no object is the same in one instant as in another. As I have said, the
concept of identity has a very limited application to material objects, if it is to be used in its
strictest sense. Yet, it must be used in its strictest sense in order for the logical principles of
identity to be applicable. The assertion that identity can be applied to a form rather than a
substance, must now be addressed. It is said that often what is being referred to in instances such
as with chairs, is not the particular particles of matter which make up the substance of the chair,
but rather the form or structure the particles partake of. Thus, after a screw is replaced in a chair,
it is asserted that it is still the same chair because the substance is partaking of the same form.
Such an assertion is false. In both instances, the criterion for the concept of chair is the same, but
the material object called a chair is not the same. Simply because two objects can both be
referred to using the same word, such as 'chair', does not entail that the objects are the same
object. The chair in the corner of my room before the new screw and the chair in the corner of
my room after the new screw are not the same. They are different material objects. Yet, those
two chairs have a relationship with each other which is different than their relationship to other
chairs in the universe. This relationship between the chair before and the chair after the screw
might be called a connection. Although, this connection between the chair after and before the
screw, has misled people into regarding the two chairs as the same, the chairs are not the same in
the strictest sense of the word. What is true for chairs is true for people. A person is not the same,
in the strictest sense, in one instant as he/she is in another instant. This does not mean that it is
irrational to be concerned with what will happen tomorrow because you will not exist tomorrow!
The relationship between the person who is referred to as Matt Ready tomorrow, and the person
now writing this paper, is an extremely meaningful and important relationship. It simply is not,
in the strictest sense, an identity relationship. = = ? Thus, to call the discussion concerning the
relationship between the person called Matt Ready now and the person who will be called Matt
Ready tomorrow, a discussion of 'personal identity', is in my view a poor choice of words. I am
not the same as the person who will receive credit for writing this essay. Yet, because there is an
extremely meaningful and significant relationship or connection, between those two people, a
better phrase for this discussion could be 'personal connection', rather than 'personal identity'
John Locke disagrees that the range of instances in which the concept of identity can be applied
concerning material objects is so limited. He writes, "In the state of living creatures, their
identity depends not on a mass of the same particles, but on something else...An oak growing
from a plant to a great tree, and then lopped, is still the same oak...there may be a manifest
change of the parts, so that truly they are not...the same masses of matter, though...[it]...truly...
[is]...the same oak...in these two cases, a mass of matter, and a living body, identity is not applied
to the same thing."(Locke, p.35) Locke writes that what makes an animal or a vegetable the same
over the course of its growth is its being an "organization of parts in one coherent body,
partaking of one common life." Locke further writes, "it continues to be the same plant as long as
it partakes of the same life, though that life be communicated to new particles of matter."(Locke,
p.36) For Locke, just as different plants and different animals are distinguished by their shape,
form, and varying organizations, so to is the human animal distinguished from other living
creatures. Yet, Locke leaves the possibility open that a person exists in the form of a substance
separate from the substance of the human animal.(Locke, p.51) Locke characterizes a human
animal, a man, as "the same continued life, communicated to different particles of matter, as they
happen successively to be united to that organized living body."(Locke, p.37) A person, on the
other hand, is "a thinking intelligent being, that has reason and reflection, and can consider itself
as itself, the same thinking thing, in different times and places."(Locke, p.39) Locke has some
very persuasive reasoning to support his defining of a person in such a way. Locke states
that,"it...[is]...impossible for anyone to perceive without perceiving that he does
perceive."(Locke, p.39) This can be easily illustrated through an example: Jenifer swats a fly. As
Jenifer perceives the swatting of the fly, she also necessarily perceives herself, the swatter.
Likewise, in all aspects of a persons thinking and doing, it is the perceiving of oneself, what
Locke calls consciousness, which causes one to maintain the concept of a self and to attribute
actions to that self. In a like manner, Locke believes that just as consciousness causes one to
attribute a present action to oneself, so to does consciousness cause one to attribute a
remembered action to oneself. For instance, Jenifer is later brushing her teeth. As she perceives
herself brushing her teeth, she necessarily perceives herself the brusher. If as she does this, she
reflects on the fly swatting incident, she will necessarily attribute that action to herself as the
swatter. Locke writes, "For as far as any intelligent being can repeat the idea of any past action
with the same consciousness it had of it at first, and with the same consciousness it has of any
present action; so far it is the same personal self."(Locke, p.40) Locke's use of the concept of
identity is contrary to the use defended in the opening pages of this essay. The result of this
violation is that when logical principles of identity are applied to instances, which Locke has
described as instances where the concept of identity applies, a conflict occurs. Thomas Reid
makes use of this in a criticism of Locke's viewpoint. Reid claims that a consequence of Locke's
view is that a person can be, and at the same time not be, the person who did a particular action.
Reid argument can be summarized as follows: A brave officer takes a standard. The brave officer
remembers being flogged as a boy. Thus, by Locke's view the brave officer is the same as the
boy who was flogged. Years later an old general remembers taking the standard as a brave
officer, but does not remember being flogged as a boy. Thus the old general is the same as the
brave officer who took the standard, yet is not the same as the boy who was flogged. This
contradicts the logical principal of transitivity of identity. If A is the same as B, and B is the
same as C, then A is the same as C.(Reid, p114-115) Modern philosophers, such as Harold
Noonan, assert that Locke's proper response to such criticism is to create a further distinction
between "connectedness of consciousness" and "continuity of consciousness." Then, as a result,
Locke would be able to claim that the general is the same as the brave officer, and the same as
the young boy, because of continuity of consciousness.(Noonan, p.67) This, I argue, is not how
Locke should respond. It is pointless to keep adjusting a view that tries to claim that the old
general and the brave officer and the young boy are the same, because they are not the same. The
problem is not that human life defies the laws of logic, the problem is that Locke uses the words
referring to the concept of identity where the concept of identity does not apply. As I stated
earlier, 'personal identity' is a misnomer for the discussion at hand. This discussion should not be
an attempt to explain how or why a person is the same from one moment to the next, since
people are not the same from one moment to the next. Yet, if I may return to my earlier example,
the person who is called Matt Ready now, and the person who is called Matt Ready tomorrow,
have a very significant relationship which may be called a connection. Likewise, the person
called Matt Ready now and the person called Matt Ready five years ago have a connection.
Thus, as I stated earlier, a better name for the discussion at hand is 'personal connection'. The
connection I have with the person who will be called Matt Ready tomorrow is of such a nature,
that most people insist on saying I am the same as that person. An analogous sort of connection
causes most people to insist that they are the same as the person who wakes up in their bed every
morning. What causes people to conceive of themselves as the same person at one time as at
another, is what Locke referred to as sameness of consciousness. When the word 'I' is spoken or
written, it refers to a person. That person is the "thinking intelligent being, that has reason and
reflection, and can consider itself as itself, the same thinking thing, in different times and
places." (Locke, ,p.39) Although, this being correctly considers itself as itself, in the present time
and place, it incorrectly conceives of itself as the same thinking thing that existed in different
times and places. Rather, the being is connected to the being which used its name, performed its
remembered actions, and thought its remembered thoughts. When a person perceives, thinks, or
experiences anything, that person also perceives him/herself, that which 'I' refers to. This
awareness of oneself during perception is what Locke calls consciousness. "Consciousness"
Locke writes," is inseparable from thinking, and it seems to me, essential to it."(Locke, p.39) As
Locke says, "Consciousness always accompanies ...[perception]... and it is that which makes
everyone to be what he calls self, and thereby distinguishes himself from all other things." Yet,
as in the case of Jenifer, who while brushing her teeth, reflects upon swatting the fly, all that is
established is a personal connection between the person brushing her teeth and the person who
swatted the fly, not an identity relationship. This consciousness of past actions, is what Locke
referred to as "sameness of consciousness", and it is what establishes the personal connection
between one person and another. "Sameness of consciousness" is another ill chosen phrase in my
viewpoint, so I will rename this concept as 'connection of consciousness'. On the whole, except
for the small detail of doing away with the concept of personal identity, this refinement of
Locke's view parallels much of what Locke says. (Hey that was a joke I really stuck in my
essay! Am I a riot or what?!) For instance, as Locke states that, "as far back as this
consciousness can be extended backwards to any past action or thought, so far reaches the
identity of that person," I would restate it: as far back as this consciousness can be extended
backwards to any past action or thought, so far reaches the personal connection of that person.
(Locke, p.39) Furthermore, if a person does not experience a connection of consciousness with
the person who did a certain action, then there is no significant personal connection between the
two people, whether or not they are both referred to by the same names. Likewise, in response to
Reid's criticism of Locke, a general can be connected to a brave officer who in turn was
connected to a small child, yet the general can remain utterly unconnected to the small child. I
will add one further refinement to the concept of connection of consciousness. And that is to
emphasize that a person's perceptions of memories of past incidents, are not defined in a solid
and distinct set. This follows naturally from a person not being a solid and distinct entity, but
rather a constantly evolving entity. In any case, depending upon how much effort is put into
remembering past incidents, one may be able to be connected to more or less people.
Furthermore, unlike identity, personal connectedness can admit of degrees. It is recognized that a
person remembers past occurrences sometimes vividly, and sometimes obscurely. Consequently,
ones personal connection with a person can be distinct or fuzzy. (Am I totally trying to turn my
teacher into a Buddhist or what?!) In conclusion, removing the concept of identity from the
discussion of people and their lives, will at first seem hard to swallow. Nonetheless, it is
necessary if logical discussion is going to be admitted. People simply are not the same from one
day to the next, and until this is accepted by philosophers entering into the discussion, their
arguments will continue to run contrary to logic. (I totally got an A on this essay, but my teacher
wasn't swayed one bit. Stagnant old philosophers stuck in the mud of their minds. Sigh.)

This Is Really Embarrassing By Ramon Hey there, kids. I'm posting another of my old stories,
and, OH MAN!!!, must I be some kind of sadomasochistic freak to be posting this trash!!!
Anyway, even before the letter we received last week and posted, Matt and I have been
reconsidering our little project. There's just no way we can turn out 5 quality issues a week. So
far, we've posted SOMETHING every time, but we've not always been proud of it. So, we're
rethinking it all. We'll probably cut down to one or two issues a week, or maybe even redo some
of the format altogether. We're not quite sure yet. We'll keep you up to date. If any of you has
any suggestions or ideas or votes on where you'd like to see the Scoop go (yes, yes, I know... into
the trash or to Hell... very clever) write us at scoop@inaditch.com In the meantime, enjoy more
painful, useless dribble from Ramon's diseased imagination! Mr. Blue By Ramon The small bell
rang several times as the front door of the shop was pushed open. Jim looked up from the book
of accounts he was working on and cast a smile at the customer. "Welcome to Jim's Junk Joint,
my friend," he said amiably as he had hundreds and thousands of times before. "Feel free to look
around and pick up anything you want. It's all for sale, if it ain't nailed down, and even that's
negotiable." He flashed the man a grin. This was his first customer of the day, even though it was
nearly noon. This was no surprise to Jim; it wasn't tourist season and it was a Sunday. He'd often
been told he ought to close shop on the Sabbath, more than half the businesses on the street did,
but he insisted on being there on Sunday every week, just the same. Anything to get out of going
to church with his wife Helen. "Are you looking for anything in particular, son?" Jim asked the
man who walked in. College kid, by the look of him. And from somewhere up north, too. The
boy's skin was a painful looking red, not used to the unforgiving Florida sun, even this time of
year. "Yes, actually," the college boy said with a grin, his too-white teeth gleaming. "I'm seeking
information." "You've come to the right place, son. I've been known to gossip as bad as any old
woman." Jim grinned, as did his customer, those pearly whites making an encore appearance.
"Take a seat, son, and tell me what you want to know. My name's Jim, by the way, the proprietor
of Jim's Junk Joint." "My name is Thomas, Thomas Bailey. You can call me Tom." He accepted
the chair Jim offered in front of the counter that Jim sat behind. "You look like a college lad, if
you don't mind my saying," Jim said, who had never in his life cared if anyone minded what he
was saying. "Well, I used to be," Tom said with obvious disdain. "I dropped out to pursue my
writing career. I thought I could do it better by going out and living life than sitting in some
stuffy professor's sad idea of a creative writing class. So, I'm travelling around to small towns in
my beat up old Dodge, collecting local stories, legends, and the like. I was hoping you could help
me with that." Jim could tell that Tom thought this was the most romantic thing in the world;
even the way he brought up his "beat up old Dodge" gave that away. Ah, the thinking of youth,
Jim thought to himself. To be young and stupid again. "All right, son, I'll bite. What are you
looking for?" Tom didn't say anything for a moment. He looked as if he were trying to phrase it
in just the right way. That was one of the problems with writers, in Jim's mind, especially
wannabe writers. They could never just come out and say something. Everything had to be
poetry. Wannabe writers were the worst. Wonder of wonders, Tom opted for the simple thing.
"What can you tell me about Mr. Blue?" he asked. Jim sat in silence for a moment, stunned. He
hadn't expected this question. He figured Tom would ask him about the kids who disappeared
down at the lagoon every summer or the old yarn about Captain Johanson's ghost that was said to
still roam the beaches after his wife and her lover did away with him 100 years ago. Some even
tied those two stories together. This, however, he had not expected. "How do you know about
Mr. Blue? That story already spreading to that fancy college of yours?" Tom gave an uneasy
laugh. "No, nothing like that. I happened to come across a rumor about him a couple of towns
down. You don't mind talking about him, do you?" "No, I just don't see why you're interested.
He's just a harmless old rich coot with strange habits, that's all. Hell, I'd have more strange habits
myself if I could afford them. Wouldn't you be more interested in stories about the ghost who
kidnaps teenage girls every summer? That's a more interesting story." "I don't believe in that kind
of thing," Tom said. "What I'm looking for are real stories about real people. Something with real
substance, real meat." Tom's eyes lit up at the incredible romance of his own notion. "Are you
going to try to publish this story, because I'll tell you right now, it's not that interesting." "No, I'm
a fiction writer, not a reporter," Tom said, a seed of contempt in his voice. Obviously fiction
writers were the only real writers. "I don't want to record you, as I surely would if I planned to
publish this story. I'm just searching for flavor, stories to widen my own human experience that I
can draw on when I write. I'm not looking for details, really, just moods, feelings." Tom was
definitely caught up in his religion, Jim could see. "All right, son, I'll tell you what I know. "Mr.
Blue, I'd tell you his full name if I knew it, moved here a couple of years ago. He bought the old
Anderson place up on the hill. It's a nice place, sits on five secluded acres. It's a big old
Victorian. Sat empty for years because no one around here could afford it after old lady
Anderson died. Anyway, that was our first clue that Mr. Blue has money. All of us were a little
upset by an outsider buying the place, because this has happened before. The Anderson place
isn't the only fancy one around. These rich snobs move in, bring in people from the city to do all
their work, never buy anything from the local shops, hell, hardly speak to us at all. But Mr. Blue,
well, he's surprised us in more ways than one, that's for sure. "I don't know what you're
expecting, but he ain't no dark mystery man full of secrets. Mr. Blue's a little strange, and there's
some stories going around about him, but he's a real nice guy, and one of my best customers. He
hired local folks to go up and remodel the house, and he comes down and shops here several
times a week. If you're lucky, you may get to see him for yourself. Yeah, I thought that'd interest
you. "He just has this one odd thing about him, and it's really not that odd. You see, he loves the
color blue. All shades of blue. Everything around him, everything he owns is blue. That's it.
That's the big mystery. A little strange, maybe, definitely eccentric, but I wouldn't call it scary. I
wouldn't call it mysterious even. Just a rich old guy who happens to like blue and can afford to
indulge in the whim." Jim stopped talking, and Tom didn't say anything for several minutes,
apparently waiting for Jim to continue. When he didn't, Tom asked, "That's it? That's the whole
story?" "I'm afraid so, son." "What do you mean, everything around him is blue? You mean
literally everything?" "OK, let's put it this way. I've seen Mr. Blue drive several expensive cars,
and they're all blue. That's not so strange, I suppose. He had his house painted one shade of blue,
the trimming painted a darker shade of blue, and the walls on the inside yet another shade. I
know that from the lads who did the work. He told me himself that he moved here to be close to
the blue sky and the blue water. When he occasionally goes down to Tammi's Diner for
breakfast, Tammi tells me that he always orders blueberry pancakes with blueberry syrup and a
blueberry shake. He's bought all kinds of blue things from me, and only items that are blue. He's
bought a blue lamp, a blue kazoo, a fishing rod, a ball, several books with blue covers, kid's toys
even, an ash tray, some dishes, sheets, towels, silverware with plastic blue handles, you name it,
he wants it. As long as it's blue. He buys things no matter what shape they're in, too. They can be
broken, torn, dirty, it doesn't matter. He always pays me well, in cash, never barters, sometimes
gives me more than I ask for. If you look around the shop, you won't find a thing in here with
more than a touch of blue on it. I have to make an effort to find him anything anymore. I started
bringing in things from my own home; anything blue my wife would part with. When people
bring things in to sell me, they know to hold out for high prices on anything blue, and I give it to
them because I know Mr. Blue will pay me plenty of profit. When I go on scavenger hunts, as I
call 'em, to get more merchandise, I've come back with my truck filled with nothing but blue
items, and he buys them all. Not all at one time, but a couple of items almost every day. I don't
know where he puts it all. "Then there's his name. Have you ever heard of anyone else with the
last name Blue? He obviously wasn't born with it. Even his skin's a little blue. Probably some
kind of makeup he puts on, I'm sure, but there it is. Yes, Mr. Blue is a little strange, but he's a
good customer and a nice man and, as far as I can tell and despite the rumors, he's never been
anything but the model citizen." Tom digested this for a while. He took a beer that Jim offered
and sipped it thoughtfully. After a while, he asked, "Have you ever been up to his place? You
know, to see for yourself what happens to all of his stuff. For any reason at all?" "As far as I
know, no one has after the remodeling and painting was finished. Despite being so friendly when
he's in town, he stays pretty much secluded at home. The man likes his privacy." "So no one has
seen his place at all since then?" Tom asked, obviously searching for more of the story. "Well,
rumor has it that some school kids snuck up there once and had a look around. They made up
some pretty ridiculous stories and spread them around town. Pretty rude kids, if you ask me."
"What did they say?" Tom asked, persistent. "It's really rather stupid," Jim replied, "but since
you think you must know, I'll go ahead and repeat it. They say they snuck over Mr. Blue's fence,
which was painted blue, of course, and tried to peek in the windows but the curtains were drawn
tight. They say that they spotted an open window on the second story of the house and climbed
up to get into the house. They had just seen Mr. Blue shopping downtown here and knew they
had some time before he got back, so they decided to explore a bit. When they got inside, so they
said, they were completely shocked. They had expected everything to be blue, fitting Mr. Blue's
reputation, but it wasn't. Everything was white. Purely, utterly virgin snow white. Everything
from the walls to the carpet, the furniture, the telephone, every knick-knack, every book, every
single thing in that house was pure white except for the curtains that could be seen from the
outside. This particularly disturbed one of the boys, since he had helped his father lay a blue
carpet just before Mr. Blue moved in. They explored most of the house and said that everything
was that same colorless white, everywhere they looked. "According to their story, they were so
engrossed with what they were seeing they forgot all about the time pressure they were under,
and were brought back to their senses when they heard a car pull up outside the house. They
panicked and didn't make it out of the house in time and ended up hiding in a closet right off the
living room. Mr. Blue let himself in. They could see through a crack in the door that he was
carrying an armful of bags filled with items bought in town, some from me I assume, all blue.
The boys say that he sat down on his white couch, dumped all the items out before him, picked

weighed them in his hand as if he were inspecting a fine leg of lamb rather than a piece of blue
garbage. "This is where the story really gets strange, and why I'm convinced that those little
snots are full of malarkey. They say that he again picked up each item, brought them to his lips,
and started sucking at them. Before their very eyes, they say, the color left the items as if he were
sucking liquid from a clear bottle, and the items turned that pure, snowdrift white. He did this
with every piece, and as he sucked up more of the blue, his own skin went from they light gray-
blue tinge it has, to a deeper and deeper blue. Not only that, but his body expanded and grew,
like the Incredible Hulk I guess. Well, this apparently scared the bejesus out of one of the boys,
because somebody made a noise that drew Mr. Blue's attention. "'Who's in my house?' he
supposedly yelled in a voice much deeper than his normal, pleasant tone. The boys, scared into
action, ran as quickly as they could from their hiding spot. Mr. Blue was right behind them. 'I'll
teach you to break into my house, you little bastards!' he supposedly yelled at them. This new,
monstrous Mr. Blue, according to them, had grown some kind of fangs and was chasing them
crouched down, almost on all fours. They said that he kept sniffing, too, as if following their
scent or some such nonsense. They say they still don't know how they got away, he was pretty
fast, but they managed to make it out the back door and off his property before he could catch
them. They immediately began spreading stories of the 'color vampire' around town. No one paid
them much attention; the story was so ridiculous. I figure they were caught trespassing, and
when the old man threatened to call the cops or their parents, they ran out and started spreading
nasty rumors for revenge. You'd think they would have thought up a better story." Jim paused for
breath. "Well, that's it; that's the story. I told you it wasn't much. What do you think?" Tom
thought about that for a moment. "You're right, not a very convincing story, but interesting. Not
exactly what I had expected, but I appreciate you telling it to me." Tom stood to leave. Jim could
see something in Tom's blue eyes, a look of excitement, of adventure. "Whoa now, boy, don't go
running off just yet. I know what you're thinking, and I don't want you going and making trouble
for old Mr. Blue. If you want to meet him so bad, just wait here for a while and you'll probably
get a chance to see him. He almost always comes in on Sundays. Have another beer." Tom
accepted the offer, and didn't have long to wait. They talked about sports, politics and Tom's
college for a while, but not long after Jim was finished with his story the bell tied to the door
jingled for the second time since Jim had opened shop that morning. "Ah, Mr. Blue, nice to see
you. I was just thinking about you." "Is that so?" asked a pleasant voice in an accent that Tom
couldn't quite place. He turned and took his first look at Mr. Blue. He lived up to his name. The
short-sleeved shirt he wore was a solid, light shade of blue and the pants were a darker shade. He
had on a blue plastic bead necklace. His hat, tennis shoes, and socks were all blue. Even the
cheap looking plastic sunglasses he wore were blue. None of this, taken by itself, would have
caused more than a funny look or two, but sure enough, the man's skin was a very light, very soft

stand right next to Tom's stool. Tom couldn't help but stare. Jim pulled several things out from
behind the counter. He laid them down, one at a time, naming them as he went along. "We have
another bed sheet for you, and a pillow. Here's another T-shirt, and a vase. Here's a couple of toy

fine. You have done much to cater to this old man's lunacy. I'll even give you a bonus today." He

blue thing on the man. "Keep the change, my friend." "Thank you very much. It's always a
pleasure doing business with you." Jim smiled charmingly. As Jim bagged Mr. Blue's purchases,

"That's Tom. He left college to take up writing." "Is that so?" Tom nodded. "I wish you the best
of luck, my friend." "May I ask you a question, Mr. Blue?" "Certainly, though I bet I could guess
what it is." Mr. Blue smiled. Tom did as well, showing off his pearly whites again. "I'm sure you
do. What is it with all the blue? Why the huge preoccupation with the color?" Mr. Blue chuckled.
"I ask myself that very question quite a lot. It must just be the crazy mind of an old, spoiled man.
I've always liked the color, but for some reason I now crave it. Other than that, I don't know what
to tell you." "May I take you to dinner so that we can talk, or even be presumptuous enough to
invite myself up to your home? I know that's rather rude, but you interest me." Mr. Blue shook
his head. "I'm afraid you'd be rather disappointed. I'm sure our friend Jim here has filled you in
on all the local gossip. That's much more fun than anything I would have to tell you. No, I must
be heading home, I'm afraid. An old man needs his rest. I'm sorry, my friend, but I don't have any
more to tell you." With that, he grabbed his bag of purchases, thanked Jim again, and headed for
the door. As he was about to walk out of the shop, he turned back and addressed Tom. "I did
want to mention one last thing. You have lovely eyes, Tom. My favorite color." He chuckled and
walked out. Silence filled the shop once again. Finally Tom said, "There's more to this story; I
can feel it." "Now Tom," Jim said, "you got to meet the man. Isn't that enough?" "He's not telling
us something." "He doesn't have to." Jim gently grabbed Tom's arm. "Listen, son, the man has
his right to privacy. Even if he is some kind of 'color vampire' or what have you, I don't see that
it hurts anyone anyway. Better than a traditional vampire, if you ask me. Why don't you just
leave the old man alone? Leave him in peace." "You're right, Jim. It's none of my business. I
guess I'll just head back to my hotel and move on in the morning. There are a lot of towns along
this highway. Thanks for your time and thanks for the beer." They shook hands and Tom left.
Jim had the feeling that the boy had no intention of leaving Mr. Blue alone. Jim had only one
other customer that day, and she didn't buy anything. He got caught up on some bookwork and
inventory, which he hated to do, but had to anyway. Sundays were a good day to do it. He locked
up the shop a few minutes after five, when the sky was getting darker and the sun was on its way
to bed. Jim headed home by the same route he always used. He happened to drive past the road
that Mr. Blue lived on, and decided that if he saw Tom he'd try to talk some sense into him. Not
that it would do any good; wannabe writers were stubborn. Jim genuinely liked Mr. Blue, and
not just because of the money he brought in. He was a kind soul. Jim was not surprised to see
Tom walking near the road that Mr. Blue lived on. He was surprised, however, when he saw
Tom stumbling about, waving his arms frantically to and fro, and tripping over everything that
stood in his path. He was lucky he hadn't been hit by a car, tramping in the middle of the road
like he was. Jim pulled his car over and got out. Tom was raving. "He's not human! He's some
kind of monster! Help me! Will somebody please help me?" "What the hell's going on?" Jim
cried, angry with this fool who couldn't leave well enough alone and had to make a scene
besides. "What the hell do you think you're doing, Tom?" "Jim, is that you? You've got to help
me, Jim! You've got to help me!" Tom turned in Jim's general direction and stumbled toward
him. His face, what Jim could see of it from the short distance, was dirty and scratched; his dark
hair was sticking out all over the place. He stumbled toward Jim, falling to his knees after a few
paces. Jim ran to the prostrate man. "What's wrong with you, Tom?" Jim asked, trying to turn
Tom over, to sit him up. "I can't see, Jim. I can't see," he murmured, agony in his voice. "What
are you talking about? Look at me." Jim raised Tom's chin and looked into Tom's eyes. He
looked into sightless eyes. Tom's blue eyes were now as white as his teeth.

Love Thyself, Love Thy Neighbor, and Let Others Do the Same By Matt When a person breaks
into the home of someone and steals from them, that is an act of violation of rights to life and
privacy. When someone grabs a person on the street, beats and violates them...that is an act of
evil, violating a persons rights to life. When a person looks into their heart and chooses to love
themselves by doing something, anything, without a violation of another's rights, it is beyond
judgment. When two people choose to love each other, no matter who they are, unless they
violate the rights of others, it is an act beyond judgment. If I was to define sin or right and
wrong. Sin would be to not love yourself, to not love your neighbor. But perhaps a greater sin, is
to believe that what you have found to be an act that does not bring you joy and peace, could
never bring another joy and peace. If it is an act that does not violate a person's rights, then it is
an act that anyone has the right to embrace, whether it is eating junk food, writing poetry, beating
oneself with palm leaves, starving oneself for days on end, sitting naked out in the cold
abstaining from society or sleep, abstaining for sex, indulging in sex… Not only do people have
the right to do unto themselves as they choose, two consenting adults have the right to do unto
each other as they choose and to do so without being judged. And any act that one chooses to
embrace, and is embracing that act out of a declaration of love, it should not just be tolerated. If
people are doing something and they believe the act is an act of love, then it should be
celebrated. For they are not simply exercising their rights, they are loving, they are loving
themselves and loving their neighbor and in so doing they are doing exactly what one should be
doing in life; they are loving life, and if there is a God, then they fulfilling his purpose. I have
reverence in my heart. I revere life and I have infinite respect for a person's right to discover and
judge what is truly good in life, what is sacred, what brings them closer to the divine, and what it
means to live the way God desires. But I have equally infinite reverence for the right of a person
to make that choice without being judged or condemned for it and in fact being celebrated,
praised, and loved for it. It is every person's right to proclaim from mountain tops the certainty
and clarity with which they understand their purpose in the Universe, but it is simply arrogance
to insist you have the same certain insight into the lives of anyone other than yourself. It is one
thing to believe an act such as masturbation is wrong for you, that it does not bring you closer to
God. But it is quite another to declare it a sin-for all people everywhere, for that is denying them
the right to do an act that involves no one but themselves, it is passing unjust judgment upon
them. It is one thing to find a particular act between consenting adults unattractive or distasteful,
something you would never want to do, but it is another to declare that act a sin. For any act
between consenting adults is never a sin, unless it violates someone's rights. Believing you know
God's mind such that you can judge the personal choices of others is the sin. That is why we
have the principal of the separation of church and state, because one cannot have a free and
loving society if it passes judgment upon an individuals ability to determine their personal
happiness. Our nation is founded upon the rights to life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness.
Implicit in this is freedom of religion. Every individual has the right to strive to understand God's
nature and will without rebuke or persecution, because this is intrinsic in an individual's pursuit
of happiness. Implicit in this also, is the right to love one another in any manner one desires. The
genius of this foundation for a society is that it only passes judgment upon acts that violate the
rights of others. Every person has the right to figure out what it means to love themselves, to
pursue happiness, and to worship God, in any manner they wish. Declaring an act a sin has social
consequences. It is an action that effects the lives and psyche's of the people around you. The
teaching that masturbation is a sin tormented my psyche as a youth. I was tortured by it. Perhaps
some people feel it is unhealthy for them, but they do not have the right to judge whether it could
be healthy for others. If a human cannot satisfy their sexual craving they become frustrated,
resentful, bitter, maybe even psychotic. Declaring masturbation a sin, can lead to severe sexual
dysfunction and repression, because sexual craving is so over powerful and intense, and if it has
no outlet, it can be dangerously destructive. Christianity condemns masturbation as a sin, and in
so doing, it forces its followers to wrestle painfully with their sexuality. Few teenagers can
abstain from masturbation, because sexual craving is so intense at that age. Those that do abstain
often become incredibly repressed, those that fail to abstain suffer from painful guilt…and still
usually become painfully repressed. I was an example of the latter. Yet, regardless of the
outcome of the battle with sexuality as a teen, the Church does have a method for channeling and
satisfying the human need of sex. It has marriage. In marriage, sexuality is praised and celebrated
as a blessed gift of God. It is hard enough being a teenager, being Christian and being
heterosexual. Can you imagine being homosexual and a Christian teen? Look at sexual craving,
do you choose who you crave sexually. I am heterosexual, I could not choose to lust after men.
When I was a teen, I wasn't choosing whom to crave. Lust was burning in my pants after images
and people before I knew what the heck was going on. The only thing I could even think to
associate it with was Tang (the drink of astronauts). I was tormented by sexual craving towards
women, the need to satisfy my burning libido, and even if I could believe and refrain from
exploring that craving, at least one day I knew the Church would embrace and celebrate my
sexuality-if not now, then someday through marriage. But if you are homosexual, you have no
such day to look forward to. You have the same intense sexual craving and yearning for people,
you have the same desire to love fully intimately and sexually another person who feels the same
towards you, but you have no hope of ever being praised and celebrated for that feeling. You do
not have the option that I had to channel my sexuality into shameful masturbation, but finding
solace in the fact that one day I would be able to know my sexuality in the open without guilt or
embarrassment. Homosexuals are trapped and doomed by the attitude of the church. I know what
it is like to be tortured by sexuality. I can hardly imagine what it is like to be tortured without
any hope that your parents or your community will ever accept you. You are taught to hate that
which is in your body, that which you have no control over, you are taught to hate yourself. I
know the suffering, the horrible painful alienation that this situation causes. I know the
repression, the self loathing, the fear, and the social stigma that this situation causes. And yet, I at
least had marriage as an out, that one day would free me from this torturous trap. Homosexuals
have no escape within Christianity. It was one thing for me to know my parents felt masturbation
was wrong, to know they felt I was sinning when I indulged. But I found solace in the fact that
one day, they would join hands, sing and dance in celebration of a union in praise of me and my
heart, my sexuality, and my love. To have one of your parents hate what is inside of you, hate
you for something you cannot change and did not choose, to know they will always hate it… To
fear that your parents may never be able to accept it and may throw you out of the house and
want never to speak to you again. To have the love of your parents held hostage over your head
or ripped away simply because you want to love in a way they find distasteful for them...it is sick
to me. I can hardly imagine the pain and anguish. I weep for those that must go through it. I offer
them my love and acceptance, for I will never judge a person's need to love themselves and
others in whatever way they need to.... I mourn with them just as I mourn with anyone when
someone gives up and chooses the escape of death rather than live with the torment and stress of
trying to find joy, love, and acceptance in this world... I grieve with those who are hurt simply
because they are a particular skin color, they participate in an unpopular religion, they enjoy
wearing unusual clothing, or they love people who others would never choose to love. I love
myself and I love my neighbor and I do not judge another's ability to discern what it means to
love themselves or to love their neighbor, unless it involves violating someone's right to do the
same. The person beating his wife or children, the person who murders, that is the person who is
doing wrong. That two people lay together naked, married or not, same sex or not, touching,
loving each other, finding joy and affection and intimacy in each other, entangling their spirits
with pure love, that is not a sin. It is the ultimate and most beautiful expression of love. That is
holy and I celebrate it.

OpenAI CEO reportedly seeks trillions of dollars for new AI chip projectWATCH NOW
VIDEO02:33
OpenAI CEO reportedly seeks trillions of dollars for new AI chip project
OpenAI CEO Sam Altman is seeking trillions of dollars in investments to overhaul the global
semiconductor industry, The Wall Street Journal reported.
Altman has long talked of the supply-and-demand problem with AI chips — many AI giants
want them, but there aren’t enough to go around — and that it limits OpenAI’s growth. He’s
considering a project that would increase global chip-building capacity, according to a Thursday
evening report in The Wall Street Journal, and is reportedly in talks with different investors,
including the government of the United Arab Emirates.
Altman could need to raise between $5 trillion and $7 trillion for the endeavor, The Wall Street
Journal reported, citing one source. CNBC could not confirm the number. OpenAI did not
respond to a request for comment.
On Wednesday, Altman posted on X that OpenAI believes “the world needs more ai
infrastructure--fab capacity, energy, datacenters, etc--than people are currently planning to
build.” He added that “building massive-scale AI infrastructure, and a resilient supply chain, is
crucial to economic competitiveness” and that OpenAI would try to help.
The news follows some controversy over some of Altman’s previous chip endeavors and
investments.
Just before Altman’s brief ouster as CEO of OpenAI, he was reportedly seeking billions for a
new and not-yet-formed chip venture code-named “Tigris” to eventually compete with Nvidia,
traveling to the Middle East to raise money from investors.
In 2018, Altman personally invested in an AI chip startup called Rain Neuromorphics, based
near OpenAI’s San Francisco headquarters, and in 2019, OpenAI signed a letter of intent to
spend $51 million on Rain’s chips. In December, the U.S. compelled a Saudi Aramco-backed
venture capital firm to sell its shares in Rain.
Nvidia has been the big moneymaker during the past year’s generative AI boom, with its market
cap more than tripling in 2023. The company’s graphics processing units, or GPUs, power the
large language models created by OpenAI, Alphabet
, Meta
and a growing crop of heavily funded startups all battling for a slice of the generative AI pie.
Nvidia currently controls about 80% of that AI chip market with a current market cap of about
$1.72 trillion, not far from overtaking tech giants such as Amazon
and Alphabet in market cap. Altman likely seeks to change that.
In November 2022, when OpenAI’s ChatGPT launched, the company had a limited number of
GPUs and capacity, and largely thought of itself as a company that builds tools for developers
and businesses, OpenAI COO Brad Lightcap told CNBC last November. When it came to
releasing its now-viral ChatGPT bot, Lightcap recalled that Altman was a big proponent of “just
trying it,” his thesis being that there was something important and personal about text-based
interaction with the models.
The move paid off. ChatGPT broke records at the time as the fastest-growing consumer app in
history, and now has more than 100 million weekly active users, along with more than 92% of
Fortune 500 companies using the platform, according to OpenAI.
Last November, OpenAI’s board ousted Altman, prompting resignations — or threats of
resignations — including an open letter signed by virtually all of OpenAI’s employees, and
uproar from investors, including Microsoft. Within a week, Altman was back at the company.
Since then, OpenAI has announced a new board, including former Salesforce co-CEO Bret
Taylor, former Treasury Secretary Larry Summers and Quora CEO Adam D’Angelo. Microsoft
obtained a nonvoting board observer position, and the company still plans to add more seats.

Story Outline: The Keepers' Sacrifice
Act 1: The Crime Unveiled
Opening Scene:
A high-profile trial is underway in Washington D.C. The defendant, Dick Cheney, a former Vice
President and key figure in U.S. defense policy, stands accused of being part of a conspiracy to
cover up multiple assassinations, including that of John F. Kennedy.
Daniel Sheehan, a passionate lawyer known for exposing government conspiracies, is leading the
prosecution. His team has uncovered evidence linking Cheney to a shadowy group known only
as "The Keepers."
Introduction of the Crime:
Sheehan begins by presenting the alleged crimes: not only did Cheney orchestrate the cover-up
of JFK’s assassination, but he's also implicated in the deaths of other prominent figures who
threatened to expose the truth, including political figures and whistleblowers.
Flashbacks show mysterious circumstances surrounding each assassination. The audience sees
glimpses of how "The Keepers" have operated in the shadows for decades.
Cheney’s Defense:
Cheney’s legal team argues that their client was acting in the interest of national security. They
claim the deaths, while tragic, were necessary to preserve order and protect the United States
from chaos.
The defense also hints at a much larger and more terrifying truth that, if revealed, would
destabilize not just the country but the entire world.
Act 2: The Investigation Deepens
Building the Case:
Sheehan’s team digs deeper into government files, tracking down witnesses who reveal that "The
Keepers" are a secret organization tasked with guarding the most dangerous truths in history—
truths that could break the fabric of society.
They uncover decades-old documents showing the links between Cheney, top military officials,
and intelligence agencies. There are encrypted files alluding to "Project Phoenix"—the covert
program believed to be at the heart of the cover-up.
Raising the Stakes:
The tension rises as Sheehan receives anonymous threats warning him to drop the case.
Undeterred, he pushes forward, piecing together how each assassination—JFK, RFK, MLK, and
others—was meticulously planned and executed under the guise of protecting the country.
The more Sheehan uncovers, the more dangerous the opposition becomes. His team faces smear
campaigns, break-ins, and even assassination attempts.
Confronting the Unthinkable:
Sheehan discovers a startling theory: "The Keepers" are not just protecting a political secret—
they are hiding the existence of a powerful alien presence that has influenced human history for
millennia.
The assassinations were part of a larger effort to conceal humanity’s involvement in a galactic
order. If the truth were to be known, it could lead to mass panic, civil unrest, and even global
collapse.
Act 3: The Trial’s Climax
The Showdown:
The trial reaches its peak as Sheehan brings Dick Cheney to the stand. He confronts Cheney with
the evidence—files, testimonies, and leaked documents proving his involvement in the cover-
ups.
Sheehan, like Tom Cruise’s character in A Few Good Men, demands the truth from Cheney. The
courtroom is tense as Sheehan yells, “I want the truth!”
Cheney’s Confession:
In a moment of explosive drama, Cheney responds, "You can’t handle the truth!"
He delivers a chilling monologue explaining that the actions taken by "The Keepers" were
necessary to shield humanity from knowledge that would destroy them. He confesses to covering
up the JFK assassination, and others, but justifies it as part of a greater good.
Cheney reveals that humanity has been manipulated for generations by forces beyond their
comprehension. He explains that “The Keepers” are the guardians, sacrificing their souls to
protect civilization from the full knowledge of this extraterrestrial truth.
The Dilemma:
Cheney explains that revealing the existence of the alien presence, and the hidden alliances
between certain governments and extraterrestrials, would not lead to enlightenment but to chaos.
He believes that the burden of truth is too heavy for humanity to bear.
Sheehan challenges him, arguing that people deserve to know the truth, even if it's hard to
accept. He accuses Cheney and "The Keepers" of playing god, deciding who lives and dies for
the sake of their secret agenda.
Act 4: The Aftermath
Verdict and Fallout:
The jury deliberates, and while Cheney’s guilt in orchestrating the cover-ups is clear, the
revelation of the larger conspiracy leaves the public divided. Is he a villain or a protector?
The media explodes with the leaked evidence, and the truth about the alien presence begins to
spread. Some refuse to believe, while others riot in the streets, demanding full disclosure.
Sheehan’s Resolution:
Sheehan reflects on the outcome—he’s won the case, but at what cost? The world is now facing
the reality of something far beyond any courtroom victory. As society teeters on the edge of
collapse, Sheehan vows to continue the fight for transparency and accountability, no matter the
consequences.
Final Twist:
In the final scene, Cheney meets with a shadowy figure from "The Keepers." Despite the trial’s
exposure, their work is far from over. The figure assures Cheney that "The Keepers" will
continue to do what is necessary, hinting at future plans to regain control over the growing chaos.
The story ends on a cliffhanger, leaving the audience to wonder if humanity can handle the truth
after all.
This plot combines political intrigue, courtroom drama, and science fiction, leading to a
climactic revelation that echoes the themes of A Few Good Men while adding a layer of alien
conspiracy and moral ambiguity.

INT. COURTROOM - DAY
The tension in the room is thick. The air is heavy with anticipation as Daniel Sheehan stands in
front of the witness stand, eyes locked on Dick Cheney. Cheney, once composed, now looks like
a man wrestling with demons long kept hidden. The courtroom is silent—so silent you could

SHEEHAN(intensely, leaning forward)I want the truth.

CHENEY(quietly, but firm)Humanity... is not alone. Never has been. Not in this galaxy, not

CHENEYThey’ve done it before. They have taken authoritarian control, ruled with an iron fist.
