1.4 The Structure of This Dissertation
This dissertation has three layers.
Layer 1: The Academic Frame (Chapters 1–3). Introduction, an analysis of the shadow tree that
masquerades as truth (Chapter 1.5), methodology, and the theoretical framework of Galactic
Facilitation. This layer follows conventional academic structure while explicitly naming the
limitations of conventional academic structure.
Layer 2: The Merkle Tree (Chapters 4–10). The body of the dissertation. Each chapter is a major
branch of the tree. Each branch contains question-blocks: a clearly stated question, a one-
paragraph answer summarizing available evidence, and a hash-link showing how that question
connects to other nodes in the tree. This is the living map of the author’s search for truth.
Layer 3: The Visual Tree (Chapter 10). Diagrams showing the branching structure of the entire
Merkle Tree, so readers can see the relationships between questions and trace any claim back to
the root.

Chapter 1.5: The Shadow Tree and the Cave
1.5.1 Plato’s Prisoners, Reconsidered
Twenty-four hundred years ago, Plato described a cave. Prisoners are chained from birth so they
can see only one wall. Behind them, a fire burns; between the fire and the prisoners, puppeteers
carry objects whose shadows fall on the wall. The prisoners, having seen nothing else, take the
shadows for reality. They develop names for the shadow-shapes, predict their movements, and
reward those among them most skilled at shadow-classification with honor and authority.
The allegory has been read for two and a half millennia as a parable about appearance and
reality, about education, about the philosopher’s painful journey toward the Forms. This
dissertation reads it as something more specific: an early description of a corrupted Merkle Tree.
The prisoners’ shadow-knowledge is internally coherent. Shadow A reliably precedes shadow B.
The motion of the bird-shadow follows predictable rules. A prisoner who claims that bird-
shadows fly backward will be corrected by other prisoners — correctly, on the prisoners’ own
terms. The shadow-tree is self-verifying within its own root hash. Hash any node against any
other shadow-node and the values check out. This is what makes the cave so stable. This is why
escape requires not better arguments but a violent reorientation of the body.
The prisoners are not lying. They are not stupid. They are operating in good faith within an
epistemic system whose root hash they have never been permitted to question. Their entire
toolkit is shadow-comparison. The puppets and the fire — the actual objects casting the shadows
— are unverifiable from their position because no node available to them hashes back to
anything outside the cave.
Plato says that when a prisoner does escape, sees the fire, and returns to report, the others mock
or kill him. This dissertation has documented the modern equivalent: career destruction, censure,
microphones muted in public meetings, the structural ridicule of UAP researchers in academia,
the Robertson Panel’s 1953 recommendation to deploy mass media against witnesses. Same
mechanism. Different century. The shadow-tree defends itself.

1.5.2 The True Tree
The Merkle Tree of Truth proposed in this dissertation has its root hash in a single open
question: What is true? From this root, six branches descend: epistemology, consensus reality,
power and secrecy, methods of inquiry, the extraterrestrial question, and post-disclosure futures.
Each branch contains question-blocks. Each block hashes against every other through explicit
cross-links. The integrity of the whole can be verified from any node by tracing the hash path
back to the root.
This tree is not the author’s private possession. It is a structure into which others enter,
contribute, and verify. Hive1.net is its digital instantiation. The April 2026 Ubiquity psi training
cohort is its embodied instantiation. The Storm is Glass is its narrative instantiation. The
Jefferson Healthcare public record is its institutional-accountability instantiation.
The Merkle Tree of Truth — root hash “What is true?”, six branches, open structure

1.5.3 The Shadow Tree
There is another tree. It has the same shape. It has the same six branches, in the same
arrangement, at the same depth. A casual observer cannot tell the two trees apart by surface
inspection. But its root hash is different.
The shadow tree’s root hash is What is permitted?
Where the true tree’s Branch A asks “Can we know what is true?” the shadow tree’s Branch A
asks “What does authority know?” Where the true tree’s Branch C asks “What forces shape
belief?” the shadow tree’s Branch C asks “What protects the institution?” Where the true tree’s
Branch D asks “How do we get closer to truth?” the shadow tree’s Branch D asks “What is
allowable evidence?” Where the true tree’s Branch E asks “What is the truth about NHI?” the
shadow tree’s Branch E asks “What may we speculate about?”
Every branch has a counterpart. Every counterpart looks structurally similar at the surface. The
peer-review system is a real verification process — within the shadow tree. Classification is a
real protective mechanism — within the shadow tree. “Conspiracy as pathology” is a real
diagnostic category — within the shadow tree. None of it is incoherent. All of it is internally
Merkle-valid.
The Shadow Tree — root hash “What is permitted?”, same shape, divergent meaning

1.5.4 The Illusion of Overlap
A casual observer comparing the two trees sees overlap. Both trees have a Branch C. Both have
something called “epistemology.” Both have processes for evaluating claims. Surely, the
observer reasons, these are the same tree, or near enough.
This is the cave’s most efficient defense: not denial, but apparent congruence. The shadow tree
does not deny that there is such a thing as epistemology. It produces an epistemology. The
shadow tree does not deny that there is such a thing as evidence. It produces criteria for
evidence. The shadow tree does not deny that there are questions about NHI. It produces a
permitted speculative literature about them, neatly contained within the entertainment branch.
But the overlap is an illusion of form. The shadows are not the puppets. The two trees diverge at
the root. And because Merkle Tree integrity propagates from root to leaf, every node
downstream of a different root hash resolves to a different answer, no matter how similar the
surface labels appear.
The two trees — apparent overlap, divergent roots, structural divergence
1.5.5 Why This Matters Methodologically
This is not metaphor for its own sake. It generates three methodological commitments that
organize the rest of this dissertation.
First, internal coherence is not sufficient evidence of truth. A claim that hashes cleanly against
other claims within a system tells you only that the system is internally consistent. The shadow
tree is internally consistent. Coherence is a necessary condition for truth, not a sufficient one.
The sufficient condition requires verification against nodes that hash back to a different — and
ideally, to the actual — root.
Second, the prisoners are not the enemy. The shadow-watchers in academia, in media, in
government, on hospital boards, are not (mostly) corrupt individuals. They are honest researchers
operating in good faith within a tree whose root hash they have not been permitted to question.
The Robertson Panel did not need to corrupt every academic. It only needed to corrupt the root.
After that, the shadow tree maintains itself by ordinary peer-review hygiene. This insight matters
because it determines tone: this dissertation does not accuse individuals; it diagnoses a structure.
Third, escape is not the goal; verification is. Plato’s philosopher escapes the cave, sees the
Forms, and returns to govern the prisoners with superior knowledge. The Merkle Tree of Truth
refuses this move. The facilitator is mechanism, not authority. The person who has seen
something the shadow tree cannot account for — Lidu’s letterboard message, the orca/whale
telepathic signature, the gathering at The Hill — does not become the new philosopher-king.
They become a node. Their experience hashes against other nodes. The structure verifies, or it
does not. Galactic Facilitation is, in this specific sense, anti-Platonic. No single escape is
sufficient. The tree is verified by the network, not by the witness.

1.5.6 The Position of This Dissertation
This dissertation is being submitted to an institution that operates partly within the shadow tree.
Ubiquity University, by founding an ET Studies program, has signaled willingness to verify
nodes against a different root. But the larger academic ecosystem — within which this
dissertation will be read, evaluated, and either circulated or buried — operates predominantly
within the shadow tree.
The author cannot escape this. Neither can the reader. Neither can the dissertation committee.
We are all, to varying degrees, prisoners in the cave. The question is not whether we have
escaped. The question is whether we are willing to construct verification structures that hash
back to something other than institutional permission.
The Merkle Tree of Truth is one such structure. The chapters that follow populate it.

1.5.7 The Hive1 Hash: Both Trees in One Operational Structure
The two-trees framework as developed across the preceding subsections is conceptual. It
distinguishes between a true tree rooted at what is true and a shadow tree rooted at what is
permitted, treats them as structurally parallel, and argues that they are distinguishable by their
root hash rather than by their surface coherence. As a piece of philosophical exposition this is
adequate. As an operational claim it has been, until now, unverifiable. The reader has no way to
test, in real time, whether a given verification system is functioning as a true tree or as a shadow
tree.
Hive1.net resolves this. The platform implements a public hash endpoint at
https://hive1.net/app/view/hive/hivehash1.php that produces, on demand, the current Merkle root
hash of the entire platform’s contributions. Anyone can open the URL. The hash regenerates
with every new node, every edit, every removal. The integrity of the whole tree is therefore
continuously, publicly, anonymously verifiable. Hive1 is not a metaphorical Merkle tree. It is a
literal Merkle tree in the cryptographic sense, deployed and running, with its root hash exposed
as a publicly readable endpoint.
This deployment forces a refinement of the two-trees framework that the conceptual exposition
could not produce on its own.
The two trees coexist in a single open data structure. Hive1 does not pre-sort claims into “true”
and “shadow.” It records all contributions. Both kinds of actors — those operating in service of
verification and those operating in service of permission — can post. The platform itself is
structurally agnostic about which tree any contribution belongs to. The Merkle hash verifies that
the contributions were not tampered with; it does not verify that they are true. Both trees, in other
words, are present in the same hashable structure.
The shadow tree identifies itself through behavior, not content. This is the operational
refinement. A shadow-tree actor on an open verification platform is not identified by the kind of
claim they make. They are identified by what they do to other claims. The shadow tree’s
signature behavior is the attempt to block possible answers to nodes — to refuse admission, to
suppress, to redirect, to delegitimize, to gatekeep. On a platform that blocks nothing, this
behavior becomes immediately visible. The shadow tree is not a different content. It is a different
relationship to openness.
Hive1 blocks nothing. This is the dissertation’s central operational falsification criterion. A
platform that blocks contributions is, in the act of blocking, operating as a shadow tree,
regardless of what reasons it gives or what root it claims. A platform that does not block — that
makes its hash public, that admits all contributions, that lets the shadow-tree actors and the true-
tree actors coexist in the same structure — is, in its non-blocking, operating as a true tree. The
criterion is structural rather than ideological. It does not require the observer to know in advance
which claims are true. It requires only the observation of who is trying to close the system and
who is not.
This refinement reaches forward to Chapter 3E. The Brotherhood Pattern documented across the
seven-year Recording Fiasco, the Peninsula Health Alliance saga, and the Ashcraft prosecutorial
response is now legible as the shadow tree’s operational signature in institutional form: a
sustained, coordinated, ostensibly-good-faith pattern of attempting to block possible answers to
nodes that the institution prefers not to verify. Every characteristic move — the assertion of
unproduced legal advice, the recessing of meetings rather than allowing recordings, the
consultant deployment to redirect substantive questions, the prosecutorial decline to investigate
— is a blocking move. The Pattern is the shadow tree wearing institutional clothing. The
dissertation has been documenting it the whole time. The Hive1 hash is the place where the
dissertation can finally name what makes the Pattern recognizable.

3E.1 Case Study 1: The Recording Fiasco (2014–2021): The Prequel
The Peninsula Health Alliance dispute did not erupt from a stable institutional culture. It erupted
from a culture that had spent the previous decade actively resisting the most elementary form of
governance verification: the recording of its own public meetings by its own elected
representatives. The Recording Fiasco — the term the author used contemporaneously — is the
institutional precondition for the PHA saga. It establishes that the Brotherhood Pattern
documented in this chapter was operating in Jefferson Healthcare’s governance for at least a
decade before the moment it became prosecutable, that the institution’s preferred response to
verification proposals was procedural delay, legal ambiguity, and social pressure on the
dissenter, and that these patterns were already documented in the public record by the same
elected commissioner whose subsequent dissent on the PHA matter would be characterized in
2025 as “defying the board majority.” The verbatim transcripts of the events summarized here
are reproduced in Appendix D.
The 2014 confrontation. The author was elected to the Jefferson Healthcare Board of
Commissioners and sworn in in early 2014. At his first regular meeting on March 19, 2014, he
placed an audio recorder on the table. The board chair, Marie Dressler, opened the meeting and
immediately asked: “Could I ask you what is in front of you? Are you recording this meeting?”
The author confirmed he was making a personal audio recording to help him remember what had
happened. CEO Mike Glenn intervened with what he characterized as the position of the
district’s legal counsel: that any recording made by a commissioner — even on a personal device
— would, by virtue of the commissioner’s role, become an official public record subject to the
Open Public Meetings Act and Records Act, and that “the recommendation from Council is that
absent of the hospital doing it, that a board member should not.” The author replied that he had
researched the matter and disagreed with that legal characterization, that recording an open
public meeting was a right he held as a citizen and did not surrender by being elected. Glenn then
stated: “It’s not like I feel like it. The law would require it, and the recommendation from
Council is that if a recording is made on behalf of the organization and as a Commissioner you
would be making it on behalf of the organization, that we have our own recording.”
The author continued recording. Board chair Dressler then recessed the meeting at 3:39 p.m. —
five minutes after it had begun — to “see if we can locate a recording — some recording device,
and if not we will just have to schedule a special meeting.” The meeting resumed at 3:43 p.m.
only after another commissioner, Tony DeLeo, announced: “Madam Chairman, if you would,
that Commissioner Ready is no longer recording the meeting.” The author, having weighed the
cost of losing meeting time against the cost of conceding, had turned off his recorder.
The 2014 letter. One week later, on March 26, 2014, the author wrote a formal letter to CEO
Glenn and Chair Dressler proposing a cooperative resolution. The proposal was procedurally
simple: the author would record meetings on his personal device, immediately upload the file to
the hospital’s IT server after each meeting (where it would be stored alongside other public
records), and the file would be available to anyone who requested it through the existing public-
records process. The letter cited Washington State Attorney General Opinion AGO 1998 No. 15,
which held that “a county legislative body may not ban the use of recording devices from the
open portion of a meeting held pursuant to the Open Public Meetings Act.” The letter closed by
noting that the author would be recording the next regular meeting on April 16, 2014, and asked
whether his recording would again result in the chair recessing or adjourning the meeting.
Chair Dressler’s response, dated March 27, 2014, did not engage with the AG opinion. It restated
that the matter was “a Board decision,” that she and Glenn had consulted counsel and “were
made aware of the legal implications to the District related to recording Board meetings,” and
that “it would certainly be best if you chose not to exercise any right you have, to record the 4/16
meeting and allow the Board the time and space to make a thoughtful and deliberate decision on
this issue.” When the author replied citing the OPMA’s own preamble — “The people, in
delegating authority, do not give their public servants the right to decide what is good for the
people to know and what is not good for them to know” — and asked for the name and contact
of the attorney whose advice the chair was citing, Dressler provided only a partial name (a
Seattle attorney, identified later as Brad Berg of Foster Pepper) and made clear that any
consultation the author wished to undertake with that counsel would be “solely and totally at
your own expense.”
The structural pattern visible in these exchanges is the one this chapter describes throughout. A
right that the elected commissioner clearly held (the right of any citizen to record an open public
meeting) was reframed by the institution as a privilege that required board permission. The
asymmetry was operationalized through the assertion that the institution’s counsel had given
advice — advice the dissenting commissioner could not see, could not verify, could not consult
the attorney about without paying personally, and which was repeatedly cited as authoritative
without being produced in writing. The legal-ambiguity-as-institutional-stalling pattern that
would later characterize the PHA deliberations is already fully present here, in 2014, eleven
years before the PHA proposal existed.
The 2016 walkout. On June 29, 2016, in Chelan, Washington, the Jefferson Healthcare
Commission convened an off-site board meeting. The author began recording. Commissioner
DeLeo announced: “We’re not going to record this meeting Matt.” The author replied: “I’m
recording it.” DeLeo: “No you’re not.” A new commissioner, Kees Kolff, who had recently
joined the board, asked the procedural question that should have ended the dispute: “There’s
nothing that prohibits Matt from recording it.” DeLeo’s response: “Yes there is. It makes it
official record.” Kolff: “There should be an official record if it’s an official meeting.”
Glenn restated the institutional position: “There is a legal opinion that recommends to not do this
actually.” Kolff, attempting to find common ground, asked whether providing the recording to
the board secretary immediately would resolve the concern. Chair Jill Buhler answered: “It does
not, because it does not follow policy.” DeLeo then moved a motion to “forbid Commissioner
Ready from recording this meeting.” The motion died for lack of clear procedural support.
DeLeo stood up from the table abruptly. The author, by his own contemporaneous account,
experienced a flash of adrenaline — not knowing whether DeLeo intended to take the recorder or
leave the room. DeLeo left, saying “See you guys later! Let me know if he turns it off.”
Kolff then made a motion to conclude. The board adjourned the meeting rather than continue
with the recording in progress. The dissenting commissioner had again been forced to choose
between recording and the board functioning. The board had again chosen to stop functioning
rather than allow the recording.
The 2019 Karma B intervention. A detail that would not become structurally significant until six
years later: at the October 14, 2019 commission retreat, the consultant facilitating the board’s
governance-policy review was a person identified in the transcripts as Karma B. When the
recording question arose during her facilitation, she redirected: “But since they are recorded
now, isn’t it a moot point?” When the author tried to surface the substantive procedural question
— whether the chair should have ruled the past attempts to stop his recording out of order —
Karma B’s facilitative move was to tell the chair “don’t rule that it’s out of order. I would say
don’t go there.” This is a verbatim instance of soft procedural redirection in service of
institutional comfort rather than substantive resolution. It is also the same consultant who, six
years later, would be hired to run a similarly redirective “trust-building” facilitation pressuring
the dissenting commissioner to be “complete” with his objections to the Peninsula Health
Alliance proposal. The consultant’s role in 2019 establishes that this facilitation pattern was not
an emergency response to the 2025 dispute. It was a known, available, previously-deployed tool.
The 2019 vote. On December 18, 2019, the author proposed a board policy: “if a commissioner
decides to record a meeting on their own device, it will be announced and no further discussion
of it will be had since they’re exercising their basic right.” The hospital attorney present, John
French, told the board: “the threshold question is whether or not a board member can record over
the objection of other board members and I don’t know the answer to that, so I would have to
research that before our next meeting.” The board nevertheless voted on the motion that same
evening. It failed 3-1. The board, in other words, voted against committing not to harass a
recording commissioner before the attorney had researched whether a recording commissioner
could be harassed.
The 2021 resolution. On January 14, 2021, after seven years of dispute, the Jefferson Healthcare
Board of Commissioners voted unanimously to add language to its policy book stating that any
commissioner who independently records an open public meeting would promptly provide a
copy to the district for public records storage. The two principles all members of the board now
endorsed:
A commissioner has the right to record any open public meeting of the commission whether
regular or special session, on site or offsite (as do all residents of the United States).
No one can (or should try to) prohibit a recording of anyone in an open public meeting, even if
they personally object to the recording.
These were the principles the AG opinion had stated in 1998. They were the principles the
dissenting commissioner had cited in 2014. They were the principles the institutional counsel had
effectively conceded but resisted operationalizing through the entirety of the intervening seven
years. The cost of the resistance, measured in board time, attorney consultations, public
confrontation, and institutional dysfunction, was substantial. The cost was paid. The principles
that finally prevailed in 2021 had been correct, and citable, and provided to the board,
throughout.
Why the Recording Fiasco matters for the PHA analysis. The PHA capture attempt, when it
materialized in 2024–2025, did not arrive in a Jefferson Healthcare governance culture that
respected verification, transparency, or the rights of dissenting commissioners. It arrived in a
governance culture that had spent the previous decade actively resisting the most elementary
form of governance verification, that had repeatedly invoked unverified legal advice to justify
the resistance, that had deployed an outside consultant to soften and redirect substantive
procedural questions, and that had treated the dissenting commissioner’s persistence as the
problem rather than the institutional resistance as the problem. Every structural feature visible in
the PHA saga — the appeal to non-public legal advice, the procedural delay tactics, the
consultant deployment, the recharacterization of dissent as defiance, the exclusion of the
dissenting commissioner from substantive deliberation — had already been operationalized at
lesser stakes for years before the PHA appeared. The Brotherhood Pattern in this district was not
a 2025 emergency response. It was a 2025 mature institutional capability that had been refined
through prior conflict.
This is the structural meaning of the prequel. The PHA saga did not corrupt a healthy governance
culture. It revealed the culture that had already been in place. The Recording Fiasco is the
longer-term hash path that verifies what 2025 alone could only assert.
The Ashcraft memo cannot be analyzed in isolation. It is the prosecutorial response to a
documented chain of governance breaches whose contours must be visible to the reader before
the memo’s protective reasoning can be evaluated. This section provides that context. It is not a
comprehensive history of the Peninsula Health Alliance dispute — that history occupies
approximately three hundred pages of The Complete Works of Matt Ready, including emails,
legal analyses, meeting transcripts, criminal complaints, public-records requests, and media
coverage. This section provides only what the reader needs to follow the memo analysis that
follows.

Case Study 2: The 2025 Peninsula Health Alliance proposal
The Peninsula Health Alliance was a proposed governance structure that would have placed two
public hospital districts — Jefferson Healthcare in Jefferson County, Washington, and Olympic
Medical Center in Clallam County, Washington — under a single combined oversight board.
The proposed allocation of board seats was seven for OMC appointees and five for Jefferson
Healthcare appointees, on a board of twelve. Such an allocation is a permanent supermajority.
Under the proposed structure, every contested decision regarding the operations, capital
allocation, service-line composition, and strategic direction of two public hospital districts —
taxpayer-owned assets in two separate counties — would be decided by the appointees of one
party, with the other party’s appointees holding only enough votes to register dissent. The
framework was developed in part by the consulting firm Juniper Advisors, engaged to facilitate
the merger discussions.
The NDA. In late 2024 and early 2025, Jefferson Healthcare CEO Mike Glenn signed a non-
disclosure agreement with Olympic Medical Center committing the institution to secrecy
regarding the merger discussions. This document was neither presented to nor approved by the
elected Jefferson Healthcare board of commissioners. The author, as a sitting commissioner
during this period, was not informed through normal governance channels of the NDA’s
existence, contents, or signing. The NDA was, by all available evidence, drafted as standard
merger-advisory practice — the kind of confidentiality instrument that consulting firms routinely
produce for transactions of this kind. Standard practice, in this instance, was incompatible with
two layers of governing authority: it was incompatible with the OPMA, because it bound a
public-asset institution to secrecy regarding deliberations that the OPMA presumes to be public;
and it was incompatible with the elected board’s authority over CEO actions of this magnitude,
because it committed the institution to a binding agreement with a counterparty without board
knowledge or approval. Neither incompatibility appears to have been registered by the
institutional actors who facilitated, drafted, or signed the document at the moment of signing.
The structural pattern is that the standard practice of one institutional domain (merger advisory)
was applied without examination to a domain where it was not legally available (public hospital
district governance).
The executive sessions. During this same period, the Jefferson Healthcare board majority
deliberated the PHA proposal in executive sessions that did not meet the criteria authorized
under Washington’s OPMA. The OPMA permits executive (closed) sessions only for narrowly
defined purposes — receiving legal advice on pending litigation, evaluating personnel
performance, considering the lease or sale of real estate where public knowledge would
adversely affect price, and a small number of other enumerated categories. Deliberating a
governance restructure that would transfer effective control of the hospital district to a different
jurisdiction’s appointees is not within those categories. The deliberations should have occurred
in open session, with the public and the dissenting commissioner present. They did not.
The discovery. In February 2025, the author — as a sitting Jefferson Healthcare commissioner
— discovered the executive-session deliberations and the existence of the NDA. He raised the
OPMA-compliance and CEO-authority concerns publicly, in board meetings and in writing to
the board, the CEO, and the institution’s attorneys. The structural argument he made was
straightforward: a public hospital district cannot legally surrender effective control of taxpayer-
owned assets to a permanent supermajority controlled by a separate jurisdiction’s appointees, the
deliberations producing such a proposal cannot legally occur in unauthorized executive session,
and the chief executive of a public hospital cannot legally sign a non-disclosure agreement on
behalf of the district without board approval.
The institutional response. The board majority responded to the author’s objections through a
documented sequence of suppression mechanisms. An outside facilitator (Karma B) was hired to
run a “trust-building” session whose facilitation method functioned to pressure the dissenting
commissioner to be “complete” with his objections and move on. The author was accused of
libel for the public statements he made about the OPMA violations. His microphone was muted
in public board meetings. He was ultimately censured by the board majority for “defying the
board majority” — a charge whose phrasing makes the structural problem visible: the censure
was not for any specific factual misstatement, but for the act of dissenting from the institutional
consensus. None of these responses addressed the underlying OPMA or CEO-authority
questions. They addressed the dissenter.
The criminal complaint. The author filed a criminal complaint with the Jefferson County
Sheriff’s Office regarding the OPMA violations and the unauthorized NDA. Detective Derek
Allen of the Sheriff’s Office conducted the criminal investigation and produced a report
documenting the findings. That report, along with the supporting attachments, was forwarded to
the Jefferson County Prosecuting Attorney’s Office for evaluation. Chief Criminal Deputy Chris
Ashcraft received Detective Allen’s investigation report. On May 14, 2025, Deputy Ashcraft
produced the internal work-product memo that the remainder of this chapter analyzes. The chain
matters: this was not a single prosecutor’s idiosyncratic call. This was the documented output of
a multi-step institutional review process — citizen complaint, sheriff’s investigation, deputy
prosecutor’s legal evaluation — in which each actor performed his assigned role and the
outcome was the production of protection rather than the enforcement of law.
The current status. The PHA proposal was not consummated, in significant part because the
author’s documentation forced the matter into public visibility before the supermajority structure
could be ratified. The 300-page public record exists. The author remains an elected
commissioner as of the date of this dissertation. The OPMA violations and the unauthorized
NDA were not prosecuted. Mike Glenn remains CEO of Jefferson Healthcare. The board
majority that censured the author remains in place. Olympic Medical Center remains
operationally separate. Juniper Advisors remains a functioning consulting practice. No actor in
the chain — institutional or individual — has faced legal consequence. The Ashcraft memo is the
document that secured this outcome.
With this background established, the memo can be examined.

3E.3 The Ashcraft Memo: A Case Study in Protective Reasoning
On May 14, 2025, Deputy Ashcraft produced an internal “work product” memo evaluating
potential criminal charges related to the Peninsula Health Alliance OPMA violations. The
memo’s full text reads:
“I thoroughly reviewed Derek’s memo and reviewed the attachments I was provided. Legal
analysis — I do not seen any evidence of traditional criminal conduct because there is a lack of
criminal intent to harm anyone, including the public. There may be OPMA violations that could
run their ordinary course but those are issues for State regulators to investigate. There is no
RICO violation because there is no criminal intent. In a RICO case you have a mix of legal and
criminal actions that all support an overarching criminal scheme, i.e., the business itself is crime
though lots of the things the organization does is legal (run a strip club, pick up garbage, etc.) in
order to hide the proceeds of the illegal activity (protection, drugs, murder). With regard to the
hospital, it’s goal is legal (providing medical care to the Olympic Peninsula), but some of what
they did might have violated OPMA. Since the goal, providing good health care, is 100% legal,
there is not a RICO case even if they intentionally violated OPMA (and I don’t see intent to
commit a crime).”
The memo’s central conclusion — that no criminal conduct occurred because there was “a lack
of criminal intent to harm anyone, including the public” — represents a fundamental inversion of
legal reasoning. Rather than evaluating whether the evidence supported criminal charges, the
prosecutor constructed a presumption of innocence based on the defendants’ institutional status
and stated good intentions. The memo does not deny that violations may have occurred. It
declines to act on them.
The author terms this pattern the Immunity Doctrine: the systematic application of prosecutorial
discretion to protect institutional actors by reframing criminal conduct as procedural violations,
jurisdictional confusion, or good-faith mistakes.

3E.4 The Intent Standard as Institutional Shield
Ashcraft’s reasoning relies on an intent standard that effectively immunizes institutional actors
from criminal prosecution. By requiring proof that defendants specifically intended to “harm the
public,” the prosecutor created an evidentiary bar that institutional actors can almost never meet,
because institutions always claim public benefit as their mission.
The logical structure of institutional immunity proceeds in four steps. First, the mission
statement defense: the organization exists to serve the public — healthcare, education, public
safety. Second, the good-faith presumption: employees and officials are presumed to be
advancing that mission. Third, intent impossibility: criminal intent cannot exist when actors
believe they serve the public good. Fourth, procedural minimization: violations become
“mistakes” rather than crimes.
This framework would protect any institutional actor whose organization has a legal mission.
Hospital administrators, school superintendents, police chiefs, and elected officials become
effectively immune from criminal prosecution because their institutional roles provide
presumptive evidence of good intent. The same actions that would constitute criminal conspiracy
if undertaken by individuals outside institutional settings become evidence of good-faith
institutional process when undertaken by “good people” in official roles.

3E.5 Jurisdictional Buck-Passing
The Ashcraft memo demonstrates a second protection mechanism: jurisdictional deflection.
When presented with potential OPMA violations by county-level actors, the county prosecutor
immediately referred the matter to “State regulators,” characterizing the violations as “issues for
State regulators to investigate.”
This represents a systematic abdication of local prosecutorial responsibility. OPMA violations
occur at every level of government — municipal, county, state. If each prosecutor refers
violations to a “higher authority,” the result is a protection system in which no actor at any level
claims responsibility for enforcement. The local prosecutor refers the matter to state regulators.
State regulators classify it as requiring local prosecutorial discretion. State prosecutors may
classify it as a civil rather than criminal matter. Civil enforcement requires prosecutorial
determination of criminal intent — which returns the question to the local prosecutor who
declined to act in the first place. Each level of the system provides the others with plausible
deniability while ensuring that institutional actors face no meaningful consequences.

3E.6 RICO Analysis as Institutional Brotherhood
Ashcraft’s rejection of RICO charges reveals perhaps the most significant aspect of institutional
protection: the prosecutor’s structural inability to perceive institutional corruption as organized
criminal activity. His analysis states that RICO requires “a mix of legal and criminal actions that
all support an overarching criminal scheme,” and then defines “criminal scheme” so narrowly
that institutional capture becomes impossible to prosecute.
According to this reasoning, an organization cannot be a criminal enterprise if its stated mission
is legal, regardless of how systematically it violates the law in pursuing that mission. This logic
would immunize not only hospitals but also police departments (mission: public safety), school
districts (mission: education), and government agencies (mission: public service) from RICO
prosecution no matter how corrupt their operations. What Ashcraft’s framework cannot register
is that the systematic violation of transparency laws, the coordinated suppression of oversight,
and the use of legal processes to conceal unlawful conduct constitute exactly the pattern of
racketeering activity that RICO was designed to address.

3E.7 The Brotherhood Protection Network
The Ashcraft memo is one document. The pattern it exemplifies is not. The author terms this
pattern Institutional Brotherhood: a network of professional relationships that creates systematic
protection for institutional actors across different agencies and jurisdictions.
In the Jefferson Healthcare case, the protection network includes hospital administrators who
coordinate secrecy, hospital attorneys who provide legal cover for violations, elected
commissioners who suppress dissent and transparency, county prosecutors who decline to pursue
criminal charges, sheriff’s departments that investigate selectively, and state regulators who
defer to local discretion. Each actor in this network provides protection for the others. The
prosecutor protects the hospital administrators, who protect the elected officials, who protect the
attorneys, who in turn maintain the political and professional relationships that sustain the
prosecutor’s position.
This is not conspiracy in the sense of a coordinated meeting in a smoke-filled room. It is
conspiracy in the structural sense: each actor, operating in good faith within professional norms,
produces protection as a byproduct of normal operation. The brotherhood does not need to plot.
It only needs to function.
The term Brotherhood is used here not metaphorically but historically. The formative
governance institutions of the early American republic — the Constitutional Convention, the
early federal courts, the political parties of the founding generation, and the professional bar that
grew up alongside them — were substantially organized through male fraternal structures, most
prominently Freemasonry. Fourteen of the first sixteen U.S. presidents had documented Masonic
ties; the architecture, ceremonial protocol, and professional networks of the early republic carry
that lineage into the present day. The internal logic of those structures — mutual protection
among similarly-positioned members, in-group preference operationalized through routine
professional courtesy, and the treatment of institutional loyalty as a moral category rather than a
procedural one — has descended through institutional culture into the contemporary professional
class. The pattern is structural, not coordinated. Participants need not be Masons, need not be
male, and need not be aware that the logic they are applying has a historical origin. They need
only inherit the institutional norms that originated in that structure and apply those norms in
good faith. The female commissioners, board chairs, and consultants who appear in the Jefferson
Healthcare record — Marie Dressler, Jill Buhler-Reinstra, the consultant Karma B — operate
within the Brotherhood Pattern as readily as any of their male counterparts. The pattern selects
for institutional position, not for biology. The historical name is preserved here because the
historical name is structurally accurate.
The structural mechanism by which the Brotherhood Pattern operates is the one named in
Section 1.5.7: blocking possible answers to nodes. Every move documented in this chapter is, at
the operational level, a blocking move. CEO Glenn citing unproduced legal advice to prevent
recording is a block on the possible answer what was actually said at the meeting. Chair Dressler
refusing to share the attorney’s name except at the dissenter’s expense is a block on the possible
answer what was the attorney’s actual position. Commissioner DeLeo’s walkout in Chelan rather
than continuing with the recording in progress is a block on the possible answer what does this
meeting contain. The hiring of Karma B in 2019 to redirect the recording question, and again in
2025 to redirect the PHA dissent, is a block on the possible answer was the dissent substantively
correct. The board majority’s censure of the dissenting commissioner for “defying the board
majority” is a block on the possible answer was the dissent factually grounded. The Ashcraft
memo declining to find criminal intent is a block on the possible answer did the institutional
actors commit prosecutable acts. Each block individually appears to a participant inside the
Pattern as a routine professional decision — protecting the institution, preserving discretion,
avoiding speculation, exercising appropriate caution. Examined collectively, against the
framework of Section 1.5.7, the blocks are the Pattern. The Brotherhood is not a conspiracy of
intent. It is a coordinated set of blocking behaviors operating in a culture that treats blocking as
professional norm. It is the shadow tree wearing institutional clothing.

3E.8 Linguistic Reframing as Protection Mechanism
Underlying the entire analytical structure of the Ashcraft memo is an unstated presumption that
institutional actors are inherently good people who make procedural mistakes rather than commit
crimes. This presumption operates automatically for certain classes of defendants — healthcare
executives, elected officials, attorneys, fellow law enforcement — while being systematically
denied to other classes.
The presumption operates through linguistic substitution. Violations become procedural
mistakes. Coordination becomes communication. Suppression becomes order. Deception
becomes miscommunication. Conspiracy becomes institutional process. This linguistic reframing
allows prosecutors to acknowledge that illegal conduct occurred while simultaneously arguing
that no crime was committed.
This is the shadow tree’s most efficient defense at the prosecutorial layer: not denial of the
underlying facts, but renaming of the facts in language that strips them of their criminal
character. The substitution operates automatically, without conscious bad faith, because the
prosecutor and the institutional actors share a vocabulary and a worldview.

3E.9 Port Townsend as a Merkle Tree Case Study
The history of corruption and moral crime by institutions in Port Townsend is itself a Merkle
Tree case study. The dissertation has, until this point, deployed the Merkle Tree as a framework
for evaluating claims about extraterrestrial presence, institutional secrecy, and disclosure. But the
framework applies recursively. Any community across time can be examined as a Merkle Tree: a
root question (what does this community claim about itself?), branches of institutional behavior
(governance, law enforcement, commerce, religion, civic memory), and nodes consisting of
specific documented events. The integrity of the community’s self-understanding is verified by
hashing nodes against one another. When the official narrative says “we are a charming
Victorian seaport with proud frontier heritage” and the documented record contains a federal-
ordered village destruction, an extralegal lynching, an 1867 ordinance prohibiting Indigenous
dwellings, an 1871 ordinance prohibiting Indigenous people from entering the city without a
white chaperone, multiple decades of subsequent institutional capture, and a 2025 prosecutorial
memo declining to enforce transparency law — the hash paths do not converge. The root hash is
corrupted. The community’s self-understanding does not match the community’s documented
behavior.
This subsection examines Port Townsend as a worked example. The selection of events is not
exhaustive; it is illustrative. The pattern is the point. The same town in which the dissertation’s
author serves as an elected hospital commissioner — and in which his microphone was muted in
public meetings for objecting to an illegal executive session — has produced documented
institutional crime, without individual accountability, across at least 154 years. Examining the
pattern establishes that the Immunity Doctrine is not an artifact of contemporary prosecutorial
practice. It is a structural feature of how this community’s institutions have processed
wrongdoing for generations.

Node 1: The destruction of qatáy village, August 23, 1871
The S’Klallam village of qatáy — Chemakum in origin, occupying the site where Memorial
Field sits today — had been continuously inhabited for thousands of years. By 1859,
approximately two hundred S’Klallam people lived there under the leadership of Chief
Chetzemoka, who had repeatedly intervened to maintain peace between his people and the
arriving white settlers, including (according to oral tradition) preventing a planned massacre of
the early Port Townsend founders. On August 23, 1871, on orders from the Superintendent of
Indian Affairs for Washington Territory, the entire village was burned to the ground. Its residents
were forcibly removed; their canoes were tied to the stern of a federal ship and towed away as
the village smoldered behind them. It is highly likely the leaders of Port Townsend actively
assisted with this action including city police and fire officials. The legal pretext was an 1867
city ordinance prohibiting Indigenous dwellings within Port Townsend, an ordinance that
“technically remained on the books” until modern day and was deployed by the Superintendent
as the basis for the destruction. The ordinance had been passed by the city’s settler-led council,
supported by the local press, and enforced by the territorial government. No individual was ever
charged with anything related to this event. There was no person to charge. The entire operation
had been performed by the institutions.

Node 2: The lynching of Kia-a-han
In an early period of Port Townsend history, a Chemakum man named Kia-a-han killed a stray
steer belonging to Percival Chamberlin, a non-Native farmer whose herd was known to roam
destructively through the area. Historical accounts indicate that Chamberlin had previously
announced that local Indigenous people could hunt his troublesome cattle so long as they
reported the kill so the meat could be shared. Kia-a-han did exactly this. Chamberlin responded
with rage. Kia-a-han fled. Chamberlin organized a posse from Port Townsend, threatened Kia-a-
han’s wife O’wo-o-ta until she revealed his hiding place, captured him, and brought him back to
town. He was hanged from a tree at the southwest corner of what is now the Camas Prairie Golf
Course, likely in front of many community witnesses, upon the limb of a fir tree that still stands
today. There was no trial. There was no warrant. There was no judge. There was a mob
organized by a private citizen, drawing participants from the broader Port Townsend community,
and the mob killed a man for allegedly killing a cow with permission. No individual was ever
charged. The community participated. The community moved on.

Node 3: The 2025 Peninsula Health Alliance Scandal
In 2024 and 2025, the Jefferson Healthcare board began closed-session deliberations regarding
the Peninsula Health Alliance, a proposed governance structure that would combine Jefferson
Healthcare and Olympic Medical Center under a single oversight board. The proposal was
facilitated in significant part by the consulting firm Juniper Advisors, engaged to support the
merger discussions and produce the governance framework. The structural feature of the PHA
proposal that this dissertation treats as documentary evidence — and which is verifiable in the
public record — is the proposed allocation of board seats: seven seats for Olympic Medical
Center appointees and five seats for Jefferson Healthcare appointees. A 7-5 split on a 12-seat
board is a permanent supermajority. Under such a structure, every contested vote regarding the
operations, capital allocation, service-line decisions, and strategic direction of two public
hospital districts — assets owned by the taxpayers of two separate counties (Jefferson and
Clallam) — would be decided by the appointees of one party, with the other party’s appointees
holding only enough votes to register dissent. This is not parity. This is not even minority
protection. This is the documented governance asymmetry that the proposal would have
installed.
The author’s primary objection as a sitting Jefferson Healthcare commissioner was
straightforward: a public hospital district cannot legally surrender effective control of taxpayer-
owned assets to a permanent supermajority controlled by a separate jurisdiction’s appointees,
and the deliberations producing such a proposal cannot legally occur in unauthorized executive
session, and the chief executive of a public hospital cannot legally sign a non-disclosure
agreement on behalf of the district without board approval. All three of these things occurred.
The author objected. The board majority responded by excluding him, censuring him, and
muting his microphone. The county prosecutor responded by declining to enforce the
transparency law. The PHA proposal was not consummated — in significant part because the
author’s documentation forced the matter into public visibility before the supermajority structure
could be ratified — but the attempt is what this node records. The attempted capture was
conducted through a documented chain of identifiable institutional actors performing assigned
roles: the consulting firm produced the framework; the CEO signed the NDA; the board majority
deliberated in unauthorized executive session; the hospital attorneys provided legal cover; the
dissenting commissioner was suppressed; the prosecutor declined to enforce. None of them,
individually, “attempted to seize control of two public hospitals.” The attempt was performed by
the institution.
A point of methodological honesty: this node documents an attempted institutional capture, not a
consummated one. The dissertation does not allege that Juniper Advisors or Olympic Medical
Center engaged in criminal conduct as defined by the statutes the county prosecutor declined to
invoke. What is documented is that a consulting firm was engaged to facilitate a transaction
whose proposed governance structure would have transferred effective control of one public
hospital district to the appointees of another, that the deliberations producing this proposal
occurred in violation of Washington’s Open Public Meetings Act, that an NDA was signed by
the chief executive without board approval, and that the dissenting commissioner who
documented all of this was institutionally suppressed. Moreover, the coverup of this process
involved many publicly false statements and coordinated actions which to the author continues to
believe appears like a conspiracy to commit fraud. Whether these documented facts constitute
criminal conduct is — per the Ashcraft memo — a question prosecutors have declined to answer.
Whether they constitute institutional capture in the structural sense the dissertation defines is a
question the Merkle Tree is built to answer. The hash path is visible. The reader can trace it.

Node 4: The Power of Local Prosecutors to permit shadow tree behavior, “The 2025
Ashcraft Memo”
The detailed analysis of this node occupies sections 3E.3 through 3E.8 above. In summary: a
sitting county prosecutor in 2025, presented with documented acts of deception and possible
conspiracy to commit fraud by the local public hospital district administrator and board
members, declined to act on grounds that the hospital’s mission was legal and that intent to harm
the public could not be established. The dissenting commissioner — the dissertation’s author —
was excluded, accused of libel, censured, and had his microphone muted in public meetings. No
individual was charged. The institutional protection mechanism functioned exactly as it did in
1871. Node 4 documents the prosecutorial response to the underlying transaction. Node 3, above,
documents the underlying transaction itself.

The structural pattern across nodes
What these four events share, across 154 years, is the production of institutional crime — or
attempted institutional capture — without individual accountability. In 1871, the federal
government, the territorial Superintendent of Indian Affairs, the Port Townsend city council that
passed the 1867 ordinance, the local newspaper, the settlers who lodged complaints, and the
soldiers who lit the fires were each performing their assigned institutional roles. None of them,
individually, “destroyed a village.” The village was destroyed by the institution. In the Kia-a-han
lynching, Chamberlin organized the posse, but no member of the posse was the one who tied the
rope or chose the tree alone — and even Chamberlin acted within a community that supplied the
participants, supplied the witnesses, supplied the absence of legal consequence. None of them,
individually, “lynched a man.” The man was lynched by the community functioning as
institution. In the PHA proposal, Juniper Advisors produced the governance framework as
engaged consultants performing standard merger-advisory work; Olympic Medical Center
pursued a structure favorable to its district as boards routinely do; the Jefferson Healthcare board
majority deliberated in executive session as boards routinely do when discussing acquisitions;
the CEO signed the NDA as CEOs routinely do; the attorneys provided cover as attorneys
routinely do; the prosecutor declined to enforce as prosecutors routinely do. None of them,
individually, “attempted to capture two public hospital districts.” The capture was attempted by
the institution. In the Ashcraft memo, the prosecutor declined to act because the hospital’s
mission was legal; the hospital’s secrecy was processed by attorneys whose role was to protect
the institution; the executive session was conducted by commissioners performing their assigned
roles; the consultant was hired to facilitate harmony rather than accountability. None of them
individually egregiously “violated the public trust.” The public trust was violated by shadow tree
norms familiar to the participants in the institutions. The author’s objections to the law breaking
in the process was seen as the inappropriate and disruptive behavior to the other board members
who formally censured this author for these actions.
Four nodes. One pattern. The hash matches. This is the Brotherhood Pattern operating across
deep time, and the Merkle Tree of the community’s actual behavior — verified node against
node — diverges from the Merkle Tree of the community’s official self-understanding. Both
trees exist. Both have internal coherence. They share the same surface labels (charming
Victorian seaport, proud frontier heritage, civic-minded community, public hospital districts
serving the people of the Olympic Peninsula). Their root hashes do not match. The shadow tree
of Port Townsend’s official memory and the true tree of Port Townsend’s documented behavior
are the same divergence the dissertation has been mapping at the federal-disclosure scale, here at
municipal scale. The mechanism is identical.

The institutional substrate
The specific institutions named in the dissertation memory note — Freemasonry and the Catholic
Church as concentrated nodes of the territorial-era good-old-boys network — are documented as
significant social and political forces in Port Townsend’s nineteenth-century power structure.
Port Townsend’s Masonic lodge was founded in 1859, four years after the Point No Point Treaty
and before the village destruction; the Catholic Church established a missionary presence in the
territory during the same period. Both institutions provided the kinship, professional, and social
infrastructure within which the city council, the territorial government, the local press, and the
merchant class coordinated. Connecting either to specific operational responsibility for the 1871
village destruction or the Kia-a-han killing requires source documentation that exceeds what is
available in the public record. What is documented is that the city government, the federal Indian
Affairs office, the territorial press, the merchant class, and the settler community functioned as
an integrated network in which legal authority, social capital, and economic interest converged to
produce these outcomes without producing a single individually-prosecutable actor. That is the
definition of institutional capture. That is the substrate that produced the 1867 and 1871
ordinances, the village destruction, the Kia-a-han lynching, the legal exclusion of Indigenous
people from the city, and — in attenuated but structurally identical form — the 2025
prosecutorial memo declining to enforce transparency laws against a captured hospital board.

Why this matters for the dissertation’s central claim
If the same town that burned a 2000-year-old village in 1871, lynched a man for killing a cow
with permission shortly thereafter, codified racial exclusion through municipal ordinance for
decades, and produced an internal prosecutorial memo in 2025 declining to enforce transparency
law against a hospital board — if that town’s institutions have processed wrongdoing through the
same Immunity Doctrine across three separate centuries — then the question of whether
contemporary U.S. federal institutions can be trusted to handle disclosure of non-human
intelligence presence is not a hypothetical. It has empirical historical answer at the local scale.
Institutions that have operated this way for 154 years do not abruptly begin operating differently
when the stakes increase. They operate the same way at every scale and every era, because the
mechanism is structural rather than situational. The Brotherhood does not need to plot. It only
needs to function.
The Merkle Tree methodology proposed in this dissertation is not a theoretical exercise. It is the
only verification structure that has been demonstrated, locally, to surface what the community’s
official self-understanding has buried. The historical record being built today around qatáy
village, the hanging tree, and the Camas Prairie golf course site is itself a Merkle-Tree-in-
progress: descendants and allies adding nodes, hashing them against the documentary record, and
forcing the community’s official narrative to verify against what actually happened rather than
against what was previously permitted to be remembered.

Acknowledgment
The Chemakum people, declared “extinct” by nineteenth-century historians, are not extinct. In
2022, Chemakum descendants formed a council to reclaim their history, culture, and language.
There is an ongoing 2026 process to designate the hanging tree as a Port Townsend landmark.
The S’Klallam people, dispersed by the 1871 forced removal, have rebuilt at Jamestown, Port
Gamble, and Lower Elwha. They remain. The historical record being built today — in part by
their advocacy, in part by allies on the Port Townsend City Council who have moved forward
with landmark-tree designation despite some objections — is itself an instance of the Merkle
Tree methodology functioning. New nodes are being added. Old hashes are being verified
against documentary and oral-historical evidence. The institutional record that erased these
events is being amended by descendants who refused to be erased. This is what verification
structures look like when they actually work.

3E.10 Implications for Post-Disclosure Governance
The Ashcraft memo demonstrates why traditional law enforcement cannot be relied upon to
address institutional capture. When the capture involves coordination among government entities
— hospital district, county prosecutor, sheriff’s department — the normal accountability
mechanisms become protection mechanisms. The same structures designed to enforce the law
become instruments through which the law is rendered inoperative against insiders.
The implications for post-disclosure governance are direct. If agents in the criminal justice
system from law enforcement to the prosecutor systematically protect institutional actors from
accountability for transparency violations at the rural-county scale, the same mechanisms — the
same intent standards, the same jurisdictional deflection, the same brotherhood norms — will
operate at the state and federal scales to protect powerful bad actors, intelligence agencies,
military contractors, and government officials from disclosure obligations regarding NHI
presence (and all secrets they coordinate to hide). The protection systems that shield Jefferson
Healthcare administrators from law enforcement are structurally identical to the systems that
have shielded the U.S. crash-retrieval program, not to mention the basic truth about the existence
of powerful local non human intelligence, from congressional knowledge and oversight for seven
decades.
This is the structural argument the dissertation makes: secrecy operates identically at every scale.
The Ashcraft memo is the rural-county scale specimen. The Washington State Auditor’s barely
noticeable recognition of the Open Public Meetings Act violations and coordinated deception
designed to usurp control of a public hospital district is an example at the state level. The 1953
Robertson Panel report and The Warren Report are the federal-intelligence scale specimens.
They are the same mechanism in different domains.

3E.11 The Merkle Tree Response
The systematic nature of prosecutorial protection demonstrates why the Merkle Tree approach to
truth verification is necessary rather than optional. When law enforcement cannot be trusted to
enforce transparency laws, alternative verification mechanisms become required infrastructure
rather than supplementary tools.
The Merkle Tree approach addresses prosecutorial protection in four ways. It removes
prosecutorial discretion from truth verification, replacing the question “did a crime occur?” with
the question “does the documentary record cohere?” — a question prosecutors cannot decline to
answer because the public can answer it themselves. It creates transparent chains of evidence that
cannot be dismissed through jurisdictional confusion, because the tree does not respect
jurisdictional boundaries. It establishes public accountability that operates independently of law
enforcement cooperation. And it documents protection patterns that would otherwise remain
invisible — the Ashcraft memo itself, through its inclusion in this dissertation, becomes a node
in the tree.
That node is doubly evidentiary: it documents the underlying OPMA violations, and it
documents the systematic prosecutorial protection that shields institutional actors from
accountability. This second layer of documentation is the more valuable one, because it is far
rarer. Most prosecutorial discretion happens invisibly, in conversations and judgment calls that
never produce a document. The Ashcraft memo, by virtue of being a written work-product memo
released through public-records process, makes visible what the brotherhood usually keeps tacit.

3E.12 Conclusion: The Immunity Doctrine Revealed
The Ashcraft memo provides rare insight into how institutional protection operates at the
prosecutorial level. Rather than evaluating evidence neutrally, prosecutors construct frameworks
that systematically protect institutional actors while maintaining the appearance of legal analysis.
The conclusion preceded the analysis. The framework was designed to produce the conclusion.
Once the framework is in place, the analysis follows automatically.
This protection system operates through intent standards that are impossible for institutional
actors to meet, jurisdictional deflection that ensures no level of government takes responsibility,
RICO interpretations that immunize any organization with a legal mission, linguistic reframing
that transforms crimes into mistakes, and professional brotherhood norms that protect colleagues
across institutions. None of these mechanisms requires conscious corruption. All of them
produce the same result.
Understanding this is essential for designing governance systems that can function in a post-
disclosure environment. If traditional law enforcement systematically protects institutional
capture at the rural-county scale, post-disclosure governance must operate through mechanisms
that bypass rather than rely on prosecutorial discretion. The tree grows only when accountability
mechanisms cannot themselves be captured. The Ashcraft memo demonstrates why new forms
of verification and enforcement will be necessary when the stakes include not just local
transparency, but species-level truth about humanity’s place in the cosmos.

Appendix D: The Recording Fiasco Transcripts (2014–2021) — Selected
Primary-Source Excerpts
This appendix preserves selected verbatim transcripts from the seven-year Recording Fiasco
analyzed in Section 3E.1. The author compiled the complete record in 2023 in a document titled
Recording Fiasco Transcripts with Good Names (pre-AI compilation), which contains audio
transcripts of multiple Jefferson Healthcare Commission meetings, contemporaneous email

original transcripts. Bracketed timestamps and editorial notes ([unclear], [crosstalk], etc.) are

made in 3E.1 against the verbatim record.

D.1 March 19, 2014 — The Opening Confrontation
Excerpted from the Jefferson Healthcare Commission meeting transcript, opening the author’s
first regular meeting as a newly elected commissioner.
Marie Dressler: …Calling the meeting to order at 3:33. This is Jefferson County Public Hospital
District N.2, Board of Commissioners meeting and Commissioner Jill Buhler is excused. Could I
ask you what is in front of you? Are you recording this meeting?
Matt Ready: Yes. I’m making an audio recording of this meeting to help me remember what has
happened.
Marie Dressler: Okay. Actually that sounds like a good opening for discussion about doing
something like that with one of the concerns with the Public Meetings Act as it is being recorded
and the Public Hospital District is responsible for safekeeping…
Mike Glenn: I think that there was going to be a discussion at tonight’s meeting about recording
board meetings, which I think is a reasonable thing to discuss. There are implications associated
with recording board meetings that recording become part of the record… So I think the
recommendation from Council is that absent of the hospital doing it, that a board member should
not.

D.2 March 26, 2014 — The Author’s Letter to CEO Glenn and Chair
Dressler
Dear Mike,
I would like for us to work together to avoid any further public confrontations or drawn out
conflicts over the issue of audio recordings of commission public meetings.
To best do my job as a hospital commissioner I require a complete record of our public meetings.
I require this complete record to be in my possession the moment our public meetings conclude
so that I might immediately review any portion of the meeting events and begin considering next
steps…
I believe the simplest solution is that I record the meetings on my personal recording device and
immediately provide a copy of the file to administration after the meeting. I could simply walk
over to the commission office, plug in my usb cable, and upload the file to a directory on the file
server. The file is already dated by the software. The hospital Information Technology
department keeps backups of all files on the file server. If anyone ever requests one of the audio
files from a meeting, then someone could simply copy the file to a thumb drive for the person…
As you noted, any handwritten notes a hospital commissioner makes during a public meeting is
subject public records standards. Audio recordings, are simply a form of note taking. We may
need to refine it, but the policy regarding commissioner notetaking you described is already in
place and as long as I make my recordings available in a timely manner, we appear to be keeping
with the policy we already have…
We have another public meeting on 4/16/2014. I would like to record this meeting. Please let me
know if my recording the meeting will result in yourself and/or the board chair delaying the
meeting progress on the agenda, recessing the meeting, or adjourning the meeting as happened at
the 3/19/2014 meeting…
Respectfully,
Matthew Ready
The letter attached the relevant excerpt from Washington State Attorney General Opinion AGO
1998 No. 15:
A county is subject to the Open Public Meetings Act which generally requires that meetings of
the governing body be open to the public and that no conditions precedent to attendance by the
public, except for orderly conduct, may be imposed. Therefore, a county legislative body may
not ban the use of recording devices from the open portion of a meeting held pursuant to the
Open Public Meetings Act. The county legislative body may impose restrictions on the use of
recording devices, but only to the extent necessary to preserve the orderly conduct of the
meeting.

D.3 March 27, 2014 — Chair Dressler’s Response
Hello Matt,
Actually, audio recording of Board meetings is a Board decision.
At the conclusion of our last meeting we, the Board, asked Mike to develop a policy, procedure
and recording methodology to present to the Board for our review and consideration. At this
time, the board can then discuss and take action, if appropriate.
Mike and I participated in a teleconference with counsel and were made aware of the legal
implications to the District related to recording Board meetings. If we are going to do this, then
we are going to do it correctly. Interestingly, according to counsel, it is not common for a Public
Hospital District to record it’s board meetings.
Based on this, Matt, it would certainly be best if you chose not to exercise any right you have, to
record the 4/16 meeting and allow the Board the time and space to make a thoughtful and
deliberate decision on this issue.
Marie Dressler Board Chair
The author replied citing the OPMA’s preamble — “The people, in delegating authority, do not
give their public servants the right to decide what is good for the people to know and what is not
good for them to know” — and asked for the name and contact information of the attorney
whose advice was being cited. Chair Dressler responded that the consultation Matt had requested
would be “solely and totally at your own expense.”

The structural significance of this excerpt is that the same redirective facilitation move — the

D.6 December 18, 2019 — The 3-1 Vote
The author proposed a board policy:
If a commissioner decides to record a meeting on their own device, it will be announced and no
further discussion of it will be had since they’re exercising their basic right.
The hospital attorney present, John French, told the board:
The threshold question is whether or not a board member can record over the objection of other
board members and I don’t know the answer to that, so I would have to research that before our
next meeting.
The board nevertheless voted that evening. The motion failed 3-1. The board voted not to
commit to non-harassment of a recording commissioner before the attorney had researched
whether a recording commissioner could be lawfully harassed.

D.7 January 14, 2021 — The Unanimous Resolution
After seven years of dispute, the Jefferson Healthcare Board of Commissioners voted
unanimously to add language to its policy book stating that any commissioner who
independently records an open public meeting would promptly provide a copy to the district for
public records storage. The two principles all members of the board now endorsed:
A commissioner has the right to record any open public meeting of the commission whether
regular or special session, on site or offsite (as do all residents of the United States).
No one can (or should try to) prohibit a recording of anyone in an open public meeting, even if
they personally object to the recording.
These were the principles the Washington Attorney General had stated in 1998. They were the
principles the dissenting commissioner had cited in 2014. They were the principles the institution
had effectively conceded but resisted operationalizing for the entirety of the intervening seven
years. The dispute resolved on the same legal foundation the dissenting commissioner had been
citing throughout. The cost of the seven-year resistance — measured in board time, attorney
consultations, public confrontation, and institutional capacity diverted from healthcare
governance — was paid by the institution and by the public it serves.

D.8 A Note on the 2023 ChatGPT Coda
The 2023 compilation of the Recording Fiasco transcripts closes with the author asking ChatGPT
to write a news story summarizing the seven-year dispute. ChatGPT initially produced a
plausible-but-mostly-accurate paraphrase. When the author asked it to attribute quotes more
carefully to the correct speakers, ChatGPT instead generated a completely fabricated story about
a “John Smith of ABC Company” announcing a merger with “XYZ Inc.” This is preserved as the
closing item in the 2023 compilation. The author intended it as wry commentary on AI
hallucination. It also functions, in retrospect, as a structurally apt closing image: the moment a
human-authored verification record was handed to a system designed to summarize, the system
invented a different story entirely and reported it with confidence. The shadow tree mechanism
reproduced in real time, in machine form, in a single conversation. The verbatim record
preserved in this appendix is the corrective.
