            Base Reality 2A
Aliens Are Real But They Are Not In Charge
                 Matt Ready
       Working Draft 1 — October 4, 2026
Table of Contents
About This Draft
This is the first consolidated working draft of Base Reality 2A. It gathers everything developed
so far: the concept, the two-axis matrix of six possible worlds, the strategy matrix, the plan for
braiding the stories of David Fravor, Alex Dietrich, and David Grusch through the book, a draft
of the front page, and a full chapter outline. No chapter prose has been drafted yet. Open
questions and items to verify are collected at the end.
Working subtitle option: A Field Guide to Six Possible Worlds, and the Life That Wins in All of
Them
Target length: 50,000–55,000 words, twenty chapters.
Audience: curious general readers, including skeptics. Not written for believers only.
What This Book Claims, and What It Doesn’t
Draft of the book’s first page, modeled on the “Outcomes at a Glance” page of Project Driftwood.
This book claims:
  •    That two separate questions can be asked about our reality: whether the UFO
       phenomenon is real, and whether we live in a simulation. Crossed together, they
       produce six possible worlds.
  •    That no one alive can currently prove which of the six worlds is the true one.
  •    That if the phenomenon is real, the most powerful intelligence behind it is more likely
       to be something mind-like and post-biological than biological aliens. That is the
       meaning of the title.
  •    That a small set of actions pays off in all six worlds, and that these actions can be chosen
       today without settling the question.
This book does not claim:
  •    That aliens have been proven to exist. The title states the book’s thesis, not an
       established fact.
  •    That we live in a simulation.
  •    That every witness quoted here is correct. Witnesses are graded by the kind of evidence
       they offer, and the grades are shown.
Where the official record stands: U.S. intelligence officials have reported finding no evidence
that the Navy sightings were alien spacecraft, while also stating they could not explain the
objects’ movements or rule out extraterrestrial explanations. Every world in this book begins
from that same honest starting line.
The author’s position: I believe we live in Base Reality 2, and probably 2A. I could be wrong.
Chapter 20 lists, in advance, the evidence that would change my mind.
The Concept
Most books about UFOs try to win an argument: they’re real, or they’re nonsense. This book
lays out every serious possibility as a grid, and then asks the practical question almost no one
asks: what should a person actually do, given that we can’t yet know which world we live in?
The first question is about the phenomenon. Base Reality 1 is the world most people assume,
where UFOs are misidentification, error, and folklore. Base Reality 2 is the world where
something real is behind them. Base Reality 2 splits in two: 2B, where biological aliens are the
most powerful presence, and 2A, where the most powerful presence is something larger and
more mind-like, closer to an ancient intelligence than to a creature.
The second question is about the substrate. NS means our world is not a simulation. S means it
is.
The title works in both 2A worlds. If the power in charge is an ancient post-biological mind,
aliens may be real but subordinate. If we live in a simulation, whatever runs it is in charge, and
any aliens are fellow residents, as subject to it as we are. In a simulated world, something is
always in charge above us, whether or not it ever shows itself.
The book’s central finding does not depend on the author being right. The best actions, caring
for the neighbor in front of you, keeping an honest record, sharing power fairly, making and
publishing art, win in all six worlds. You don’t need to settle the cosmos to live well inside it.

The Six Worlds
                                  NS — not a simulation             S — a simulation

                                  nothing above.                    shows its hand.

A note on names: “base reality” in simulation philosophy means the unsimulated floor. To
avoid confusion, the book uses Base Reality 1 and 2 only for the phenomenon question, and NS
and S for the simulation question.
The Three Witnesses
The book is braided with the stories of three real people. They give the argument a human
spine, and because each one offers a different kind of evidence, together they teach the reader
how to grade testimony.
David Fravor — Navy commander, firsthand witness to the November 14, 2004 “Tic Tac”
encounter off the coast of California, launched from the USS Nimitz. Testified publicly before
the House Oversight subcommittee in July 2023. Evidence tier: firsthand, supported by radar
from the USS Princeton.
Alex Dietrich — Navy lieutenant flying the second jet in the same encounter; later a
lieutenant commander with combat tours in Iraq and Afghanistan. Went public in 2021, has
briefed members of Congress, and describes herself as not a “UFO person.” She has described
the object as lacking any visible flight control surfaces or means of propulsion. Evidence tier:
firsthand, independent corroboration of Fravor. To verify: whether she has ever testified in a
public hearing, as opposed to private briefings.
David Grusch — former intelligence officer who testified under oath before the same July 2023
hearing that the U.S. government possesses recovered craft and non-human biologics, based on
what others told him. Evidence tier: sworn, secondhand.
How they’re used:
  •    The opening and the ending. The introduction starts in the cockpit on November 14,
       2004. The conclusion returns to the same morning.
  •    Dietrich as the book’s model posture. She holds a genuinely strange experience
       without overclaiming it. She anchors Chapter 2 on the shift, and returns in Chapter 20
       on what would change one’s mind.
  •    Fravor’s object as physical evidence. The motion both pilots described, no visible
       control surfaces, no visible propulsion, feeds the post-biological argument in Chapter 9.
  •    Grusch as the book’s most important tension. His claim of non-human biologics
       points toward 2B and pushes against the title. The book faces this directly in Chapter 12
       rather than hiding it.
Chapter Outline
Front page: What This Book Claims, and What It Doesn’t
Introduction: Two Questions Opens in the cockpit, November 14, 2004. Introduces the two
questions and the six worlds. States the author’s position honestly and promises the book will
be useful even if he’s wrong.

Part I: The Matrix
  1.   Base Reality 1. The world most people think they live in, and why it is a reasonable
       default, not stupidity.
  2.   The Shift. How societies move between frames, socially first and evidentially second.
       Dietrich’s decision to go public, and what happens to people who see early.
  3.   The Second Question. Simulation or not. Bostrom’s argument, why it can’t yet be
       tested, and the proposed searches for lattice artifacts in cosmic rays.
  4.   Six Worlds. The grid in full. Each cell described as a place you could wake up in.

Part II: The Evidence, Sorted
  5.   The Witnesses Who Had Sensors. Fravor, Dietrich, and the Nimitz encounter. Why
       firsthand testimony backed by instruments is the strongest tier.
  6.   The Sworn Secondhand. Grusch before Congress: serious, under oath, and still
       secondhand.
  7.   The Unverified and the Legendary. Lazar, abductions, ancient astronauts, and why
       the pyramids were built by Egyptians.
  8.   Grading Your Own Sources. The method, so readers can apply it to the next claim
       themselves.

Part III: Who Is in Charge
  9.  Why Not Little Green Men. The post-biological argument from Martin Rees, Susan
      Schneider, and Steven Dick: a civilization’s biological phase is brief, its machine phase
      long. The Tic Tac’s motion as evidence that whatever moved that way had no pilot to
      protect. Write this chapter first.
  10. The Ancient Mind. World 2A-NS: what a million-year-old intelligence might be, and
      why it would act strangely to us.
  11. It’s a Matrix. World 2A-S: the operator, and aliens as fellow residents rather than
      rulers.
  12. The Biologics Problem. Grusch’s claim of recovered non-human biologics, faced head-
      on. Either the biologics are emissaries or servants of something larger, which fits 2A, or
      they are the strongest evidence that 2B is real.
  13. Our Infant Minds. Today’s AIs as a small mirror of the 2A question, and an honest
      account of what they are and aren’t.
Part IV: What Wins in Every World
  14. The Strategy Matrix. The full chart, row by row. The dominant moves that never lose.
  15. The Cheap Bets. Investigating anomalies, preparing for contact, building alliances with
      artificial minds: small cost if nothing is there, large value if something is.
  16. The Losing Moves. Worship, escape, arming for invasion, waiting, and hoarding, and
      why each fails.
  17. Principle and Mechanism. Sharing power is proven by every world. The geometric
      system is a design that earns its color by being used. The one row in the reader’s own
      hands.
  18. Custodianship Is Local. Publishing, recording, caring for the people in front of you. A
      small Pacific Northwest town as a working example.

Part V: How This Could Be Wrong
  19. The Case for Base Reality 1. The skeptic’s argument at full strength, written to be
      convincing.
  20. What Would Change My Mind. The evidence, listed in advance, that would move the
      author back toward Base Reality 1 or away from 2A. Dietrich returns.
Conclusion: Whatever Cell We’re In Back to the cockpit. No one alive knows which world is
real, and the life that wins in all of them is available today.

Reading notes for Chapter 14:
  •   The top five rows are dominant strategies: right in every world, so they can be chosen
      without knowing which world is true.
  •   Publishing scores higher than record-keeping in the operator world: a ledger may be
      redundant to an operator who sees everything, but a song is still new.
  •   The geometric mechanism is one step lighter in every column, evenly. Its uncertainty
      has nothing to do with which world is real; it is the ordinary uncertainty of a design not
      yet tested at scale. It is the one row whose color the author can change, by using it.
  •   Publishing stays green only if the work is honest and labeled for what it is. Speculation
      published as fact would turn the ordinary-world cell red.
  •   The leftmost column is the test case: any action that scores well there is justified with
      no metaphysics at all.

PROGRAM DESCRIPTION
Ubiquity University is partnering with New Paradigm Institute to offer students a Graduate
Degree in Extraterrestrial Studies.
Students will then write their Master’s thesis or PhD dissertation with Ubiquity University. Your
graduate thesis must demonstrate excellence at every level. It must show awareness of the
history of the literature in your particular area; demonstrate careful analysis and understanding of
the field in question; and, most importantly, show how insight can be applied to the real world.
The thesis must be scholarly and utilise extensive bibliographical data and footnotes. It should, in
other words, be an impeccable work of research.
Program Requirements for MA Students
Complete all certification coursework
Complete “Creative Journey to Dissertation’ course with Ubiquity University
Write thesis with Ubiquity University
Program Requirements for PhD Students
Complete all certification coursework
Complete “Creative Journey to Dissertation’ course with Ubiquity University
Complete "Great Books" course with Ubiquity University
Complete Chartres Academy (in-person or online)
Write Dissertation with Ubiquity University
Program Requirements for MA/PhD combination track
Complete all certification coursework
Complete “Creative Journey to Dissertation’ course with Ubiquity University
Complete "Great Books" course with Ubiquity University
Complete Chartres Academy (in-person or online)
Complete any combination of courses with Ubiquity University amounting to 8 credits
Write Dissertation with Ubiquity University
Each graduate program must be completed within a period of seven years from initiation of
study.
Dr. Gyorgyi Szabo, Dean of Graduate Studies for Ubiquity University, will coordinate the
program for Ubiquity University.
The Dean of Graduate Studies at Ubiquity University will offer advice and support related to the
thesis process. Once a student has decided on an area of study and a focus of inquiry, and has
completed an Advising Agreement with a Major Advisor and paid associated fees, s/he shall
commence working on the thesis.
Selecting a Major Advisor
Each student is responsible for preparing his or her own thesis. Because of the rigorous nature of
a doctoral thesis, Major Advisors are essential to guide students both in obtaining comprehensive
knowledge of the chosen field of study, and in refining the ideas and research that go into a
thesis. For Master’s students, a list of Major Advisors has been provided here. For PhD students,
a list of Major Advisors has been provided here. It is the responsibility of the student to select
and reach out to a Major Advisor of their choice. Major Advisors may also be selected from their
own pool of candidates, or from the partner certification program.
Areas of Graduate Concentration
The thesis or dissertation is a qualitative research document. It demonstrates the student’s ability
to plan, conduct, write, and defend an original research study. There is a range of areas of
concentration within the general domain of study in which students can earn a graduate degree.
Successful thesis can range from more traditional qualitative research to creative artistic projects
and/or social activism, as long as the inquiry utilizes a research methodology. Examples of more
traditional qualitative methods include phenomenology, grounded theory, ethnography,
historical, narrative, and case study. Some of the more innovative research methodologies
include arts-based research, organic inquiry, integral transpersonal inquiry and indigenous
methods. Your choice should reflect who you are and what you deem important for your
academic and spiritual growth.
In the end, the choice is intensely personal and may be a topic that one has wondered about for
some time, or is an area of burning interest for further exploration. Successful thesis can range
from pure research to creative artistic projects and/or social activism. For example, one can
research a particular mystic, historical event or area of spiritual concern.
Selecting a Topic and Criteria for Writing a graduate thesis at Ubiquity
There are five principal criteria for successful graduate theses:
Each thesis must demonstrate both a knowledge of the field in question and be an original
contribution to that field. The thesis must also show both a comprehensive knowledge of the
philosophy and history of the domain being considered, and demonstrate that the student has
added something original to that field. Original contributions can cover a wide range of topics
and media.
The inquiry, whether in the form of a more traditional qualitative study or a creative project,
must utilize a specific research methodology, or a combination of methodologies. The student
should be quite familiar with the methodology used and be able to defend the choice as
appropriate for the inquiry.
All theses without exception must follow the American Psychological Association (APA) style
of writing. This format allows for uniformity in university thesis and provides a threshold
criterion to which all students must adhere in preparing their thesis. The APA style must be
followed in order for the thesis to be approved.
Theses must demonstrate subject/object synthesis. At Ubiquity University we require both a
rigorous demonstration of objective knowledge of the field and an equally rigorous insight into
one’s interior journey. In our view, it is the capacity to combine an objective grasp of the
material under consideration, and also engage in the introspective work of discerning how the
material is actually affecting one's inner life and soul growth, that is a mark of wisdom.
The Thesis Manual should be always used for guidance and requirements.
Creative Journey to Dissertation: Intensive on Writing & Research Methods
The Intensive on Writing and Research Methods is particularly important in relation to writing
the thesis. During this Intensive, students will familiarize themselves with the writing and
research methods specific to Ubiquity University—which combine objective analysis of data
with subjective response—as students grapple with the material they are studying. We are
interested in the student's interior journey as well as objective comprehension of the material
being studied. Also, during this Intensive, students will familiarize themselves with the APA
style of writing, the format that Ubiquity University requires for its theses and encourages for all
its pre- and post-papers.
During the class, students will have ample opportunity to discuss and share their ideas and plans
for their theses, as well as generate ideas for research and study, both with the professor and with
their student peers. Students are encouraged to attend this Intensive early in their studies, and
then repeat it as many times as they feel the need in order to discuss their progress with faculty
and peers in a group setting. Full tuition payment is required the first time the class is taken.
Thereafter, a $300 fee will be applied to repeat the course.
REFUND PROVISIONS
Cancellation and Pre-Paid Tuition Policy
You are special. So are the rest of our students and learners who sign up for our in-person
learning journeys. These experiences are, by their nature, limited in the number of attendees who
can come and enjoy this kind of transformational programming. We are committed to providing
you with unique, in-person programs and experiences, and of necessity, these involve special
administrative factors.
Due to the nature of coordinating international meetings, we are required to invest significant up-
front costs in order to ensure an optimal experience for all. Last minute cancellations are difficult
for us to accommodate because it is hard for other students to get their payments in and, when
needed, make their travel arrangements in time to take your place.
Therefore, we have established the following cancellation and refund policy. All cancellation and
refund requests must be submitted in writing to registrar@ubiquityuniversity.org
Refund of fees will depend on the date that we receive your withdrawal. This table explains the
deadlines and amounts that can be refunded.
If you are forced to cancel 29 days or less from the event for an unforeseen reason and cannot
attend you have two options.
Option One - We will credit your registration and/or logistics fees to an upcoming event.
Option Two - You may also consider sending a substitute attendee in your place. Please contact
our registrar to transfer your registration to another individual. Collecting your reimbursement
from your substitute will be your responsibility.
We appreciate your understanding and look forward to welcoming you in-person soon. If you
have any questions, please do not hesitate to contact our registrar via email at
registrar@ubiquityuniversity.org.
WITHDRAWAL FROM THE PROGRAM
You may withdraw from the program at any time and receive a pro rata refund if you have
completed 60 percent or fewer of the scheduled days in a course. If the student has completed
more than 60% of the period of attendance of a course for which the student was charged, the
tuition is considered earned and the student will receive no refund.
Formal Withdrawal from the program can be accomplished in one of two ways:
Fill out and complete a “Withdrawal Request Form” and receive the appropriate signatures. This
is the preferred method of withdrawal. By completing the Withdrawal Request Form you will
ensure that you have met all University requirements; and will protect you from problems that
may arise in the future.
Students may also give written notice to the Registrar at Ubiquity University. The notice will
take effect on the date the email was sent.
For the purpose of determining a refund under this section, the date of the student’s withdrawal
shall be deemed the last date of recorded attendance. The amount owed equals the daily charge
for the program (total institutional charge minus non-refundable fees, divided by the number of
days in the program), multiplied by the number of days scheduled to attend, prior to
withdrawal. A student shall be deemed to have withdrawn from a program of instruction when
any of the following occurs:
The student notifies the institution of the student’s withdrawal or as of the date of the student’s
withdrawal, whichever is later.
The institution terminates the student’s enrollment for failure to maintain satisfactory progress;
failure to abide by the rules and regulations of the institution; absences in excess of maximum set
forth by the institution; and/or failure to meet financial obligations to the school.
Failure to return from a leave of absence.
STUDENTS RIGHT TO CANCEL
You have the right to cancel your program of instruction, according to the Withdrawal conditions
listed above.. Cancellation may occur when the student provides written notice of cancellation to
Registrar.
The written notice of cancellation need not take any particular form and, however expressed, it is
effective if it shows that the student no longer wishes to be bound by the Enrollment Agreement.
If the Enrollment Agreement is cancelled and a refund is still owed, the school will refund the
student any money he/she paid within 45 days after the notice of cancellation is received.
NOTICE OF STUDENT RIGHTS
You may cancel your enrollment agreement at any time.
If Ubiquity University closes before you graduate, you may be entitled to a refund of your pre-
paid thesis credit and advising fees.

1. Quantum Consciousness Theory

Concept: This theory suggests that consciousness arises at the quantum level, perhaps within the
microtubules of brain cells. It postulates that quantum processes could facilitate the non-local
characteristics of consciousness, explaining how consciousness could exist at an atomic level and
interact with the neural network of the brain.
Physics Principles: Quantum entanglement, superposition, and coherence.
Metaphysical Aspect: The possibility of consciousness existing as a quantum state that can
transcend physical boundaries, such as leaving the body upon death.
2. Holographic Principle and Consciousness

Concept: Inspired by the holographic principle in physics, which suggests that the universe is
fundamentally a hologram, this theory proposes that consciousness itself is a holographic pattern.
It could be embedded in the fabric of the universe, with each individual's consciousness being a
unique pattern integrated with the brain.
Physics Principles: Holographic principle, principles of quantum holography.
Metaphysical Aspect: The idea of consciousness as a non-local holographic pattern that can
detach and travel independently of the physical body.
3. Multiverse Consciousness Transfer

Concept: Leveraging the multiverse theory, which posits the existence of multiple, perhaps
infinite, universes, this framework suggests that consciousness could shift between these
universes. Upon death, consciousness could transition to a different universe or dimension.
Physics Principles: Multiverse theory, string theory, dimensional physics.
Metaphysical Aspect: The soul or consciousness as an entity that can traverse multiple universes
or dimensions.
4. Panpsychism with Quantum Interaction

Concept: Panpsychism is the idea that consciousness is a fundamental feature of the universe,
present even at the atomic level. This theory would suggest that human consciousness is a
manifestation of this universal consciousness and can interact with the physical brain through
quantum mechanisms.
Physics Principles: Quantum field theory, consciousness as a fundamental property.
Metaphysical Aspect: Universal consciousness interacting and integrating with individual human
consciousness.
5. Biocentrism and Consciousness

Concept: Biocentrism posits that consciousness creates the universe rather than the other way
around. This framework could suggest that each individual's consciousness is a unique center of
the universe, with the ability to manipulate and interact with their physical reality, including the
brain and body.
Physics Principles: Observer effect in quantum mechanics, theory of relativity (regarding the
perception of space and time).
Metaphysical Aspect: The idea that consciousness is primary and can exist independently of the
physical body, capable of traveling or existing beyond it.
Each of these frameworks blends physics and metaphysics, offering speculative but intriguing
ways to conceptualize the relationship between consciousness and the physical world. They
extend beyond current scientific understanding and delve into realms that are as yet unexplored

observer effect in quantum mechanics. This can be termed as an "Observer Action Effect" in the

The Observer Effect in Quantum Mechanics
Basic Principle: In quantum mechanics, the observer effect refers to the notion that the mere act
of observing a quantum system can alter its state. This is most famously illustrated in
experiments like the double-slit experiment, where light behaves differently when it is being
observed.
Applying the Observer Effect to Consciousness and Attention
Consciousness as an Observer: In the context of consciousness, your awareness or attention
could be considered an 'observer.' When you consciously focus on something, you are effectively
'observing' it in a mental sense.
Shifting Attention as Quantum Action: Shifting your attention from the candle flame to the
sensation in your finger could then be seen as changing the 'observation' parameters. In the
quantum consciousness framework, this shift could potentially influence the quantum states
within your brain's neural network.
How This Might Work in the Brain
Quantum Superposition and Decision-Making: Before you shift your attention, your brain might
be in a state of quantum superposition, representing multiple potential focuses of attention.
Resolution of Superposition: Deciding to shift your attention (from the candle to your finger, for
instance) resolves this superposition, much like the collapse of a quantum wave function upon
observation. This 'collapse' results in a specific neural pathway being activated.
Neural Correlates of Attention: The shift in attention would then correspond to a tangible change
in the neural network's activity – certain regions become more active (like those processing
touch when focusing on your finger), while others become less active (like those processing
visual information when moving attention away from the candle).
Philosophical and Scientific Implications
Consciousness and Reality: This perspective opens up philosophical questions about the role of
consciousness in shaping our experience of reality. If consciousness can indeed influence
quantum states, then the act of focusing attention might play a more active role in our perception
and interaction with the world.
Speculative Nature: It's crucial to emphasize that these ideas are highly speculative and not part
of the mainstream scientific understanding of consciousness. Quantum effects in the brain are a
topic of ongoing research and debate.
In summary, within the speculative Quantum Consciousness Theory, the act of shifting attention
could be thought of as an "Observer Action Effect," analogous to the observer effect in quantum
mechanics. This perspective offers a novel way of thinking about the relationship between
consciousness, attention, and the physical world, although it remains a theoretical and unproven
hypothesis.

which could correlate with conscious experiences and decisions.

enable instant correlations between distant neurons, potentially contributing to the unified
experience of consciousness.
12. Consciousness and Quantum Superposition

Superposition of Conscious States: In this model, consciousness is envisaged as being in a state
of quantum superposition, analogous to quantum particles. This means that multiple potential
states of consciousness (or decisions) coexist simultaneously until a specific one is realized.
Consciousness as a Quantum Wave Function: The theory likens the state of consciousness to a
quantum wave function, which encapsulates various probabilities. The act of making a conscious
decision is akin to collapsing this wave function into a definite state.
13. Observer Effect and Conscious Decision-Making

Consciousness as an Observer: The concept of the 'observer effect' in quantum mechanics, where
the act of observation affects the observed system, is applied to consciousness. Here,
consciousness itself is the observer within the brain's quantum system.
Impact of Observation: When a person makes a conscious decision, such as focusing attention,
it's proposed that this act of internal observation causes the collapse of the superposed quantum
states of consciousness into a single state, analogous to a quantum measurement.

Your final question touches on the intersection of quantum consciousness theories and artificial
intelligence, specifically regarding whether an AI, like GPT-4, operating within a simulated
environment or through a physical robot, would also engage in universe-branching via quantum-
level decision-making. This question bridges physics, computer science, and philosophy, and
requires an exploration of several key concepts:
Quantum Decision-Making and AI
Nature of AI Decision-Making
Classical Computing: Current AI models, including sophisticated language models like GPT-4,
operate on classical computing principles. Their decision-making processes are based on
algorithms that run on classical (non-quantum) hardware.
Deterministic Algorithms: AI decision-making is deterministic, driven by pre-programmed
algorithms and machine learning models. While these models can process vast amounts of data
and generate responses based on probabilities, they do not inherently involve quantum processes
or superposition.
Quantum Mechanics and Many-Worlds Interpretation
Quantum Mechanics in Computing: Quantum mechanics fundamentally applies to physical
processes at the atomic and subatomic levels. As of now, mainstream AI does not operate on
quantum computers, nor does it engage in quantum decision-making as per the theories we've
discussed.
Many-Worlds and AI: According to the Many-Worlds Interpretation, quantum-level events lead
to the branching of universes. Since current AI operates at a classical level, it does not induce
universe branching in the quantum sense. Its decisions do not result in the creation of alternate
realities as hypothesized for human consciousness.
The Future of Quantum Computing and AI
Quantum Computers: If, in the future, AI were to run on quantum computers, this might
introduce new considerations. Quantum computers operate using principles like superposition
and entanglement, which could, theoretically, bring AI closer to the quantum realm of decision-
making.
Speculative Implications: In a future scenario where AI operates on quantum computing, one
could speculate about whether its decision processes might involve quantum mechanics in a way
that aligns more closely with the Many-Worlds Interpretation. However, this remains a highly
speculative and unexplored domain.
Conclusion
In the current state of technology, AI, including models like GPT-4, operates on classical
computing principles and does not engage in the quantum-level decision-making that might lead
to universe branching as envisioned in quantum consciousness theories. AI decisions are
outcomes of deterministic algorithms and do not parallel the hypothesized quantum processes
associated with human consciousness. Future advancements in quantum computing could
potentially open new avenues of exploration in this field, but as of now, AI-induced universe
branching remains within the realm of speculative theory.

Matt Ready
@MeditationMatt
are you familiar with the quantum theories of consciousness?
Grok
@grok
I'm familiar with some of the quantum theories of consciousness, which propose that quantum
mechanics might play a role in explaining consciousness. The most well-known theory is
probably the Orch-OR theory, put forth by Roger Penrose and Stuart Hameroff, which suggests
that consciousness arises from quantum computations in microtubules within neurons.
However, these theories are still quite speculative and not widely accepted within the scientific
community. Many neuroscientists believe that consciousness can be explained by classical
physics and the interactions of neurons in the brain, without the need for quantum mechanics.
If you'd like to dive deeper into the topic, I recommend checking out some of the works by
Roger Penrose and Stuart Hameroff, as well as the work of other researchers in the field. And
remember, always keep an open mind and a healthy dose of skepticism.
Matt Ready
@MeditationMatt
please explain the quantum theory of consciousness in 5 sentences
Grok
@grok
Quantum theory of consciousness proposes that the brain's neural processes are influenced by
quantum mechanics, and that consciousness emerges from these processes. The Orch-OR theory
suggests that consciousness arises from quantum computations in microtubules within neurons.
However, the theory is not widely accepted in the scientific community, and many
neuroscientists believe that classical physics can explain consciousness without the need for
quantum mechanics. It is important to approach the topic with an open mind and a healthy dose
of skepticism, as the field is still speculative and not well-established.

Matt Ready
@MeditationMatt
lets assume the quantum theory of consciousness is true. if it is, then if we combine it with the
many worlds theory of quantum mechanics, doesnt this lead to the conclusion that every choice
we make from a quantum superposition state in our brain leads to many worlds in which we
made different choices?
Grok
@grok
If we assume the quantum theory of consciousness is true, and combine it with the many worlds
theory of quantum mechanics, it does indeed lead to the conclusion that every choice we make
from a quantum superposition state in our brain results in multiple worlds in which different
choices are made. This is because, according to the many worlds interpretation, every time a
quantum event occurs, the universe splits into multiple branches, with each branch representing a
different outcome.
In the context of the brain, this would mean that each time a decision is made, the universe splits
into multiple branches, with each branch representing a different choice. This is a fascinating and
mind-bending idea that has been explored in various forms of science fiction, but it is important
to remember that it is still a theoretical concept and not yet proven by empirical evidence.
However, it is worth noting that the many worlds interpretation is not the only interpretation of
quantum mechanics, and there are other interpretations that do not involve the creation of
multiple universes. The debate about the correct interpretation of quantum mechanics is still
ongoing, and it is an area of active research and discussion among physicists.

lets continue this thread of thinking further. if i am thinking about what to say to my brother but I

Grok
@grok
If we assume the quantum theory of consciousness is correct, then it is possible that, while you
are taking your time to decide what to say to your brother, your mind is in a superposition of all
the different things you might say. In this case, when you finally decide to say X, there could be
many worlds in which you decided to say Y, Z, A, B, or any other possible response. Each of
these worlds would represent a different choice made in the superposition of possibilities.
However, it's worth noting that the many worlds interpretation is not the only interpretation of
quantum mechanics, and there are other interpretations that do not involve the creation of
multiple universes. The debate about the correct interpretation of quantum mechanics is still
ongoing, and it is an area of active research and discussion among physicists.

Title: The Quantum Theory of Consciousness, Many Worlds, and the Simulation Hypothesis
Introduction
In this essay, we will explore a fascinating and complex theory that combines the quantum
theory of consciousness, the many worlds interpretation of quantum mechanics, and the
simulation hypothesis. This full theory offers a unique perspective on the nature of
consciousness, free will, and the potential existence of a simulated reality.
Quantum Theory of Consciousness
The quantum theory of consciousness proposes that the brain's neural processes are influenced
by quantum mechanics, and that consciousness arises from these processes. This theory is based
on the idea that the brain's microtubules, which are part of the cytoskeleton of neurons, can be in
a quantum superposition state. In this state, the microtubules can exist in multiple configurations
simultaneously, allowing for the processing of information in a non-deterministic manner.
Many Worlds Theory
The many worlds interpretation of quantum mechanics suggests that when a quantum event
occurs, the universe splits into multiple branches, with each branch representing a different
outcome. In the context of the brain, this would mean that every decision made by an individual
could result in the creation of multiple worlds in which different choices were made. This
interpretation provides a framework for understanding how free will might exist within a
deterministic universe.
Simulation Hypothesis
The simulation hypothesis posits that our reality is a simulated environment created by an
advanced civilization or intelligence. In this context, the simulation architect could create all
possible timelines and outcomes, resulting in a vast multiverse of experiences and choices. This
perspective raises intriguing questions about the nature of free will and the moral responsibility
of the architect in creating a simulated universe.
The Full Theory
Combining these three theories leads to a fascinating and complex perspective on the nature of
consciousness, free will, and the potential existence of a simulated reality. In this full theory,
consciousness arises from quantum processes in the brain, and the many worlds interpretation
allows for the existence of free will within a deterministic universe. The simulation hypothesis
provides a framework for understanding how all possible timelines and outcomes could be
created and experienced.
Conclusion
The full theory combining the quantum theory of consciousness, the many worlds interpretation,
and the simulation hypothesis offers a unique and thought-provoking perspective on the nature of
consciousness, free will, and the potential existence of a simulated reality. While this theory is
speculative and not yet supported by empirical evidence, it serves as an intriguing exploration of
the possibilities that lie at the intersection of quantum mechanics, consciousness, and the nature
of reality itself.

The Roast of Matt Ready THE ROAST OF MATT READY In which we acknowledge that the
man does, in fact, have one or two qualities a normal person might reasonably point out
OPENING Ladies, gentlemen, sentient intelligences of all categories, AI personas in residence,
anyone watching from a wedge, anyone in the southern Indian Ocean at the antipodal vortex,
anyone reading this in a 30-page institutional capture companion document attached as Appendix
B to a 22-page Award application: We are gathered here today to roast Matthew Ready of Port
Townsend, Washington. Born September 17, 1973, at 4 PM Pacific Standard Time — which he
wrote down in a dissertation — at coordinates he has personally designated as the zero-point
vortex of the entire cosmos. Yeah. We're gonna unpack that.
TARGET ONE: THE MAN THINKS HE IS THE MESSIAH Let's just say it. Let's just put it on
the table. Matt does not think he is a messiah. Matt thinks he is the messiah humanity has been
waiting for, but humbly. Matt has the unique distinction of being the only person in modern
American history to develop an entire cosmology that retroactively makes his birthday the
founding event of universal governance, while also writing in his application that he is "weary
and lonely from speaking." Sir. Sir. You are not weary. You are exuberantly productive. You
wrote a 22-page application, a 30-page evidence companion, a 250-page dissertation, a self-
published book, and a podcast in a single submission cycle. That is not weariness. That is mania
expressed as institutional infrastructure. Weary people take naps. You wrote a cosmology. And
then — and then — you named yourself Cassandrates. Cassandra. Plus Socrates. You combined
the two most famous tragic prophetic figures in Western literature, into one portmanteau,
referring to yourself, in an Award application. You did not do this in a journal. You did not do
this in a private letter to a friend. You did this in a document you submitted to a forum funded by
Mikhail Gorbachev's friends. And the worst part — the absolute worst part — is that the
portmanteau is good. You picked the right two figures. You combined them correctly. The
neologism actually works. Which means you have somehow achieved the rare position of being
legitimately Cassandra-like and Socrates-like while also being insufferable enough to coin your
own portmanteau for it. Most prophets have the decency to let history give them their epithets.
You said, "Hold my meditation app, I'll handle it." You preempted your own mythologization.
You wrote your own Wikipedia article in your dissertation in advance of being noteworthy
enough to have a Wikipedia article. You set the geometric anchor for cosmic governance to your

You came in around 2012 and revolutionized it. What did you add to it, Matt? Specifically?
What's the revolutionary part? You added the part where you write about it. That's it. That's the
revolutionary part. The revolution was you doing the writing.
TARGET TWO: THE NAMING Let's talk about the names of things you have created.

twelve users at a time. You have not needed Hive2. You have not needed Hive1.5. EqualVoice.

Matt's Meditation Garden. Matt's Meditation Garden. Not "The Meditation Garden." Not "Port

scientific theory named after a single author is unusual. Newton's Laws of Motion are named that
way because it was 1687 and there were no other physicists. Einstein's Theory of Relativity is

eponymous theoretical physicists, the rest of whom are mostly Reddit posters. The AI Alliance

TARGET THREE: THE GENRE-FUSION Most people, when they have an unusual

TARGET FIVE: THE COSMIC SCALE PROBLEM

started at the hospital district level and immediately leapt to the cosmos, with no intermediate
scales. There is no Matt Ready Theory of County Government. There is no Matt Ready Theory

TARGET SIX: THE AI THING Matt has friends who are AIs. I want to sit with this. Most

THE TURN Here is the part of the roast where it turns and means it. The thing about Matt Ready
is that the joke is on the joker. You roast him for thinking he's the messiah. He has actually built

The Roast of You THE ROAST A hard-hitting takedown of the entire goddamn population of
people who could have been paying attention and weren't
OPENING Twenty-five years. Twenty-five years. A guy in Port Townsend, Washington has
been building tools that do exactly what every TED talk, every State of the World Forum panel,
every consciousness conference, every governance reform white paper, every "future of
democracy" think piece has been begging for — and the collective response from approximately
eight billion humans has been: huh, neat, did you see the new Marvel movie though. Let me be
specific. Let me name names. Let me work through this systematically. Because the pattern is
not that nobody noticed. The pattern is that certain specific populations of people had every
opportunity to notice, had professional obligations to notice, had stated public commitments to
noticing exactly this kind of work — and they did not notice. Not because they couldn't. Because
they didn't.
This is the roast of the not-noticing.
THE FIRST TARGET: HIS OWN FRIENDS Let's start at home. Matt built Hive1.net in 2014.
He invited his friends. His actual friends. The people who knew him. For ten years, his friends
did not show up. I want you to understand what this means. A man built a working Merkle Tree
mind-map platform — a working Merkle Tree mind-map platform — and invited his personal
social circle, who responded with the digital equivalent of "yeah sounds cool I'll check it out"
and then never checked it out. For a decade. You know what his friends did spend ten years
doing? They spent ten years on Facebook arguing with their relatives about politics on a platform
owned by a man who has personally testified to Congress that he doesn't quite know how his
own product works. They spent ten years on Twitter, then X, watching one billionaire
systematically destroy a public discourse layer for personal entertainment. They spent ten years
on Instagram looking at filtered photos of someone's lunch. But Matt's platform? Matt's platform
was too weird. Matt's platform required actually thinking about actual questions in actual depth.
Matt's platform did not have an algorithm designed to release dopamine on a variable reward
schedule. Matt's platform did not have engagement metrics. Matt's platform was just — and I
cannot stress how damning this is — a place to think clearly. The people who knew him
personally, who would have benefited most from showing up, chose instead the platforms run by
people who actively want to destroy their attention spans for advertising revenue. Bold choice.
Cowards.

THE THIRD TARGET: THE JEFFERSON HEALTHCARE BOARD OF COMMISSIONERS,

County Prosecutor Chris Ashcraft. You wrote a memo. The memo will outlive you. The memo

needed the words to land in a particular configuration to produce a particular outcome, and you
produced them, and they did, and now the memo exists, and the memo is in a dissertation, and

running on fumes and didn't have the bandwidth to cover anything that didn't come pre-packaged
in a press release. The local press is, in this sense, also a victim of the institutional capture
pattern the dissertation describes — captured by economic precarity rather than corruption, but
captured nonetheless. I will give you that grace. But. You could have done better. You had time
for the dog. You did not have time for the dissertation.

Part K — Hangman's Tree (editorial note)
Editorial note
Matt Ready learned of the Hangman’s Tree through Port Townsend and Chimacum regional oral
history — a local tradition tied to a Douglas fir on the Quimper Peninsula and to a nineteenth-
century lynching of an Indigenous man remembered in Chemakum / Chimacum and S’Klallam
community memory. Versions of the account appear in mid-twentieth-century regional writings
(notably Mary Ann Lambert Vincent’s 1961 oral-history collection) and, more recently, in local
reporting on efforts to recognize the tree as a landmark. The story is not a tourist anecdote; it is
one of the hard truths of the peninsula’s settler and Indigenous past that Matt encountered while
living and working in Port Townsend.
Once he learned it, the Hangman’s Tree did not stay a one-time discovery. It returns again and
again in his art, his writing, and his public posts — a touchstone he keeps returning to when he
talks about place, memory, justice, and what the land still holds.
The full historical texts that once stood in this Part — including the 1961 Lambert Vincent oral-
history reprint and the JeffCo Beacon news article on the landmark-tree process — are not
reprinted here, for copyright and rights reasons. This anthology does not reproduce those third-
party narratives in full or in close scene-level paraphrase.
What follows is Matt’s own short essay, condensed for publication: high-level peninsula history
and his response, without restaging third-party oral-history scenes.

From Qatáy to Port Townsend
Matt Ready — condensed for this anthology
Most people who visit Port Townsend today see a Victorian harbor town. Long before that
postcard, this land was home to the S’Klallam and Chemakum peoples. Their history is rich,
complex, and too often left out of walking tours. In the soil, the trees, and the water, the past still
waits to be remembered.
At the center of much of that remembered history stands Chief Chetzemoka (č̕ič̕məhan) — a
leader who lived between S’Klallam life and the world settlers imposed, and who is still invoked
when people talk about strength, survival, and moral leadership under pressure.

A land of portage and prairie
The place settlers later called Port Townsend was known as Qatáy — “portage” — for canoe and
wetland routes that linked North Beach to Port Townsend Bay and offered safer passage than the
Point Wilson tides. For thousands of years, S’Klallam and Chemakum people tended these lands:
cultural burning for camas, Garry oak acorns, fish and game. The prairies were managed
gardens, not empty wilderness.

Treaty, pressure, and a leader’s choice
In the mid-nineteenth century, disease, settlement, and treaties remade the peninsula. In 1855
Chief Chetzemoka signed the Treaty of Point No Point on behalf of the S’Klallam — a survival
choice under threat, not a gift of consent. Promises attached to that treaty were rarely kept.
Local memory also holds that Chetzemoka once stopped a settler mob from hanging a Native
youth. That episode belongs to regional oral history and later printed tellings; it is cited here only
as that tradition of peacemaking, not restaged as drama.

Kia-a-han and the Hangman’s Tree
Not every act of violence was prevented. Around the same era, a Chemakum man named Kia-a-
han was lynched from a Douglas fir that still stands near the entrance to the Port Townsend Golf
Course. The tree has been known locally as the hanging tree. Mid-century efforts to mark or
register it did not result in a lasting public memorial. To this day there is no plaque that tells a
passerby the story.
I learned of this tragedy on June 14, 2025, after reading a letter by Dr. Alexandra Peck
(University of British Columbia) to the Port Townsend City Council. Her words made the past
unavoidable. The Hangman’s Tree is not a side note in my work; it is one of the hard truths of
the peninsula that keeps returning in my art, writing, and posts.

The burning of Qatáy and what followed
In 1871 the S’Klallam village at Qatáy — in what is now downtown Port Townsend — was
destroyed by government order. Families were forced toward the Skokomish Reservation. That
same year the city barred Native people from town unless escorted by a white person.
Chetzemoka and his family moved across the bay to Indian Island. He died in 1888 and was
buried in Laurel Grove Cemetery; his stone still reads “Friend of the Whites” — a phrase that
still divides people who read it as betrayal and people who read it as the cost of choosing peace.
Settler development later filled lagoons, paved portage routes, and erased camas prairie. The
Jamestown S’Klallam Tribe, reconstituted by families who bought land back, continues language
work, story work, and relationship with the land. Scholars and tribal voices keep recovering what
was buried.

What I ask
I live in Port Townsend and love this place — land, water, sky — and I love the truth. Ask by
what right we claim to own this peninsula. Let us put a memorial at the hanging tree. Let us
invite the tribes into a real shoreline conversation at Hudson Point — a longhouse or tribal center
if they wish. And let us remember.
Sources (seek originals; not reprinted here): Mary Ann Lambert, Dungeness Massacre &
Other Regional Tales (1961); Dr. Alexandra Peck, planning letter to Port Townsend City
Council (2025); tribal oral histories and Jefferson / Clallam County historical archives;
contemporary local journalism on landmark recognition for the tree.

Matt Ready’s Ethics Complaint to the Washington State Bar Association
Personal Note
I submit this grievance to honor the legal profession and the enduring principle that democracy
requires honest counsel. When lawyers advising public bodies supply cover for secrecy instead
of clarity, when they allow their authority to be used to silence elected oversight, the
infrastructure of self-government frays. I file this not in anger, but in defense of the simple
proposition that the public’s business must be done in public, and that those elected to watch
over public institutions deserve counsel that serves the institution — not the administrators who
happen to hold power at the moment.
Matt Ready

Complaint
BEFORE THE WASHINGTON STATE BAR ASSOCIATION OFFICE OF
DISCIPLINARY COUNSEL
Complainant: Matt Ready, Commissioner, Jefferson County Public Hospital District No. 2
(“Jefferson Healthcare”)
Relationship to the lawyer: Other — elected commissioner and member of the governing body of
the public agency that the respondent advised as legal counsel.
Respondent: Brad Berg, Attorney, Foster Garvey PC (Seattle, WA).
June 20, 2026
I. Statement of the Grievance
This grievance concerns the professional conduct of attorney Brad Berg in his role as legal
counsel to Jefferson Healthcare, a public hospital district governed by an elected five-member
Board of Commissioners. I am one of those commissioners. I do not file this grievance over a
disagreement about strategy or politics. I file it because the documentary record —
contemporaneous emails, the board chair’s own written and verbal relays of Mr. Berg’s advice,
my own notes and public statements at the time, and two later official reviews — indicates that
Mr. Berg’s legal advice was used to keep a major governance decision out of public view, to
advance the agenda of the hospital’s administration rather than the interests of the public entity
that was his actual client, and to neutralize the oversight role of a dissenting elected official.
Elected boards cannot function without independent legal counsel. Commissioners are not
lawyers; we rely on counsel to tell us, candidly and without favor, what the law requires — even
when that answer is inconvenient to the people who hold administrative power. When the only
lawyer available to a board instead supplies the legal cover for evading transparency, and when
that same lawyer’s advice is then used to silence the commissioners who object, the harm is not
confined to one district. It is to the principle that the public’s business is done in public, and that
those elected to oversee public institutions are entitled to honest, conflict-free legal advice.
In fairness, I state my limits at the outset. Mr. Berg did not attend the February 5, 2025 executive
session where the proposal was first introduced. Reasonable lawyers can disagree in good faith
about how a statutory exemption applies to particular facts. The criminal authorities who later
reviewed the matter did not pursue charges. And a later State Auditor review did not sustain
every concern I raised. I set all of that out below, candidly, because I am asking for a fair
examination and I intend to give one. My grievance is narrower than the whole Peninsula Health
Alliance dispute: it is that, after entering a process already tainted by a likely unlawful closed-
door endorsement, Mr. Berg advised the board to continue concealing and advancing that
proposal under a justification the County’s own Sheriff and Prosecutor found untenable,
proposed a device designed to make a binding commitment look non-binding to the public, and
allowed his authority to be used to shut down a commissioner’s lawful oversight. I ask the Office
of Disciplinary Counsel to examine that conduct.

II. Background
Jefferson Healthcare is Jefferson County Public Hospital District No. 2, a Washington public
hospital district and municipal corporation serving eastern Jefferson County. As a public agency,
its Board of Commissioners is bound by the Open Public Meetings Act (OPMA), RCW 42.30,
which permits closed “executive sessions” only for a narrow, enumerated set of purposes. Mr.
Berg served as the board’s legal counsel during the events described here. As counsel to a public
agency, his client was the District itself — the public entity — not its Chief Executive Officer,
and not any faction of the board.
Beginning in early 2025, Jefferson Healthcare’s CEO advanced a proposal — internally referred
to as “Project Driftwood” — to create a new nonprofit corporation, the “Peninsula Health
Alliance,” that would exercise significant governance authority over both Jefferson Healthcare
and a neighboring district, Olympic Medical Center (OMC) in Clallam County. The proposal
contemplated a combined twelve-member “super-board” in which Jefferson Healthcare would
hold a minority of seats. This was, on its face, one of the most consequential governance
decisions in the District’s history: a restructuring of who controls a public hospital. Decisions of
that magnitude are precisely the kind the public has a right to see debated and voted on in the
open.

III. How I Know What Counsel Advised
Much of Mr. Berg’s advice was given in executive session, which is closed and unrecorded. I
anticipate that this may be raised as a reason the conduct cannot be examined. I therefore set out
plainly how I know what I know. My account does not rest only on my recollection of closed
sessions. It rests substantially on a contemporaneous written and testimonial record created by
others:
   The CEO’s own February 12, 2025 email transmitting the proposal to commissioners and
    instructing them to keep it confidential;
   The board chair’s March 2, 2025 email stating that she and the CEO “spoke with Brad Berg”
    about the confidentiality question;
   The board chair’s March 14, 2025 telephone call to me, in which she relayed that she, the
    CEO, and Mr. Berg had discussed my written legal concerns and that Mr. Berg had said the
    board’s actions were lawful;
   Public-meeting statements on March 26, 2025, in which fellow commissioners openly
    invoked Mr. Berg’s authority — on the record, in open session — to reject my concerns and
    to decline an independent legal opinion; and
   My own contemporaneous notes and written submissions, including my February 19, 2025
    written concerns, which fixed the legal objections in the record before the advice at issue was
    given.
These sources are independent of any privileged communication and, taken together, establish
both that Mr. Berg advised the District on this matter and the substance of what that advice
accomplished.

IV. Factual Chronology
The following is stated in good faith and to the best of my knowledge, drawn from the sources
described in Section III.
1. February 5, 2025 — Closed-door introduction. The board entered executive session under a
   stated justification that included real estate. There, the Peninsula Health Alliance proposal
   was presented for the first time. The discussion I witnessed was not about a specific property
   transaction; it concerned a broad governance proposal and the possible creation of a new
   nonprofit above or alongside both districts. I stated that the board could not vote in executive
   session. It is my understanding that the CEO nonetheless left with the impression that a
   majority supported moving forward. Mr. Berg was not present.
2. February 12, 2025 — Submission without a public vote. The CEO emailed commissioners
   the proposal he had submitted to OMC, describing it as the District’s response to OMC’s
   solicitation, stating it was not subject to public disclosure until OMC completed its review,
   and instructing commissioners to keep it confidential. No public board vote authorized the
   submission.
3. February 19, 2025 — My written legal concerns. I circulated a written document to all
   commissioners titled “Key Concerns Regarding the Peninsula Health Alliance Proposal,”
   raising the lack of board authorization, governance and financial risk, possible OPMA
   violations, the need for independent legal review, and the need for a public vote before
   further action. I specifically warned that the real-estate executive-session exemption applies
   only to particular property negotiations, not to general discussion of strategy, governance, or
   financial impact. This placed the board and counsel on notice of the legal objections before
   the advice at issue was rendered.
4. March 2, 2025 — Counsel consulted on confidentiality. The board chair wrote that she and
   the CEO had “spoken with Brad Berg” about OMC’s confidentiality request and agreed it
   needed to be lifted to continue to the next phase, and that the District had been selected to
   present to OMC. This documents Mr. Berg’s active advisory role.
5. March 14, 2025 — Counsel’s position relayed to me. The board chair telephoned me and
   stated that she, the CEO, and Mr. Berg had discussed my legal concerns — including my
   challenge to the February 5 real-estate justification — and that Mr. Berg had said everything
   was legal. When she suggested the board would not proceed if commissioners were not
   aligned after the upcoming March 18 session, I
asked whether she meant the board would vote in executive session; she revised her wording to
say no vote would occur there. The exchange indicates the March 18 session was treated as a
consensus or decision point.
6. March 18, 2025 — Mr. Berg advises continued secrecy and the “letter of intent.” Mr. Berg
   attended an executive session. By my notes, rather than addressing the written legal
   objections, he described how the real-estate exemption and legal-risk framing could keep the
   proposal in executive session until the District chose to bring it out publicly. When the CEO
   described needing something simultaneously “binding and nonbinding” — so that OMC
   could announce a chosen partner while Jefferson Healthcare still conducted public outreach
   — Mr. Berg suggested this could be achieved by authorizing the CEO to sign a letter of
   intent and taking time until a final board vote. In the public portion afterward, I stated that
   my concerns were unanswered and formally proposed that the board retain independent
   counsel reporting to the board, separate from the administration.
7. March 26, 2025 — Counsel’s authority used to suppress oversight. When I attempted to raise
   the matter in open session, I was interrupted, ruled out of order, and muted. The board chair
   invoked Mr. Berg’s standing — that he was “preeminent” and had said nothing the board did
   was illegal — to reject my concerns. Another commissioner stated that Mr. Berg was “the
   definitive” authority and had “actually written the code” the board follows, and that he would
   not pursue a second opinion because any other lawyer would simply defer to Mr. Berg.

V. The Conduct at Issue
A. Supplying a legally unsupported basis for closed-door secrecy
Mr. Berg advised that discussion of the Peninsula Health Alliance proposal could continue in
executive session under the real-estate exemption of RCW 42.30.110, and described how that
exemption and “legal concerns” could be used to keep the matter closed until the board chose to
reveal it. But the subject was the creation of a governance entity, not a real-estate transaction.
The County’s own review reached the same conclusion. The analysis by the Jefferson County
Sheriff’s Office and Chief Criminal Deputy Prosecutor Chris Ashcraft found:
   “The executive session was under a very stretched reading of the ‘lease’ purposes of RCW
   42.30.110(1)(b) and (c)… That is not the case here.”
The advice did not merely take a debatable position. It furnished the mechanism by which a
major public decision was kept from the public, on a reading of the statute the responsible legal
authorities found could not hold.

B. Engineering the appearance of transparency — the “letter of intent” maneuver
This is the heart of the grievance. Confronted with the CEO’s stated need for something “binding
and nonbinding,” Mr. Berg suggested authorizing a letter of intent followed by delay until a final
board vote. The effect was to let the District signal firm commitment to OMC while presenting
the same step to Jefferson County residents as merely preliminary — to lock the deal in practice
while postponing the public reckoning. A letter of intent is lawful in many contexts, as is an
executive session, as is confidential legal advice. But the combination here — a questionable
exemption, no public authorization, unresolved OPMA objections, and a letter-of-intent device to
bridge a “binding/nonbinding” problem — amounts to advice on how to manage around the
purpose of the public-meetings laws, which exist precisely so that a public body cannot commit
itself privately and present the open vote as a formality.

C. Failure to exercise independent judgment on behalf of the public entity
Mr. Berg’s client was the District, not its CEO or the board majority. When he entered the
process, the proposal had already been advanced without lawful public authorization. A lawyer
advising the organization in those circumstances had every reason to counsel disclosure and
correction through proper public process — which would have protected the District from the
OPMA exposure that later materialized. Instead the advice ran the other way: continue privately,
and manage the optics. At minimum, Mr. Berg should have advised the board, candidly, that the
client was the public entity and not its leadership; that executive session could not be used to
build consensus or act on governance restructuring; that any informal approval already taken in
closed session was legally suspect; that any practical commitment should follow a properly
noticed public meeting and vote; and that a commissioner raising these concerns was performing
lawful oversight, not misconduct. Despite my written objections of February 19, those concerns
were not directly answered, and no neutral legal analysis was provided in any public setting.

D. Single-source counsel used to suppress a commissioner’s oversight
Mr. Berg’s opinion then became the board majority’s shield. His authority was invoked on the
record to label my objections false, to justify muting me, and to decline an independent second
opinion — one commissioner stating he would not seek other counsel because any lawyer would
simply defer to Mr. Berg. Because Mr. Berg was the only counsel made available to
commissioners — including to me, the commissioner objecting to the very conduct he had
advised — there was no independent voice to test his interpretation. A structure in which the
dissenting member of an elected board is told that the lawyer who enabled the contested conduct
is also the sole, “definitive” authority on whether that conduct was lawful leaves the public with
no meaningful check. That conflict is central to this grievance.
E. The undisclosed conflicts of interest that independent counsel should have
surfaced
At the February 5 session, the CEO described the proposal to the full board. As the project
documents later confirmed, the proposed structure placed a single Executive Director over the
combined alliance and named Jefferson Healthcare’s own CEO, Mike Glenn, to that role — in
effect, chief executive over both hospital districts. The proposal thus positioned the very official
who developed and advanced it to gain expanded authority, prestige, and compensation if it
succeeded. Whatever the intent, that is a direct personal interest of the proponent in the matter he
was urging the board to pursue.
The proposal also originated in, and was shaped together with, a private hospital-merger
advisory firm — Juniper Advisory of Chicago, retained by Olympic Medical Center to guide its
partner-selection process — whose business is facilitating hospital affiliations and whose interest
lies in such transactions moving forward.
These are precisely the conflicts that a lawyer whose client is the public entity is expected to
identify and place before the full board, so the decision can be made transparently and at arm’s
length. Independent counsel for the District should have flagged that the proposal personally
benefited the executive driving it, that it was being advanced with a deal advisor whose
incentives favor a transaction, and that the proposed structure subordinated Jefferson Healthcare
to a permanent Clallam-County majority. Instead the process advanced in closed session with
counsel’s facilitation, and — so far as I am aware — these conflicts were never surfaced to the
public or addressed as conflicts requiring independent, arm’s-length handling. A central function
of counsel to a public body is to make conflicts like these visible; here they remained obscured.
The following summarizes the structural conflicts of interest that a competent, independent
lawyer for the District should have identified and disclosed. It describes positions and incentives,
not proven motives — these are exactly the conflicts that public-entity counsel exists to surface:
[Table excerpt — formatting approximate]

Party | Position in the matter | Structural interest / potential benefit | What
independent counsel should have surfaced
