F. A pattern across a decade: how counsel’s advice has reached this board
The conduct described above was not the first time the District’s legal advice reached its elected
board only after passing through — and being reshaped by — its administration. I raise the
following earlier episode not as a freestanding grievance; it was resolved years ago, and I am not
asking the Office to reopen it. I raise it because it shows that the mechanism at the center of this
complaint is not a single 2025 lapse. It is how this board has received its lawyer’s advice for
more than a decade: filtered through the CEO, withheld from or contradicted to the
commissioners, and never tested with counsel and the full board in the same room.
The origin (2014–2016). The matter began over something deliberately small: whether a
commissioner could make an audio recording of a public meeting. Soon after I took office in
2014, I began recording meetings so there would be an accurate record of what was said and
decided. Before I first recorded, CEO Mike Glenn and Commissioner Dressler consulted Mr.
Berg, the District’s counsel, about the question. I then spoke with Mr. Berg directly, by
telephone, to learn his position for myself. He told me, in substance, that I had the right to record
the meetings, and that a reasonable solution to the record-keeping question was to provide a copy
of each recording to the organization.
The written opinion, and five years of silence. In 2016, the administration obtained a written
legal opinion from Mr. Berg’s firm addressing the same question, but the administration did not
reveal that opinion to the full board until 2021, when the board voted to obtain a written legal
opinion on the matter. That written opinion was consistent with the position Mr. Berg had given
me by phone. Yet the full board — including me — was never told the opinion existed, and was
denied access to it, despite my repeated requests for written legal answers between 2016 and
2021. It had been shared with at least one commissioner before 2021. For five years, a written
legal answer to the very question we were fighting about sat in the administration’s hands while
the board it would have settled was kept from it.
The contradiction. Throughout those years, up to 2021, I repeatedly asked the board to clarify the
law — because interfering with a commissioner’s recording appeared to violate statute, and the
board urgently needed a lawful and ethical method, consistent with Robert’s Rules of Order, for
handling the situation. Mr. Berg never appeared before the full board to clarify the law on the
matter — the very step that, once finally taken in 2021, opened the door to an immediate and
sensible resolution. For years the commissioners, the people legally responsible for the District,
were denied access to the legal answer, at a cost measured in wasted time, wasted energy, and
lost trust.
How it ended (2021). Only in 2021 was the written opinion finally provided to the full board.
Once we could simply read it, the board promptly adopted a sensible policy on recording with a
personal device and voted to move on. A conflict that had consumed five years ended within
weeks of the board being allowed to see the legal answer that had existed since 2016.
The same pattern, eleven years later. The 2025 events trace the identical shape. Mr. Berg’s
advice again reached the board through the CEO and chair rather than directly: I was told that the
chair, the CEO, and Mr. Berg had discussed my concerns and that Mr. Berg had said the board’s
actions were lawful. When I asked the board to test that advice with independent counsel, his
authority was again invoked to refuse — one commissioner calling him “the definitive person on
this particular type of issue” who had “actually written the code that we follow,” and the chair
stating that counsel “has said that nothing we have done is illegal” and was “preeminent in this
discussion.” And again, Mr. Berg never sat with the full board to let his advice be questioned in
the open. The recording episode shows this was not a one-time lapse under pressure. It is how
counsel has operated with this board across two separate controversies, eleven years apart.
The moral ground — for a legal scholar and a high-school assembly alike. A public hospital
district is not the property of the people who run it. It belongs to the public — to the patients,
taxpayers, and neighbors of this county. The elected commissioners are the public’s eyes and
ears inside the institution; we are how ordinary people keep watch over something that touches
their health and their savings. But commissioners are not lawyers. We cannot oversee anything if
we do not know what the law actually requires, and for that we depend on the District’s attorney
to tell us the truth — plainly, and to all of us.
There are two ways that trust can be broken without the lawyer ever speaking a single false
word. The first is to lock the answer in a drawer: the written advice exists, it would settle the
question, and it is simply kept from the people who need it. The second is quieter — the lawyer’s
honest answer is carried to the board by someone who repeats it backwards, and the lawyer, the
one person who knows it has been turned upside down, says nothing. Picture a referee who hears
a coach tell the players the wrong rule and stays silent. Picture a game of telephone in which the
one person who knows the original message declines to correct it. The harm is the same as a lie,
and the person best placed to prevent it chose not to.
That is why this is the lawyer’s burden and not only the administrator’s. The administrator has a
stake in the outcome — which is the very reason the law gives a public body its own counsel,
whose loyalty runs to the institution and to the law rather than to any official within it. When the
lawyer allows his advice to be filtered, withheld, or inverted on its way to the board, the board
cannot do its job, and the public the board represents is governed by people kept in the dark on
purpose. Oversight becomes theater. The open vote becomes a formality, because the real
decision — and the real understanding of the law — happened where the public could not see.
We ask the people we entrust with power on the public’s behalf to wield it with integrity — the
soldier and the officer with the force they may use, the physician with a life in their hands. We
must ask the same of the lawyer who guards the law and the truth that elected officials depend
on. The lawyer’s instrument is not a weapon; it is the law itself and the public’s trust in it. Used
dishonestly it draws no blood, but it can quietly strip a community of its voice in its own
government. Those entrusted with the most consequential instruments must serve with honor, or
the institutions that rely on them fail.
A civics class puts it simply: democracy depends on the people, through their representatives,
knowing the rules and deciding. A scholar states the same principle more formally — that those
charged with oversight must have unimpeded access to the legal and factual basis of the
decisions for which they are accountable. They are the same principle. Strip an elected board of
honest, direct access to its own lawyer’s advice, and you have not merely wronged one
commissioner. You have quietly removed the public from its own government.
What I do and do not allege. I want to be precise about the limits of this. I do not allege that Mr.
Berg’s advice in 2014 or 2016 was wrong; by my account it was correct and matched the written
opinion. I do not allege that preparing an opinion for the administration was itself improper. And
I do not claim to know everything Mr. Berg was told about how his position was being
represented to the board. What I ask the Office to examine is narrower: whether a lawyer whose
client is the full elected board of a public agency meets his duties of candor and loyalty when his
advice is withheld from that board for years and contradicted to their faces, and he does not act
to correct the record with the board directly. The duty to set the client straight arises when
counsel knows or should know his advice is being distorted to the client’s detriment. Whether
Mr. Berg knew is a question for the Office; that the distortion occurred, and that he did not
convene the full board to correct it, I can attest.
Why it belongs here. This earlier episode bears on the same duties raised above — RPC 1.13 (the
client is the organization, acting through its full board, not its CEO) and RPC 2.1 (candid,
independent advice). I include it so the Office can weigh the 2025 conduct for what the record
suggests it is: not an isolated misstep, but the latest instance of an established practice in which
this board’s access to its own lawyer has been controlled by the administration the lawyer was
supposed to keep within the law.

VI. The Later Independent Reviews (Presented in Full)
Sheriff and Prosecutor. I submitted a complaint to the Jefferson County Sheriff’s Office; the
matter was reviewed and routed to Chief Criminal Deputy Prosecutor Chris Ashcraft. I state
plainly that no criminal charges were pursued, and this grievance does not depend on criminal
conduct. The review nonetheless found the executive-session justification a “very stretched”
reading of the statute and OPMA violations likely, and recognized that the role of legal counsel
could raise ethical questions distinct from criminal liability. That is the appropriate forum for
those questions, and the reason I bring them here.
State Auditor. I include the Auditor’s review because a fair grievance shows the whole picture,
including what cuts against me. In a letter dated May 1, 2026, the Auditor determined that the
February 5, 2025 executive session discussed matters unrelated to its stated purpose. The Auditor
did not find that the March 18 session strayed from its stated purpose, and did not identify
proposal-related actions requiring public discussion, board approval, or financial or legal review.
I do not overstate this: the Auditor did not sustain every concern I raised. But it confirmed the
central predicate — that the February 5 session, which set this process in motion, exceeded its
lawful scope. That sharpens, rather than answers, the question presented: once Mr. Berg became
involved after February 5, did his advice work to correct that public-meeting problem, or to
preserve the secrecy and move the process forward without adequate public correction?

VII. Rules of Professional Conduct Implicated
I am not a lawyer and do not ask the Office to accept my characterization of which rules apply. I
respectfully ask the Office to examine whether Mr. Berg’s conduct was consistent with the
following:
   RPC 1.1 (Competence). Whether competent representation required meaningful inquiry into
    the February 5 session, the February 12 submission, the absence of a public vote, and the
    written concerns of February 19 — before advising that the board’s actions were lawful and
    could continue in closed session.
   RPC 1.13 (Organization as Client). Whether Mr. Berg properly treated the District itself as
    his client and acted in its interest — rather than the CEO’s or the majority’s — once he had
    reason to know the organization was being committed to action that likely violated the law
    and could be imputed to it.
   RPC 2.1 (Advisor). Whether he exercised independent professional judgment and rendered
    candid advice about transparency, public-meeting law, and the risk of appearing to commit
    the District before public engagement — rather than advice on how to sustain confidentiality
    and structure a letter of intent.
   RPC 1.7 (Conflict of Interest). Whether his representation of the District was materially
    limited by his alignment with the CEO and chair, or by his own prior advice now under
    challenge, such that the board should have been advised to obtain independent counsel.
   RPC 1.2(d). Whether his advice crossed from analyzing a questionable situation into
    recommending a means — closed-session confidentiality plus a letter of intent plus delayed
    public process — by which the District could advance the proposal while avoiding timely
    public scrutiny.
   RPC 8.4(c) and (d). Whether advice structured to make a commitment appear nonbinding to
    the public while functioning as a commitment, and the use of his authority to suppress lawful
    oversight, involved conduct that is deceptive or prejudicial to the public’s right to open
    government.

VIII. Why This Matters Beyond This District
Every elected board in Washington — every hospital district, school board, port, and council —
depends on the same arrangement: lay officials, accountable to voters, relying on professional
counsel to keep them within the law. That arrangement works only if counsel’s loyalty runs to
the public entity and to the law, not to whichever administrator signs the engagement or
commands the majority. Public entities depend on lawyers who tell elected officials the hard
truth, not merely how to make a desired action look procedurally defensible. When legal advice
instead becomes a tool to keep the public out of decisions it has every right to witness, and is
then used to silence the officials elected to ask hard questions, the premise of public oversight
collapses. I bring this grievance because the record indicates the conduct here crossed the line
from honest counsel to helping a public board avoid the public it serves.

IX. Relief Requested
I do not ask the Office to decide the merits of the Peninsula Health Alliance proposal. I ask it to
review this grievance and determine whether Mr. Berg’s conduct warrants further investigation
or discipline. In particular, I ask the Office to examine whether Mr. Berg:
8. adequately investigated the February 5 session before advising that the process could
   continue under executive-session confidentiality, and whether he advised that any closed-
   session straw poll would be unlawful or ineffective;
9. advised that broad governance restructuring could not be kept in executive session merely
   because the proposal might touch on real estate;
10. advised or supported a “letter of intent” approach allowing OMC to treat the District as
    committed while residents were told public input and a final vote were still pending;
11. communicated his advice candidly to the full board, or primarily through the CEO and chair;
    whether his role became materially limited; and whether he should have advised the board to
    obtain independent counsel; and
12. by his advice or silence, contributed to the suppression of commissioner oversight, including
    the muting of my microphone and the rejection of an independent legal opinion.

X. More Documentation Available
Because the form limits total pages, I have kept this narrative concise and can provide all my
records upon request.
I affirm that the information I am providing is true and accurate to the best of my knowledge.
Some facts are based on my direct participation as a commissioner, some on my notes, some on
emails and public-meeting transcripts, and some on later official reviews. I have read Lawyer
Discipline in Washington and I understand that all information I submit can be disclosed to the
lawyer I am complaining about and others.
Matt Ready, 6/20/2026
Commissioner, Jefferson County Public Hospital District No. 2

9/24/2026 Matt unPublished Essay on X “The Quietest Way to
Lose a Democracy is Allow the Lawyers to Rule”
You already know the facts, so I will not spend our time reciting them. You know about the
alliance that was built in closed rooms before the public was told it existed. You know that
when I said so out loud, my microphone was switched off. And some of you know the older
story: that it once took years, and a withheld legal opinion, to settle a question as small as
whether a commissioner could turn on a tape recorder. I am not here to re-argue any of that. I
am here to tell you what I think it means, because the meaning is larger than me, larger than
one lawyer, and larger than one small hospital district on the edge of the continent.
Here is what connects those two stories, more than a decade apart. In neither one did anyone
fire a shot. No one robbed a vault. No one was dragged into an alley. What happened was
quieter than that, and that is exactly why it is dangerous. In both stories, the people you elected
to watch over a public institution were kept from their own lawyer's honest answer. The law
existed. The answer existed. It simply was not allowed to reach the people who needed it to do
their jobs.
We are trained to recognize corruption when it is loud. We picture briefcases of cash and
shredded documents. But the loud kind gets caught. It is the quiet kind that endures, the kind
that wears a suit, cites a statute, and calls itself procedure. The quiet kind does not break a
single law in a way you can photograph. It just decides who gets to see the law. And whoever
controls who sees the law controls everything decided in its name.
Think about what a public hospital actually is. It is not the property of the people who run it. It
belongs to you: to the patient in the infusion chair, to the family at the birth center at two in
the morning, to the taxpayer who funds it whether or not they ever walk through its doors. You
cannot run it directly. So you elect a handful of neighbors to be your eyes and ears inside it.
That is all a commissioner is: a pair of eyes you send into a room you cannot enter yourself.
And here is the simple, devastating fact. Eyes that are not allowed to see are worth nothing.
Blind a board to its own lawyer's advice, and you have not merely wronged a commissioner.
You have quietly walked the public out of its own government and locked the door behind it.
Now let me say the hardest part plainly, because I believe it.
We ask extraordinary things of the people we hand power to. We give a soldier a weapon that
can end a life, and we ask that they carry it with honor. We give a police officer the authority to
use force, and we demand restraint and honesty. We place a living person in the hands of a
surgeon, and we trust them not to betray that body on the table. We accept that these people
hold terrible instruments, and we hold them, rightly, to a terrible standard.
I am here to tell you that we must ask exactly as much of the people who hold the law.
The lawyer who advises a public body holds an instrument too. It is not a rifle or a scalpel. It is
the law itself, and the trust we place in it. Wielded dishonestly, that instrument draws no blood.
But it can do something a weapon cannot. It can take a free people's voice in their own affairs
and make it disappear so smoothly that no one even hears the sound. The warrior who fights
with a weapon and the one who fights with an idea are bound by the same oath. Each must
serve with honor, or all of us who depend on them fail together.
On February 5, 2025, I sat in a closed room and was told, under the name of a real estate
discussion, things the public had every right to hear. In that moment I could see the whole road
ahead: the momentum of the room, the colleagues who would close ranks, the long cost of
saying no. I said no anyway. I wrote to everyone I thought might have the courage to correct it.
I spoke in public. Not for revenge. Not to win a fight I have already been living inside for years.
I did it to ask a single question, out loud, where it cannot be switched off:
Does the standard still mean anything?
When the people's representatives are handed a false version of their own lawyer's advice, and
the one person who knows it is false stays silent, is that still wrong? Or have we quietly agreed
that loyalty to the powerful counts for more than loyalty to the law?
I do not yet know how that question will be answered. That is not up to me. But I know this. A
democracy is not tested by whether it survives the loud attacks; those it can see coming. A
democracy is tested by whether it can still notice the quiet ones: the withheld memo, the
inverted opinion, the microphone switched off at the convenient moment. The quiet ones are
how a free people loses its government without ever being told it is gone.
And I have learned what happens when you keep noticing. The quiet does not stay quiet. On
May 23, 2025, an elected commissioner of our neighboring hospital district wrote, on his official
account, that I was a "dufus," and that back in his old Chicago neighborhood, I'd be "swimming
with the fishes." I do not claim he meant it literally. I claim something simpler. That is the
sound the quiet makes when someone refuses to be quiet with it. The withheld memo and the
mob joke are not two different stories. They are the same story at two volumes.
So here is what I ask of you, because the facts you already know are not the point. The standard
is the point. Keep the lights on. Make them show you the law, in writing, in public, to all of you
at once. And when you ask the question that gets you ruled out of order, ask it again.
To the lawyers here: build the bar this moment needs. An association of public-service counsel
who swear to tell a public body the legal truth, all of it, to all of its members, no matter what
any executive would prefer to hear.
And to everyone else: the entire machinery of secrecy depends on one thing, that eventually
you will grow tired and stop asking. So do not. That is the whole job. That is the entire defense
of a free people. Just keep asking, in the open, until they answer.
I now wait.
